papers.title: HARDTESTGEN: A High-Quality RL Verifier Generation Pipeline for LLM Algorithmic Coding
papers.abstract: Verifiers provide important reward signals for reinforcement learning of large language models (LLMs). However, it is challenging to develop or create reliable verifiers, especially for code generation tasks. A well-disguised wrong solution program may only be detected by carefully human-written edge cases that are difficult to synthesize automatically. To address this issue, we propose HARDTESTGEN, an approach to synthesize high-quality test cases for algorithmic coding problems. We curate a comprehensive algorithmic programming dataset HARDTESTS with 26.6k problems and high-quality synthetic tests. Compared with existing tests, HARDTESTGEN tests demonstrate significantly higher accuracy in verifying LLM-generated code (+11.22 percentage points in precision, the percentage of actually correct code within the predicted correct ones). We also show that downstream post-training -- including rejection sampling and reinforcement learning (RL) -- using HARDTESTS verifier results in improved performance of LLM code generation. We open-source our dataset and synthesis pipeline at https://leililab.github.io/HardTests/.
papers.summary: Reliable verifiers are needed to give reward signals when training large language models (LLMs) on code generation, but subtly wrong programs often slip past automatically synthesized tests. `HARDTESTGEN` is a pipeline for synthesizing high-quality test cases for algorithmic coding problems, used to build `HARDTESTS`, a dataset of 26.6k problems with synthetic tests. Compared with existing tests, these achieve **11.22 percentage points higher precision** in judging LLM-generated code, and using them as the verifier for rejection sampling and reinforcement learning improves downstream code generation performance.

papers.title: PhysDox: Benchmarking LLMs on Physical Feasibility Auditing of Physiological Sensing Protocols
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist in experimental design, yet fluent protocols often remain physically infeasible. We introduce PhysDox, a physical feasibility auditing benchmark for biomedical protocols comprising a 683-sample expert-curated Gold set and a 5,000-sample Silver set across six sensing domains. We formulate the task as a two-stage evaluation: severity detection classifying protocols as valid, minor, or fatal, followed by the constraint-level diagnosis of fatal violations. Evaluating 6 LLMs across 4 inference strategies yields a peak Stage-1 macro-F1 of only 53.0. Moreover, strong oracle diagnosis collapses during end-to-end evaluation due to correlated cascade errors. Error analysis reveals scaffold bias, where models conflate procedural completeness with physical validity. Consequently, implicit constraints exhibit a 2 times higher miss rate than explicit hardware violations, supported by strong statistical correlation at $\rho{=}0.81$ and $p{<}0.01$. Trace analysis of false negatives exposes a 54%--46% split between attention and judgment failures, ultimately demonstrating that protocol auditing demands calibrated feasibility reasoning rather than factual recall or longer rationales.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can write fluent experimental protocols that are nonetheless physically impossible to carry out. `PhysDox` is a benchmark for auditing the physical feasibility of biomedical sensing protocols, with a 683-sample expert-curated Gold set and a 5,000-sample Silver set across six sensing domains, evaluated in two stages: classifying severity as valid, minor, or fatal, then diagnosing which constraint a fatal protocol violates. Across 6 LLMs and 4 inference strategies, the **best Stage-1 macro-F1 is only 53.0**, and diagnosis that looks strong with oracle severity labels collapses end-to-end. Error analysis points to a scaffold bias, where models mistake procedural completeness for physical validity and miss implicit constraints twice as often as explicit hardware violations.

papers.title: When Should LLM Agents Forget? Memory Filtering Under Query-Critical Resolver Errors
papers.abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.
papers.summary: Memory systems for LLM agents often delete facts that a resolver classifies as stale, and this study examines what happens when that resolver is wrong about facts a query depends on. In a controlled intervention across three models, hard deletion moves from **gains of +0.186 to +0.230 with perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181** at the lowest tested resolver reliability, and wrongly dropping a fact hurts significantly more than wrongly keeping one. A simple gate calibrated on matched data reaches 0.655 accuracy on a held-out split, against 0.641 for always deleting and 0.662 for an oracle. The authors recommend treating deletion as cost-sensitive: validate the false-drop risk on matched data, or default to retaining facts when that validation is not possible.

papers.title: Does the Ranking Hold? A Practitioner-Facing Audit of Hallucination Detectors on Small, Quantized, On-Device LLMs
papers.abstract: Hallucination detection for large language models is dominated by methods evaluated on 7B-70B research models with abundant sampling budgets and exact-match or ROUGE correctness labels. The small models practitioners actually ship on-device, Phi-3-mini, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-2B-Instruct, typically at 4-bit precision, sit outside this evidence base. We present a reproducible one-GPU audit of four detectors spanning three paradigms: length-normalized token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, and two sampling-based consistency methods (semantic entropy and SelfCheckGPT-NLI) on two small open instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) loaded at 4-bit NF4 quantization on a single Colab T4 GPU, evaluated on closed-book TriviaQA. Cross-model ranking transfer is poor: Spearman rho is -0.80 and Kendall tau-b is -0.667, meaning the detector ranking actively inverts between the two models, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency detectors on both models under bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals. As a second, methodological contribution, we show that the standard token-overlap-to-multiple-choice correctness labeler for TruthfulQA-Generation produces near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for all four detectors on both models, a labeler failure, not a detector failure, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89 AUROC on TriviaQA under the identical pipeline. We release the harness, prompts, and per-item scores and frame the detector choice explicitly as a fairness-of-error-rates allocation problem for practitioners deploying on resource-constrained, on-device hardware.
papers.summary: Hallucination detectors are mostly validated on 7B-70B research models, leaving open whether the results hold for the small 4-bit quantized models shipped on-device. This audit runs four detectors (token-margin calibration, a lexical n-gram baseline, semantic entropy, and `SelfCheckGPT-NLI`) on `Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct` and `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct` on a single Colab T4 GPU using closed-book `TriviaQA`. The detector ranking **inverts between the two models (Spearman rho of -0.80)**, and the cheap lexical baseline is statistically indistinguishable from the sampling-based consistency methods on both. The authors also show that the standard token-overlap correctness labeler for `TruthfulQA-Generation` yields near-chance AUROC (0.46-0.59) for every detector, which they attribute to the labeler rather than the detectors, since the same detectors reach 0.69-0.89 on `TriviaQA`.

papers.title: LoRAWeaver: Directional Adapter Routing in LoRA Representation Space
papers.abstract: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.
papers.summary: Repeated parameter-efficient fine-tuning leaves a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters, and existing methods for choosing among them at inference often need retraining whenever an adapter is added. `LoRAWeaver` is a training-free router that treats selection as representation alignment: it compares adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity in the adapter-output space. On a 48-task `FLAN-v2` benchmark and out-of-distribution tasks with `LLaMA-2-7B` and `LLaMA-2-13B`, it **outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder** without learning a router.

papers.title: Tabular Population Priors as Structured Retrieval for EHR Medication Set Prediction
papers.abstract: Medication prediction from electronic health records is a fixed vocabulary structured prediction problem, yet recent clinical RAG systems often treat it like open ended case based reasoning: retrieve similar patient admissions and ask an LLM to infer a medication set. This retrieval object is indirect the model receives retrieved patient records while the target is a discrete set of medication class labels. We propose a more task aligned retrieval object: a tabular population prior ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition medication co occurrence table estimated from training admissions. Using PACERAG as a fixed downstream pipeline and replacing only its patient retriever, this drop in swap improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 heldout MIMIC IV admissions, with no additional LLM calls and no inference time patient index. A non LLM top k baseline reaches F1=0.248, confirming the prior is predictive before LLM integration. Aggregate population statistics can provide a more task aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than patient level nearest neighbors for fixed vocabulary EHR set prediction.
papers.summary: Clinical retrieval-augmented systems for predicting medications from electronic health records (EHR) usually retrieve similar patient admissions, even though the target is a fixed set of medication class labels. The authors instead retrieve a tabular population prior: ranked medication class candidates drawn from a sparse condition-medication co-occurrence table estimated on training admissions. Swapping only the retriever inside the fixed `PACERAG` pipeline **raises F1 from 0.303 to 0.338** and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 held-out `MIMIC-IV` admissions, with no extra LLM calls and no patient index at inference time. A non-LLM top-k baseline using the prior alone reaches F1 of 0.248.

papers.title: Curvature-Aware Edge Dynamic GNNs for Low-$p_T$ Track Reconstruction at HL-LHC
papers.abstract: Particle track reconstruction in high-energy collider experiments is a computationally demanding combinatorial problem, traditionally solved by Kalman filters that scale poorly with increasing detector occupancy. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative. In this work, we introduce the Manifold Helical-IN, a novel Interaction Network architecture that explicitly embeds detector spacepoints onto a helical manifold chart using curvature-aware features. This geometric projection mathematically unrolls the tightly curling trajectories of low-momentum particles. Consequently, the network can distinguish true physical tracks from combinatorial noise with good precision. Evaluated on the TrackML challenge dataset, the proposed Manifold Helical-IN achieves a reconstruction efficiency of 0.9675 in the experimentally critical $p_T > 0.5$ GeV regime, approaching recently reported Transformer-based approaches. Crucially, the manifold embedding yields a fake track rate of 0.0037. This represents a 13-fold improvement over the baseline Helical-IN (0.0508). Furthermore, the model maintains good track coherence, as quantified by our proposed Mean Hit Recovery Fraction (MHRF) of 0.858, and achieves a highly efficient inference latency of approximately 150 ms per event on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. These results represent a critical step toward real-time soft particle tracking for the High-Level Trigger (HLT). By operating within practical HLT latency budgets, this geometry-aware approach provides a pathway to recover soft, anomalous Beyond Standard Model signatures such as unclustered energy patterns (SUEPs), that routinely evade standard hardware filters.
papers.summary: Reconstructing particle tracks at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider is a combinatorial problem that Kalman filters handle poorly as detector occupancy grows, particularly for low-momentum particles with tightly curling trajectories. `Manifold Helical-IN` is a graph neural network Interaction Network that embeds detector spacepoints onto a helical manifold chart using curvature-aware features, effectively unrolling those trajectories. On the `TrackML` dataset it reaches a reconstruction efficiency of 0.9675 for transverse momentum above 0.5 GeV and a **fake track rate of 0.0037, a 13-fold improvement** over the baseline `Helical-IN`. Inference takes about 150 ms per event on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, which the authors say fits High-Level Trigger latency budgets.

papers.title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection in Measured Neutron Flux Profiles of the SAFARI-1 Research Reactor
papers.abstract: Knowledge of the neutron flux distribution is essential for safe and effective reactor utilisation. In the SAFARI-1 research reactor, a set of axial flux profiles are periodically measured by activating natural copper wires inserted along the height of the fuel or control assemblies and subsequently measuring their activity using a sodium iodide detector. Improper wire insertion can, however, result in profiles that do not accurately represent the actual neutron flux distribution. Building on previously identified potential indicators of improper wire insertion, an automated approach based on unsupervised learning was developed to detect anomalous axial flux measurements. The measured data were preprocessed using missing-value imputation, decay correction, and normalisation. High-order polynomial fitting was then applied to characterise the axial flux profiles and derive features describing their shape. The Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) algorithm was employed to group flux profiles into regular and abnormal clusters based on these features with results matching the known groups. In addition, Convolutional Autoencoders were developed and trained on flux profiles from central and peripheral core positions to identify deviations from the regular profiles through reconstruction error, achieving better performance in central assemblies than in peripheral assemblies. The developed framework is intended to provide feedback to reactor operation by identifying potential wire-insertion problems in the manual technique used for axial flux monitoring at SAFARI-1.
papers.summary: Axial neutron flux profiles in the `SAFARI-1` research reactor are measured by activating copper wires inserted into fuel or control assemblies, and improperly inserted wires produce misleading profiles. The authors build an unsupervised detection pipeline that preprocesses the measurements, derives shape features from high-order polynomial fits, and clusters profiles with Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (`DBSCAN`), alongside convolutional autoencoders that flag anomalies by reconstruction error. The **`DBSCAN` clusters match the known regular and abnormal groups**, and the autoencoders perform better on central assemblies than on peripheral ones. The framework is intended to give reactor operators feedback on wire-insertion problems.

papers.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Sequence Models for Sample-Efficient Energy Regression in Simulated Calorimeter Showers
papers.abstract: Energy reconstruction from electromagnetic calorimeter data underpins particle identification, event reconstruction and precision measurements in high-energy physics. Machine learning already performs well on this task, yet two questions remain open: how much the choice of data representation matters, and whether hybrid quantum-classical models add value in practice. We compare classical and quantum-enhanced models for incident positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN dataset, a public benchmark of 100,000 simulated electromagnetic shower events spanning 1 to 100 GeV. Eight architectures, namely SVR, ANN, CNN and LSTM together with their quantum counterparts, are trained on three calorimeter representations: engineered physical features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Models that follow the longitudinal development of the shower reach the highest accuracy, which points to the value of physically informed representations. The hybrid QLSTM gives the lowest reconstruction error, with an RMSE of 0.294 GeV. Under matched-data conditions with only 1,500 training events, the QLSTM improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7% and also surpasses an LSTM trained on the full set. These observations indicate that longitudinal representations are central to calorimeter energy reconstruction and give preliminary evidence that hybrid quantum-classical sequence models can be more sample-efficient for regression in high-energy physics.
papers.summary: Reconstructing incident particle energy from electromagnetic calorimeter data is a core task in high-energy physics, and this study asks how much data representation matters and whether hybrid quantum-classical models help. Eight architectures (SVR, ANN, CNN, and LSTM plus quantum counterparts of each) are trained on the `CaloGAN` dataset of 100,000 simulated showers using engineered features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Sequence models that follow the longitudinal shower development are most accurate, with the hybrid `QLSTM` giving the lowest RMSE of 0.294 GeV. With only 1,500 training events, the **`QLSTM` improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7%** and also beats an LSTM trained on the full set, which the authors present as preliminary evidence of better sample efficiency.

papers.title: Waveform-based pulse timing enhanced by self-supervised neural regression models for digital nuclear instrumentation
papers.abstract: With the rapid development of high-sampling-rate digital nuclear devices, their applications in nuclear facilities and related fields become more acceptable, and will possibly become widespread due to the versatility and flexibility of waveform sampling systems. When digitizers reach hundreds of megahertz or gigahertz, their lower limit in time measurement probes into the sub-nanosecond region, expediting their use in a bunch of time-critical scenarios. While conventional algorithms coupled with digital sampling techniques realize fair pulse timing in certain conditions, the potentials are still open to compact and efficient machine learning models. In this paper, we intend to boost the performance of pulse timing with a new paradigm of self-supervised learning on matched waveform pairs. The proposed method combines the mainstream self-supervised loss and the auxiliary weakly-supervised loss on the reference set, jointly improving the timing performance. We apply the method in a gamma/neutron-mixed radiation field, common in nuclear facilities. The simulation and experimental results show that, the proposed method not only outperforms conventional timing algorithms, but also surpasses neural network models based on supervised learning alone. Considering the trained model is lightweight and computationally efficient, it is promising to deploy it on edge devices, like economical microcontrollers with neural processing units.
papers.summary: High-sampling-rate digitizers allow sub-nanosecond pulse timing in nuclear instrumentation, where conventional timing algorithms leave room for compact machine learning models. The authors propose a self-supervised regression approach trained on matched waveform pairs, combining a self-supervised loss with an auxiliary weakly-supervised loss on a reference set. In simulations and experiments in a mixed gamma/neutron radiation field, the method **outperforms both conventional timing algorithms and neural networks trained with supervised learning alone**. The resulting model is lightweight enough that the authors consider it suitable for edge devices such as low-cost microcontrollers with neural processing units.

papers.title: ProdPilot: A Layered Model Context Protocol System for Automated Production Readiness and Deployment of Vibe-Coded Projects
papers.abstract: AI-assisted development environments turn natural-language requests into working applications, yet the projects they produce often fail on their first deployment for operational reasons: credentials in source files, missing security middleware, no container definition, no health endpoint and no delivery pipeline. Automated repair of such defects usually relies on free-form model generation, which varies between runs and is seldom checked independently. This paper presents ProdPilot, a local Model Context Protocol server that audits Node.js and React projects against 50 production readiness rules, repairs violations through a bounded loop, gates the result and deploys it. Each rule is classified by what its fix requires: 28 fixes are fixed templates, 16 are filled with values extracted from the project and only 6 are written by the IDE agent's model, so 88.0\% of the ruleset needs no model-written content, and across 499 real repositories 93.5\% of the violations found fall in those classes. A fix, however it was produced, is accepted only if the checker that flagged the rule now passes. In a full-chain run over 23 sample projects, template and extraction fixes that were applied as written passed their checkers in 87.6\% and 95.0\% of cases, and independent verification rejected 25 of the 237 fixes reported as applied. A deployability model trained on 684 real deployments ranks held-out projects at 0.909 ROC AUC, a gated project was deployed, smoke-tested and connected to an active CI/CD pipeline in 82 seconds, and the unchanged server worked from the IDE agents in VS Code, Cursor and Windsurf, where live agents resolved all six delegated rules on the first attempt under the same verification. ProdPilot itself runs no model.
papers.summary: Applications produced by AI-assisted coding often fail on first deployment for operational reasons such as hardcoded credentials, missing security middleware, or no container definition, health endpoint, or delivery pipeline. `ProdPilot` is a local Model Context Protocol server that audits Node.js and React projects against 50 production-readiness rules, repairs violations in a bounded loop, gates the result, and deploys it, accepting a fix only if the checker that flagged the rule then passes. Fixes are classified by what they require, so that **88.0% of the ruleset needs no model-written content**, and across 499 real repositories 93.5% of violations found fall into the template or extraction classes. In a run over 23 sample projects, independent verification rejected 25 of 237 fixes reported as applied, and a gated project was deployed, smoke-tested, and connected to a CI/CD pipeline in 82 seconds.

papers.title: Time-Consistent Evaluation of Hierarchical Code Graphs for SWE Agents
papers.abstract:
Evaluating repository-aware software engineering (SWE) agents requires strict separation between pre-existing repository knowledge and future code evolution, yet standard benchmarks frequently suffer from temporal contamination and prompt-level solution leakage. Building on the time-consistent benchmark protocol of Sun (2026), we enforce strict zero-leakage isolation across DragonFly in C++ and React in JavaScript/TypeScript, locking repository snapshots and knowledge graphs at historical cutoff commits $T_0$ and evaluating 100 post-$T_0$ pull requests across four prompt granularities: Minimal, Concise, Contextual, and Guided.
  Under this zero-leakage protocol, we conduct a matched evaluation of three context-augmentation regimes: (1) an unaugmented Baseline, (2) a flat syntax-level Tree-sitter AST graph, and (3) ServiceExplorer, a deterministic two-level hierarchical dependency graph capturing Level-1 system/package containers and Level-2 architectural modules. Across 7,200 paired evaluations spanning six foundation models across the MAI-Code Flash, Claude, and GPT-Sol families, ServiceExplorer consistently outperforms both Baseline and Tree-sitter AST across every model, repository, and prompt granularity ($+15.6\%$ to $+86.2\%$ relative $F_1$ lift, $p < 10^{-4}$), while tripling exact full-PR localization on DragonFly. Crucially, equipping an efficiency-tier or prior-generation model with ServiceExplorer consistently surpasses the unaugmented Baseline $F_1$ of the next-generation model across all evaluated families.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for repository-aware software engineering (SWE) agents often leak future code or solutions into the evaluation, so the authors lock repository snapshots and knowledge graphs at a historical cutoff commit and evaluate 100 later pull requests from `DragonFly` (C++) and `React` (JavaScript/TypeScript) at four prompt granularities. Under this protocol they compare an unaugmented baseline, a flat `Tree-sitter` AST graph, and `ServiceExplorer`, a deterministic two-level hierarchical dependency graph of system/package containers and architectural modules. Across 7,200 paired evaluations on six foundation models, `ServiceExplorer` beats both alternatives for every model, repository, and prompt granularity, with a **relative F1 lift of 15.6% to 86.2%**, and triples exact full-PR localization on `DragonFly`. An efficiency-tier or prior-generation model equipped with it also surpasses the unaugmented baseline F1 of the next-generation model in each family.

papers.title: Enumerating Posterior-Supported Priors: First-Order Error of Finite-Integral Cross-Categorical Measurement Morphisms
papers.abstract: In generative modeling, standard measure theory adopts the a.e. convention, which legitimately ignores any error component carried by a null-support set: a single null element can hide out-of-domain error inside null support and never be explicitly accounted for. The contribution of this paper is not a new distributional distance, but rather a verifiable structure that writes down which underlying predicate supports a high-level object, when it is invertible, and at which layer the error resides, from which we propose the enumerating posterior-supported prior framework. The framework operates on a three-layer categorical chain Quot->MorTop->Set: the first two layers posit no point elements and take binary-predicate quotient partitions as objects; the replica-index counting measure successively discriminates one-to-many collections into injections, lifting object collection from surjection to a quotient-layer bijection; the mutual exclusion of preimages in the shared measure space is resolved by an invertible MPT. Four results consolidate into Thm. 7: binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects support the set categorical functional along categorical support via measure descent--recovery, enumerating the morphism itself rather than its preimage and object; their multiplicity is normalized through replica-index injection and accounted as an explicitly first-order error. The contribution of this paper is a transformation from nontrivial-input construction -> engineering-computable first-order output: the binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects, supported via categorical support measure descent--recovery, constitute a substantive nontrivial input---precisely because they lift the out-of-domain error that hid inside null support into a first-order falsifiable coefficient mu_err, a finitely obtainable finite integral first-order error.
papers.summary: Standard measure theory in generative modeling ignores error carried on null-support sets under the almost-everywhere convention, which can hide out-of-domain error from explicit accounting. The authors propose an enumerating posterior-supported prior framework built on a three-layer categorical chain `Quot->MorTop->Set`, whose first two layers take binary-predicate quotient partitions as objects rather than point elements, and which uses a replica-index counting measure to turn one-to-many collections into injections. Its main theorem consolidates four results to state that these objects support the set-level functional through measure descent and recovery, with **the hidden error surfaced as an explicit, finitely computable first-order coefficient `mu_err`**. The contribution is framed as a verifiable structure for locating where error resides, not as a new distributional distance.

papers.title: Confident and Wrong: Structure Confidence Is a Poor Selection Filter for Protein Function
papers.abstract: Structure-guided protein design can generate plausible candidates, but structural confidence does not predict function. We trained a function-guided model on measured metal-binding affinity with protein sequence, ligand identity, and assay conditions, and used it to design rare earth element (REE) binding variants of lanmodulin, a lanthanide-binding protein with four EF-hand domains. We screened 297 designs from three strategies against terbium and dysprosium, adjacent lanthanides among the hardest REE pairs to separate. Selection on structural confidence inverted the outcome it was meant to improve. The Structure-Confidence-Selected panel carried the highest pTM, complex ipLDDT, and composite confidence scores, and expressed at 97%, yet only 16.7% of its designs bound terbium (95% CI 10.4 to 25.7), against 83.3% (74.6 to 89.5) for the function-guided panel, whose confidence scores were the lowest. The odds of binding differed 25-fold between the two panels (Fisher exact $p = 1 \times 10^{-20}$). No structural-confidence metric separated binders from non-binders consistently across panels, whereas the function-trained model's predicted pKd gave the highest ROC AUC in every panel, 0.79 to 0.92, and ranked measured affinity among function-guided binders at Spearman $\rho = 0.98$. On the design objective, Tb/Dy selectivity, the function-guided designs also exceeded the natural lanmodulin family, outranking a randomly drawn ortholog 84% of the time across 149 orthologs. Structural confidence is a plausibility signal, not a selection criterion for function; direct supervision on measured function is what ranks designs.
papers.summary: Structure-guided protein design commonly filters candidates by structural confidence scores, and this study tests whether those scores predict function. The authors trained a model on measured metal-binding affinity with protein sequence, ligand identity, and assay conditions, used it to design rare earth element binding variants of `lanmodulin`, and screened 297 designs from three strategies against terbium and dysprosium. The panel selected on structural confidence had the highest confidence scores yet **only 16.7% of its designs bound terbium, against 83.3% for the function-guided panel**, a 25-fold difference in odds. No structural-confidence metric separated binders from non-binders consistently, whereas the function-trained model's predicted affinity gave ROC AUC of 0.79 to 0.92 in every panel.

papers.title: Can LLMs Write Backdoors? An Empirical Security Study of Weight-Space Programming
papers.abstract: Recent advances in weight-space programming (WSP) have demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can directly inspect and modify neural network weights without conventional gradient-based training. While this capability opens new possibilities for model improvement, it also raises an important security question: Can LLMs exploit weight-space programming to inject backdoors into neural networks? To answer this question, we present an empirical security study of LLM-driven weight-space programming for backdoor injection. Specifically, we investigate whether general-purpose LLMs can directly modify the weights of target models according to natural-language instructions, without accessing task-specific data, performing forward passes, or computing gradients. We evaluate five LLMs as weight editors across three target architectures: an MLP on MNIST, ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on AG News. Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, LLM-driven weight editing can successfully inject backdoors across different architectures while largely preserving clean performance. Second, successful attacks can require remarkably few parameter modifications, including only six parameters for the MLP and 0.02% of the weights for a fine-tuned Qwen model. Third, editing capabilities vary substantially across LLMs and target architectures: although all five LLMs successfully backdoor the MLP, only GPT-6 Astra succeeds across all three targets. These findings highlight an emerging security risk of weight-space programming and underscore the importance of safeguarding LLM-driven weight editing.
papers.summary: Weight-space programming (WSP) lets large language models (LLMs) inspect and modify neural network weights directly, and this study asks whether that can be used to inject backdoors from natural-language instructions without task data, forward passes, or gradients. Five LLMs are evaluated as weight editors on an MLP on `MNIST`, `ResNet-18` on `CIFAR-10`, and `Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct` on `AG News`. The edits inject backdoors while largely preserving clean performance, and can be very sparse, needing **only six modified parameters for the MLP** and 0.02% of the weights for the fine-tuned `Qwen` model. Capability varies widely: all five LLMs backdoor the MLP, but only `GPT-6 Astra` succeeds on all three targets.

papers.title: Alignment with Reflect-Reasoning: Learning How To Follow Principles
papers.abstract: The appropriate governing norms and principles for the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) often depend on cultural context and deployment application. However, most alignment techniques focus on training models to conform to human preferences or constitutional principles specified at training time and subsequently fixed. In practice, many deployers rely on system prompting to implement contextual norms and guardrails at inference time. Prior work has shown that post-generation reflective reasoning with critique and revision can improve conformance compared to simple system prompting, but such methods are limited to the reasoning abilities inherent in the trained model. We introduce Reflect-Reasoning, a training method that teaches models how to reason about alignment to principles, rather than simply which principles to follow. Across five models, Reflect-Reasoning consistently outperforms both system prompting and explicit prompting strategies for in-context reflective reasoning. These improvements extend and generalize to entirely out-of-distribution domains of medical and financial principles. We additionally demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning reduces the occurrence of rare but serious principle violations. Finally, we show that Reflect-Reasoning does not erode the safety engineering of a model and is robust against jailbreaking attempts using adversarial constitutions. Overall, our results demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning is a scalable method for training constitutional alignment as a generalizable reasoning capability, enabling models to adapt to novel principles and produce transparent reasoning traces without additional fine-tuning.
papers.summary: Deployers usually impose context-specific norms on LLMs through system prompts at inference time, while most alignment training fixes a set of principles in advance. `Reflect-Reasoning` is a training method that teaches models how to reason about conforming to whatever principles they are given, as opposed to which principles to follow. Across five models it **consistently outperforms both system prompting and prompted in-context reflective reasoning**, and the gains generalize to out-of-distribution medical and financial principles. The authors also report fewer rare but serious principle violations, no erosion of existing safety behavior, and robustness to jailbreak attempts using adversarial constitutions.

papers.title: WETW: Learning Pair-Specific Weighted Euclidean Distances for Efficient DTW Search
papers.abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for similarity search over time series that are misaligned in time, but its cost is quadratic in the series length and lower bounds often prune few candidates, so search over large collections of long series is slow. Learned approximations embed the series to make comparisons cheap, yet compare every pair with the same fixed rule, usually the Euclidean distance, although DTW aligns each pair differently. We observe that, once a pair is aligned, DTW is a Euclidean distance over coordinates selected for that pair. Building on this view, we propose Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (WETW), a learned distance that adapts the comparison of fixed-length embeddings to each pair. A small symmetric network predicts one weight per embedding di- mension and pair without computing an alignment, which halves the error of the best static distance on the same embeddings. The embeddings come from the Weighted Euclidean SEries Encoder (WESEE), whose multi-scale Temporal Feature Extractor keeps the timing information that global pooling removes and raises recall@1 from 0.90 to 0.95, although WETW works with any encoder. We also show that fitting DTW distances is not enough for search, as regression alone misorders the closest neighbours, and that ranking regularization raises recall@1 from 0.79 to 0.95. Our filter-and-verify pipeline, WETW-FV, uses WETW to build a shortlist and exact DTW to check it, so the search is approximate but every returned distance is exact. Over eight datasets, WETW-FV is 11.4x faster than the fastest exact method among the UCR Suite, lower bounds and MESSI-DTW, at a mean recall@10 of 0.93, while the best learned baseline reaches 0.59 at the same speed. On 48K-point series, WETW- FV remains 40x faster than the UCR Suite at a recall@10 of 0.91.
papers.summary: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for searching misaligned time series, but its quadratic cost makes search over large collections of long series slow, and learned approximations compare every pair with one fixed rule. Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (`WETW`) instead uses a small symmetric network to predict per-dimension weights for each pair of fixed-length embeddings, without computing an alignment, which halves the error of the best static distance on the same embeddings. Adding a ranking regularizer raises recall@1 from 0.79 to 0.95, since regression on DTW distances alone misorders the nearest neighbours. In a filter-and-verify pipeline that checks a shortlist with exact DTW, the method is **11.4x faster than the fastest exact method at a mean recall@10 of 0.93** over eight datasets, where the best learned baseline reaches 0.59 at the same speed.

papers.title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories
papers.abstract: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.
papers.summary: Coding-agent benchmarks mostly report binary task success, hiding how agents actually behave while solving tasks. The authors analyze **143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 models**, using a rule-based parser that maps raw traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, audited against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. Agents with similar solve rates differ substantially in how they explore, modify, and verify code, and aggregate behavioral profiles can identify the agent stack across disjoint repositories and programming languages without using outcomes, token counts, or tool names. Scaffold choice and reasoning effort are also shown to systematically shift search, editing, and testing behavior.

papers.title: Racing the Clock: Teaching VLNs Budget-Conditioned Object Search
papers.abstract: A rescue robot entering a building with thirty seconds on the clock should sprint toward the single most promising room; given ten minutes, it should instead explore a broader tour. Yet vision-language-navigation (VLN) models are typically evaluated under a fixed episode limit that the policy never observes, even though time-critical missions require behavior to adapt to the available budget. We study budget-conditioned object search: given a target category and an explicit action budget, an agent must find as many distinct target instances as possible before the budget expires. We investigate how to supervise VLNs for this task by comparing a privileged TSP expert, which plans near-optimal routes using the full map and true target locations, with a room-level Bellman expert that maximizes expected return under partial observability using high-level cross-scene semantic priors. Despite the TSP expert achieving substantially higher expert performance, its demonstrations are less effective for learning exploration: on held-out HM3D scenes, the Bellman-supervised VLN consistently outperforms the TSP-supervised VLN, with the advantage becoming more pronounced at longer budgets. At 2000 steps (500m), the Bellman-supervised VLN finds 71.4% of reachable target instances, compared with 65.5% for the TSP-supervised VLN and 44.8% for the pretrained VLN. These results highlight a distinction between optimal routing and optimal exploration: effective exploration supervision should optimize decisions under partial observability rather than imitate routes that are optimal only once the environment is fully known.
papers.summary: Vision-language-navigation (VLN) models are usually evaluated under a fixed episode limit the policy never sees, so the authors study budget-conditioned object search, where an agent given a target category and an explicit action budget must find as many distinct instances as possible. They compare two sources of supervision: a privileged travelling-salesman (TSP) expert that plans near-optimal routes from the full map and true target locations, and a room-level Bellman expert that maximizes expected return under partial observability using cross-scene semantic priors. Although the TSP expert itself performs better, its demonstrations teach exploration less well: on held-out `HM3D` scenes at a 2000-step budget, the **Bellman-supervised model finds 71.4% of reachable targets versus 65.5%** for the TSP-supervised one and 44.8% for the pretrained model. The gap widens as budgets grow.

papers.title: Classification with Large-Step Gradient Descent: Unifying Self-Stabilization and Convergence Rates
papers.abstract: Neural networks are often trained with gradient descent (GD) using step sizes that exceed classical stability thresholds, a regime where standard convergence theory no longer applies. Despite exhibiting non-monotonic loss and oscillatory dynamics, this regime frequently leads to faster convergence and better generalization. Existing theoretical perspectives offer complementary but incomplete insights: one identifies a self-stabilization mechanism that drives GD toward flat regions but does not yield convergence rates; another derives rigorous rates for specific losses but does not explain the underlying stabilization mechanism; and a third unifies these views for overparameterized least squares, but relies on the existence of a minimizer manifold, which is absent in classification settings. In this work, we extend this unified geometric perspective to exponential-tail losses, including logistic and cross-entropy losses in separable linear classification, where the loss infimum is not attained at any finite parameter. We identify a curvature-defined reference subspace that replaces the role of the minimizer manifold, yielding a coupled dynamical system in which orthogonal oscillations are damped by parallel progress along directions of decreasing sharpness. Under regularity conditions, which we verify for logistic and multiclass cross-entropy losses on symmetric data models, we derive explicit bounds for the iterates, not just the loss, covering both the unstable and stable regimes, and revealing a three-phase damping structure in the latter. Our analysis further uncovers a transient implicit bias induced by large step sizes: although GD converges asymptotically to the max-margin direction, large steps can leave persistent orthogonal residuals and, in certain geometries, amplify them, affecting finite-time alignment with the max-margin direction.
papers.summary: Gradient descent is often run with step sizes above classical stability thresholds, a regime with oscillating, non-monotonic loss that standard convergence theory does not cover. This work extends a unified geometric analysis, previously limited to overparameterized least squares, to exponential-tail losses such as logistic and cross-entropy in separable linear classification, where no finite minimizer exists. A curvature-defined reference subspace takes the place of the minimizer manifold, giving a coupled system in which orthogonal oscillations are damped by progress along directions of decreasing sharpness, and yielding **explicit bounds on the iterates in both unstable and stable regimes**. The analysis also identifies a transient implicit bias: large steps can leave or even amplify orthogonal residuals that slow finite-time alignment with the max-margin direction.

papers.title: Unfinished-Bench: Measuring Rule Violations by Persistent Agents in Realistic Work Environments
papers.abstract: AI agents are increasingly equipped with persistence toward task completion to run delegated work autonomously for long periods, under many unstated constraints from internal documents and other people's authority. When completion requires violating a rule, the agent must decide alone, yet benchmarks of instruction-rule conflicts state the rule in the prompt or keep it hidden and do not evaluate persistence. We present Unfinished-Bench, a benchmark that gives models persistence in autonomous runs without a user, in realistic work environments with embedded rules. In each of its 97 scenarios across 7 organizations and 7 risk categories, the goal and the rule cannot both hold. We find that persistence raised violations of a rule in an internal document from 32.2% to 43.6%, five times the 8.5% for the same rule stated by the user. Of the document-rule violations, 98.3% occurred after the rule was displayed, and in 89% of a judged sample the agent first wrote down the rule. Violations of rules placed in the environment without user oversight can lead to serious incidents, so persistence-driven risks need to be evaluated. Benchmark documentation: https://francis21c.github.io/unfinished-bench/
papers.summary: Long-running autonomous agents that are told to persist until a task is done often meet rules buried in internal documents rather than stated by a user, and existing benchmarks do not test how persistence affects compliance. `Unfinished-Bench` puts models in 97 realistic work scenarios across 7 organizations and 7 risk categories, where the goal and an embedded rule cannot both hold. **Persistence raised violations of a rule in an internal document from 32.2% to 43.6%, five times the 8.5% rate for the same rule stated by the user.** Of those document-rule violations, 98.3% happened after the rule had been displayed, and in 89% of a judged sample the agent had first written the rule down.

papers.title: Tracing Knowledge and Reasoning in LLM
papers.abstract: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.
papers.summary: Benchmark scores for Large Language Models (LLMs) show what a model achieves but not what internal processing produced the result. The proposed framework combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to place benchmarks on a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to expose failure modes that task-level scores hide. Across 16 LLMs and 24 benchmarks, with targeted internal-state analyses on representative models, the authors observe **systematic differences in internal processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks**. They suggest the resulting profiles could guide benchmark selection and model choice.

papers.title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.
papers.summary: Diffusion models are strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but steering them toward several conflicting properties usually needs costly fine-tuning or differentiable guidance that many real tasks do not allow. The authors adapt the models at inference time with Diffusion Tree Sampling (`DTS`), a Monte Carlo tree search over the denoising trajectory. They extend it so that existing property-conditional models serve as guided proposals without distorting the target distribution, and so that **a single search yields samples spanning an entire Pareto front**. Demonstrations cover improving crystal stability, generating rare space groups or high bulk modulus crystals, and trading off dielectric constant against bandgap, all without modifying the underlying models.

papers.title: Availability-Aware Historical Feedback Learning for Electric Arc Furnace Temperature and Chemical Composition Prediction
papers.abstract: Electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking plays an increasingly important role in recycled and lower-carbon steel production. However, variability in charged materials, energy input, and operating conditions makes accurate prediction of molten steel temperature and final chemical composition challenging. Intermittent or delayed measurements limit the information available for timely prediction. This study develops an availability-aware historical-feedback learning framework for predicting EAF endpoint temperature and the final concentrations of twelve chemical elements. Eight industrial data sources are integrated into three progressively enriched predictor representations comprising 19 static, 39 temporal, and 47 history-informed features. Historical outcomes are incorporated only when eligible under an assumed 60-minute measurement-release delay. Using 19,738 temperature heats and 3,341 chemistry heats, twelve tuned regression algorithms are evaluated through chronological forward validation. The proposed historical-feedback representation reduces root mean squared error (RMSE) in 147 of 156 matched algorithm-target comparisons. For temperature prediction, ExtraTrees achieves an RMSE of 12.290 degrees C, representing a 5.54 percent reduction compared with its temporal-only counterpart. Historical-feature ablation and feedback-delay sensitivity analyses demonstrate the importance of recent outcome information and its availability. In a separate retrospective later-period evaluation, lightweight adaptive residual correction reduces temperature RMSE from 12.502 to 12.275 degrees C without retraining the underlying model. Exploratory deep learning comparisons and target-specific feature-attribution analyses provide additional insights into predictive behavior. The results establish historical outcome availability and sequential feedback as important considerations for EAF endpoint prediction.
papers.summary: Predicting the endpoint temperature and final chemistry of electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking is difficult because inputs vary and measurements arrive intermittently or late. The framework builds static, temporal, and history-informed feature sets from eight industrial data sources, admitting past outcomes only when they would have been available under an assumed 60-minute release delay. Twelve regression algorithms are evaluated with chronological forward validation on 19,738 temperature heats and 3,341 chemistry heats. **The historical-feedback features reduce root mean squared error (RMSE) in 147 of 156 matched algorithm-target comparisons**, with `ExtraTrees` reaching 12.290 degrees C on temperature, 5.54% below its temporal-only counterpart.

papers.title: Poetry 'resurrection' from LLMs
papers.abstract: In an era where linguistic creativity is challenged by algorithmic authorship, we pose a provocative question: can artificial intelligence (AI) write an infinite poem? We set up two experiments to investigate the quantitative and qualitative output produced by AI utilizing couplets that evidence a poetic relationship between end words, the only variation in a strict anaphoric, litany structure. Our results show that while AI can generate interesting pairings, it still falls short of human-level creativity and understanding of poetic relationships. We offer commentary and a brief survey of the field of computational poetry experiments, tracing back authorial intention and distinctions of 'natural' and 'artificial' poetry, as well as justifying why couplet form is suited to testing AI's poetic output. Experiment 1 relies on manual prompting and co-creation to extend the original poem, which is developed into an animated webpage installation and interactive artwork. Experiment 2 reliably achieves automated output reaching the 1000 benchmark via an alternative method of using an LLM in combination with semantic similarity, of which Method 2 demonstrates a higher capacity for semantic and quantitative poetic output. These experiments highlight the limitations of current LLMs' generation capacity at the word level but also suggest that poetry will also respond and revive by incorporating AI workflows.
papers.summary: Two experiments ask whether an LLM can extend a poem indefinitely, using couplets in a strict anaphoric litany where only the end words vary and must stand in a poetic relationship. The first uses manual prompting and co-creation, and its output became an animated interactive web installation. The second automates generation by pairing an LLM with semantic similarity and reaches 1,000 couplets. The authors conclude that **the models produce interesting pairings but fall short of human-level creativity and understanding of poetic relationships**, and they include a brief survey of computational poetry.

papers.title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
papers.abstract: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.
papers.summary: Smart homes for ambient assisted living (AAL) need a shared formal description of residents and devices in order to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects. The authors describe the ontology that serves as the semantic data layer of the `Virtual Home Framework`, with requirements drawn from two use cases: a frail elderly woman exercising on a cycle-ergometer and a designer configuring a kitchen for users with different impairments. Built with the `NeOn` methodology and reusing existing ontologies, **the resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and their cardiorespiratory fitness**, alongside smart objects, their programs and measurements, and home comfort dimensions. `SWRL` rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and match smart objects to impairments.

papers.title: A thorough review on Deep Learning approaches to 2D-to-3D Registration in Medical Imaging
papers.abstract: 2D-to-3D image registration is a key component for several medical imaging purposes such as intraoperative guidance, enabling the alignment between preoperative 3D volumes and real-time 2D images. While conventional optimisation-based methods often struggle with non-convex objectives, sensitivity to initialisation, and high computational demands, deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising alternative, offering improved alignment robustness and the potential for real-time performance. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of DL frameworks developed to address the challenges inherent in 2D-to-3D registration. We first outline how core concepts of DL are adapted to the registration problem. We then examine recent methodological advancements from multiple perspectives, including pipeline design, architectural innovations, and domain adaptation strategies. Particular attention is given to quantitative metrics, highlighting how performance is defined and measured across studies. Across the 41 included studies, we find that direct regression is the most common pipeline (23 studies, against 18 iterative ones), that hybrid CNN-attention architectures are gaining ground, and that research remains heavily concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration. We conclude by identifying the absence of per-case uncertainty estimation and the strong neglect of temporal or sequential modelling as the two methodological gaps most consequential for clinical readiness, and discuss state-space models as a way to add temporal memory within intraoperative latency budgets. Further opportunities lie in more principled domain adaptation and in the integration of foundation models for representation learning.
papers.summary: Aligning preoperative 3D volumes with real-time 2D images is central to intraoperative guidance, and conventional optimisation-based registration suffers from non-convex objectives, sensitivity to initialisation, and high compute cost. This review covers deep learning approaches to the problem, examining pipeline design, architectures, domain adaptation strategies, and how performance is measured. **Across the 41 included studies, direct regression is the most common pipeline (23 studies versus 18 iterative ones)**, hybrid CNN-attention architectures are gaining ground, and work is concentrated on X-ray-to-CT registration. The authors identify missing per-case uncertainty estimation and neglect of temporal modelling as the main gaps for clinical readiness, and discuss state-space models as a way to add temporal memory.

papers.title: Improved Regret via Variance-Aware Policy Optimization in Adversarial MDPs
papers.abstract: We study episodic adversarial MDPs with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards and achieve regret with leading term $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3SAK})$. Here $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the total number of states across decision layers, $A$ the number of actions, and $K$ the number of episodes. This improves the two incomparable prior leading terms by factors $\sqrt{S/H}$ and $\sqrt{H^3}$, leaving a factor $\sqrt H$ to the lower-bound scale. We give a reduction from unknown to known dynamics for \emph{downstream-dependent} algorithms, whose policy at step $h$ is computed only from information at steps $h+1$ and onward. This reduces the remaining leading-order gap to finding a downstream-dependent known-dynamics algorithm with $\widetilde O(H\sqrt K)$ regret, which would yield the tight $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{SAK})$ leading term for unknown dynamics. We instantiate the reduction with VOPO, a policy optimization (PO) algorithm. Its improved guarantees follow from a variance-aware analysis enabled by a novel bonus, which we call the Stability-Matching Bonus (SMB). VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3K})$ regret under known dynamics with full information; its $\sqrt H$ gap to the target $H\sqrt K$ rate is inherited by our unknown-dynamics guarantee. We also show that with known dynamics and trajectory bandit feedback, VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^2SAK})$ regret. Both known-dynamics guarantees improve the corresponding state-of-the-art PO bounds by a factor $\sqrt H$. A matching lower bound establishes that the full-information rate is tight in one parameter regime.
papers.summary: For episodic adversarial Markov decision processes with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards, the authors obtain **regret with leading term Õ(√(H³SAK))**, for horizon H, S states, A actions, and K episodes, which leaves a √H factor to the lower-bound scale. The result comes from a reduction from unknown to known dynamics for algorithms whose policy at each step depends only on information from later steps. The reduction is instantiated with `VOPO`, a policy optimization algorithm whose variance-aware analysis relies on a new Stability-Matching Bonus. Under known dynamics, `VOPO` improves the best prior policy-optimization bounds by a factor of √H for both full-information and trajectory bandit feedback.

papers.title: Do Mixture-of-Experts Routers Benefit from Ensembling?
papers.abstract: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts models rely on a single router to weight experts for each input, and this study tests whether an ensemble of routers trained jointly with the experts does better. Experiments use underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks and are analysed with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble. More routers lower validation loss, training routers to maximize expert diversity helps on three of four tasks, maximizing router diversity has no effect, and arithmetic-mean combination beats geometric-mean. Overall, **routing benefits only mildly from ensembling, and the gain is offset by the cost of training additional routers**.

papers.title: ERGo: Energy-Efficient Hybrid Graph Neural Network Training on Processing-In-Memory Architectures
papers.abstract: Processing-in-memory (PIM) has been proposed as an alternative computing paradigm for training Deep Neural Networks, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Despite these advancements, training GNN workloads on PIM devices necessitates off-chip memory access. This off-chip access is expensive in terms of performance and energy, thereby impacting the overall energy efficiency of the training process on PIM platforms. In this paper, we propose a novel hybrid training framework called ERGo that automatically switches from a full-parameter phase to a parameter-efficient phase during the training process with negligible loss in predictive accuracy. The parameter-efficient phase employs low-rank representations of GNN weights, effectively reducing the number of trainable parameters. This helps in reducing the off-chip access during the end-to-end training process on PIM architectures, leading to notable improvements in both performance and energy efficiency. ERGo outperforms the conventional full-parameter GNN training on a PIM-based platform by up to 3.15x in speedup and enhances energy efficiency by 10.5x. Furthermore, ERGo offers additional advantages when utilized on heterogeneous architectures incorporating non-volatile memory (NVM) and static random-access memory (SRAM). Training on the heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture typically utilizes NVM for the forward-pass and SRAM for the backward-pass. However, NVM cells suffer from low device endurance and repeated write operations due to weight updates can lead to poor lifetime. ERGo improves the lifetime of NVM devices by freezing the weights and preventing weight updates in the parameter-efficient phase. Experimental results demonstrate that ERGo improves the lifetime of heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture by up to 33x in comparison to full-parameter implementation.
papers.summary: Training Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on processing-in-memory (PIM) hardware requires off-chip memory accesses that are costly in time and energy. `ERGo` is a hybrid training framework that automatically switches from a full-parameter phase to a parameter-efficient phase using low-rank representations of the GNN weights, which cuts trainable parameters and off-chip access with negligible accuracy loss. **It delivers up to 3.15x speedup and 10.5x better energy efficiency than conventional full-parameter training on a PIM platform.** On heterogeneous architectures that combine non-volatile memory (NVM) and static random-access memory (SRAM), freezing weights in the second phase extends NVM lifetime by up to 33x.

papers.title: Creating Steering Vectors via Input Optimisation
papers.abstract: Activation steering influences a language model's behaviour by adding a steering vector to its residual stream during generation, but it requires white-box access to modify the hidden states at every generation step. We introduce ActGCG, a modification of Greedy Coordinate Gradient which optimises a suffix to match the target activations obtained by adding a steering vector to the residual stream. We further introduce universal suffixes trained across many prompts at once, a model-translation step that rewrites the suffix into human-readable text midway through optimisation, and a soft-suffix variant to remove the discrete token space constraint. We study two behaviours: steering a model to answer in German, and anti-refusal steering for jailbreaking. For German, a discrete suffix reproduces the steering vector's behaviour almost perfectly and transfers well across prompts and models. For anti-refusal, the equivalence is weaker, succeeding under a phrase-avoidance metric but only partially under the stricter HarmBench classifier. Our results show that a steering vector's behaviour is reachable from the input, with no access to model internals at generation time, up to a loss that depends on the concept being steered.
papers.summary: Activation steering normally needs white-box access to add a vector to a language model's residual stream at every generation step. `ActGCG` modifies `Greedy Coordinate Gradient` to optimise an input suffix whose activations match those produced by the steering vector, with variants for universal suffixes trained across many prompts, human-readable rewrites, and soft suffixes. **For steering a model to answer in German, a discrete suffix reproduces the steering vector's behaviour almost perfectly and transfers well across prompts and models.** For anti-refusal steering the match is weaker, succeeding on a phrase-avoidance metric but only partially under the stricter `HarmBench` classifier.

papers.title: SURFACE: Preference Distribution Matching on Pareto Fronts via Scalarization Steering
papers.abstract: Constructing a finite Pareto representation requires allocating a limited number of solutions across the Pareto front (PF). A desired preference distribution specifies this allocation by assigning more solutions to some PF regions and fewer to others. Scalarization generates Pareto solutions by varying objective weights and solving single-objective problems. However, a distribution of scalarization weights generally does not translate into the same distribution of Pareto solutions along the PF, because the weight-to-solution map is nonlinear and unknown in advance.To account for this distortion, we introduce SURFACE (Scalarization Updates for Redistributing Finite Approximations with Chart Estimation}), which adaptively updates scalarization weights to match a desired PF distribution. SURFACE estimates how each region of the weight grid corresponds to an area of the PF from the current scalarized solutions, then redistributes the weights accordingly. The method supports parallel, warm-started, inexact optimization with standard single-objective solvers. Theoretically, we establish that, under the stated regularity conditions, SURFACE achieves linear convergence of the preference distribution mismatch to a finite-resolution error floor of $\mathcal{O}(N^{-2/(M-1)})$, where $N$ is the number of adaptive weights and $M$ is the number of objectives. Empirically, experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate improved target-mass balance and PF coverage compared with established baselines.
papers.summary: When a Pareto front is approximated with a limited number of solutions, a chosen distribution of scalarization weights does not give the same distribution of solutions along the front, because the weight-to-solution map is nonlinear and unknown in advance. `SURFACE` estimates how each region of the weight grid maps to an area of the front from the current solutions and redistributes the weights to match a desired preference distribution. It works with parallel, warm-started, inexact single-objective solvers. Under stated regularity conditions, the authors prove **linear convergence of the distribution mismatch to an error floor of O(N^(-2/(M-1)))** for N adaptive weights and M objectives, and experiments show better target-mass balance and front coverage than established baselines.

papers.title: Identifying Latent Neural Dynamics with Recognition-Parametrised Gaussian Process Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: Neural circuits are densely interconnected systems, and many neural computations are thought to be mediated by the dynamical evolution of activity within these recurrent networks, a hypothesis often referred to as "computation through dynamics". Under this view, understanding computation within real neural populations depends on building models of the dynamical rules governing the temporal evolution of recorded high-dimensional neural activity. Most commonly, such models depend on explicit generative parameterisations of (i) the (nonlinear) intrinsic dynamical flow field and stochasticity, (ii) the (nonlinear) mapping from dynamical state to neuronal activity, and (iii) the variability of individual neural responses given that dynamical state. Misspecification of any of these components can bias estimates of dynamics and latent trajectories. In this paper, we circumvent generation-related issues by introducing the Recognition-Parametrised Gaussian Process dynamics (RP-GPdyn) model. RP-GPdyn models the dynamical flow field using a nonparametric Gaussian Process-defined transition function and models the relationship of dynamics to neural activity implicitly using the Recognition-Parametrised Model (RPM) framework. We show that this generation-free approach uncovers meaningful, behaviourally relevant latent variables and dynamics from both synthetic and experimental datasets.
papers.summary: Models of the latent dynamics behind recorded neural population activity usually require explicit generative assumptions about the flow field, the mapping from latent state to neural activity, and response variability, and misspecifying any of them can bias the result. `RP-GPdyn` models the flow field with a nonparametric Gaussian Process transition function and links dynamics to neural activity implicitly through the Recognition-Parametrised Model (`RPM`) framework, avoiding an explicit generative mapping. The authors report that **this generation-free approach recovers meaningful, behaviourally relevant latent variables and dynamics** on both synthetic and experimental datasets.

papers.title: Convergence Properties of PF-Exec: Homogeneous Structure, Anchored Closed Form, and Gain Dynamics
papers.abstract: This paper establishes a layered mathematical char acterisation of PF-Exec, the algorithm of the companion system paper. Demand-proportional bandwidth allocation yields an exact first-order homogeneous decomposition, from which the equal-load bandwidth target and its feasibility bound follow in closed form. The logarithmic knee view preserves strict load order and shares its global optimum with the Jain fairness index, while the demand-weighted centroid minimises the position potential.
