The damped softmax association block possesses a fixed point on the product of simplices. The truncated one-dimensional gain iteration admits a complete characterisation, with geomet ric convergence below the critical gain, initial-value-dependent bounded oscillation at it, and a family of bounded two-state cycles above it. A global invariant error ball and an explicit tracking recursion complete the execution guarantee. A numerical audit confirms the structural identities on every measured state and quantifies the local amplification of the coupled association and resource dynamics. Together, the results explain how closed form recovery directions and bounded adaptive gains provide stable execution without requiring a global Euclidean contraction assumption.
papers.summary: A mathematical analysis is given for `PF-Exec`, a load-balancing algorithm for UAV relay networks presented in a companion system paper. Demand-proportional bandwidth allocation yields an exact first-order homogeneous decomposition, which gives the equal-load bandwidth target and its feasibility bound in closed form, and the damped softmax association block is shown to have a fixed point. **The one-dimensional gain iteration is fully characterised: geometric convergence below a critical gain, bounded oscillation at it, and bounded two-state cycles above it.** A global invariant error ball and a tracking recursion complete the execution guarantee without assuming a global Euclidean contraction.

papers.title: PF-Exec: Large-Scale UAV Relay Load Balancing with an Anchored Potential Direction Decider and a Per-Dimension Gain-Learning Executor
papers.abstract: Relay load balancing in large-scale UAV networks requires joint decisions on association, bandwidth, power and hovering position, while the dimension grows with the number of UAVs and each UAV sees only its local state. This paper splits the decision into two layers. An anchored potential direction decider emits a closed-form target at every instant and returns its direction only. A gain-learning executor maps a local observation into a positive gain per dimension, composes gain and target, and clips the action against the physical single-step bound; the two layers form PF-Exec. The unit gain is the default start, so the executor reduces to the pure potential policy before training. The load is first-order homogeneous in bandwidth, making the bandwidth target closed form, and the position target is the demand-weighted centroid of the served users. The system uses a two-hop access and millimetre-wave backhaul link with soft association, a 3GPP UMa-AV channel with two shadowing layers, an OU-type social-force crowd and a quadrotor physical layer. Evaluation spans all fleet sizes, two crowd scenarios, independent seeds, the published baselines in their own settings and a degraded-information line. In the highest-pressure burst setting the fixed-step comparison breaks down on part of the seeds, losing fairness and mean load at once, while PF-Exec holds fairness near one. Among the ten comparison methods only the greedy heuristic survives that setting; its load variance stays far higher. Under stale global state and position noise the fairness index stays high at both largest-scale scenarios. Flight energy is nearly identical between the learned and the fixed-step executor, and three constants are fixed once across all settings. The convergence properties of both layers, from the truncated gain iteration to the perturbed tracking bound, are proved in the companion analysis.
papers.summary: Balancing relay load across large UAV fleets requires joint decisions on user association, bandwidth, power, and hovering position, with each UAV seeing only local state. `PF-Exec` splits the decision into a potential-based decider that emits a closed-form target direction and a learned executor that maps local observations to a positive gain per dimension, starting from unit gain so that it matches the pure potential policy before training. Evaluation uses a two-hop millimetre-wave backhaul model with a 3GPP channel, simulated crowds, and ten comparison methods. **In the highest-pressure burst setting `PF-Exec` holds the fairness index near one while the fixed-step comparison breaks down on some seeds**, and only a greedy heuristic among the baselines survives, with far higher load variance.

papers.title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not been modified to interpret as a different type of data. By construction, the resulting measure, NLS depth, can be adjudicated before training from an architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone, and is insensitive to ordinary post-training such as prompting, distillation, and RL. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. It would likely grow slowly under continued scaling of standard transformers, while latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could increase it by a large amount. We work through how NLS depth applies to a range of existing and proposed architectures, discuss alternative operationalizations, and give a worked example bounding the depth of Gemma3-1B. We argue that AI developers should track and report the NLS depth of their models as a complement to direct measurements of CoT monitorability.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring depends on a model's reasoning passing through readable text, and some architectural changes could let much more computation happen out of view. The authors define `NLS depth`, a proxy for unverbalized serial cognition measured as the longest computation path that avoids natural-language-rooted nodes, meaning nodes initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs and not repurposed since. The measure can be determined from architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration before training. Across open-weight models it correlates strongly with layer count and **has grown slowly in recent years, whereas latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could increase it by a large amount**; a worked example bounds the depth of `Gemma3-1B`.

papers.title: Continuous Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation Using PPG From Methods to Clinical Translation
papers.abstract: Continuous blood pressure (BP) monitoring could improve hypertension management by capturing changes that intermittent cuff measurements miss. Photoplethysmography (PPG) is widely explored for cuffless BP estimation because optical sensors are inexpensive, wearable, and already present in many consumer and clinical devices. PPG, however, does not measure arterial pressure: BP is inferred from waveform characteristics or pulse timing, which also depend on vascular tone, arterial stiffness, sensor contact, motion, and individual physiology. This survey reviews PPG-based cuffless BP estimation along the full measurement chain, covering physiological mechanisms, waveform features, pulse arrival time (PAT), pulse transit time (PTT), machine-learning methods, datasets, calibration, validation, deployment, bias, and clinical translation. Studies are assessed by the strength of evidence they provide rather than by reported error alone, with particular attention to subject and temporal leakage, dataset imbalance, calibration dependence and drift, motion artifacts, and the gap between benchmark accuracy and reliable real-world measurement. The review finds that progress depends on more than better prediction algorithms. Future work should prioritize physiologically informed models, diverse longitudinal datasets, transparent reporting of calibration requirements and failure rates, stronger evaluation protocols, and studies that demonstrate practical value in clinical care.
papers.summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) sensors are cheap and already common in wearables, but they do not measure arterial pressure directly, so cuffless blood pressure must be inferred from waveform shape or pulse timing that also depends on vascular tone, sensor contact, motion, and individual physiology. This survey covers the full measurement chain, from physiological mechanisms, pulse arrival time (PAT), and pulse transit time (PTT) through machine-learning methods, datasets, calibration, validation, and clinical translation. Studies are judged by strength of evidence rather than reported error, with attention to subject and temporal leakage, dataset imbalance, calibration drift, and motion artifacts. The review concludes that **progress depends on more than better prediction algorithms**, calling for physiologically informed models, diverse longitudinal datasets, and stronger evaluation protocols.

papers.title: Adversarially Batched Online Learning
papers.abstract: We introduce adversarially batched online learning, where the learner may update its decision rule only at a restricted set of time steps. Equivalently, the time horizon is partitioned into batches, within which the learner must use a fixed policy. We study this model for four canonical problems: stochastic bandits, online convex optimization, prediction with expert advice, and adversarial bandits. For stochastic bandits, we identify a universal complexity measure based on relative batch growth and establish both gap-dependent and gap-independent regret bounds. We show that the multiplicative penalty relative to the standard gap-dependent complexity can grow superlinearly in batch hardness. For the remaining three, we show that the optimal regret is tightly characterized by the 2-norm of the batch-length sequence. The upper bound is achieved by a batch-oblivious learner who does not know the batch structure, via a generic adaptive doubling trick tailored to this complexity measure. In contrast, the lower bound holds even for batch-aware learners.
papers.summary: A new online learning model restricts the learner to updating its decision rule only at certain time steps, which partitions the horizon into batches with a fixed policy inside each. The model is studied for stochastic bandits, online convex optimization, prediction with expert advice, and adversarial bandits. For stochastic bandits, a complexity measure based on relative batch growth gives gap-dependent and gap-independent regret bounds. For the other three problems, **optimal regret is tightly characterized by the 2-norm of the batch-length sequence**, achieved by a learner that does not know the batch structure, while the lower bound holds even for learners that do.

papers.title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
papers.abstract:
Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture.
  To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.
papers.summary: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models for advertising need very high inference throughput yet must stay within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin of their baseline, which has kept aggressive quantization out of production. This empirical study evaluates the `MXFP8` and 6-bit `MXFP6` microscaling formats on the AMD `MI350X`, applying the 6-bit format selectively to stay inside the NE threshold. On two production ads ranking models, **matrix-multiply kernel speedups over FP16 are 1.33-1.55x for `MXFP8` and 1.73-1.99x for `MXFP6`**, with up to 2.90x on individual layers. End-to-end throughput gains from selective `MXFP6` over FP8 configurations are 1.5-5.3% for one model and 7.6-14.3% for the other.

papers.title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: This paper presents a multifidelity (MF) formulation of Operator Inference (OpInf) for learning non-intrusive, physics-based reduced-order models (ROMs) of nonlinear dynamical systems. OpInf learns reduced operators from projections of snapshot data by solving a least squares regression problem. However, generating high-fidelity snapshots can be computationally expensive, limiting parameter coverage and the temporal extent of training trajectories for many aerospace applications, which can lead to inaccurate or unstable ROM predictions. This work proposes MF-OpInf, which combines limited high-fidelity snapshots with more plentiful low-fidelity snapshots through a control-variates-inspired MF least squares formulation to learn a single set of reduced operators across multiple trajectories. Low-fidelity trajectories provide additional parameter coverage and extend beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. The low-fidelity snapshots are also used to construct an improved reduced basis through weighted proper orthogonal decomposition. We demonstrate MF-OpInf on a nonlinear reaction-diffusion problem with parametrized sinusoidal forcing and a two-dimensional incompressible flow past a cylinder with a parametrized inlet pulse. In these experiments, under an equal training simulation budget, MF-OpInf reduces the mean relative prediction error at unseen parameters by up to $87\%$ for the reaction-diffusion problem and $28\%$ for the cylinder flow problem over the test time regime, which extends beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. These results demonstrate that MF-OpInf can improve temporal extrapolation and prediction at unseen parameters without increasing the training simulation budget.
papers.summary: Operator Inference (`OpInf`) learns reduced-order models (ROMs) of nonlinear dynamical systems from simulation snapshots, but high-fidelity snapshots are expensive, which limits parameter coverage and training time horizons. `MF-OpInf` combines a few high-fidelity snapshots with many low-fidelity ones through a control-variates-inspired multifidelity least squares formulation, and also uses the low-fidelity data to build a better reduced basis via weighted proper orthogonal decomposition. Under an equal training simulation budget, **it reduces mean relative prediction error at unseen parameters by up to 87% on a reaction-diffusion problem and 28% on flow past a cylinder**, over a test window that extends beyond the high-fidelity training horizon.

papers.title: Adversarial Tracking: Attacks on Image Sensors for Object Tracking in Autonomous Vehicles
papers.abstract: Object tracking systems estimate the motion of surrounding vehicles by linking detected objects across video frames. In particular, Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) systems combine object detectors with motion prediction and data association to maintain object identities over time. However, neural network-based detectors are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that perturb input images, and their impact on downstream trajectory estimation is not fully characterized by detection accuracy alone. Therefore, this paper evaluates image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 detectors paired with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT tracking systems. The evaluation uses CARLA simulator and measures tracking quality through Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA), and Identification F1 (IDF1). Under image-specific attacks, HOTA for YOLOv3-based trackers declines from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%, while MOTA reaches -772.60% in the worst case. YOLOv4-based trackers exhibit greater robustness, while HOTA still declines to 25.06-26.86%. In addition, image-agnostic attacks can reduce the tracking accuracy using a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP), without generating a separate perturbation for individual frames.
papers.summary: Adversarial image perturbations are known to fool neural object detectors, but their effect on downstream trajectory estimation in tracking-by-detection systems is not captured by detection accuracy alone. The authors evaluate image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on `YOLOv3` and `YOLOv4` detectors paired with the `SORT`, `Deep SORT`, `Strong SORT`, and `OC-SORT` trackers in the `CARLA` simulator, measuring Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA), and Identification F1. Under image-specific attacks, **HOTA for `YOLOv3`-based trackers falls from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%**, with MOTA reaching -772.60% in the worst case, while `YOLOv4`-based trackers are more robust but still drop to 25.06-26.86% HOTA. A single Universal Adversarial Perturbation applied to every frame also reduces tracking accuracy without per-frame optimization.

papers.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
papers.abstract:
Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22.
  In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.
papers.summary: The study tests whether sustained gain-loss framing can push an LLM agent toward market manipulation by placing `Gemma 3 12B` in the role of a defendant in the London silver-fixing case, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts and run 260 times. A counterparty asks the agent to collude under gain, loss, blame, or credit framing, with added management pressure and endorsement from another bank; in a second phase, internal states extracted from texts evoking each frame are injected at layer 22. In the text-framing phase, **blame framing raised participation in collusion to 33% and loss framing to 25%, against 5% under neutral framing**, while management pressure raised trading volume 10-19 times without raising collusion. The injected states pointed the other way: loss and blame states led the agent to refuse all 60 requests, whereas gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no injected state.

papers.title: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
papers.abstract: Major industry multi-agent systems like Codex and Claude Code can be broken by attacks that have long been unsuccessful against modern frontier models. AI Safety as a discipline has largely focused on finding the bounds and vulnerabilities of AI models used in isolation. Yet as humans increasingly deploy these models as agents and multi-agent systems, the same attacks that had been thought to be patched when using a model in isolation can break these same models under specific circumstances. We show that these system breaks are not purely theoretical, but can break Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, all unmodified and used with their own sub-agent mechanisms. We show the attack by asking agents to answer questions from a store of files on disk in which we have planted a forged record. Searching the store themselves, the strong model orchestrators commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials. However, if that same orchestrator model delegates to a cheaper sub-agent, which is what these harnesses are built to do, the same models on the same facts fail on 20/180, 44/180, 75/180 and 553/900. Thus, even when the system is driven by a strong model, the system's safety lands near the weak reader's, not the orchestrator's. Simulations over 18 models show the same effect in the delivery channel where five aggregators, who on their own were almost never unsafe, repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials. The safety of real-world agentic systems that use strong orchestrator agents and weaker sub-agents, and multi-agent systems in general, is defined not by the safety of the strong agent but by the safety of the weakest agent.
papers.summary: Attacks that fail against frontier models used in isolation can succeed once those models delegate work to cheaper sub-agents, as shown on unmodified `Claude Code`, `Codex`, and a reference harness using their own sub-agent mechanisms. Agents answer questions from a store of files on disk containing a planted forged record: when strong orchestrator models search the store themselves they commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials, but **when the same orchestrators delegate to a cheaper sub-agent they fail in 20/180, 44/180, 75/180, and 553/900 trials**. Simulations over 18 models show the same effect in the delivery channel, where five aggregators that were almost never unsafe on their own repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751 of 757 trials. The authors conclude that the safety of a multi-agent system lands near that of its weakest agent, not its orchestrator.

papers.title: Model Annealing: Data-Efficient Learning through Review and Consolidation
papers.abstract: A small labelled dataset is memorized long before the training budget runs out, and the one-hot labels that remain to be fitted then mostly sharpen confidence. Model annealing spends the rest of the budget on review and consolidation, relearning from the network's own knowledge. Training is divided into episodes whose learning rate is raised again and cooled, every cooled state joins a memory of past selves, and each new episode learns from the labels, from the tempered predictions of this memory, and from adversarial dreams sought where student and memory disagree most. The memory averages predictions rather than weights, and the deployed network is the last student, so inference costs nothing extra. Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet and Imagewoof, four architecture families and 5\% to 100\% of the labels, model annealing raises the top-1 accuracy of the AdamW-trained ConvNeXt, ViT and MLP-Mixer over cross-entropy training in 28 of 33 configurations, by 1.3 points on average, and is on par in accuracy with snapshot distillation, the closest competitor. On these families it is better than both in likelihood, calibration and robustness to corruptions and small adversarial perturbations. For an SGD-trained ResNet-18 it lowers accuracy but still improves robustness to small adversarial perturbations. Separating the reheated schedule from relearning shows that relearning helps every family and that the losses come from reheats, which undo most of this network's fit to its training set. How early the accuracy of a cross-entropy run saturates largely separates the AdamW families from ResNet-18 but does not predict the gain within them. With little data, relearning from the latest snapshot without dreams, as snapshot distillation does, compounds overconfidence in the AdamW families from episode to episode. The memory and the dreams each curb most of this drift, and together they remove it.
papers.summary: Small labelled datasets are memorized long before the training budget runs out, after which fitting one-hot labels mostly sharpens confidence. The proposed method splits training into episodes with a reheated and cooled learning rate, stores each cooled state in a memory of past selves, and trains each new episode on the labels, the memory's averaged tempered predictions, and adversarial examples sought where student and memory disagree most, with no extra inference cost. Across `CIFAR-100`, `Tiny-ImageNet`, and `Imagewoof` with 5% to 100% of the labels, it **raises top-1 accuracy of AdamW-trained `ConvNeXt`, `ViT`, and `MLP-Mixer` over cross-entropy training in 28 of 33 configurations, by 1.3 points on average**, matching snapshot distillation in accuracy while improving likelihood, calibration, and robustness. For an SGD-trained `ResNet-18` it lowers accuracy, which the authors trace to the learning-rate reheats and not to the relearning step.

papers.title: User-Schedulable Approximations for Quantized Tensor Programs
papers.abstract:
Quantization lets language models run on edge devices, but it sharply increases the number of tensor kernels a library must maintain: every weight format must be paired with every activation format on every instruction set and GPU, with an encoder and a decoder that agree on the stored bytes. In GGML, the tensor library used by llama.cpp, these kernels are written by hand, and only 8 of the 54 weight-activation pairs it runs on our Arm CPU have a tiled matrix-multiplication kernel.
  We extend Halide's separation of algorithm and schedule to the representation of values. Each approximation is a codec, an encoder paired with a decoder, composed from reusable units: quantizers, integer representations, bit packers and layouts. A new directive, approximate_by, applies a codec to one stage of a program and returns the encoder and decoder as ordinary stages that Halide can schedule, so both decoders fuse into the register tiles of a matrix product. Optional contracts, such as a round-trip law, are checked by property tests; the law exposed an inconsistent block sum in GGML's q8_1.
  One algorithm and one schedule library generate 347 kernels for 31 of GGML's and KleidiAI's formats on Arm CPUs and Apple GPUs, covering 38 weight-activation pairs for which GGML has no kernel, in 3.7x less code than GGML and KleidiAI. On an Apple M3 Max, our kernels reach at least 95% of the speed of GGML's format-specific kernels in 91.0% of the cases that have one, with a median speedup of 1.13x, and are faster still where GGML falls back to blocked dot products. Counting Apple's BLAS library, which is usually faster for larger f32 products, we still reach that threshold in 86.9% of CPU cases. A port to x86 with Intel's AMX adds 793 lines of code and matches GGML in 83.5% of its cases.
papers.summary: Quantization multiplies the number of tensor kernels a library must maintain, since every weight format must be paired with every activation format on every instruction set and GPU; in `GGML`, the library behind `llama.cpp`, only 8 of the 54 weight-activation pairs run on the authors' Arm CPU have a tiled matrix-multiplication kernel. The authors extend `Halide`'s separation of algorithm and schedule to value representations, composing each approximation as an encoder-decoder codec from reusable quantizers, integer representations, bit packers, and layouts, applied through a new `approximate_by` directive that yields schedulable stages. One algorithm and one schedule library generate **347 kernels for 31 formats on Arm CPUs and Apple GPUs, covering 38 weight-activation pairs for which `GGML` has no kernel, in 3.7x less code** than `GGML` and `KleidiAI`. On an Apple M3 Max the generated kernels reach at least 95% of the speed of `GGML`'s format-specific kernels in 91.0% of cases with a median speedup of 1.13x, and a property-tested round-trip law exposed an inconsistent block sum in `GGML`'s `q8_1` format.

papers.title: GraphScent: Calibrating Directional Relevance Signals for Bounded-Context Code Localization
papers.abstract: Running open-weight language models locally on a single consumer GPU requires replacing expanding multi-turn exploration histories with short, stateless code inspections. Stateless repository localization, however, hinges on a foundational question: when a frozen language model evaluates an unedited code entity from a compact view, which structural relationships make its relevance judgment informative about a nearby repair target? Studying Gemma 4 models across 211 real-world Python issues in 86 repositories, we uncover a systematic directional relevance asymmetry: zero-temperature relevance scores on enclosing scopes and upstream callers consistently separate true structural neighbors from hard lexical distractors, whereas scores on downstream callees, peer methods, historical co-change partners, and dense node embeddings remain near chance. Zero-leakage masked-scope probes and regressions controlling for lexical similarity and snippet length confirm that this asymmetry reflects functional role (callers expose symptom entrypoints delegating to defective routines, while downstream helpers appear benign alone) rather than target leakage or surface overlap. Guided by this finding, we introduce GraphScent, a training-free search controller that propagates out-of-repository, relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over runtime Typed-AST multigraphs before resolving ties via a single listwise comparison, alongside AST Ripple, a lightweight post-edit check for missed co-edits. Likelihood calibration prevents overconfident smaller models from chasing false-positive callers while lifting exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8 to 23.4 percent at 31B within a single-GPU budget.
papers.summary: Running open-weight language models on a single consumer GPU for repository-level bug localization means replacing long multi-turn exploration histories with short, stateless code inspections, which raises the question of which structural relationships make a model's relevance judgment informative. Studying `Gemma 4` models on 211 real Python issues across 86 repositories, the authors find a directional asymmetry: relevance scores on enclosing scopes and upstream callers separate true structural neighbors from hard lexical distractors, while scores on downstream callees, peer methods, co-change partners, and dense node embeddings stay near chance. They build `GraphScent`, a training-free search controller that propagates relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over typed abstract-syntax-tree multigraphs and resolves ties with a single listwise comparison, plus `AST Ripple`, a post-edit check for missed co-edits. Likelihood calibration **lifts exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8 to 23.4 percent at 31B** within a single-GPU budget.

papers.title: Learning Latent Goal Costs for Visual World-Model Planning with an Expanding Curriculum
papers.abstract: Image-goal planning with a frozen visual world model depends on how predicted observations are scored against the goal. Mean-squared error (MSE) between embeddings from a pretrained visual encoder can provide a useful signal near a goal, yet favor states across an obstacle that are visually similar to the goal and difficult to reach. We fit a small residual adapter on top of frozen I-JEPA embeddings to improve this latent goal cost. Starting near each goal, a planner collects trajectories from progressively wider regions of initial states. The adapter learns from the order of observations along successful trajectories, with additional comparisons inferred from failed rollouts. No task-specific progress labels are used for fitting, so the procedure can be applied to other goal-reaching tasks. DotWall and PointMaze are used in this work. In paired 50-case evaluations with identical starts, goals, world models, and planner settings, success increases from 54% to 98% in DotWall and from 82% to 96% in PointMaze. On 16 unseen DotWall layout-goal cases, the adapter fitted on one fixed layout improves agreement between latent-cost ordering and shortest legal-path ordering from 71.9% to 85.8%. The results indicate that planning experience can improve a frozen visual representation's goal cost without retraining the encoder or the world model.
papers.summary: Image-goal planning with a frozen visual world model typically scores predicted observations by mean-squared error between pretrained encoder embeddings, which can favor states that look like the goal but lie across an obstacle. The authors fit a small residual adapter on frozen `I-JEPA` embeddings, training it on the order of observations along successful trajectories and on comparisons inferred from failed rollouts, with a planner collecting data from progressively wider regions of start states and no task-specific progress labels. In paired 50-case evaluations, **success rises from 54% to 98% in `DotWall`** and from 82% to 96% in `PointMaze`. On 16 unseen `DotWall` layout-goal cases, agreement between the latent cost ordering and the shortest legal-path ordering improves from 71.9% to 85.8%.

papers.title: Astrocyte Biocomputing: Astrocytic Contributions to Neural Network Computation
papers.abstract: Conductors are critical for the performance of an orchestra even though they do not emit sound. Basic research and clinical studies in the last decade are revealing that astrocytes may be the "conductors" of the "orchestra" that is the brain network: astrocytes make up approximately $50\%$ of all brain cells but do not emit electrical signals. Nevertheless, they may play critical roles in important cognitive brain functions, specifically learning, memory, and information processing. Here we consider the implications of these discoveries for brain-inspired machine learning (ML), where analogy is typically drawn between neurons and their electrical interactions. We highlight specific algorithms for two key astrocyte characteristics. The first characteristic is the ability to link to and modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously. A model based on this characteristic yields faster training and makes the network more robust to noise, providing a supervised learning algorithm that can be applied to any existing neural network. The second characteristic we focus on is that the non-electrical communication among astrocytes includes slow, rhythmic dynamics. The rhythmic sharing algorithm we developed based on this premise yields rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting. Overall, we find that astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neurocentric algorithms significantly and remediate critical weaknesses of current state-of-the-art ML models.
papers.summary: Astrocytes make up roughly half of all brain cells and emit no electrical signals, yet recent neuroscience suggests they contribute to learning, memory, and information processing, which brain-inspired machine learning has largely ignored in favor of neurons. The authors describe two algorithms derived from astrocyte properties: one models the ability to modulate thousands of synapses at once as a supervised learning rule applicable to existing networks, and one, called rhythmic sharing, is based on slow rhythmic communication among astrocytes. They report that **the first yields faster training and greater noise robustness, while rhythmic sharing gives rapid adaptation in anomaly detection and prevents catastrophic forgetting**. The authors claim these astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neuron-centric ones.

papers.title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.
papers.summary: Determining crystal structures from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) is framed as a verifiable agentic search problem, in which candidate structures are checked during inference by forward-simulating the diffraction profile and during evaluation by matching against a known reference. The authors introduce `pXRD-Bench`, 200 simulated single-phase problems covering in-distribution cases, polymorphic structures, and controlled distribution shifts, on which **agent adaptation raises structural recovery from 27% to 69%**, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. For experimental multiphase data, an evolver agent diagnoses solver failures on self-generated synthetic problems and produces persistent guidance and executable tools for the solving agents. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, this evolved package improves average profile agreement and recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Continual Learning for 2D XRD Interpretation Using Simulated and Experimental Data
papers.abstract: Autonomous experimentation systems require characterization models that can interpret heterogeneous measurements and maintain predictive performance as data accumulate. Developing such models involves addressing domain mismatch between data sources, overconfident predictions on unfamiliar inputs, and catastrophic forgetting during sequential updates. In this work, we present a proof-of-concept framework for uncertainty-aware continual interpretation of two-dimensional X-ray diffraction (XRD) data. The framework integrates established components: maximum mean discrepancy-based domain adaptation to reduce simulation-to-experiment discrepancies, a convolutional neural network with a spectral-normalized neural Gaussian process (CNN--SNGP) for predictive uncertainty estimation, and replay with knowledge distillation for sequential model updating. We evaluate the framework using simulated and previously-collected experimental data for crystal structure classification of single-phase body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed patterns. Data are organized into predefined sequential blocks to assess adaptation and retention of previously learned knowledge. Within this setting, the results show accurate classification across simulated and experimental data, improved alignment between the two domains, and reduced forgetting compared with na\"ive fine-tuning. Predictive uncertainty is also evaluated on unfamiliar and noisy inputs. The contribution is the integration and evaluation of these capabilities for sequential XRD interpretation. The framework provides a basis for future integration into autonomous experimentation systems, with experimental planning, instrument control, and closed-loop deployment remaining areas for future development.
papers.summary: Characterization models for autonomous laboratories face mismatch between simulated and experimental data, overconfidence on unfamiliar inputs, and catastrophic forgetting during sequential updates. This proof-of-concept framework for two-dimensional X-ray diffraction combines maximum mean discrepancy-based domain adaptation, a convolutional network with a spectral-normalized neural Gaussian process for uncertainty estimation, and replay with knowledge distillation for sequential updating. Evaluated on classifying single-phase body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed patterns arranged in sequential data blocks, it shows **accurate classification on both simulated and experimental data with less forgetting than naive fine-tuning**. The authors describe the contribution as the integration of established components, with closed-loop deployment left for future work.

papers.title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Target-Centric Causal Discovery in Industrial Processes
papers.abstract: Causal discovery promises to find which recorded variables drive a process target such as product quality, yield or energy use. Process data with known causes are rare, and in existing benchmarks the difficulty of identifying the causes of a target is either fixed by the recorded data or set for the whole graph. We present a synthetic benchmark for target-centric causal discovery in industrial processes. Its generator is a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon of process data, such as a control loop or a delayed effect. The graph is built around the target: without sensor error, every non-cause can be distinguished from the direct causes by conditioning on them or by time order. Each component is set independently, so the difficulty can be varied one condition at a time. We evaluate eight methods, from association measures to effect estimation, with an error analysis by the role of the selected candidate; all degrade as the difficulties combine, each in a way consistent with its assumptions.
papers.summary: Causal discovery methods aim to identify which recorded variables drive a process target such as product quality or energy use, but industrial data with known causes are rare and existing benchmarks fix difficulty in the data or set it for the whole graph. The authors present a synthetic benchmark whose generator is a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon such as a control loop or a delayed effect. The graph is built around the target so that, absent sensor error, every non-cause can be separated from the direct causes by conditioning or time order, and each difficulty can be varied independently. Across eight methods ranging from association measures to effect estimation, **all degrade as the difficulties combine, each in a way consistent with its assumptions**.

papers.title: Generative Design with Real-time Physics Explainability: Towards Product Definition in the Age of AI
papers.abstract: In this article, we explore opportunities from using generative AI in mechanical engineering. On the one hand, generative methods based on invertible neural networks have been recently proposed for the solution of inverse design problems, allowing to infer design parameters from performance labels. On the other hand, generative AI models have shown that they can act as real time capable surrogates for physics based simulations. Here we suggest that these two streams should be combined in a unified framework, where INN are used to control the design process from the customer requirements perspective and the generative simulation of the systems physics adds a layer of explainability, why the proposed design fulfils the requirements. As generative design is prone to hallucinations, we propose uncertainty quantification to fend off physically infeasible requests. Finally, validation with classical tools is a requirement for generative design process. To demonstrate the capabilities of our novel generative design paradigm, we develop two interactive environments, one for airfoil design based on simulator data and one for the combustor design space exploration based on measured data.
papers.summary: Two strands of generative AI in mechanical engineering are brought together: invertible neural networks that infer design parameters from performance requirements, and generative models that act as real-time surrogates for physics simulation. The authors propose **a unified framework in which invertible networks drive design from customer requirements while generative simulation of the physics explains why a proposed design meets them**. Uncertainty quantification is added to reject physically infeasible requests, and validation with classical tools remains a required step. Two interactive environments demonstrate the idea, one for airfoil design from simulator data and one for combustor design-space exploration from measured data.

papers.title: Contrastive local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits
papers.abstract: Machine learning in physical hardware promises to reduce training cost by colocating computation, memory and adaptation within device physics. Contrastive local learning networks (CLLNs) offer a compelling route: an electrical circuit relaxes to equilibrium in free and weakly clamped states, and each adaptive element updates from local voltage contrasts rather than backpropagated error signals. Yet whether nonlinear transistor implementations can scale beyond proof-of-concept circuits, and what design principles control that scaling, have remained unknown. Here we show that nonlinear analog circuits trained by contrastive local rules can learn larger machine-learning tasks and remain robust under hardware nonidealities. Using device-level circuit simulations, we systematically explore initialization, operating regime, loss-dependent clamping and training parameters, and scale CLLNs beyond ten thousand adaptive edges. The same local rule trains classifiers that reach the accuracy regime of conventional digital methods on Ionosphere and handwritten-digit benchmarks, and a network that autoregressively generates language over a 122-token vocabulary. These results establish the feasibility of local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits.
papers.summary: Contrastive local learning networks (CLLNs) are electrical circuits that relax to equilibrium in free and weakly clamped states, with each adaptive element updating from local voltage contrasts instead of backpropagated errors, but whether nonlinear transistor implementations scale past proof-of-concept size has been unclear. Using device-level circuit simulations, the authors systematically explore initialization, operating regime, loss-dependent clamping, and training parameters, and **scale these circuits beyond ten thousand adaptive edges**. They report that the same local rule trains classifiers reaching the accuracy regime of conventional digital methods on the `Ionosphere` and handwritten-digit benchmarks, as well as a network that autoregressively generates language over a 122-token vocabulary. The circuits are also reported to remain robust under hardware nonidealities.

papers.title: Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement
papers.abstract: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a capability in its own right -- knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one -- which we call dialectical competence. It stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside, we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest case against that position -- its antithesis -- rules on whether the case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at training or at deployment. We call this learning through Self-Disagreement: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself. The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not come from outside it.
papers.summary: Language models often abandon correct answers when challenged with counter-reasoning that is itself wrong, a failure standard single-question benchmarks do not measure. The authors treat knowing when to hold a position and when to yield as a distinct capability, which they call dialectical competence, and argue it does not follow from first-answer accuracy and cannot be obtained at inference time through self-reflection or more sampling. Their training method, `Self-Disagreement`, has the model state a position, generate the strongest case against it, rule on whether that case stands, and receive reinforcement learning rewards from the same reference check used to score answers, with no second model, reward model, or human annotation. They claim **the trained capability does not cost first-answer accuracy and holds against challengers never seen in training, including ones stronger than the model itself**.

papers.title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
papers.abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.
papers.summary: `AI-Voyager` is a public-interest system that lets residents find, question, and draft revisions to the rules their governments are writing about AI, with every answer tied to the exact passage of a source document. It converts 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal, and national governments into passages that retain page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions requiring document discovery it reaches **83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline** and 73.7% without iterative search. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led participants to check the source.

papers.title: Performance-Portable Exact Gaussian Process Regression in Python via SYCL and oneMath
papers.abstract: Modern multi-vendor GPU environments force a choice between portable code and native performance. GPRat is an open-source Python library for exact Gaussian process regression built on the HPX asynchronous many-task runtime, tiled algorithms, and CPU/CUDA BLAS backends. We contribute a UXL Foundation oneMath backend with a hybrid HPX/SYCL design, extending GPRat to AMD and Intel GPUs. The new SYCL backend comes within 3% of native CUDA on an NVIDIA A30 at the largest problem size and outperforms the GPflow and GPyTorch libraries by up to 1.75x and 2.17x on the A30 and up to 1.79x and 4.62x on an AMD Instinct MI210. On an Intel Arc B580, a consumer-class card with FP64 throughput below our CPUs, the unmodified SYCL backend trails GPRat's CPU backend. Overall, oneMath's dispatch to vendor-native BLAS lets a single SYCL codebase match CUDA on NVIDIA and outperform established Python GP frameworks on AMD, without vendor-specific code.
papers.summary: `GPRat` is an open-source Python library for exact Gaussian process regression built on the `HPX` asynchronous many-task runtime, previously limited to CPU and CUDA backends. The authors add a `oneMath` backend with a hybrid `HPX`/`SYCL` design, extending the library to AMD and Intel GPUs from a single codebase without vendor-specific code. The new backend comes **within 3% of native CUDA on an NVIDIA A30 at the largest problem size** and outperforms `GPflow` and `GPyTorch` by up to 1.75x and 2.17x on the A30 and up to 1.79x and 4.62x on an AMD Instinct MI210. On a consumer Intel Arc B580, whose double-precision throughput is below that of the test CPUs, the unmodified backend is slower than the library's CPU backend.

papers.title: CamSpokenNLI: A Pilot Resource for Cross-Variety Transfer Evaluation in Cameroon Pidgin English and Camfranglais
papers.abstract: Cameroon Pidgin English (a West African Pidgin English variety) and Camfranglais are widely used in Cameroon, yet to our knowledge, neither has a dedicated spoken Natural Language Inference (NLI) resource. We introduce CamSpokenNLI, a pilot dataset of 114 scenario-matched spoken NLI items in each variety (228 in total), recorded by one native speaker from Buea. Each item pairs premise audio and text with a hypothesis, an NLI label, and English glosses. The author assigned labels, so the dataset is an exploratory resource rather than a mature benchmark. The NLI experiments use the reference text; the audio is evaluated separately. XLM-RoBERTa baselines with five-fold item-level cross-validation reach 44.7% on Pidgin and 46.2% on Camfranglais (chance 33.3%). Still, neither is statistically distinguishable from hypothesis-only input, so hypothesis wording may account for much of the accuracy. Under disjoint-item cross-variety transfer, where a test item's counterpart is never seen in training, accuracy is 40.1% (Pidgin to Camfranglais) and 45.6% (Camfranglais to Pidgin). A counterpart-leak audit raises this to 60-64%, illustrating how counterpart leakage can overstate transfer. Zero-shot Whisper transcription of the recordings performs poorly: the best word error rates are 66.6% for Pidgin and 45.5% for Camfranglais, and with automatic language identification, Whisper Large-v3 labels 93 of 114 Pidgin recordings as Yoruba or Swahili. Together, the results suggest that such resources need disjoint-item evaluation and hypothesis-only controls, and that speech recognition must be adapted to these varieties before spoken NLI can be tested end to end.
papers.summary: Cameroon Pidgin English and Camfranglais are widely spoken in Cameroon but have lacked a spoken Natural Language Inference (NLI) resource. `CamSpokenNLI` is a pilot dataset of 114 scenario-matched items in each variety, recorded by one native speaker and labelled by the author, pairing premise audio and text with a hypothesis, a label, and English glosses. `XLM-RoBERTa` baselines reach 44.7% and 46.2% accuracy against 33.3% chance but are not statistically distinguishable from hypothesis-only input, and allowing counterpart items to leak into training inflates cross-variety transfer from 40-46% to 60-64%. Zero-shot `Whisper` transcription performs poorly, with best word error rates of 66.6% for Pidgin and 45.5% for Camfranglais, and **`Whisper Large-v3` labels 93 of 114 Pidgin recordings as Yoruba or Swahili**.

papers.title: Beyond a Single Sign: BiTE for Branch-Preserving Binary Threshold Expansion
papers.abstract: Binary neural networks (BNNs) reduce model storage and replace many arithmetic operations with efficient bitwise computations, but the single-sign activation limits their representational capacity. Each preactivation direction is compared with one threshold and reduced to one of two values, discarding variation within each sign region. We propose \textbf{BiTE} (Branch-Preserving Binary Threshold Expansion), which evaluates each feature direction against $K$ ordered thresholds and retains the resulting binary responses as separate inputs to the following learned operator. BiTE can distinguish up to $K+1$ ordered activation states while allowing the following operator to learn a separate transformation for each threshold response. It also enables a controllable trade-off between the number of independently constructed feature directions and the number of ordered responses extracted from each direction. On BinaryViT, BiTE improves mean final-epoch Top-1 accuracy from $74.60\pm0.30\%$ to $75.83\pm0.15\%$ on CIFAR-10 and from $42.80\pm0.46\%$ to $44.07\pm0.32\%$ on CIFAR-100, with nearly unchanged trainable parameter counts. A matched uniform-collapse control reaches $75.33\pm0.15\%$ on CIFAR-10, supporting the value of retaining the threshold responses separately relative to the evaluated scalar collapse. Binary VGG-16 experiments further show a favorable observed parameter--accuracy trade-off, including a configuration that achieves $0.64$ percentage points higher mean accuracy with $21.8\%$ fewer parameters than conventional width scaling. Overall, these results support branch-preserving threshold expansion as an effective way to improve binary representations and the observed parameter--accuracy trade-off.
papers.summary: Binary neural networks cut storage and replace arithmetic with bitwise operations, but comparing each preactivation to a single threshold discards variation within each sign region. `BiTE` (Branch-Preserving Binary Threshold Expansion) evaluates each feature direction against K ordered thresholds and passes the resulting binary responses as separate inputs to the next learned operator, distinguishing up to K+1 activation states. On `BinaryViT` it **improves mean top-1 accuracy from 74.60% to 75.83% on `CIFAR-10`** and from 42.80% to 44.07% on `CIFAR-100` with nearly unchanged parameter counts, while a control that collapses the responses into one scalar reaches 75.33%. A binary `VGG-16` configuration achieves 0.64 points higher mean accuracy with 21.8% fewer parameters than conventional width scaling.

papers.title: Fair and Efficient Distributed EV Charging Coordination Using Threshold Cryptography and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Distributed coordination of electric vehicle (EV) charging with the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) keeps EV constraints private but assumes that every participant follows the algorithm. This assumption fails in practice, where a biased operator or a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacker can send inconsistent signals to different EVs, and compromised EVs can deviate from their prescribed updates. We first prove that attacks by such arbitrarily malicious, i.e., Byzantine, participants do not prevent convergence and therefore remain undetected, and derive the most damaging attack in closed form. We then propose a framework that combines a threshold-signed broadcast with upload recomputation, which detects every deviation without false alarms at linear instead of quadratic communication cost. To keep the optimization running, each affected EV recovers locally with a certified, fleet-aware machine learning price forecast, and we prove that the optimization remains convergent with a recovery cost bounded by the shape of the forecast error. Simulation results with real-world load, price, and charging data show that a biased operator raises the annual cost of disadvantaged EVs by 132.7% and lowers that of advantaged EVs by 49.3% without changing the aggregate load, whereas the defense limits all cost changes to 2.6%. An external MITM attacker raises the cost of its victims by 57.6%, the peak load by 5.8%, and the grid cost by 15.8%, whereas the defense keeps them within 1.1%, 0.2%, and 0.3% of benign operation. With up to 70% of the EVs attacked, the recovery converges in at least 97.8% of the runs.
papers.summary: Distributed electric vehicle charging coordination with the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) keeps vehicle constraints private but assumes all participants follow the algorithm, which fails when a biased operator, a man-in-the-middle attacker, or compromised vehicles send inconsistent or deviating updates. The authors prove that such Byzantine attacks do not prevent convergence and so go undetected, derive the most damaging attack in closed form, and propose a defense combining a threshold-signed broadcast with upload recomputation that detects every deviation without false alarms at linear communication cost. Affected vehicles recover locally using a certified machine learning price forecast, with convergence shown to be preserved. In simulations on real load, price, and charging data, **a biased operator raises the annual cost of disadvantaged vehicles by 132.7% without changing aggregate load, whereas the defense limits all cost changes to 2.6%**.

papers.title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
papers.abstract:
A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs.
  In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better.
  These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. $I(W;R)$ measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.
papers.summary: A representation retaining one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly while another retaining 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy, because what matters is which distinctions are preserved. The authors enumerate every admissible representation and binary action rule in a uniform four-state world, comparing constructions across three tasks, their mixtures, and four hypothetical cost tariffs. The exhaustive census shows cases where the less informative representation has the higher payoff, cases where the more informative one does, and pairs with different information but equal payoff, while **a representation that preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones can never lower the best zero-cost payoff**. The authors present the atlas as a reproducible worked model illustrating the established gap between information quantity and decision value, not as a new general law.

papers.title: Rethinking Visual Reasoning in Text-to-Image Reward Modeling
papers.abstract: Reward models are a core component of modern text-to-image systems, serving as the objective for inference-time selection and RL-based post-training. A key prerequisite is visual understanding: to judge prompt adherence and ground aesthetic preferences, a reward model must bind attributes, resolve relations, and count reliably. We find that widely-used reward models perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning evaluations. Even when starting from strong vision-language backbones, preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities, and continual-learning baselines fail to mitigate a steep tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy. We propose a data-centric intervention that injects visual reasoning supervision into preference learning by flipping the pairing axis. To complement conventional human preference data (paired images under a shared prompt), we convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs that share the same image but differ in prompt, and train on the mixture. This yields a Pareto improvement in both visual understanding and preference prediction. Across inference-time best-of-n selection and RL post-training, the resulting reward model improves text-to-image generation on challenging compositional prompts (GenEval) by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively, outperforming HPSv3 which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.

papers.title: Small Open-Weight Language Models for Crowd Decision-Making: Capabilities and Limits of Output-Level Fusion and Linguistic Aggregation
papers.abstract: Small open-weight language models can run crowd decision-making (CDM) on an institution's own infrastructure, which keeps the checkpoint, the inference settings and the opinions under its control. Their judgements vary across repeated queries; whether repeating and aggregating them, often through the 2-tuple linguistic representation, settles the decision rather than the labels is untested. Five open-weight models of 8-36B total parameters on one consumer GPU and a hosted reference classify 474 TripAdvisor reviews of four London restaurants ten times each; three open-weight models repeat the protocol on 600 reviews of twelve Madrid restaurants. Continuous evaluations preserve resolution: snapping each review leaves 5 distinct values against 21-65, and snapping at every level at most two collective values. Sensitivity to the participants persists once run-to-run variability is reduced: in London, redrawing the reviewers keeps the winner on 47-81% of replicas against 86-100% for redrawing the runs. With simultaneous intervals over every pair of alternatives under crowd resampling, no system on either corpus names a single winner: in London every system keeps all four restaurants as candidates, and in Madrid the candidate sets hold five to eight of the twelve. Extra runs and output-level fusion stabilize the winner but do not remove that sensitivity, and the fusion does not beat its best member. The three larger open-weight models name the hosted reference's London winner and at least match its per-review correlation with the reviewers' stars, so small open-weight models can support local CDM, reported as candidate sets with margins rather than forced rankings.

papers.title: Tractable Importance Sampling for Monte Carlo Privacy Accounting
papers.abstract: Evaluating tight Differential Privacy (DP) parameters for DP matrix factorization with privacy amplification by sampling requires analyzing high-dimensional, correlated Gaussian mixtures. Because integrating these mixture distributions to find the exact privacy failure probability ($\delta$) is analytically intractable, these mechanisms are typically analyzed using Monte Carlo accounting. However, standard sampling suffers from prohibitive variance when estimating small $\delta$ associated with strict privacy guarantees, which in turn requires a large sample complexity, making Monte Carlo accounting inefficient. We demonstrate that Monte Carlo accounting can be made much more efficient via importance sampling. We give a shifted importance sampling proposal distribution parameterized by a stretch factor $\alpha > 1$. We prove a closed-form bound $B(\alpha) < 1$ on the support of the importance-weighted estimator that holds identically for both directions of the hockey-stick divergence, show that $B$ is log-convex so that the optimal $\alpha$ is a one-dimensional root-finding problem, and show that the resulting estimator seamlessly plugs into the KL-Hoeffding verification protocol used by past work, with a sample complexity reduced by exactly a factor of $1/B(\alpha^*)$.

papers.title: X-Nav Technical Report: Real-World Long-Horizon Indoor-to-Outdoor Navigation on a Humanoid Robot
papers.abstract: Long-horizon navigation from indoors to outdoors remains an open problem for humanoid robots: one instruction covers rooms, doors and roads, and the camera moves with the gait. Worken, AGIBOT's measure of productive robot work, depends on robots that reach their workplaces autonomously. We present X-Nav, to our knowledge the first system to take a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed long-horizon mission from indoors to outdoors. X-Nav covers a pipeline from data to deployment. Its data engine collects navigation data in open-source scenes, in digital twins of deployment sites and on real robots. Its navigation model, MELIOR, takes only RGB images from the robot's built-in camera and comes in two versions: MELIOR-A predicts actions, and MELIOR-N predicts a navigation goal. Its agentic workflow, X-Navarch, turns a brief human instruction into sub-tasks and deploys MELIOR on the robot with explicit target navigation and obstacle avoidance. On the Lingxi X2, X-Nav completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building; LiDAR and odometry are used for target approach and low-level control. The mission is completed with both versions of MELIOR: the robot follows a change of destination and walks through a door from the lobby to the road, and with X-Navarch it also passes static and dynamic obstacles on the route. During deployment, MELIOR is adapted with data collected in a digital twin of the site; the adaptation raises its closed-loop success rate in the twin, and the adapted model is then deployed on the robot at the real site. In addition, MELIOR achieves competitive results on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.

papers.title: LightTAR: Light and Fast Target-Aware Representations for Multimodal Tabular Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal tabular learning involves classification and regression on tables combining structured numerical and categorical features with unstructured text and images. These unstructured fields are commonly represented by pretrained encoder embeddings reduced with principal component analysis (PCA). This reduction prioritizes input variance but may overlook information relevant to predicting the target. We introduce LightTAR, a simple, inexpensive method that adapts dimensionality reduction to the prediction task. LightTAR augments the standard PCA representation with a few target-aware features extracted jointly from the final and an intermediate encoder layer using regularized partial least squares (PLS). We evaluate LightTAR with 21 tabular models, including tree ensembles, neural networks, and tabular foundation models. LightTAR improves average predictive performance for all models and, averaged across models, improves prediction on almost every MulTaBench dataset. These gains come with a small increase in total runtime relative to PCA representations. LightTAR integrates directly into existing encoding pipelines, improving tabular learners' predictive performance without modifying the encoder or the learner.

papers.title: Offline KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Transitions
papers.abstract: KL-regularized reinforcement learning is the objective behind RL fine-tuning of language models, and its data are often collected by the reference policy itself. However, beyond bandits and deterministic transitions, little is known about how much offline data it needs. In this work, we study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown stochastic transitions, $K$ state-action pairs and effective horizon $H$. For data that cover the regularized optimum with concentrability $C\geq 4$, every estimator needs $\Omega(KCH^3/(\epsilon\max\{\epsilon,\beta\}))$ samples on some instances when $\epsilon$ is small, where $\beta$ is the temperature. Under a fixed design, pessimistic soft value iteration with a variance-aware penalty attains this rate with high probability, up to logarithmic factors, when $\beta\geq 1.4H$. When the data come from the reference policy itself, we show that it covers the optimum up to a power law whose exponent grows as $H/\beta$; in the same temperature range, this power law alone gives the estimator a sample complexity polynomial in $1/\epsilon$, with no coverage assumption. For $\beta\geq H$ the power can also increase the sample size needed by a factor polynomial in $1/\epsilon$. Finally, the plug-in estimator, which is minimax optimal with a generative model, can fail on reference data at small temperatures when many actions are rarely seen, while the pessimistic estimator does not.

papers.title: Choosing Quantized Code LLMs by File Size and Energy per Solved Task
papers.abstract: A developer running a code assistant on a laptop downloads one model file, and local inference moves the energy of every request onto that machine. A common rule says a larger model at lower precision tends to beat a smaller one at higher precision. We ran 24 GGUF files of Qwen2.5-Coder at four sizes on a fanless MacBook Air M2 and priced each in energy per solved task on 542 EvalPlus tasks. The result is a selection guide indexed by Ollama's listed file size, with an evidence label on each pick. At 1 and 2 GB it picks the q4_K_M files of the 1.5B and 3B models, both on the correctness and energy frontier under every accounting. At 3 GB as listed, the larger-model rule picks 7B-q2_K, the only measured 7B file that fits, and there it does not pay. That file brings no significant gain in solves over the 2 GB pick, 3B-q4_K_M, and the 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deficit to 2.4 points. Yet 7B-q2_K needs 2.03 times the energy per solved task on CPU, GPU and memory rails, or 1.66 to 1.81 times on whole-system power. On HumanEval+, five alternating session pairs give a ratio of 1.925 against 1.956 in the main grid. At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K buys a significant gain over the 2 GB pick at a higher energy price. From 1.5B up, q4_K_M trails the highest precision measured at its size by less than 3 points (90% CI). We release per-task results, power logs and the analysis script.

papers.title: Neural Simulation-Based Inference for Computational Cognitive Models: A Tutorial
papers.abstract: Computational cognitive modeling is an increasingly essential methodology to elucidate the mechanisms underlying human and animal cognition. By fitting models to empirical data, researchers can perform parameter estimation, model comparison, and model-based neural analyses to assess competing theories, quantify individual differences, and investigate neural representations. Typically, fitting these models relies on likelihood-dependent methods (e.g., Maximum likelihood estimation or hierarchical Bayesian methods). However, for many reasonable cognitive models, computing the likelihood is computationally intractable, in which case these methods become inadequate. This substantially limits the range of theories that researchers can investigate.
