Simulation-based inference with neural networks (neural SBI) has emerged as a powerful toolkit to overcome this hurdle. By training deep neural networks on datasets generated through model simulations, neural SBI learns the relation between observable data and cognitive models. This approach enables all the applications of standard modeling while bypassing the likelihood computation, without constraints on empirical data size. Despite its successful adoption across diverse scientific fields, neural SBI remains underutilized in cognitive modeling, partly due to a lack of accessible, domain-tailored guidance. This tutorial addresses this gap by providing a clear workflow for applying neural SBI to cognitive models. We also provide practical use cases and recommendations for reducing the computational and simulation burden, facilitating efficient implementation in real-world research settings. By lowering the technical barriers to neural SBI, this tutorial aims to empower cognitive scientists to investigate richer theory spaces and ultimately propel scientific discovery.

papers.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
papers.abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.
papers.highlight_summary:
Multi-agent LLM systems are usually benchmarked against a single greedy pass, which mixes any benefit of inter-agent communication with the known gains from simply drawing more samples or spending more inference compute. This synthesis re-reads nine prior evaluations (516 multi-agent configurations) through a resource-accounting protocol called `PACE` and finds that once the baseline is given comparable samples or budget, coordination mostly fails to pay for itself.

- The method sorts every comparison onto a four-rung baseline ladder (greedy single pass, sample-matched, budget-matched, Pareto sweep) and records a six-dimension resource vector (thinking tokens, total tokens, cost, latency, sample count, tooling), backed by stylized propositions showing that communication cannot add information when all agents see the same evidence.
- Against sample- or budget-matched baselines, multi-agent systems average **−0.042** in accuracy (about 4 points) and equal or trail the baseline in **74%** of 474 contrasts, with an exploratory multilevel model giving a pooled log-odds of −0.195 (95% CI −0.320 to −0.070).
- Baseline strength explains much of the apparent benefit: in the five studies reporting both baselines, swapping greedy decoding for a sampled baseline shifts the difference by **−0.038** on average, and in one worked case five-agent debate looks **+0.045** better than greedy but **−0.031** worse than five-sample majority voting.
- The one positive exception is a Pareto comparison on `MMLU-Pro`, where debate and mixture-of-agents beat self-consistency by **+1.3** and **+2.7** points at comparable compute, and the authors argue that real gains require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across different models.
- The evidence base is not a systematic literature search, one study supplies 180 of the 516 configurations, resource parity was not checked contrast by contrast, and cost ratios come from a single study (a median of **8.1×** versus greedy chain-of-thought), so the authors treat the pooled estimates as exploratory.

papers.title: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters
papers.abstract: Behavioral clusters learned over user or item interactions drift as behavior evolves: some fragment into sub-behaviors, some converge, some disappear, and new patterns emerge. Two paradigms dominate the maintenance of evolving clusterings. Threshold triggers fire a pre-specified action when a hardcoded statistic crosses a cutoff; refit-and-track (MONIC-style) re-clusters every window and infers transitions from how the new clusters align with the previous window's. Both hardwire the decision into a threshold or a re-clustering rule. We study an alternative in which a large language model (LLM) makes the lifecycle decision in place. Given a threshold-free, whole-population view of the current cluster set (statistical health, labels, member texts, residual mass), the LLM decides per cluster whether and how to act (split, merge, retire, create, or no-action) without re-clustering. Because the useful signal channel depends on how informative the labels are, we fix a richness-conditioned policy in advance: statistics when label distinctiveness is low, fused statistics+semantics when it is high. On three public datasets spanning label richness (YooChoose 0.17, MOOC 0.50, News-Category 0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three, with far fewer interventions and stronger restraint than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC steelman (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003, bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero). The gain is concentrated more in precision than recall. The useful modality shifts from statistics to semantics/fusion as richness rises. Semantics hurt on YooChoose, fusion is roughly neutral on MOOC, and the semantic channel is required on News. One base prompt template and one fixed policy serve all three datasets, whereas the tuned baseline collapses when moved between them. We treat this shift as a practitioner diagnostic observed on three datasets, not a validated law.

papers.title: Safety Side Effects of Preventative Persona Steering: An Empirical Audit
papers.abstract: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.

papers.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
papers.abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.

papers.title: Finite speed Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac processes and their applications in generative modeling
papers.abstract: We study the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-Kac (OU-K) process, where instead of a Brownian motion, a finite-speed Kac process defines the driving process. The OU-K process can be analyzed through a rescaled, time-inhomogeneous Kac process, characterized by a switching rate from the Kac part, and a convergence rate from the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) part. The law of this inhomogeneous Kac process describes the solution of a wave equation, the Euler-Poisson-Darboux (EPD) equation. For Kac switching rates being multiples of the OU convergence rate, we can explicitly derive this EPD solution via the sum of (the derivative of) two Legendre polynomials, restricted between two Dirac points representing the wave fronts. Using the framework of piecewise-deterministic Markov processes (PDMP), we describe the conditional velocity fields of the OU-K process via our polynomial-law-formula. This allows us to apply the OU-K process in a generative flow model. Since the OU-K velocity fields prove to be bounded by the finite Kac speed, the usual time truncations of diffusion models become unnecessary. We demonstrate advantages over diffusion and flow matching models in terms of generation sharpness on singular data sets, while achieving competitive results on CIFAR-10 image generation.

papers.title: Joint World Action Models through Differentiable Trajectory Optimization
papers.abstract: Joint world action models (WAMs) generate future actions and states together, modeling world-action trajectories rather than actions alone. However, trajectory imitation does not ensure that these trajectories are task-effective or consistent with dynamics. We present \textbf{world action trajectory optimization (WATO)}, which optimizes generated actions and future states jointly for control. WATO uses both as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization problem and differentiates the task loss through the optimized trajectory to train the generator. This makes generated trajectories task-aware and dynamics-consistent while using trajectory optimization only during training. At deployment, WATO directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model, without iterative trajectory optimization. Across $7$ visual control environments, WATO improves average success from $79.9\%$ for the imitation joint WAM to $91.7\%$, outperforming strong model-based, goal-conditioned RL, and generative control baselines. Compared with cross-entropy method (CEM), WATO is on average $11.5\times$ faster and uses $600.5\times$ fewer world model evaluations at deployment.

papers.title: Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-View 3D Transformers via Regime-Aware Attention Approximation
papers.abstract: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.

papers.title: A mesh-free deep energy method for phase-field modeling of thermally driven brittle fracture
papers.abstract: Phase-field simulation of thermally driven fracture requires resolving localized crack bands whose paths are unknown in advance and thermal boundary layers whose thickness evolves during the transient. Neural energy-based computations of thermal fracture have so far started from defects placed in advance. This paper proposes a mesh-free deep energy method based on multiresolution neural representations that predicts spontaneous crack nucleation, crack spacing, and selective crack propagation and arrest under transient thermal loading. Two networks, each with its own multiresolution encoding, represent the displacement and phase fields and the transient temperature, and the mechanical energy and the incremental functional of the backward Euler heat equation are estimated on integration points redrawn at every iteration. Restricting irreversibility to the crack set, carrying the optimizer state across load steps and decaying the learning rates within each step help prevent spurious damage accumulation. On two notched plates the initiation peak loads agree closely with an independent finite element reference. On a quenched glass strip under an analytical temperature field the crack path changes from straight to oscillatory and then to branched, with an oscillation threshold close to the linear stability prediction. Under a prescribed boundary temperature a quenched ceramic slab forms a crack array of the type observed in experiment, with a spacing close to that of a published benchmark. On the slab and a quenched annulus the arrays are denser than those of a finite element computation on the same material field. No crack paths, nucleation sites or crack-adapted meshes are prescribed.

papers.title: Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search for Real Agent Regressions
papers.abstract: Generating an evaluation suite from an agent's specification is diversity-driven search: a generator fills a descriptor space (requirements $\times$ personas $\times$ scenario kinds), and the suite it emits is an archive, then scored like a benchmark by its mean pass rate, which throws away the search's product. We inject 7 controlled defects into a $\tau^2$-bench agent across two domains. Coverage yields a ceiling: if a defect's traced footprint holds $b$ scenarios that pass at baseline, it can itself contribute at most $b/N$ to a suite of $N$. For 4 of 5 traceable defects that ceiling lies at or below the detection threshold $\theta = 0.10$, so no within-footprint effect can move the suite past it; in both domains the tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario it can (exactly its ceiling) while the suite-level pass rate moves the other way. Defects split into two regimes: trace-aligned ones, where per-cell scoring recovers the tool-removal defect in full and reveals a second as a significant improvement, and trace-orthogonal ones, whose footprint is behavioural: forced escalation is detected in retail at a traced coverage of exactly zero. Diversity along the generator's own axes helps only where it aligns: at fixed suite size a happy-path-only suite detects nothing, while a kind-diverse one detects the orchestration defect in 5 of 20 draws. Evaluation archives should be scored per cell and should publish coverage as a first-class property.

papers.title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say
papers.abstract: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.

papers.title: CoTTAGE: An Explainable Judge for Text-to-Audio Generation
papers.abstract: Rapid progress in text-to-audio (TTA) generation demands reliable and explainable automatic evaluation. However, existing metrics fail to simultaneously deliver high correlation with human judgments and meaningful, audio-grounded explanations, forcing reliance on labor-intensive human evaluation that bottlenecks model development iteration. To address this, we propose CoTTAGE, a reasoning-based evaluator for text relevance (REL) and audio quality (OVL). Following a reason-then-predict paradigm, CoTTAGE first generates an audio-grounded rationale to diagnose errors before predicting scores. Supported by over 10K newly collected human OVL annotations, CoTTAGE is first trained via supervised fine-tuning and then refined with reinforcement learning using a Thurstone-based preference objective that converts sampled score distributions into pairwise preference probabilities and rewards agreement with rankings derived from human judgments. Across six benchmarks spanning REL and OVL, CoTTAGE achieves state-of-the-art correlation with human judgments while producing human-preferred explanations to accelerate TTA development.

papers.title: Binarization as an Attack Surface in Weightless Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) are lightweight classifiers that binarize their inputs and learn by storing binary patterns in lookup memories, which makes them attractive for resource-constrained tasks such as intrusion detection. Because a small perturbation that crosses no binarization threshold leaves the binary input unchanged, WNNs may appear naturally robust to adversarial examples; a perturbation that does cross a threshold, however, can still change the prediction. We study this tension in WiSARD, the canonical RAM-based WNN, and in two variants that replace its memories with Bloom filters, Bloom WiSARD and BTHOWeN. A continuous perturbation reaches these classifiers only by crossing an encoding threshold, changing at least one binary tuple, and redirecting a memory query; we formalize this mechanism with a threshold-crossing bound and a response-margin certificate for standard Boolean WiSARD. Controlled MNIST experiments compare linear and data-driven thermometer encodings under model-agnostic sensitivity probes, a score-based Simulated Annealing attack, and surrogate-transfer attacks. Changing only the encoding while keeping each model otherwise fixed shows that encoding granularity can trade a small clean-accuracy loss for a large decrease in attack success. On the Bot-IoT, CICIDS, and UNSW-NB15 intrusion-detection datasets, adversarial perturbations lead WNN detectors to classify many attacks as normal traffic and to raise false alarms, even when their aggregate accuracy remains high.

papers.title: Classifier-Guided Latent Diffusion for Small-Molecule Generation
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a promising class of generative models for molecular design because of their ability to learn complex chemical distributions and support conditional or guided generation. In this work, we investigate a latent diffusion pipeline for property-guided small-molecule generation. The proposed framework represents canonicalized SMILES strings using a frozen ChemBERTa encoder, trains a Transformer-based decoder to reconstruct SELFIES strings from molecular latent embeddings, and learns an unconditional denoising diffusion model in the ChemBERTa latent space. To enable property-directed generation, a differentiable latent property predictor is used to guide the diffusion sampling process. Generated SELFIES strings are converted to SMILES, validated using RDKit, and evaluated using molecular validity, uniqueness, novelty, and predicted property scores. We study guidance toward two drug-relevant binary endpoints: blood--brain barrier permeability and inhibition of human $\beta$-secretase 1. The results suggest that latent diffusion over pretrained molecular embeddings can generate chemically valid and novel molecules while enabling controllable steering toward desired molecular properties.
papers.summary: Property-guided small-molecule design is framed as a latent diffusion problem: canonicalized SMILES strings are encoded by a frozen `ChemBERTa` model, a Transformer decoder is trained to reconstruct SELFIES strings from those latents, and an unconditional denoising diffusion model is learned in the embedding space. A differentiable latent property predictor then steers sampling toward chosen endpoints, with outputs converted back to SMILES and checked with `RDKit` for validity, uniqueness, and novelty. Guidance is tested on two drug-relevant binary endpoints, blood-brain barrier permeability and inhibition of human beta-secretase 1, and the reported result is that **latent diffusion over pretrained molecular embeddings yields chemically valid, novel molecules while remaining steerable toward target properties**.

papers.title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost
papers.abstract: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $\alpha = V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $\alpha$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $\alpha$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $\alpha$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $\alpha$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.
papers.summary: Imitation-learned manipulation policies trained on noisy object positions partially ignore the noisy reading, and this work quantifies how much. Because demonstrators move toward the object, the robot's own proprioceptive state acts as an anchor, and the policy weights the sensor reading by alpha = V/(V + s squared), where s squared is reading noise and V the anchor's error variance; V is much smaller than a linear model of demonstrations suggests, explaining why classical errors-in-variables regression overestimates alpha. Measured once, V **predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two `robomimic` tasks with mean absolute error 0.025 versus 0.37 for classical errors-in-variables regression**. The discount does not transfer to deployment: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent offset exceeded alpha in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, and lower alpha correlated with lower success, steeply for diffusion policies; all experiments are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.

papers.title: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. In practice, practitioners use runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters to decide when a run should be stopped, upgraded, or assisted. However, these heuristics may stop runs that would otherwise succeed or allow failing runs to continue. To address this limitation, we introduce LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical learning framework that derives its learning objective from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention. In particular, LeBet learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening when the evidence reaches a prescribed threshold. Under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, we derive finite-sample guarantees for false-positive control (validity) and detection power conditional on the training data, using the same trajectories for learning and calibration without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. To address the intractable combinatorial optimization problem in our learning formulation, we use stochastic local search that leverages the monitor's Boolean structure to propose rule edits aimed at improving empirical separation. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves $34.46\%$ of input-plus-output tokens and increases output precision from $18.33\%$ to $21.59\%$. The empirical false-positive rate is $13.64\%$. Our results show how to formalize the learning problem over interpretable rule sets with statistical conditions and establish training-conditional guarantees for reliable intervention based on partial histories.
papers.summary: Runtime monitors for long-running autonomous agents are usually heuristics such as turn limits and keyword filters, which can halt runs that would have succeeded or let doomed runs continue. `LeBet` (Learn then Bet) instead learns an interpretable OR-of-AND rule monitor and accumulates evidence with a fixed betting statistic, intervening once evidence crosses a threshold, with finite-sample false-positive and detection-power guarantees derived under within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability rather than independent and identically distributed trajectories. The combinatorial rule-learning problem is attacked with stochastic local search over Boolean rule edits. On `SWE-bench Lite` with `Ministral 3 8B`, the learned monitor **saves 34.46% of input-plus-output tokens while raising output precision from 18.33% to 21.59%**, at an empirical false-positive rate of 13.64%.

papers.title: Provable Cross-Modal Transfer of Hierarchical Concept Structure in CLIP Embeddings
papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP are trained to align images and text, not to represent taxonomies. Yet empirical studies show that CLIP embeddings exhibit hierarchical structure aligned with the hierarchy of semantic concepts. A theoretical characterization of why such hierarchy emerges from a non-hierarchical objective remains open. In this paper, we formalize this phenomenon as Hierarchical Angular Separation (HAS), a geometric property whereby each non-leaf concept embedding is more similar to its descendants than to off-branch concepts. Empirically, we show that HAS holds approximately in raw images and randomly initialized CLIP image embeddings, while in text embeddings it holds approximately only after contrastive learning. To theoretically explain this asymmetry, we analyze an unconstrained features model in which the image embeddings are fixed and only the text embeddings are trained. At the global minimizer, the text-side HAS violation percentage at each node is at most the image-side HAS violation and near-violation percentage. The key mechanism is the hierarchical co-occurrence structure of image-text pairs, which biases text embeddings toward root-centered image prototypes. For a linear contrastive loss, we derive a closed-form solution that makes this mechanism explicit. We extend the analysis to the InfoNCE loss and establish analogous guarantees under sufficient regularization. Synthetic experiments validate the theory and show that HAS is transferred even beyond the regimes covered by our analysis.
papers.summary: Contrastive vision-language models are trained only to align images with text, yet their embeddings show taxonomy-like structure, and this work gives a theoretical account of why. The phenomenon is formalized as Hierarchical Angular Separation (HAS), where each non-leaf concept embedding is closer to its descendants than to off-branch concepts; empirically HAS holds approximately in raw images and even randomly initialized `CLIP` image embeddings, but on the text side only after contrastive training. Analyzing an unconstrained features model with fixed image embeddings and trainable text embeddings, the authors show that at the global minimizer **the text-side HAS violation rate at each node is bounded by the image-side violation and near-violation rate**, with hierarchical co-occurrence of image-text pairs biasing text embeddings toward root-centered image prototypes. Closed-form results are given for a linear contrastive loss and extended to `InfoNCE` under sufficient regularization, with synthetic experiments showing transfer even outside the analyzed regime.

papers.title: Pattern-Based Matrix Analysis Under Permutations
papers.abstract: Low-rank approximation captures one important notion of matrix simplicity: a matrix is simple if it is well described by a low-dimensional linear model. This paper studies a complementary notion. We consider matrices that become structurally simple only after permuting rows and columns, so that their mass concentrates in a prescribed geometric pattern such as a band, block-diagonal, arrowhead, or related form. We introduce a pattern distance that measures how close a matrix is to a given pattern after optimal reordering, giving a common framework for structural problems such as latent ordering, community detection, and bandwidth minimization. The problem is NP-hard in general; we derive an alternating algorithm based on Linear Assignment subproblems. We further introduce a pattern-plus-low-rank decomposition that combines permutation-structured fitting with a low-rank residual, whose permutation step is pattern fitting on the residual; its gains across pattern families persist at a matched parameter budget and are substantially reduced under a density-matched random-mask control. We evaluate the framework on synthetic recovery tasks, real correlation and graph adjacency matrices, and transformer attention heads, showing that a single universal algorithm recovers qualitatively different forms of matrix structure.
papers.summary: Low-rank approximation captures one notion of matrix simplicity; this work studies a complementary one, where a matrix becomes structurally simple only after reordering rows and columns so its mass concentrates in a prescribed geometric pattern such as a band, block-diagonal, or arrowhead form. A pattern distance measures closeness to a target pattern under optimal reordering, unifying latent ordering, community detection, and bandwidth minimization; the problem is NP-hard, so an alternating algorithm built on linear assignment subproblems is proposed, along with a pattern-plus-low-rank decomposition whose permutation step fits the pattern to the residual. Across synthetic recovery tasks, real correlation and graph adjacency matrices, and transformer attention heads, **a single universal algorithm recovers qualitatively different forms of matrix structure**, with gains persisting at a matched parameter budget and shrinking substantially under a density-matched random-mask control.

papers.title: Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified? A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly combine sensed time series with external text such as expert reports and news, yet how reliably models use text that agrees or conflicts with the sensed history remains unclear. We introduce the first real-world diagnostic benchmark organized by text-history relationship: 1,762 text-window pairs across sensor telemetry (Weather), web-service traffic (Wikipedia), and market data streams (Finance), each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified by whether the text's direction agrees with the historical trend, opposes it, or is not stated. Across ten pretrained models evaluated zero-shot, we investigate text selection and combination under text-history relationships (RQ1) and error diagnosis and horizon-scaled revision control (RQ2). For RQ1, we compare two types of text on paired Weather windows: one directly forecasts temperature changes, while the other describes related weather conditions, such as winds and fronts. Under Aligned, the first type yields the lowest error for most models. Under Conflicting, it increases most models' error above the no-text baseline; we therefore add only its stated magnitude and timing to the second type. Compared with either type alone, this combination lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. For RQ2, an error decomposition attributes the error increase to oversized revisions, and a training-free rule that limits them outperforms forecasts both with and without text for the four models with this trade-off, lowering MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%. Our dataset is available at https://github.com/Shelton1202/ACU-Bench.
papers.summary: Forecasting systems for Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) increasingly mix sensed time series with external text, but it is unclear how models behave when the text agrees with or contradicts the history. `ACU-Bench` provides 1,762 text-window pairs over weather telemetry, Wikipedia web traffic, and financial data, each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified according to whether the text's stated direction matches the historical trend. Evaluating ten pretrained models zero-shot, directly predictive text gives the lowest error when Aligned but **pushes most models above the no-text baseline when Conflicting**; feeding only its stated magnitude and timing alongside descriptive context lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. An error decomposition attributes the degradation to oversized forecast revisions, and a training-free rule capping revision size cuts MASE by 4.49% to 21.98% and lifts DA by 2.99% to 9.71% for the four affected models.

papers.title: OCTAVE: A Capability-Resolved Benchmark for End-to-End HTML5 Game Generation
papers.abstract: Complete game generation requires agents to coordinate rules, interactions, states, and presentation over a long development process. A single aggregate score obscures which capabilities are implemented and which requirements remain unmet. We present OCTAVE, a benchmark for complete HTML5 game generation organized around eight Capability Dimensions, with 180 tasks and 1,800 Evaluation Requirements drawn from real player requests, commercial-mechanics reconstruction, and human expert design. It covers PC Web, Mobile Web, 2D, and 3D. Requirements distinguish Completeness, assessing publicly specified core implementation, from Richness, assessing hidden, deeper system relationships. Static source-code judgments provide requirement-level diagnosis across capabilities and task conditions. Evaluation of 11 model-harness combinations yields 33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness; 19.9% of generation records are static gate failures or missing artifacts. Excluding same-model self-evaluation, even the best combination remains below 50% on both public and hidden requirements. Richness is not harder than Completeness under every task condition. Systems perform relatively better on Core Rules and Numerical Design, while AI/NPC and Feedback and Game Feel show more prominent gaps. Requirement difficulty offers coarse stratification but is only weakly negatively correlated with pass rates. A limited human cross-check finds that requirements judged satisfied by humans but failed by the automated evaluator are the main direction of disagreement. OCTAVE extends evaluation beyond aggregate scores to diagnosis localized by requirement, capability, and task condition.
papers.summary: Generating a complete game requires coordinating rules, interactions, state, and presentation over a long build, and a single aggregate score hides which capabilities actually landed. `OCTAVE` organizes end-to-end HTML5 game generation into eight capability dimensions with 180 tasks and 1,800 evaluation requirements drawn from real player requests, reconstructions of commercial mechanics, and expert design, spanning PC web, mobile web, 2D, and 3D, and separating Completeness (publicly specified core implementation) from Richness (hidden, deeper system relationships). Across 11 model-harness combinations, average scores are **33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness, with 19.9% of generation records failing static gates or missing artifacts**, and excluding same-model self-evaluation no combination clears 50% on either axis. Systems do relatively better on core rules and numerical design than on AI/NPC behavior and game feel, and a limited human cross-check finds the automated judge mostly errs by failing requirements humans accept.

papers.title: Agent-written heuristics versus commercial solvers on unsolved job-shop benchmark instances
papers.abstract: Commercial solvers are the standard tool for difficult scheduling problems. We study whether a frontier large language model, used as a coding agent with open-source tools only, can match them in quality and speed. We report every run, and independent checkers verify every schedule. On the 100,000-operation job shop tai_100_1000_1, an agent-written solver reached 525,515, below OptalCP, Hexaly, and CP Optimizer. Unchanged, it improved all ten instances of the family and closed two. With equal budgets on the same workstation, it ended 0.0-1.8% above the lower bound, against 2.6-5.8% for CP Optimizer and 2.4-4.4% for Hexaly. On the Behnke-Geiger flexible job shops, an agent-written tabu search improved 11 of 32 open instances. With two transport robots, an agent-written solver improved seven of ten MKT instances. New lower bounds show that four published MKT values cannot be attained on the distributed instance files. Agent-run improvement campaigns closed eight further instances.
papers.summary: Difficult scheduling problems are normally handed to commercial solvers, and this study asks whether a frontier language model acting as a coding agent with only open-source tools can match them. Every run is reported and independent checkers verify each schedule produced. On the 100,000-operation job shop instance tai_100_1000_1 the agent-written solver reached 525,515, below `OptalCP`, `Hexaly`, and `CP Optimizer`, and unchanged it improved all ten instances of that family while closing two; under equal budgets on the same workstation it **finished 0.0-1.8% above the lower bound versus 2.6-5.8% for `CP Optimizer` and 2.4-4.4% for `Hexaly`**. An agent-written tabu search improved 11 of 32 open Behnke-Geiger flexible job shop instances, an agent-written solver improved seven of ten MKT instances with two transport robots, and new lower bounds show four published MKT values are unattainable on the distributed instance files.

papers.title: Representational Geometry as a Diagnostic for Adversarial Robustness
papers.abstract: Adversarial training is a common technique for making neural networks more robust to small, intentionally crafted input perturbations, and robustness is commonly measured through accuracy under attack. By exploring inter-network representations across different adversarial training objectives, we can analyze whether multiple networks organize their latent representations similarly. We study Multilayer Perceptrons trained on MNIST under three adversarial training regimes and compare the resulting population training dynamics and geometry to those of a vanilla network. We use M-PHATE to embed data samples across training epochs and examine how the geometry of the data changes during training under adversarial objectives. On penultimate-layer representations we measure displacement between clean and perturbed points, distributional distance through maximum mean discrepancy, and nearest-neighbor recovery. Our visualizations and quantitative analyses show that adversarial training leads to structural changes in how networks organize internal data representations, and robust accuracy and representational stability can rank the same defenses in opposite ways. These findings support a discussion of re-evaluating how practitioners approach the auditing of model robustness by treating latent representations and their training trajectories as diagnostic artifacts across sets of networks.
papers.summary: Adversarial robustness is usually judged by accuracy under attack, which says nothing about how defended networks organize their internal representations. Multilayer perceptrons trained on `MNIST` under three adversarial training objectives are compared against a vanilla network using `M-PHATE` embeddings of samples across training epochs, plus penultimate-layer measurements of clean-to-perturbed displacement, maximum mean discrepancy between distributions, and nearest-neighbor recovery. Adversarial training produces structural changes in representational geometry, and **robust accuracy and representational stability can rank the same defenses in opposite orders**, which the authors use to argue for treating latent representations and their training trajectories as auditing artifacts.

papers.title: What Do Multilingual Self-Supervised Speech Encoders Know About Sentence Meaning?
papers.abstract: Self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) have been scaled up to thousands of languages and millions of hours of audio, yet little is known about how these models structure semantic knowledge across languages. In this work, we probe sentence-level semantics in massively multilingual S3Ms across 76 languages, using linear maps from frozen speech representations into a frozen text embedding space, evaluated by cross-modal retrieval. Sentence meaning is linearly accessible but highly uneven across languages and resource tiers. Cross-lingual probes can match language-specific probes on languages never seen in probe training, but per-model monolingual decodability does not predict transfer. Within the OmniASR wav2vec family, scaling from 300M--7B disproportionately benefits high-resource languages, and ASR tuning sharply improves semantic decodability while making representations more language-specific. However, semantic content is entangled with acoustics, inflating apparent performance on single-speaker corpora.
papers.summary: Self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) now span thousands of languages and millions of hours of audio, but how they encode meaning across languages is largely unexamined. Sentence-level semantics are probed in massively multilingual S3Ms across 76 languages by fitting linear maps from frozen speech representations into a frozen text embedding space and scoring cross-modal retrieval. **Sentence meaning is linearly accessible but very unevenly so across languages and resource tiers**, and cross-lingual probes can match language-specific ones even on languages unseen during probe training, though monolingual decodability does not predict transfer. Within the `OmniASR` wav2vec family, scaling from 300M to 7B parameters mostly benefits high-resource languages, automatic speech recognition tuning sharply improves semantic decodability while making representations more language-specific, and semantic content stays entangled with acoustics, inflating scores on single-speaker corpora.

papers.title: Co-Sight Harness: Externalized Control Assets and Deterministic Enforcement for Long-Horizon Business Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon business workflows fail in two ways: errors accumulate as a chain of activities lengthens, and the knowledge an activity needs is written in a different vocabulary from the user's request. We study whether such workflows can be made reliable without changing the language model. Our method keeps the backbone fixed and moves the workflow definition, state and domain knowledge into versioned control assets outside the model. A state machine and machine-checkable acceptance gates enforce these assets during execution; an independent auditor grades the resulting trace. The assets are updated only after a regression check and human approval .We evaluate the method on three deployed workflows exceeding 200 steps. On Domain A, a 120-case end-to-end evaluation set shows unattended completion rising from 50% to 100%, retrieval recall from 56% to 91.67%, and end-to-end latency dropping from 440 to 159 minutes, with scenario-analysis recall rising from 45% to 93%. Two other domains were taken over by teams that did not write the assets, one in four days and one in seven days. A controlled ablation separates the two failure sources. The code is available at https://github.com/ZTE-AICloud/Co-Sight/tree/master/Co-Sight%20Harness.
papers.summary: Long-horizon business workflows fail both because errors compound over long activity chains and because the knowledge an activity needs is phrased differently from the user's request. The `Co-Sight Harness` keeps the backbone language model fixed and externalizes the workflow definition, state, and domain knowledge into versioned control assets, enforced during execution by a state machine with machine-checkable acceptance gates and graded afterward by an independent auditor, with asset updates gated on a regression check and human approval. Across three deployed workflows of over 200 steps, a 120-case end-to-end evaluation on one domain shows **unattended completion rising from 50% to 100%**, retrieval recall from 56% to 91.67%, scenario-analysis recall from 45% to 93%, and end-to-end latency falling from 440 to 159 minutes. Two further domains were taken over by teams that had not authored the assets, in four and seven days respectively, and an ablation separates the two failure sources.

papers.title: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system
papers.abstract: Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological information. Compared with the operational 0.25$^\circ$ Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical forecasting system, ChlCast reduces mean absolute error and root mean square error by 70.74% and 47.63%, respectively, against satellite-derived Level-4 chlorophyll-a fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations. Coastal case studies further show that the 4-km forecasts retain coastal gradients and localized concentration maxima that are weakened by coarse-grid averaging. These results demonstrate the potential of observation-driven deep learning for high-resolution forecasting of surface chlorophyll-a variability at the near-global scale.
papers.summary: Short-term forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration inform marine ecosystem monitoring, but the coupling of physical transport with biological processes makes conventional numerical biogeochemical models costly. `ChlCast` produces daily 10-day forecasts at roughly 4-km resolution between 60 degrees south and 60 degrees north, combining factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture trained on historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatology. Against the operational 0.25-degree Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical forecasting system, it **cuts mean absolute error by 70.74% and root mean square error by 47.63% relative to satellite-derived Level-4 fields**, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations. Coastal case studies show the finer grid preserves gradients and localized concentration maxima that coarse-grid averaging smooths away.

papers.title: RaFL: An Empirical Study of Random Filter Losses for Image Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Pixel losses train image reconstruction networks toward a point statistic of the target distribution, often averaging away fine textures under uncertainty. Perceptual losses alleviate this issue using pretrained features, but those features are inherently domain-specific. We study a random filter loss (RaFL) that compares prediction and target through filters with random weights, avoiding both pretrained features and task-specific loss engineering. RaFL combines random convolutions, random Fourier features, and random wavelet filters, automatically balancing their contributions through gradient-norm matching, eliminating manual loss-weight tuning and grid search. We systematically investigate three design choices: filter family, weight resampling schedule, and weight initialization. Based on validation PSNR and stability across random seeds, we select the configuration that uses all three filter families, redraws filters every optimization step, and employs Gaussian initialization. We evaluate RaFL on three 2D and two 3D image reconstruction tasks. RaFL outperforms a pixel loss on three tasks and matches it on two, and demonstrates stable performance across random seeds on all five tasks. RaFL adds less than 2% to the backbone's forward FLOPs and no inference cost, requiring $182\times$ fewer loss FLOPs than a VGG19 perceptual loss. These findings suggest that RaFL is a simple, tuning-free, and domain-agnostic loss objective for 2D and 3D image reconstruction.
papers.summary: Pixel losses push image reconstruction networks toward a point statistic of the target distribution, washing out fine texture under uncertainty, while perceptual losses fix this using pretrained features that are tied to a particular domain. A random filter loss (`RaFL`) compares prediction and target through randomly weighted filters instead, mixing random convolutions, random Fourier features, and random wavelet filters whose contributions are balanced automatically by gradient-norm matching, removing loss-weight tuning. Ablations over filter family, resampling schedule, and initialization select all three families with per-step redrawing and Gaussian initialization; across three 2D and two 3D reconstruction tasks **`RaFL` beats a pixel loss on three tasks and matches it on two while needing 182 times fewer loss FLOPs than a `VGG19` perceptual loss**, adding under 2% to forward FLOPs and nothing at inference.

papers.title: Cross-Linguistic Acoustic Biomarkers of Cognitive Impairment Across Interactive and Single-Speaker Speech Tasks
papers.abstract: Multilingual dementia detection is essential for scalable and equitable screening. In recent years, automated speech analysis has emerged as a promising approach for supporting dementia detection by enabling non-invasive and scalable assessment of cognitive function. However, existing studies that use automated speech analysis often rely on one type of task, such as picture description, and use black-box models. These studies often neglect the role of task and language. To address these gaps, we performed a cross-linguistic and cross-task acoustic analysis that integrates a conversational dataset with structured speech tasks across four languages (Spanish, Mandarin, English, Japanese). We applied statistical, linguist-/clinician-guided, and machine learning model-based feature selection to derive compact acoustic feature sets while maintaining classification performance. This enabled systematic comparison of cognitive impairment-relevant features across datasets and tasks. Our results revealed that acoustic features did not generalize uniformly across tasks and languages. Temporal features remained robust across all datasets, consistently capturing timing disruption regardless of language or task. In contrast, speech rate showed strong task dependence -- emerging as informative mainly in single-speaker tasks with externally anchored content and pacing, but becoming less reliable when speech content was highly individualized. Pitch-related features further exhibited language-specific patterns, favoring chroma-related features in tonal languages (e.g., Mandarin) and F0-related features in non-tonal languages. These findings caution against indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous speech data and underscore the need for interpretable, context-aware approaches to multilingual dementia detection using automated speech analysis.
papers.summary: Automated speech analysis is a candidate for scalable dementia screening, but most studies use a single task type such as picture description and opaque models, leaving the roles of task and language unexamined. This analysis combines a conversational dataset with structured speech tasks across Spanish, Mandarin, English, and Japanese, applying statistical, expert-guided, and model-based feature selection to derive compact acoustic feature sets that preserve classification performance. **Acoustic markers did not generalize uniformly across tasks and languages**: temporal features capturing timing disruption held everywhere, speech rate was informative mainly in single-speaker tasks with externally anchored content, and pitch features split by language type, favoring chroma-related features in tonal Mandarin and fundamental-frequency features in non-tonal languages. The authors warn against pooling heterogeneous speech data indiscriminately.

papers.title: Federated Soft Poly-Level Learning Over a Distributed Network with Guaranteed Convergence
papers.abstract: Multi-level learning/optimization, e.g., bilevel optimization, has been recognized for its versatile applicability across a broad array of domains, spanning from signal processing to machine learning. However, most existing works focus on bilevel and trilevel optimization. In contrast, multi-level optimization problems involving four or more hierarchical levels, which we term poly-level learning (PLL) problems, remain largely unexplored.In addition, in practical PLL, data may be distributed across multiple nodes over a distributed network. Nevertheless, extant studies on PLL predominantly focus on the non-federated setting, necessitating the collection of data to central servers and thereby posing potential privacy risks. To this end, we propose a Federated Poly-Level Learning (FPLL) framework over a distributed network to tackle the PLL problems with soft constraints in a federated manner. FPLL hinges on a novel non-linear cut, i.e., $L$-cut, for the level-wise relaxation to the PLL problems. Additionally, the proposed federated algorithm is designed with adjustable parameters that allow for a flexible trade-off between its computational complexity and performance efficiency, enabling users to tune it according to specific application requirements. We also carry out non-asymptotic analysis to derive the iteration complexity for the proposed FPLL to achieve the $\epsilon$-Pareto stationary point. Extensive experiments have been undertaken to elucidate the superior efficacy of the proposed method.
papers.summary: Multi-level optimization is well studied at two and three levels, but problems with four or more hierarchical levels, here called poly-level learning (PLL), remain largely unexplored, and existing PLL work assumes data is centralized, which raises privacy concerns. Federated Poly-Level Learning (`FPLL`) handles soft-constrained PLL problems over a distributed network using a new non-linear cut, the L-cut, for level-wise relaxation, with adjustable parameters trading computational complexity against performance so users can tune for their deployment. **Non-asymptotic analysis gives the iteration complexity needed to reach an epsilon-Pareto stationary point**, and experiments are reported in support of the method.

papers.title: A Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization in Model Merging
papers.abstract: Model merging constructs multi-task models without expensive joint training but often suffers from parameter interference. Some solutions mitigate this by constraining finetuning using data from the other tasks to be merged, violating the core independence and privacy assumption of model merging. Recent work offers preliminary empirical evidence that a universal, task-agnostic proxy distribution can substitute for such data, but leaves open when and why it suffices. To this end, we propose a \textit{Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization}, which characterizes the relationship between a proxy distribution and the distribution of other tasks to be merged through spectral coverage ($\alpha$) and leakage ($\beta$). Based on the framework, we derive a unified parameter interference bound: smaller $(\alpha, \beta)$ provably yields lower parameter interference through better spectral alignment. To exploit such a proxy, we augment the training objective with a proxy regularizer. Evaluating this regularizer during fine-tuning requires a concrete mechanism. We study three instantiations, including (J) an exact evaluation via Jacobian-vector products, (F) a frozen curvature approximation using the Fisher information matrix, and (O) an output-drift formulation that constrains the model's functional deviation on the proxy directly. We prove that all three coincide under the NTK linearization, where existing analyses of such regularizers stop, and go further to characterize standard non-linear fine-tuning, bounding how far each instantiation departs from its linearized reference and obtain a three-way hierarchy, zero for (J), proxy-independent for (F), and proxy-quality-scaling for (O). Empirical validation on the commonly used vision-language model CLIP confirms these theoretical predictions.
papers.summary: Merging independently finetuned models into one multi-task model avoids joint training but suffers parameter interference, and some fixes constrain finetuning using data from the other tasks, breaking the independence and privacy premise of merging. A spectral framework characterizes when a universal task-agnostic proxy distribution can substitute for that data, via spectral coverage (alpha) and leakage (beta), yielding **a unified interference bound in which smaller coverage and leakage provably give lower parameter interference**. Three ways of evaluating the resulting proxy regularizer during finetuning are studied: exact Jacobian-vector products, a frozen Fisher information curvature approximation, and a direct output-drift penalty. All three coincide under neural tangent kernel linearization, and the analysis extends to non-linear finetuning with a three-way hierarchy of departure from the linearized reference, zero for the Jacobian form, proxy-independent for the Fisher form, and proxy-quality-scaling for output drift, with experiments on `CLIP` matching the predictions.

papers.title: Logically Consistent Accurate Forecasts
papers.abstract: Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. For example, forecasts for related events often fail to satisfy the axioms of probability, which in turn implies that related forecasts cannot simultaneously be correct and undermines their utility for decision makers. Enforcing consistency is not trivial -- naive approaches (e.g., projection onto the set of consistent forecasts) can degrade accuracy. We argue that the key to overcoming the apparent tradeoff between consistency and accuracy lies in the reasoning which supports each forecast. We finetune a supervisory language model that leverages this reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies while improving the accuracy of related forecasts. On ForecastBench, our method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing measures of structural inconsistency by 82-90%. We interrogate our method via a comprehensive series of baselines and ablations, and find that no alternative method matches our gains in consistency and accuracy simultaneously.
papers.summary: Agentic forecasting systems built on large language models now rival expert human forecasters but produce forecasts for related events that violate the axioms of probability, which means related predictions cannot all be correct and limits their use for decisions. Simply projecting forecasts onto the consistent set restores coherence at the cost of accuracy; instead, a supervisory language model is finetuned to use the reasoning behind each forecast to reconcile inconsistencies and sharpen related forecasts jointly. On `ForecastBench`, the method **improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented `GPT-5.1` forecaster by 9.3% while cutting structural inconsistency measures by 82-90%**, and a battery of baselines and ablations finds no alternative matching both gains at once.

papers.title: The Polyak-{\L}ojasiewicz Paper: A 10-Year Retrospective
papers.abstract: In 2016, we wrote a paper introducing the phrase "Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition" for an old idea, unsure of how readers would react. The paper ultimately had a larger impact than we expected, and we are surprised and honoured to receive the 2026 PKDD ECML Test of Time Award. With 10 years of hindsight, this note offers an informal and candid retrospective on the PL condition. We take a look back at the origins of the paper, give an AI-assisted refined version of the main theorem, review criticisms of the work, and discuss a variety of related ideas and extensions.

papers.title: Complex Schr\"odinger Bridges
papers.abstract: Diffusion bridges have emerged as versatile frameworks for facilitating transformations between arbitrary data distributions. However, these approaches are hindered by an immense optimization space and its underlying high-order structures. This paper explores a variant of diffusion bridges for solving real-world problems in complex vector spaces governed by scaling and rotation laws, such as Hamiltonian structures. To address this, we introduce conformal optimal transport (COT), a complex-valued transportation framework designed for physical systems with geometric and dissipative dynamics under a geometric lifting. Building on this, we propose a new class of dynamical diffusion bridges, called complex Schr\"odinger bridges (CSBs), whose derived algorithms can handle diffusion-based tasks using a conformal geometric prior. For scalability, we propose image-to-image CSB (I$^2$CSB), a tractable diffusion-bridge technique with an analytic spiral posterior. Finally, we implement a physics-informed CSB algorithm within simulations of quantum electrodynamics, mimicking the logical behavior of quantum logic gates. Our extensive results validate the underlying theory while highlighting advantages of complex-valued diffusion.
papers.summary: Diffusion bridges transform between arbitrary data distributions but face an enormous optimization space with high-order structure. This work targets complex vector spaces governed by scaling and rotation laws, such as Hamiltonian systems, introducing conformal optimal transport (COT), a complex-valued transport framework for physical systems with geometric and dissipative dynamics under a geometric lifting, and building on it a class of dynamical bridges called complex Schrödinger bridges (CSBs) that carry a conformal geometric prior. For scalability, an image-to-image variant with an analytic spiral posterior is derived, and a physics-informed version is run inside quantum electrodynamics simulations mimicking quantum logic gates. **The experiments support the theory and show advantages for complex-valued diffusion over real-valued bridges.**

papers.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.
papers.summary: Serving large language models locally preserves privacy, removes per-token cost, and survives disconnection, but existing local servers bind one runtime to one machine, so several agents sharing a model with an interactive user contend badly and idle machines go unused. `Superfluid` drives `llama.cpp`, `MLX`, or `BaseRT` in isolated worker processes behind a single scheduler that prioritizes interactive requests over agent work, computes a shared prompt once, and durably logs every token before it reaches the client, while also presenting a heterogeneous fleet as one API endpoint with speed-weighted dispatch and join-or-fail tolerance. Serving `Qwen3.8-27B` on an Apple M5 Pro with eight agents active, **a chat receives its first token in 1.5 seconds versus 291-612 seconds on `llama-server`, `Ollama`, and `mlx_lm.server`**. Across six machines from three chip vendors and 64 simulated users, throughput grew from 112 to 534 tokens per second with median time to first token falling from 99 to 12 seconds, and twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras sustained 10,656 tokens per second over 38,563 requests from 384 agents without failure.

papers.title: See Every Block Once: Variance-Reduced Post-Training for Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Policy gradient methods are widely used to align large language model outputs with human preferences, but the log-likelihoods they require cannot be directly computed in Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs). MDLM post-training therefore relies on a surrogate objective based on the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), and recent work estimates a blockwise variant of this objective via Monte Carlo methods to support blockwise generation. However, existing estimation schemes randomly sample the block index, so they may evaluate the same block more than once and leave some blocks unevaluated. This introduces variance arising from block selection into the estimates. In this work, we propose a full-block estimator that evaluates every block exactly once and averages the results. We theoretically show that the proposed estimator remains unbiased while eliminating the between-group variance arising from block selection, thereby achieving lower variance than the baseline for the same sample size. In experiments on five benchmarks spanning mathematics, planning, and coding, our method achieves the highest accuracy on four benchmarks and outperforms the random block sampling baseline by an average of 12.79 points.
papers.summary: Policy-gradient post-training needs log-likelihoods that Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) cannot compute directly, so existing methods use a blockwise Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) surrogate estimated by randomly sampling block indices, which can hit some blocks repeatedly and miss others. The authors propose a full-block estimator that evaluates every block exactly once and averages the results, and prove it stays unbiased while removing the variance that comes from block selection. Across five benchmarks covering mathematics, planning, and coding, it achieves the best accuracy on four and beats the random block sampling baseline by **an average of 12.79 points**.

papers.title: Efficient Genotype Classification from 3D MRI in ADPKD via Density-Aware Point Sampling and E(3)-invariance
papers.abstract: Early detection of genetic kidney diseases, especially autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), is crucial because certain genotypes such as truncating PKD1 mutations cause rapid kidney growth and early progression to end-stage kidney disease. MRI-based genotype inference is a potential low-cost complement to genetic testing. However, although many deep learning methods have been developed for classifying various MR images, applying them to ADPKD remains challenging: (1) abdominal MR images are generally too large to be handled by deep learning models designed for smaller images like brain MRI, and (2) the amount of labeled data for ADPKD genetic mutations is insufficient to train deep learning models. In order to address these challenges, we propose E3PN, an efficient 3D MRI-based ADPKD genotype classification network that relies on point sampling and E(3)-invariance. We utilize a point representation of 3D MRI, which consumes less GPU memory than a voxel representation. For further memory efficiency, 3D points are sampled from a mixture distribution over the two kidneys in each image. Since E(3)-invariance has been shown to improve data efficiency, we also incorporate it into our model through coordinate canonicalization. On our ADPKD dataset, E3PN trains 163 times faster and uses 103x less GPU memory than a 3D ResNet, while also improving F1 from 0.165 to 0.226 over both baselines. These results establish a first benchmark for five-way ADPKD genotype classification from 3D MRI and show that point sampling and coordinate canonicalization yield two-orders-of-magnitude efficiency gains with a modest but consistent improvement in F1.
papers.summary: Inferring the genetic mutation type behind autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) from abdominal MRI is hampered by very large 3D images and scarce labeled data. `E3PN` represents each scan as 3D points sampled from a mixture distribution over the two kidneys, and adds E(3)-invariance through coordinate canonicalization to improve data efficiency. On the authors' ADPKD dataset it **trains 163 times faster and uses 103x less GPU memory than a `3D ResNet`**, while raising F1 from 0.165 to 0.226 on five-way genotype classification. Absolute accuracy remains low, and the authors present the result as a first benchmark for the task.

papers.title: Creative Product Design under Brand Image Constraints
papers.abstract: Industrial design requires creative visual exploration while satisfying constraints that are often product-specific and implicit. Existing text-to-image (T2I) approaches can generate creative designs through concept blending or multi-agent self-enhancement, but they provide limited mechanisms for ensuring that generated designs remain consistent with such constraints. We focus on brand image as a representative design constraint and propose a framework for brand-aware redesign generation. Given a product name, the framework constructs a brand image survey report that summarizes product and market information, derives a creative direction from the report, and integrates this direction into a self-enhancement loop in which generated images are critiqued and prompts are revised. We evaluate the framework on 50 redesign tasks across five product categories, comparing it with Naive T2I, IP-Adapter/IT-Blender, and unconstrained self-enhancement under the same T2I backbone. By a VLM-as-Judge protocol to measure creativity and brand identifiability, the proposed framework achieves a more favorable trade-off between the two objectives, with particularly clear gains in highly constrained categories such as automotive and motorcycle, where the plausible design space is relatively limited compared with that of other product categories. These results suggest that dynamically eliciting and textualizing brand image can guide creative product design generation under brand image constraints.
papers.summary: Text-to-image (T2I) systems can produce creative product designs but offer little control over implicit constraints such as staying recognizable as a given brand. Given a product name, the proposed framework builds a brand image survey report from product and market information, derives a creative direction from it, and feeds that direction into a self-enhancement loop that critiques generated images and revises prompts. On 50 redesign tasks across five product categories, scored by a vision-language model acting as judge, it achieves **a better trade-off between creativity and brand identifiability** than `Naive T2I`, `IP-Adapter`/`IT-Blender`, and unconstrained self-enhancement, with the clearest gains in tightly constrained categories such as automotive and motorcycle.

papers.title: Knowledge After Collapse: Context and Wording Shape Factual Accessibility in Language Models
papers.abstract: When a language model accepts a false correction in a factual discussion, its next answer can depend on how the conversation continues. We introduce Knowledge Answer Divergence (KAD), an event-conditioned evaluation protocol that distinguishes initial false-answer adoption from subsequent persistence, recovery, and abstention. KAD freezes the conversation at the first explicit adoption of a designated false target and branches independent probes from that exact history. This enables matched comparisons of post-adoption behavior and history-management interventions that a single susceptibility score cannot capture. We evaluate eight local checkpoint conditions and six hosted endpoints, alongside an audited 300-question rerun. In corrected Llama 3.2 Instruct 3B controls, a neutral-history branch yields 42/46 correct responses, compared with 16/46 under full history. A matched cue-placement control changes false adoption by 27.3 percentage points in Qwen 3.5 4B. Twelve independently authored pressure templates demonstrate substantial sensitivity to wording. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of KAD for evaluating factual reliability beyond initial susceptibility, enabling systematic comparisons of false-answer persistence, recovery conditions and conversational interventions.
papers.summary: Once a language model accepts a false correction during a factual discussion, what it says next depends on how the conversation continues, which a single susceptibility score does not capture. `Knowledge Answer Divergence` (`KAD`) is an evaluation protocol that freezes the conversation at the first explicit adoption of a false answer and branches independent probes from that exact history, separating persistence, recovery, and abstention. Across eight local checkpoint conditions and six hosted endpoints, `Llama 3.2 Instruct 3B` gave **42/46 correct responses under a neutral-history branch versus 16/46 under full history**.
