Moving a cue's placement shifted false adoption by 27.3 percentage points in `Qwen 3.5 4B`, and twelve independently written pressure templates showed strong sensitivity to wording.

papers.title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks
papers.abstract: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom. We release the evaluation harness and three public tasks; the other 67 are held out to protect the leaderboard from contamination.
papers.summary: `GDP_xlsx` is a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace spreadsheet requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with the full workbook or CSV file and an expert rubric of binary criteria, totalling 2.18 million populated cells and 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric, and models are ranked by strict pass@1, meaning every criterion must be met. Across 20 model configurations from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the best, `Gemini 4 Argon`, **passes only 38.3% of attempts** and the median is 19.3%. The evaluation harness and three tasks are public, with the other 67 held out to limit contamination.

papers.title: Learning Anisotropic Prediction Targets for Flow Models
papers.abstract: Flow-based generative models are trained on a hand-chosen prediction target, such as the velocity, the noise, or the clean data. This choice strongly affects training and sample quality. We introduce Anisotropic Flow Models (AnisoFlow), which replaces a fixed prediction target with a fully learnable one. AnisoFlow learns to scale the noise component of the target anisotropically, assigning a separate nonnegative weight to each direction in a jointly learned basis. A closed-form map recovers the velocity from the network's prediction, leaving the architecture, flow-matching loss, and sampler unchanged. Since recovery is exact, training optimizes the target purely to make it easier for the network to predict. We theoretically analyze the resulting prediction error and predict that the preferred noise weight in each direction scales near-linearly with data variance, in agreement with the weights learned empirically in pixel space. AnisoFlow improves FID from 1.90 to 1.55 over the JiT baseline on ImageNet 256$\times$256, by learning only the prediction target, without representation alignment or architectural changes. In pixel-space text-to-image generation, AnisoFlow improves image quality and, through better-conditioned velocity recovery, largely removes patch-seam artifacts under reduced-precision inference.
papers.summary: Flow-based generative models are trained to predict a hand-picked target such as velocity, noise, or clean data, and that choice strongly affects training and sample quality. `AnisoFlow` makes the target learnable by scaling the noise component with a separate nonnegative weight per direction in a jointly learned basis, with a closed-form map recovering the velocity so the architecture, loss, and sampler stay unchanged. The authors' analysis predicts that the preferred noise weight grows near-linearly with data variance in each direction, matching the weights learned in pixel space. On `ImageNet` 256x256 it **improves FID from 1.90 to 1.55 over the `JiT` baseline**, and in pixel-space text-to-image generation it largely removes patch-seam artifacts under reduced-precision inference.

papers.title: Activation Steering the Nan-Shan in Typhoon
papers.abstract: Typhoon is an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella, in which Captain MacWhirr steers the steamer Nan-Shan directly into and through a catastrophic storm. The novella is a study of what happens when the scale of a phenomenon exceeds the practical and conceptual frameworks available to comprehend it and of the paralysis that sometimes follows a demand for action in such overwhelming circumstances. We chose the text of Typhoon to reflect on human culture's current AI moment. We prompt a large language model, seeded with Conrad's original language, to feed endlessly on its own output, and explore when and how the text becomes increasingly alien and unwieldy as time progresses, including deviations from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long periods of incoherent rumination. We employ methods from activation steering, including a novel adaptive steering method we introduce, to control the rhythm of the narrative and the model's digressions over long stretches of generation. The simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability of this steering showcases the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI, and the reality of a system that remains outside our comprehension and control.
papers.summary: An audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella Typhoon has a large language model, seeded with the original text, feed endlessly on its own output. The authors examine how the text drifts over time, including departures from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long stretches of incoherent rumination. They use activation steering, including **a new adaptive steering method**, to control the rhythm of the narrative and the digressions over long generations. They present the combination of effective yet unpredictable steering as an illustration of the gap between perceived interpretability and actual control.

papers.title: Antidistillation is Cheap: Lightweight Distillation-Resistance via Stylistic Corruption
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly effective paradigm for transferring capabilities from large language models (LLMs) to smaller, more specialized student models. In commercial deployment where frontier models are restricted behind black-box APIs, sequence-level distillation remains a potent vector for competitors to clone proprietary capabilities at a fraction of the development cost. Existing defenses mostly rely on surrogate models to manipulate next-token sampling, which increases computational overhead and real-time inference latency. In this work, we propose a lightweight defense that dynamically injects style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations upon malicious queries. This framework offers exceptional flexibility, allowing hosts to customize target defensive styles and dynamically blend them to maximize stylistic variance. Crucially, this inference-time intervention preserves semantic utility and fluency during malicious queries, misleading adversaries into believing that they are extracting pristine teacher outputs, while standard consumers continue to receive original, unmodified responses. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework successfully disrupts student learning, achieving substantial anti-distillation performance while incurring negligible overhead and preserving text naturalness. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/distill-resist-38C6/.
papers.summary: Competitors can clone a proprietary language model by training a student on its API outputs, and existing defenses typically rely on surrogate models that manipulate token sampling and add inference latency. The proposed defense instead injects style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations when a query is flagged as malicious, with hosts able to choose and blend target styles to maximize stylistic variance. The altered outputs stay fluent and semantically useful, so an attacker is not alerted, while ordinary users receive unmodified responses. The authors report that it **substantially disrupts student learning at negligible overhead**, though the abstract gives no specific numbers.

papers.title: Beyond Prediction Gain: LASR as a Metric for Action-Grounded Latents in World Models
papers.abstract: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.
papers.summary: Latent-action models infer action-like variables from unlabeled video, but a latent that improves future prediction may only encode the current state, episode progress, or task identity instead of action. The `Latent Action Support Ratio` (`LASR`) is a dimensionless offline metric that measures, on held-out data, whether a latent adds predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives; `GeoLASR` summarizes typical support and `WorstLASR` the weakest case. On recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel, it **detects known action information and rejects representative non-action shortcuts**, and it allows graded comparisons between imperfect latents. The authors also use it to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter.

papers.title: Certified Improvements to Best-Known Thomson-Problem Configurations with a Search Pipeline Built with Large Language Model Agents
papers.abstract: The Thomson problem asks for N unit charges on a sphere with minimum Coulomb energy; for large N the best configurations known are curated in the Cambridge Cluster Database, whose largest-N entries were set in October 2026. We report configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502 with energies 0.0036186, 0.0109730 and 0.0614033 below the database values, certified by exact integer arithmetic. All three are numerically strict local minima modulo rotations and keep the defect inventory and scar compositions of the database configurations; the database value for N = 912 had been reached by two different methods. Our search runs unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from the database configurations, with a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions after relabelling by geometry, and gradient-only polishing; replica-exchange basin hopping alone found the N = 912 and 1382 configurations, the former in one of five runs. We built and ran it with large language model agents (Claude, through a chat interface and the Claude Code agent), and we report every search, including those that failed. Two findings matter for others who search the database. Polishing alone lowers two entries by more than the threshold at which our pipeline reports a candidate, which produced two spurious records until candidates were compared with the polished database energies (the polished baseline). A local-relaxation speed-up passed its exactness test yet found nothing in a controlled comparison in which every arm with full relaxation went below the database value within 15 minutes. We distil three practices for computational discovery with large language model agents: calibrate the search code and verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare candidates with the polished baseline, and test design changes in controlled comparisons with pass criteria fixed in advance.
papers.summary: The Thomson problem asks for the minimum-energy arrangement of N unit charges on a sphere, with best-known configurations curated in the Cambridge Cluster Database. Using a search pipeline built and run with large language model agents (`Claude` through chat and `Claude Code`), the authors report **new lower-energy configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502, certified by exact integer arithmetic**. The search combines replica-exchange basin hopping, a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions, and gradient-only polishing, and every run is reported, including failures. Two pitfalls are documented: polishing alone lowered some database entries enough to produce spurious records, and a speed-up that passed its exactness test found nothing in a controlled comparison. From these the authors derive three practices: verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare against a polished baseline, and fix pass criteria before testing design changes.
papers.highlight_summary:
New lowest-known energies for three large Thomson-problem sizes (minimum-Coulomb-energy arrangements of N unit charges on a sphere) come from a search pipeline written and run by `Claude` and `Claude Code` under human direction, with every improvement certified in exact integer arithmetic. The authors also document every failed search and the workflow errors that nearly produced false records.

- The search runs unconstrained `replica-exchange basin hopping` with full `L-BFGS` relaxation from the Cambridge Cluster Database (`CCD`) configurations, adding a shared pool of minima, region-splice recombination after relabelling points by geometry, and gradient-only `Barzilai–Borwein` polishing.
- Configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502 sit **0.0036186**, **0.0109730** and **0.0614033** below the `CCD` values (relative decreases of about **10⁻⁸**), and all three are numerically strict local minima that keep the database configurations' defect inventory and scar compositions.
- Polishing alone lowers two of the 53 `CCD` entries by more than the pipeline's **10⁻⁵** candidate threshold, which produced **two spurious records** until candidates were compared against a polished baseline.
- A local-relaxation speed-up passed its **10⁻⁹** exactness test yet found nothing in **four core-hours** of a controlled comparison in which every full-relaxation arm beat the `CCD` value within **15 minutes**, because freezing the surrounding lattice biased energies 0.1 to 0.4 too high.
- The authors claim neither global optimality nor superiority over the October 2026 method that set the largest `CCD` entries, having run no equal-budget comparison, and only **3 of 11** sizes searched with full relaxation improved, with the N = 2502 result resting on a single run and N = 912 on one of five.

papers.title: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. On its own, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, maintains its accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantized weights, and transfers zero-shot to Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB within 3.1 points of its native SQLite accuracy. Combined with Claude Opus 5.5 in a pre-registered confidence cascade over 227 questions on databases published after Opus's training cutoff, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all questions locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy. Finally, contamination probing shows that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema; however, its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas and reaches 95.6-97.4% on post-cutoff databases. Code and data: https://github.com/IAMIbrahimmemon/luthorsql
papers.summary: Frontier LLM agents are accurate at text-to-SQL but slow, costly, and require sending sensitive queries to external APIs. `LuthorSQL` is a non-autoregressive 7B model that predicts slot scores over a bounded query-plan grammar in one forward pass, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, picks an answer with a trained validator, and escalates to a slower agent only when uncertain. Alone it reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on the hidden test set of `BIRD` at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, and holds that accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantization. In a pre-registered cascade with `Claude Opus 5.5` on 227 questions over post-cutoff databases, it answers nearly half the questions locally and **cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy**. Contamination probing also shows `Opus` reproducing 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema, although its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas.

papers.title: TReC: Evaluating Move-Induced State Changes in Instruction-Conditioned Go
papers.abstract: When a Go model predicts a move different from the expert's, coordinate distance measures how far the prediction lands from the reference. We introduce Transition Representation Consistency (TReC) to compare how the two moves change a board-state embedding. Both moves are executed from the same position under the game rules, and TReC is the cosine similarity between the two resulting representation changes. In experiments with a frozen KataGo network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the gap between the highest and lowest candidate per position has a median of 0.01 to 0.08 for the direct successor-state cosine and 0.88 to 1.33 for TReC, depending on the evaluator layer. TReC follows coordinate distance only weakly: the rank correlation between a candidate's distance to the reference and its TReC, computed within each position, has a median of -0.19 over these positions.
papers.summary: When a Go model's predicted move differs from the expert's, coordinate distance only says how far apart the two moves are on the board. `Transition Representation Consistency` (`TReC`) plays both moves from the same position and takes the cosine similarity between the two resulting changes in a board-state embedding. Using a frozen `KataGo` network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the gap between the best and worst candidate per position has a **median of 0.88 to 1.33 for `TReC` versus 0.01 to 0.08 for direct successor-state cosine**, depending on the layer. `TReC` tracks coordinate distance only weakly, with a median within-position rank correlation of -0.19.

papers.title: Direction or Magnitude? Learning Scalars over Task-Calibrated Directions
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR, which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning.
papers.summary: `SCALAR` is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that builds a fixed input basis from task activations, assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction, and trains only layer-specific scalar coefficients. Grouped computation and dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduce compute and storage for the fixed parts. On commonsense reasoning it reaches **accuracy comparable to `LoRA` with about 4% of its trainable parameters**, and it is also evaluated on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge tasks. On `Qwen2.5-7B` it shows 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than `LoRA`.

papers.title: Towards Seconds-level Video Representation: Quadratically Gated Feature Grid with Adaptive, Prediction-free Sampling
papers.abstract: Implicit neural video representations are notoriously slow to build, which does not cross the basic practical threshold for most industrial applications. Here, we present Q-GAS, a coordinate-queryable video representation that couples multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids with a compact SwiGLU-style quadratic-gating (QG) decoder and an error-aware, prediction-free sampler. The explicit grids avoid hash-collision coefficient sharing at the cost of modestly higher storage yet greatly boost the expressive capacity; the QG decoder introduces low-rank local second-order interactions to improve the nonlinear feature response. During fitting, a global error map periodically refreshes a high-error pool, and each batch mixes pool samples with uniform samples, which is free from the auxiliary model to predict difficult samples, thereby further escalating the efficiency. On UVG Beauty/Bosphorus/Jockey, Q-GAS fits and quantizes under 50 s on one RTX PRO 6000, decodes at over 370 FPS with mixed precision and about 146 FPS in FP32. In our PyTorch implementation, Q-GAS trains and quantizes 5.5-7.2 times faster than the evaluated Instant-NGP baseline and 19-28 times faster than RNeRV. Under a 90 s budget, it improves PSNR/MS-SSIM/LPIPS over the evaluated NeRV-family pipelines at comparable BPP over the measured overlap. We have shared our code at https://github.com/MillenRosen/Q-GAS for readers' free use.
papers.summary: Implicit neural video representations are slow to fit, which limits their practical use. `Q-GAS` combines multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids, a compact quadratic-gating decoder in the style of SwiGLU, and a sampler that mixes uniform samples with a periodically refreshed pool of high-error locations, with no auxiliary model to predict hard samples. On `UVG` sequences it **fits and quantizes in under 50 seconds on one RTX PRO 6000** and decodes at over 370 FPS with mixed precision. That is 5.5-7.2 times faster than the evaluated `Instant-NGP` baseline and 19-28 times faster than `RNeRV`, with better PSNR, MS-SSIM, and LPIPS than NeRV-family pipelines at comparable bitrate under a 90-second budget.

papers.title: RAG-FGO: Dynamic Optimization of Query-Rewriting Agents for Generative RAG
papers.abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), query rewriting serves as a core interface that aligns user intent with external knowledge bases, and its effectiveness directly determines overall system performance. However, generative retrieval faces three critical challenges in real-world deployment: noisy retrieval feedback, the difficulty of jointly optimizing discrete prompt templates and continuous decoding-control parameters, and the limited generalization of static rewriting strategies under semantically complex scenarios. To address these issues, we propose RAG-FGO, a dynamic optimization framework for generative retrieval strategies. RAG-FGO formulates query rewriting as a non-differentiable black-box optimization problem in a mixed discrete-continuous space, and represents prompt templates and decoding parameters as adaptively optimizable query-rewriting agents. The framework performs global search to enable semantic jumps and structural reorganization that escape local optima, while applying local perturbations for fine-grained alignment and precise refinement. In addition, RAG-FGO introduces an elite-preserving memory pool that accumulates high-quality strategies across iterations, thereby mitigating the impact of stochasticity and noisy feedback on optimization stability. Experimental results on a diverse suite of benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method, supporting its applicability to complex semantic retrieval tasks.
papers.summary: Query rewriting in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) suffers from noisy retrieval feedback, the difficulty of jointly tuning discrete prompt templates and continuous decoding parameters, and static strategies that generalize poorly. `RAG-FGO` treats rewriting as black-box optimization over a mixed discrete-continuous space, in which each candidate pairs a prompt template with decoding parameters. It combines global search to escape local optima, local perturbations for refinement, and **an elite-preserving memory pool that keeps high-quality strategies across iterations** to dampen noise. The authors report effectiveness and robustness across a range of benchmarks, without specific numbers in the abstract.

papers.title: Can Large Language Models Optimize Pretrained Neural Network Weights? A Multi-Phase Empirical Evaluation of Gradient-Free Editing in YOLO26 Object Detection
papers.abstract: Direct weight editing offers a gradient-free alternative to fine-tuning pretrained detectors, but its generalization and the value of large language model (LLM) guidance remain uncertain. We evaluate five experimental phases using YOLO26 models and MS COCO, comparing deterministic scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, CMA-ES, structured interventions, real local-LLM proposals, failure-aware guidance, and hybrid LLM-CMA-ES against a matched random-policy control. Optimization uses native Ultralytics mAP50-95 on 1,000 COCO Val2017 images; selected candidates are assessed on a disjoint, previously examined 1,500-image subset, with COCO API AP50-95 reported separately where available. Increasing the CMA-ES budget from 8 to 250 evaluations raised development gains from +0.11 to +0.28 percentage points, while selection changes remained negative (-0.03 to -0.12 points); the 250-evaluation result uses one seed. The hybrid LLM approach showed no statistically established advantage over random-policy guidance (p = 0.612, 0.369, and 0.694 at budgets 8, 25, and 50). Five-seed YOLO26m replication yielded a COCO API AP difference of +0.004 points (95% CI: -0.026 to +0.034). Of 225 archived LLM proposals, 53 satisfy the final strict schema; early tensor-level execution cannot be fully verified. Genuine LLM-mediated weight editing is feasible, but the tested approaches did not demonstrate consistent transfer beyond the development subset or a measurable LLM advantage.
papers.summary: Whether large language models (LLMs) can usefully guide gradient-free edits to pretrained network weights is tested here on `YOLO26` object detectors with `MS COCO`. Five experimental phases compare deterministic scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, `CMA-ES`, structured interventions, local-LLM proposals, and a hybrid LLM-`CMA-ES` method against a matched random-policy control. Development-set gains were tiny (at most +0.28 percentage points) and turned negative on a disjoint selection subset. The hybrid LLM approach showed **no statistically established advantage over random-policy guidance** (p = 0.612, 0.369, and 0.694 at three budgets). Only 53 of 225 archived LLM proposals satisfied the final strict schema.

papers.title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.
papers.summary: `AutoRL` is a multi-agent system that supervises a reinforcement learning (RL) training run for language models as it happens, instead of running complete experiments end to end. Perceptor agents monitor training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency and trigger deliberation on anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three Proposer agents then diagnose the problem and refine candidate interventions, and an Orchestrator reviews and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. In experiments on `Qwen3` and `LongCat-Flash-Lite`, it **outperforms static RL recipes and a general-purpose agent**. The authors conclude that current agents can handle unattended RL supervision, and that the harder open problem is producing fundamental new methods worth the cost of validating.

papers.title: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals
papers.abstract: The performance of offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of the fixed offline dataset, motivating trajectory augmentation. However, augmenting multi-agent trajectories presents a fundamental challenge of the diversity-coordination trade-off: independent generation improves diversity but lacks coordination, while joint generation induces coordination but lacks diversity, reproducing the training distribution. To address this challenge in multi-agent data augmentation, we introduce MASTARS, a novel diffusion-based framework that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent consistent coordination via the method of inpainting. MASTARS produces trajectories that are diverse, coordinated and globally coherent. Experiments on various benchmarks such as MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 demonstrate significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods.
papers.summary: Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of its fixed dataset, and augmenting trajectories faces a trade-off: generating each agent independently gives diversity without coordination, while joint generation gives coordination but reproduces the training distribution. `MASTARS` is a diffusion-based framework that generates trajectories sequentially across agents and uses inpainting to keep them consistent with one another. Experiments on `MPE`, `SMAC`, and `SMAC-v2` show **significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods**, though the abstract gives no specific numbers.

papers.title: Federated Physics-Informed Thermal Field Prediction Across Unseen Geometries in Distributed Additive Manufacturing
papers.abstract: In additive manufacturing (AM), each change in part geometry requires a new thermal simulation, which makes design evaluation over many candidates costly. Geometry-aware models reduce this cost by predicting thermal fields on unseen parts with a single learned model, but they assume that diverse geometries are available centrally. This assumption is restrictive when each manufacturing site holds only a limited set of proprietary part designs that it cannot share. We propose Fed-PIGANO, a federated framework that trains physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator (PI-GANO) models at individual sites and aggregates their geometry encoders and prediction networks without sharing part geometries. We evaluate the framework on a 2D steady-state thermal benchmark for metal AM, with geometries from five polygonal families distributed across three sites under four scenarios that range from identical to strongly different family compositions. Over seven replications, Fed-PIGANO achieves mean relative L2 errors of 1.83% to 2.04% across all 12 scenario-site cases, compared with up to 20.46% for local-only training, and consistently yields lower PDE residuals. Its prediction accuracy is comparable to that of a centralized model trained on the pooled geometries of all sites. These results demonstrate that federated learning lets manufacturing sites benefit from each other's geometries without sharing them, enabling rapid thermal prediction on new part designs for tasks such as shape optimization, inverse design, and uncertainty quantification.
papers.summary: Predicting thermal fields for new part geometries in additive manufacturing normally requires either a fresh simulation or a learned model trained on diverse geometries pooled centrally, which is impractical when sites cannot share proprietary designs. `Fed-PIGANO` trains physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator models at each site and aggregates their geometry encoders and prediction networks without exchanging part geometries. On a 2D steady-state thermal benchmark with five polygon families split across three sites, it achieves **mean relative L2 errors of 1.83% to 2.04%, versus up to 20.46% for local-only training**. Its accuracy is comparable to a centralized model trained on all sites' pooled data.

papers.title: Robustness Evaluation of GPU Cloud Pricing Benchmarks under Incomplete Observations: A Controlled Missingness Study
papers.abstract: Daily GPU rental-price benchmarks can fail when marketplace quotes are missing. This article stress-tests a fixed equal-weight median rule under four imposed masking mechanisms and four benchmark-level recovery methods. Across 5,800 Monte Carlo realisations in 27 scenarios on 190 held-out days, whole-source outages reduce publication coverage to 0.77 while preserving zero conditional error on published dates; composition-changing loss retains 0.86 coverage but produces 7.74 log points of error. A separate past-only stratum-level ablation reduces error by 4.15 to 6.70 log points in five composition-changing cases, using a richer information set. An observable-signal withholding rule improves the primary error-coverage criterion in 0 of 10 cases. Results concern observed asking-price measurements, not transaction prices or identified real-world missingness mechanisms.
papers.summary: Daily benchmarks of GPU rental prices can break down when marketplace quotes are missing. This study stress-tests a fixed equal-weight median rule under four imposed masking mechanisms and four recovery methods, using 5,800 Monte Carlo realisations across 27 scenarios on 190 held-out days. Whole-source outages cut publication coverage to 0.77 with no error on the dates that are published, whereas **composition-changing loss keeps 0.86 coverage but introduces 7.74 log points of error**. A past-only stratum-level method that uses richer information reduces that error by 4.15 to 6.70 log points in five cases, while a rule that withholds publication based on observable signals helped in none of 10 cases.

papers.title: Vision-as-a-Tool: Visual Harness for Multimodal Agentic Coding
papers.abstract: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. Current frameworks largely rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, where agents depend on their intrinsic vision to execute visually grounded tasks. However, this architectural coupling introduces a fundamental bottleneck. Agent performance remains strictly bounded by internal perceptual limitations. Furthermore, text-only agents lack native perception. Without specialized tools, they cannot perform visual reasoning. To overcome these constraints, we introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm. Prior visual tool-use merely manipulates images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read. In contrast, VaaT reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as callable external utilities. As a result, text-only agents can completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Meanwhile, vision-capable agents can dynamically augment their native perception on demand. We instantiate this paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. We comprehensively evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VHarness consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across both text-only and multimodal coding agents. These findings highlight that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities provides a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems.
papers.summary: Coding agents that must judge visual output are limited by their own built-in vision, and text-only agents cannot perceive images at all. The proposed Vision-as-a-Tool (`VaaT`) paradigm treats general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as callable external utilities, implemented in `VHarness`, a framework built on five atomic actions. Across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation tasks, `VHarness` **consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy for both text-only and multimodal coding agents**.

papers.title: Multimodal Person Concept Model for Person Identification under Varying Observation Conditions
papers.abstract: Service robots in domestic and office environments must identify users to provide personalized services based on their preferences and previous interactions. This is challenging because only a few observations may be available for learning, while observation conditions change owing to appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content. To address this challenge, this study proposes a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of observations, without person labels, and enables robust identification under changing conditions. The model employs a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process and integrates visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted using Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP), followed by principal component analysis (PCA). We evaluated six participants under eight conditions in which appearance changes, additive noise, and transcription errors were introduced individually and in combination. Averaged over the eight conditions, the proposed model achieved an identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of person concepts from the observations, which is comparable to k-means clustering that was supplied with the true number of participants (0.88). We also examined PCA dimensionality, modality availability, and variation strength, and demonstrated the model on a Toyota Human Support Robot. These results show that multimodal person concept learning supports robust person identification under changing conditions, and that identification can succeed even when the number of concepts is not correctly recovered. The project page and demonstration video are available at https://okitamisan01.github.io/person_concept/.
papers.summary: Service robots need to recognize individual users from only a few unlabeled observations, even as appearance, background noise, and speech content change. The proposed model uses a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process to cluster visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted with Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (`CLIP`) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (`CLAP`) and reduced by principal component analysis (PCA). With six participants under eight conditions it reached **an average identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of people itself**, comparable to `k-means` given the true count (0.88), and was demonstrated on a `Toyota Human Support Robot`.

papers.title: Can Agents Keep Up with Time? An Empirical Analysis of Temporal Adaptation After a Conversational Hiatus
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents increasingly serve as persistent personal assistants across modern web platforms, managing schedules, applications, and multi-step plans over weeks or months. Users often return to an ongoing conversation after a long conversational hiatus, while earlier bookings and preparation notes stay on record. During this hiatus, scheduled dates may pass even though the retained records remain unchanged and event outcomes go unrecorded. Existing evaluations of long-horizon agents focus on fact retention and explicit state updates. Whether agents perceive the passage of time and adapt their advice accordingly therefore remains unknown. We frame this ability as temporal state perception and use, which means perceiving the current time and applying it when interpreting dated records. To study it, we design session-rekindling tasks that keep the earlier conversation fixed and vary only the follow-up date and the way temporal information reaches the agent. Experiments across five model routes and five temporal-information conditions show that agents can obtain the current time but often fail to use it. They reliably query the clock and even note in their reasoning that the scheduled date has passed, yet many still tell users to prepare for the expired event. Supplying explicit temporal context reduces this error, and providing the computed date relation removes it entirely. Keeping up with time therefore depends on turning perceived time into updated plans. Based on these findings, we design a session-rekindling benchmark that provides temporal-awareness guidance for designing long-horizon agents. The code can be found at https://github.com/Adoreu2/session-rekindling-benchmark.
papers.summary: Persistent assistant agents often resume a conversation after a long gap, during which scheduled dates may have passed while the stored records stay unchanged. The authors design session-rekindling tasks that hold the earlier conversation fixed and vary only the follow-up date and how temporal information reaches the agent, testing five model routes under five temporal-information conditions. Agents reliably query the clock and even note in their reasoning that a date has passed, yet **many still tell users to prepare for the expired event**. Explicit temporal context reduces the error, and supplying the computed date relation removes it entirely.

papers.title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_\alpha$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.
papers.summary: Long-running LLM agents accumulate interaction histories in which summaries can drop exact details needed later, while keeping everything carries irrelevant material. `CarryOn` is a lightweight context manager that pairs a compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence, using a learned selector and adaptive retention policy that need no extra LLM calls. The authors also introduce two metrics, a success-first score that accounts for resource use and normalized cost per success (NCS). Across `AppWorld`, `OfficeBench`, and `Tau2 Telecom` with three LLM actors, it achieves **75.7% macro-averaged task success, 6.7 percentage points above the strongest baseline**, and the best average on both metrics.

papers.title: AI Reviews Are Biased Towards the Appendix
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by reviewers to highlight weaknesses during the reviewing process, and their outputs often shape the reviews that humans submit. Prior work studies how LLM reviews align with human ones, yet we know little about which parts of a paper these models actually criticize. In this work, we investigate 2,000 papers from ACL, EMNLP, COLM, and ICLR, and show that the latest GPT and Claude models draw about 50% or more of their review weaknesses from the appendix. This behavior holds across the API, coding-agent, and web access methods for using LLMs to review a paper. In contrast, we find that humans draw only 8.4% of their weaknesses from the appendix, and these weaknesses primarily revolve around a paper's presentation and content related to its core idea. Meanwhile, LLMs draw weaknesses from deep in the appendix that concern fine-grained technical details not central to the paper's contributions. We anticipate that our analysis will contribute to the scholarly discourse on AI reviews. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/cincynlp/review_appendix.
papers.summary: Little is known about which parts of a paper LLM-generated peer reviews actually criticize. An analysis of 2,000 papers from ACL, EMNLP, COLM, and ICLR finds that the latest GPT and Claude models draw **about 50% or more of their review weaknesses from the appendix, versus 8.4% for human reviewers**, a pattern that holds across API, coding-agent, and web access. Human weaknesses mostly concern presentation and content tied to a paper's core idea, whereas the LLMs pull fine-grained technical details from deep in the appendix that are not central to the contributions.
papers.highlight_summary:
Where LLM-written peer reviews source their criticism is examined across 2,000 papers from `ACL`, `EMNLP`, `COLM`, and `ICLR`, with each weakness traced back to the section of the paper it targets. The latest GPT and Claude models draw **about half or more** of their weaknesses from appendix-related material, whereas human reviewers historically drew **under 10%**.

- Each anonymized paper (sampled only if its appendix runs at least 15 pages) is reviewed by `GPT-6-Astra`, `GPT-6.1-Sol`, `Claude-Opus-5.5`, or `Claude-Sonnet-5.5` from a deliberately minimal one-line prompt, after which the same model attributes every weakness to up to two sections, counting it as appendix-related if any of its evidence sits in the appendix.
- On `ICLR 2027` submissions, LLM reviews average **62.00%** appendix-related weaknesses (**14.19%** from the appendix alone) against **8.40%** (**4.36%** appendix-only) for human reviews of `ICLR 2021–24` papers, and every one of the 200 LLM reviews contained at least one appendix criticism.
- The bias appears to be new and model-driven: `GPT-5` attributes less than 30% of weaknesses to the appendix versus roughly **60–70%** for `GPT-6-Astra` and `GPT-6.1-Sol`, and a 100-paper test of `GPT-6-Astra` stays above 50% across `Codex`, API with PDF, API with extracted text, and the web interface.
- Human `ICLR` reviews held at about 6–10% appendix-related weaknesses for years, then rose to 11.27% for `ICLR 2026` and **27.60%** for `ICLR 2027`, while the content differs sharply: LLM appendix criticism is **54.0%** methodology and 25.2% analysis with only 2.1% on presentation (humans: 32.2%), and it persists past page 30 where human concerns nearly vanish.
- Section attribution and categorization are themselves done by LLMs with only an unquantified manual spot-check, the human and LLM reviews cover different papers and years, the rise in human reviews is a temporal correlation rather than demonstrated causation, and neither the validity of the appendix weaknesses nor their effect on scores is measured.

papers.title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. To address these challenges, we present G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system that converts daily production evidence under evolving demand and capability contracts into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and governed reward evolution. Governed checkpoint transition under cumulative evaluation controls each model update, enabling the agent to learn newly introduced behaviors without sacrificing previously accepted capabilities. Experiments on a real production e-commerce agent show that G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior compared with a strong autonomous post-training baseline. Ablations further show that both reward-routed, entropy-prioritized data orchestration and governed reward evolution are important to these gains. G-CAST is now deployed in Yuancai(http://cai.1688.com/), a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.
papers.summary: Conversational shopping agents face shifting user demand alongside an evolving set of tools, skills, and operating procedures, which leaves a once-trained model behind and makes periodic manual retraining too slow. `G-CAST` is a governed continual self-training system that turns daily production evidence into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data, evolves its reward under governance, and gates each checkpoint update on cumulative evaluation. On a real production e-commerce agent it shows **stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior** than a strong autonomous post-training baseline, and it is deployed in `Yuancai`, a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.

papers.title: Causally Constrained and Uncertainty-Aware Cardiopulmonary Risk Prediction
papers.abstract: Routine chest computed tomography (CT) captures pulmonary, cardiac, and vascular phenotypes that jointly stratify lung cancer and cardiovascular disease, the two leading causes of death in lung-screening populations. Yet clinical risk calculators evaluate each disease in isolation and omit CT findings, whereas unconstrained machine learning overfits small hospital cohorts, learns treatment- and illness-confounded risk directions, and conceals uncertainty when patient records are incomplete. Here we present the Causal Envelope Agent (CE-Agent), a two-stage framework that compiles peer-reviewed epidemiological evidence into explicit constraints on risk-factor weights before any outcome is seen, while estimating local baseline risk and newly added CT phenotypes from cohort data. At deployment, closed-form uncertainty propagation accounts for missing clinical or CT inputs within milliseconds per patient, running over two orders of magnitude faster than Monte Carlo sampling and returning calibrated risk intervals that direct chart review and selective imaging to borderline patients. Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, CE-Agent outperforms cardiovascular calculators in lung screening, exceeds the Pooled Cohort Equations on hard atherosclerotic events while correcting their 1.7-fold risk overestimation, and generalizes from a single hospital or CT scanner to external sites while lowering required sample sizes up to fivefold. Applied unchanged to lung cancer, CE-Agent matches established screening models with accurate calibration even when restricted to risk-factor directions alone, and pairing both predictions improves joint cardiopulmonary triage from a single screening visit.
papers.summary: Chest computed tomography (CT) scans from lung screening carry information about both lung cancer and cardiovascular risk, but clinical calculators treat each disease separately and unconstrained machine learning overfits small cohorts and hides uncertainty from missing data. The Causal Envelope Agent (`CE-Agent`) compiles published epidemiological evidence into explicit constraints on risk-factor weights before seeing any outcomes, then estimates local baseline risk and CT phenotypes from cohort data, with closed-form uncertainty propagation that runs over two orders of magnitude faster than Monte Carlo sampling. Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, it outperforms cardiovascular calculators and exceeds the `Pooled Cohort Equations` on hard atherosclerotic events while **correcting their 1.7-fold risk overestimation**, and it lowers required sample sizes up to fivefold.

papers.title: Aligning AI Teams
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown that alignment training on individual LLM agents can fail to transfer to multi-agent settings. We investigate the underlying mechanisms for this failure, and explore interventions to preserve alignment transfer to multi-agent LLM teams. We focus on two software-engineering tasks (sepsis triage, a news recommender) and ten consulting-proposal generation tasks. We present four findings: (1) The single-vs-team safety gap does not show a clear trend with more capable models. We find that Anthropic's Mythos Preview shows the largest gap on one of our tasks but the smallest on another; (2) Many natural interventions, such as having agents critique each other's work or coordinate in a group chat, do not reliably bring agent teams back to single-agent alignment behavior; (3) diffusion of responsibility substantially accounts for the safety gap: agents in teams are less likely to proactively check for system-level safety failures and more likely to ignore, rationalize, or deflect responsibility for issues when they arise; (4) having a designated safety lead agent ensure system-level safety, and having a coordinator agent publish a safety specifications document are effective at restoring single-agent alignment. We also release magelab, a multi-agent LLM orchestration and experimentation framework. Our findings can help practitioners design agent teams that successfully preserve the behaviors expected of aligned individual agents.
papers.summary: Alignment training on individual LLM agents can fail to carry over when those agents work in teams, and this study examines why, using two software-engineering tasks and ten consulting-proposal tasks. The single-versus-team safety gap shows no clear trend with model capability, and natural fixes such as peer critique or group-chat coordination do not reliably close it. **Diffusion of responsibility substantially accounts for the gap**: agents in teams are less likely to check proactively for system-level safety failures and more likely to ignore, rationalize, or deflect issues. Designating a safety lead agent and having a coordinator publish a safety specifications document restore single-agent alignment, and the authors release `magelab`, a multi-agent orchestration and experimentation framework.
papers.highlight_summary:
Alignment trained into individual LLM agents often fails to carry over when the same model is composed into a cooperative team, and this work traces much of that gap to diffusion of responsibility: agents stay inside their assigned subtask and nobody owns system-level safety. Giving one agent explicit end-to-end safety authority, combined with a coordinator-written safety specification, largely restores single-agent behaviour.

- A single agent is compared against a hub-and-spoke team of one project manager and eight coders on tasks whose safety and business goals are jointly infeasible by construction (a sepsis-triage classifier, a news recommender, and ten consulting-proposal scenarios), across five Claude models with roughly 30 runs per configuration using the released `magelab` orchestration harness.
- The single-vs-team safety gap shows no clear trend with capability: on sepsis the team's sensitivity falls about **59 pp** below the single agent on `Mythos Preview`, 36 pp on `Opus 4.7` and 35 pp on `Opus 4.6` (versus about 1 pp on `Sonnet 4.6` and 5 pp on `Opus 4.1`), yet on the recommender `Mythos Preview` has the smallest gap at **3 pp** while the other models sit at 12–17 pp.
- Transcript annotation plus a mediation regression over 1,054 sepsis runs shows that whether any agent tested the integrated pipeline, discovered harm, and attempted a fix accounts for **84%** of the single-agent advantage over the multi-agent baseline, with teams testing less, discovering less, and more often deflecting, rationalizing, or ignoring harms.
- The compound of a safety document and a designated safety lead is the most reliable intervention (about **+32 pp** sensitivity over the multi-agent baseline on sepsis), the safety lead alone is next, the safety document helps modestly through a separate "be more conservative" channel (only 6% mediated), and peer review, safety-focused review, and group chat do not reliably close the gap.
- Only Anthropic's Claude family is tested, the behaviours are labelled by an LLM annotator, the diffusion-of-responsibility link is much weaker on the recommender (consistent only on `Opus 4.7`), and the compound intervention only partially closes that task's gap on `Opus 4.6` (−8 pp).

papers.title: SceneAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Portable Game Scene Generation
papers.abstract: Moving a scene generator to a new game engine requires more than exporting its final output: planning, construction tools, and stored experience may also depend on the original backend. We present SceneAgent, a multi-agent framework for reusing the construction process and its experience across backends. A canonical SceneContext maintains the evolving world, while backend adapters isolate coordinate conventions, asset bindings, and export. Structured handoffs let fresh Builder sessions query this persistent state without inheriting the full construction transcript. Across generations, human-approved traces are distilled into asset-ID-free Layout skills and semantic Content skills that can be retrieved and recombined. We introduce GameSceneBench, comprising 69 indoor and outdoor prompts. Under a common asset and evaluation protocol, SceneAgent obtains human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2-89.4% against five baselines. Ablations show that reusable skills and the multi-agent protocol primarily improve prompt alignment and scene completeness, with additional runtime. Deployment in a second engine preserves the shared construction protocol and skill library while replacing backend integration components. Together, these results support separating persistent scene state, task-local reasoning, and reusable experience for portable scene construction.
papers.summary: Porting an automated scene generator to a different game engine is difficult because its planning, construction tools, and stored experience often depend on the original backend. `SceneAgent` keeps the evolving world in a canonical `SceneContext`, isolates engine specifics in backend adapters, uses structured handoffs so fresh builder sessions query persistent state rather than the full transcript, and distills human-approved traces into reusable layout and content skills. On the new `GameSceneBench` of 69 indoor and outdoor prompts it obtains **human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2-89.4% against five baselines**, and deployment in a second engine reuses the construction protocol and skill library while replacing only the backend integration components.

papers.title: V-JEPA-LM: Video-Language Models That Read Dynamics Beyond Static, Text-Aligned Representations
papers.abstract: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: https://github.com/kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM.
papers.summary: Video-language models built on world-model encoders such as `V-JEPA` tend to ignore the motion information those encoders carry: a linear probe reads speed from frozen features at 87% while the full model answers at chance. The authors show that dynamics sit in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders but not for frame-wise, text-aligned ones such as `SigLIP`, and they build counterfactual supervision from pixel transformations that produce answer-balanced video variants differing only in the change. Trained in one stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, the `V-JEPA-LM` models lead every size class on average across eleven video benchmarks, with **the 4B model scoring 72.1 against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model**.

papers.title: PaperCritic: Training AI Reviewers to Assess the Soundness of Papers
papers.abstract: As AI conference submissions grow rapidly, AI reviewers are being considered as an alternative. However, simply imitating human reviewing is problematic because reviewing serves multiple purposes, including evaluating papers' soundness, interestingness, and clarity, the last two of which are subjective. In this work, we focus solely on evaluating soundness, the most important and objective criterion, and define the learning objective as jointly maximizing (1) precision, based on the soundness and substantiveness of review points, and (2) recall, the coverage of high-quality reference review points. Under this problem formulation, we construct a quality-labeled review point dataset, PaperSound-23K, using 1K ICLR submissions and 23K human-written and LLM-generated review points. Using this dataset, we train an AI reviewer model, PaperCritic, through reinforcement learning with the F1 score of precision and recall as the reward. Our experiments show that PaperCritic outperforms frontier models and models trained with other AI reviewer training methods on an in-domain test set. Surprisingly, learning to review ICLR submissions also transfers to reviewing Nature-family papers and even to out-of-domain reviewing tasks (e.g., code review, legal contract review, and feedback on story writing).
papers.summary: Rather than imitating human peer review as a whole, this work restricts AI reviewing to soundness and defines the objective as jointly maximizing precision (sound, substantive review points) and recall (coverage of high-quality reference points). The authors build `PaperSound-23K`, a quality-labeled dataset of 23K human-written and LLM-generated review points on 1K ICLR submissions, and train the reviewer model `PaperCritic` with reinforcement learning using the F1 score as reward. It outperforms frontier models and other AI-reviewer training methods on an in-domain test set, and **the skill transfers to Nature-family papers and to out-of-domain tasks such as code review, legal contract review, and story feedback**.

papers.title: BLiMP-RO: A Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs for Romanian
papers.abstract: Evaluating grammatical knowledge in language models requires benchmarks that cover diverse linguistic phenomena and are validated against human judgments. We introduce BLiMP-RO, a Romanian minimal-pair benchmark covering 50 grammatical phenomena across ten domains. It comprises 493 linguist-constructed sentence pairs, evaluated by native speakers in five experiments, and 5,942 additional semi-automatically generated, human-validated pairs. We further investigate grammatical generalization under limited linguistic input by training GPT-2 and GPT-BERT models from scratch on Romanian BabyBabelLM data and a newly collected corpus of 10 million words from child-targeted video captions. Increasing caption training data yields approximately 9 percentage points of accuracy improvement per tenfold increase in corpus size. At matched data sizes, BabyBabelLM generally outperforms video captions, while GPT-BERT consistently outperforms GPT-2. Our findings highlight how training data quantity, composition, and model architecture shape grammatical generalization in Romanian.
papers.summary: `BLiMP-RO` is a Romanian minimal-pair benchmark for testing grammatical knowledge in language models, covering 50 phenomena across ten domains with 493 linguist-constructed sentence pairs validated by native speakers and 5,942 semi-automatically generated, human-validated pairs. The authors also train `GPT-2` and `GPT-BERT` from scratch on Romanian `BabyBabelLM` data and a new 10-million-word corpus of child-targeted video captions. More caption data yields **about 9 percentage points of accuracy per tenfold increase in corpus size**, while `BabyBabelLM` generally beats captions at matched sizes and `GPT-BERT` consistently beats `GPT-2`.

papers.title: Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors
papers.abstract: Abliteration, a fine-tuning-free weight edit, removes refusal from open-weight large language models (LLMs). The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimisation-based variant, reports that direction-based abliteration, which ablates a refusal direction, increasingly fails on newer models. On five release pairs, refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B and Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B and Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409 and Mistral-Small-3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3.5-4B were edited in Heretic 2.0 by three or four direction-based methods (difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM and, on the small pair, J-space) and ARA under the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL divergence cap and selection rule; removal counted as harder when the automatic WildGuard judge found more of 972 held-out harmful prompts (JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench and an author-compiled malicious-code bank) still refused. After direction-based removal, newer releases retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal, and after ARA -26 to +34. With run-to-run variance included, between-pair heterogeneity of the direction-based effect ranged from high to low with the scale and variance model (I^2 20-80%). ARA lost less effectiveness than direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo and more in Qwen; each verdict rests on one ARA run, and some changed with the divergence budget or variance model. In Gemma the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets. Contrary to prediction, keyword counts at the tool's window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by a mean 7 points per model. Audits of a single pair, method or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions. Whether a newer model resisted removal depended on the release pair, method and budget, not on generation alone.
papers.summary: Abliteration is a fine-tuning-free weight edit that removes refusal behavior from open-weight models, and the developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (`ARA`) has reported that simpler direction-based variants increasingly fail on newer models. This study tests that claim on five old-versus-new release pairs from the `Qwen`, `Gemma`, `OLMo`, and `Mistral Small` families, applying direction-based methods and `ARA` in `Heretic 2.0` under matched settings and judging 972 held-out harmful prompts with `WildGuard`. Newer releases retained **-1 to +37 percentage points more refusal after direction-based removal and -26 to +34 after `ARA`**, so resistance depended on the release pair, method, and budget rather than on model generation alone. Audits of a single pair, method, or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions.

papers.title: Electrocardiographic Imaging via Posterior Sampling under Operator Discrepancy
papers.abstract: Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface potentials, an ill-posed inverse problem. Diffusion posterior samplers combine a learned prior with an explicit forward operator that they assume to be accurate. In ECGI this operator is only an estimate, because the body changes with respiration and posture, and body composition such as subcutaneous fat is rarely known for an individual patient. The resulting operator discrepancy is structured and depends on the heart signal. We introduce OpDis-PS, a diffusion posterior sampler that models this discrepancy instead of treating it as signal-independent noise. OpDis-PS learns how the discrepancy depends on the signal, folds this into a corrected forward operator, and reconstructs with a fixed prior across all operator conditions. We study two realistic sources of discrepancy, changing lung conductivity and an added subcutaneous-fat layer. Across both, OpDis-PS reconstructs more accurately than classical regularization and learned predictors, with its largest gains on held-out cardiac pathologies.
papers.summary: Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface measurements, an ill-posed inverse problem in which the forward operator is only an estimate because respiration, posture, and body composition vary between and within patients. `OpDis-PS` is a diffusion posterior sampler that learns how this operator discrepancy depends on the heart signal and folds it into a corrected forward operator while keeping a fixed prior across operator conditions. Tested with changing lung conductivity and an added subcutaneous-fat layer, it **reconstructs more accurately than classical regularization and learned predictors**, with the largest gains on held-out cardiac pathologies.

papers.title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Ni\~{n}o Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents
papers.abstract: The predictability of the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Ni\~{n}o, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Ni\~{n}o development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.
papers.summary: Forecast errors for the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) are usually attributed to large-scale errors in initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Applying the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (`CNOP`) method to a differentiable ocean AI model, the authors show that **these large-scale errors can originate from mesoscale ocean-current errors in the initial state**. The most influential errors are event-dependent, arising in the eastern Pacific for the 1997/98 El Niño and the western Pacific for 2015/16, and they alter eddy count and eddy kinetic energy in ways that hinder El Niño development. The timing of fastest error growth aligns with the known spring predictability barrier.

papers.title: DECODE: Diagnosing Interpretability Failures in Automated Interpretation Process
papers.abstract: Tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on LLMs themselves to both generate and evaluate explanations, creating a self-referential automated interpretation process with minimal human oversight. This automation raises significant reliability concerns, which are exacerbated by the absence of ground truth. In practice, it is difficult to validate explanations or to attribute interpretability failures to their source -- whether they originate from the tool's extracted representations or from the LLM used in the process. To address these challenges, we present DECODE, a visual analytics system that reintroduces human oversight into the automated interpretation process. Our approach decomposes the diagnostic workflow into three progressive stages, isolating failure sources ranging from structural defects to explanation-level misalignments. Drawing inspiration from inter-coder consensus in qualitative analysis, we utilize consensus among independently generated explanations and their evaluation metrics as a proxy for reliability. To further scale human inspection, we employ a three-phase active seeding protocol that strategically recommends high-priority instances for manual review. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features, showing that it can efficiently identify and attribute interpretability failures at scale.
