papers.summary: Automated interpretability pipelines increasingly use LLMs both to generate and to evaluate explanations of model internals, which makes it hard to tell whether a bad explanation stems from the extracted representations or from the explaining LLM. `DECODE` is a visual analytics system that brings human oversight back into this loop through a three-stage diagnostic workflow that separates structural defects from explanation-level misalignments. It uses consensus among independently generated explanations and their evaluation metrics as a reliability proxy, plus a three-phase active seeding protocol that recommends high-priority instances for manual review. A case study on **16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features** shows it can identify and attribute interpretability failures at scale.

papers.title: Fuse-All MoE Inference Kernel with Load Balancing on TPUs
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures activate only a subset of experts for each token, allowing large language models (LLMs) to scale parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation per token. However, intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads limit the efficiency of MoE inference on TPUs. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce Fuse-All MoE, a TPU kernel design that jointly optimizes expert computation, output communication, and load balancing. The kernel fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes, retaining expert computation intermediates on chip. Fixed token-slot destinations allow scheduling and expert placement to change while preserving routing semantics. In prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving, Fuse-All MoE balances EP16 prefill workloads through scheduling and expert redistribution, while symmetric EP8TP2 shares active expert computation between the two TensorCore devices within each chip during decode. Our experiments show that Fuse-All MoE reduces kernel runtime for a measured skewed EP16 prefill workload from 2.3x to 1.09x the same fixed reference time for a balanced workload. Across 32-512 decode tokens, symmetric EP8TP2 reduces kernel latency by up to 21.3% relative to fused EP16. With accompanying serving stack optimizations, the integrated system improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models activate only some experts per token, but on TPUs their inference is slowed by intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads. `Fuse-All MoE` is a TPU kernel that fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes so intermediates stay on chip, and uses fixed token-slot destinations so scheduling and expert placement can change without altering routing. For a skewed prefill workload it cuts kernel runtime from 2.3x to 1.09x of a balanced reference, and a symmetric decode configuration lowers kernel latency by up to 21.3%. With accompanying serving-stack optimizations, the integrated system **improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the `Megablox` EP16 baseline**.

papers.title: AI-aided Decision-Making in Education - Uncertainty, Explainability, and Human Responsibility
papers.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based systems have become increasingly integrated into various aspects of everyday life, including education, understanding how these systems make decisions is of paramount importance. AI holds significant potential to enhance educational practices through the facilitation of personalized and adaptive learning, automation of assessment procedures, and assistance with administrative tasks. However, the opacity of AI-based decision-making in education (especially with deep learning and generative AI models) can hamper decision-making, especially when outcomes appear unjustified or incorrect. In this chapter, we argue that three key principles (uncertainty, explainability, and human responsibility) are essential for the legitimate use of AI in educational settings. Acknowledging the inherent uncertainties in AI-based decisions, analogous to those in human decision-making, is fundamental. Explainability is critical for ensuring that the functioning and outcomes of AI applications are transparent and comprehensible to both educators and learners. Furthermore, human responsibility is crucial, particularly in human decision-making, which remains indispensable across all stages of AI development and deployment. By examining these three principles, this chapter provides a comprehensive guide for stakeholders seeking to integrate AI thoughtfully and effectively into the educational system.
papers.summary: AI systems used in education for personalized learning, automated assessment, and administrative tasks often make decisions that are opaque, which is a problem when outcomes appear unjustified or incorrect. This book chapter argues that **three principles (uncertainty, explainability, and human responsibility) are essential for the legitimate use of AI in educational settings**. It discusses acknowledging the uncertainty inherent in AI-based decisions, making system behavior comprehensible to educators and learners, and keeping humans responsible throughout development and deployment, and is framed as a guide for stakeholders.

papers.title: FlexCast: Flexible Context Learning for Time Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) based on autoregressive (AR) next-token prediction entangle two factors: variable-context conditioning and prediction-unit factorization with autoregressive rollout. Strong AR performance therefore does not reveal whether generalization stems from the flexible training distribution, the local prediction target, the left-to-right inference process, or their combination. We propose FlexCast, a flexible context-target learning framework that disentangles these factors. FlexCast reformulates forecasting as variable-length masked prediction over time series patches: during pretraining, it dynamically samples visible context and masked target patches, exposing the model to diverse context-target configurations without sequential decoding. At inference time, the same pretrained model supports one-step forecasting, confidence-based iterative refinement, and next-token-style generation through a unified mask-and-predict interface, enabling controlled comparison of inference schedules under identical architecture, data, and objective. Evaluated on BLAST and multiple zero-shot benchmarks, FlexCast achieves accuracy competitive with or better than strong TSFM baselines while substantially reducing inference latency. Ablations confirm that context diversity and contiguous target masking drive performance, while left-to-right decoding does not yield consistent gains once flexible context-target relationships have been learned, suggesting that the key benefit of AR-style TSFMs lies in flexible training rather than sequential inference. The code is available at https://github.com/BenchCouncil/FlexCast.
papers.summary: Autoregressive time series foundation models (TSFMs) mix together variable-context training, the local prediction target, and left-to-right decoding, so it is unclear which of these drives their generalization. `FlexCast` recasts forecasting as variable-length masked prediction over time series patches, sampling visible context and masked targets during pretraining and supporting one-step, iterative-refinement, and next-token-style inference from the same model. On `BLAST` and several zero-shot benchmarks it matches or beats strong baselines with substantially lower inference latency. Ablations indicate that **the benefit of autoregressive-style models comes from flexible training rather than sequential inference**, since left-to-right decoding gives no consistent gain.

papers.title: Disentangling Forgetting from Utility: Lightweight LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Null-Space Projection
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) pose significant security risks by retaining private or hazardous information, creating an urgent need for unlearning techniques that excise specific knowledge without compromising general utility. However, prevailing fine-tuning-based unlearning methods struggle to achieve this balance, often suffering from computational inefficiency and unintended utility degradation due to the entangled nature of knowledge within model parameters. To disentangle forgetting from utility, we propose UUE, a theoretically grounded framework that reformulates unlearning as controllable model editing. First, UUE projects parameter updates into the orthogonal left null space of retained knowledge representations, strictly ensuring that the editing process causes minimal interference to the model's general capabilities. Second, distinct from targeted mapping, we introduce a convex untargeted objective that derives a closed-form analytical solution to effectively disrupt undesired knowledge by pushing forget-set embeddings toward their antipodal points. We implement UUE via lightweight, pluggable adapters (including a low-rank variant, UUE-L), enabling efficient deployment without modifying the frozen backbone. Extensive experiments on TOFU and WMDP benchmarks demonstrate that UUE and UUE-L achieve superior unlearning efficacy, significantly outperforming existing methods.
papers.summary: Removing private or hazardous knowledge from an LLM through fine-tuning is computationally costly and tends to degrade general capabilities, because knowledge is entangled across parameters. `UUE` reformulates unlearning as model editing: it projects parameter updates into the left null space of retained-knowledge representations to limit interference, and uses a convex untargeted objective with a closed-form solution that pushes forget-set embeddings toward their antipodal points. Implemented as pluggable adapters on a frozen backbone, including a low-rank variant `UUE-L`, it is reported to **outperform existing unlearning methods on the `TOFU` and `WMDP` benchmarks**.

papers.title: Active Learning of Temporal Specifications through Distinguishing Queries
papers.abstract: Temporal specifications are essential for verification and monitoring, yet writing formulas that capture the intended behaviour is difficult. Active learning derives such specifications through interaction between a learner and a teacher, but remains underexplored for temporal logics. Existing approaches require the teacher to answer equivalence queries and to construct counterexamples, and they often rely on SAT-based learning procedures that restart the search after each new example. We present an active-learning framework for LTLf in which the teacher only labels traces and answers natural-language questions about the intended behaviour. The learner maintains an enumerated version space of candidate formulas, generates traces that distinguish candidates, and uses the teacher's hints to rank candidates or to restrict the search. We prove consistency with the observed examples, identification within bounded hypothesis classes with a bound on the number of queries, and a PAC guarantee for the final hypothesis. In experiments with a simulated teacher on 36 targets, including targets in four standard environments, the learner identifies every target when it compares all rivals, with fewer than seven queries beyond an initial sample of ten traces on average. Correct hints reduce the number of queries by up to 16% and the number of generated candidates by a fifth, and hints used for ranking never prevent identification, even when incorrect. Our enumeration-based version space is faster than the SAT-based approach of previous learners at every target size.
papers.summary: Writing temporal-logic formulas that capture intended behaviour is hard, and existing active learners require a teacher who can answer equivalence queries and construct counterexamples. The proposed framework for `LTLf` asks the teacher only to label traces and answer natural-language questions, while the learner keeps an enumerated version space of candidate formulas, generates traces that distinguish them, and uses hints to rank or prune candidates. The authors prove consistency, bounded-query identification, and a PAC guarantee. With a simulated teacher on 36 targets, the learner **identifies every target with fewer than seven queries on average beyond an initial sample of ten traces**, and its enumeration approach is faster than the SAT-based alternative at every target size.

papers.title: UltraBERT-JEV: Encoder models for System One Applications
papers.abstract: We study encoder models that pick one of several options in a single forward pass, without generating text. This technical report compares recipes for fine-tuning UltraBERT-380M with one mask per option. The four recipes differ in how an option is scored and how the scores become probabilities; one follows the expert gate of DeepSeek-V3. Trained on the same data as Qwen3-0.6B with the LLM-as-Jev recipe (67.6% test accuracy), the encoder reaches 69.7% to 72.1%. Scoring an option by "yes" minus "no" instead of "yes" alone gives the larger gain, from 69.7% to 71.3% on the test set and from 57.8% to 59.6% on external benchmarks (56.1% for the decoder). Sigmoid normalisation adds 0.8 test points; a square-root softplus adds none. One request at a time on an NVIDIA A100, the encoder takes 29 ms per decision against 68 ms, but uses more peak memory (2.8 against 2.2 GiB). An auxiliary head, trained on human-marked evidence and on labels selected with a reward adapted from SelfCite, predicts in the same pass the sentences annotated as support for the answer.
papers.summary: Encoder models that choose among several options in a single forward pass, without generating text, are compared across four fine-tuning recipes for `UltraBERT-380M` that differ in how each option is scored and how scores become probabilities. Trained on the same data as a `Qwen3-0.6B` decoder using the `LLM-as-Jev` recipe (67.6% test accuracy), the encoder reaches **69.7% to 72.1% accuracy while taking 29 ms per decision against 68 ms** on an NVIDIA A100, though with higher peak memory (2.8 versus 2.2 GiB). Scoring an option by yes minus no rather than yes alone gives the largest gain, and an auxiliary head trained with a reward adapted from `SelfCite` predicts supporting evidence sentences in the same pass.

papers.title: Process Mining-Enabled Federated Anomaly Detection for the Industrial IoT
papers.abstract: While federated anomaly detection enables the integration of local data insights across diverse nodes to reduce false positives, it inherently struggles with non-IID data. In practice, industrial IoT plants often operate under varying conditions and experience diverse environmental phenomena, resulting in significant heterogeneity in the monitored time series. In such settings, standard federated learning approaches fail to perform nuanced aggregation that accounts for these cross-node differences, ultimately leading to increased false positive rates. In this paper, we propose a process mining approach to evaluate the similarity of local node data against a reference provided by a global node. The global node utilizes these similarity metrics to dynamically weight local models during aggregation, producing personalized updates distributed across the network. We evaluate our approach using industrial IoT time-series data collected from manufacturing plants operating under distinct conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that our process mining-enabled federated anomaly detection pipeline achieves superior performance, yielding a 46.52% and 11.99% relative improvement in F1-score compared to isolated local training baselines and standard FedAvg, respectively, alongside a 51.24% relative reduction in false positives over standard federated aggregation.
papers.summary: Federated anomaly detection across industrial IoT plants suffers when sites operate under different conditions, because standard aggregation ignores this heterogeneity and false positives rise. The proposed pipeline uses process mining to measure how similar each local node's data is to a reference from the global node, then weights local models by that similarity to produce personalized updates. On time-series data from manufacturing plants, it reports a **51.24% relative reduction in false positives over standard federated aggregation**, with F1-score improvements of 46.52% over isolated local training and 11.99% over `FedAvg`.

papers.title: OmniScore-Bench: Evaluating Vision-Language Models on Musical Score Reading
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about musical scores, but their ability to recognise notation, recover its structure and interpret its musical meaning requires separate evaluation. Existing optical music recognition (OMR) resources establish detection and transcription measurements; a transcription score alone leaves the strengths and bottlenecks of a VLM score reader unresolved. We introduce OmniScore-Bench, an evaluation of OMR capabilities in VLMs through 3,000 questions spanning six aspects and 24 task subtypes. Each question specifies a visible scope, reference annotations and an answer schema, enabling automatic evaluation from symbol localisation to musical consistency and evidence-linked question answering. Our assessment of twelve VLMs reveals operation-specific capability profiles and different transcription leaders across excerpt, single-page and multipage tasks. Controlled analyses examine the roles of score images, auxiliary givens and additional page context. On the tested subset, image removal exposes visual dependence in pitch and repeat interpretation while measuring how much performance remains with public context alone. Separate format and content analyses distinguish answer-format violations from musical errors. OmniScore-Bench supports diagnosing which score-reading operations VLMs perform reliably and which require improvement.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about musical scores, but a single transcription metric does not show where their score reading succeeds or fails. `OmniScore-Bench` evaluates optical music recognition (OMR) abilities through 3,000 questions covering six aspects and 24 task subtypes, each with a defined visible scope, reference annotations, and an answer schema for automatic grading. Testing twelve VLMs shows operation-specific capability profiles and **different transcription leaders across excerpt, single-page, and multipage tasks**. Ablations that remove the image expose visual dependence in pitch and repeat interpretation, and separate analyses distinguish answer-format violations from musical errors.

papers.title: Protection-Oriented Assessment of Machine Learning-Based Fault Detection in Power Systems
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML)-based fault detectors are increasingly proposed for power system protection, yet aggregate metrics can obscure the consequences of false and missed trips. We present a protection-oriented assessment of three ML detectors and a sequence-current reference on PROTECT-90, comprising 9,022 simulated fault episodes on a 90 kV double-circuit line. The assessment combines five window conditions, causal window-end labelling, episode-grouped cross-validation, and operating-point selection under a fixed security budget. It reports security, dependability, detection timing, decision margins, and episode-level nuisance assertions. Gradient-boosted trees, a convolutional neural network, and logistic regression achieve AUC-ROC values above 0.999, yet at a security budget of $10^{-3}$ their developed-fault missed-trip rates range from 0.007% to 1.99%. Post-clearing false-trip rates of approximately 0.12-0.16% per window coexist with nuisance assertions in 11.3-19.1% of episodes. Among the analysed physical descriptors, missed trips are most consistently associated with higher fault resistance within the sampled range. An analytical current proxy suggests a fault-current gradient only partly reproduced by waveform-derived current (rank correlation 0.62). No single topology state or faulted phase consistently dominates within the sampled domain. Because PROTECT-90 contains fault episodes only, security is assessed on pre-fault and post-clearing windows rather than independent non-fault disturbances.
papers.summary: Machine learning (ML) fault detectors for power system protection are usually judged by aggregate metrics that hide the cost of false and missed trips. Three detectors (gradient-boosted trees, a convolutional neural network, and logistic regression) plus a sequence-current reference are assessed on `PROTECT-90`, a set of 9,022 simulated fault episodes on a 90 kV double-circuit line, using episode-grouped cross-validation and operating points chosen under a fixed security budget. Although all three models exceed 0.999 AUC-ROC, at a security budget of 0.001 their **missed-trip rates on developed faults range from 0.007% to 1.99%, and nuisance assertions occur in 11.3% to 19.1% of episodes**. Missed trips are most consistently associated with higher fault resistance.

papers.title: Delayed Effects of Temporary Weight Decay in Muon Pretraining
papers.abstract: A temporary optimization intervention can increase validation loss when it ends yet reduce it at the final training budget. We demonstrate this with temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers with 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 3.4B parameters. For models up to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect. At 162M, changing window duration alters final loss even at approximately matched total shrinkage. Most strikingly, a schedule selected at 162M and transferred without retuning to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay when removed, overtakes it only after 73% of training, and ultimately finishes 0.028 nats better while also outperforming the best sampled constant-decay baseline. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger after the intervention ends. An approximate norm-dynamics recurrence captures the slow convergence of these relative steps, and fixed-norm replays of the measured trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference. At 162M and 405M, norm-reset experiments show that smaller weight norms at the end of the decay window explain most of the final loss improvement. A separate Gram intervention exhibits related post-removal norm and relative-step dynamics. These results show that temporary optimization schedules can have delayed effects long after removal and should therefore be evaluated at the intended final training budget, not only at removal.
papers.summary: A temporary optimization intervention can look harmful when it ends yet help by the end of training, shown here with temporary weight decay in decoder-only Transformers of 162M to 3.4B parameters trained with the `Muon` optimizer. A decay schedule selected at 162M and transferred unchanged to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay at removal, overtakes it only after 73% of training, and **finishes 0.028 nats better while also beating the best sampled constant-decay baseline**. The mechanism is a persistent weight-norm deficit that keeps relative step sizes larger after the decay ends, which norm-reset and fixed-norm replay experiments support. The authors conclude that such schedules should be evaluated at the final training budget rather than at the point of removal.

papers.title: DySENSE: Dynamic Spatiotemporal ENergy Synthesis and Emulation with Satellite Imagery
papers.abstract: Cities account for over two-thirds of the world's energy and more than 70% of global carbon dioxide emissions. City energy is essential for achieving the 2050 net-zero target and the UN's Sustainable Development Goals 7 and 11. Although existing studies have made progress, they are limited by data and methodological gaps. Existing studies are largely predictive for existing cities rather than generative for future cities; fine-grained, aligned monthly dynamic energy data are scarce; and existing GenAI models struggle to generate dynamic urban functional monthly energy. We present DySENSE, a joint multimodal GenAI framework that synthesizes static urban satellite imagery together with spatially aligned, dynamic monthly building energy consumption maps. We decouple long-term static urban morphology from short-term dynamic energy consumption. By conditioning on static urban land use, DySENSE can generate realistic, diverse and new static urban imagery with aligned energy maps. By conditioning on dynamic monthly and climate prompts, DySENSE can jointly generate dynamic, monthly energy consumption maps while keeping the urban morphology static. Experiments across four cities (New York, Washington, Norfolk, Busan) demonstrated that DySENSE can generate annotated high-fidelity synthetic energy data using less than 25% labelled data, boosting downstream prediction performance by 8% mIoU, and achieving strong energy dynamic consistency. Compared to existing methods, DySENSE significantly improved prediction performance (8.7% accuracy) and reduced prediction error (9%-18% CVRMSE, ASHRAE). DySENSE offers an effective foundation for energy-efficient cities, peak-load analysis, building performance simulation and dynamic demand response for city, energy, and building science. The data and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/skl24/MUSE2 and https://github.com/kailaisun/DySENSE
papers.summary: Fine-grained, spatially aligned monthly data on urban building energy use is scarce, and existing generative models struggle to produce it. `DySENSE` is a joint multimodal generative framework that synthesizes satellite imagery together with aligned monthly building energy consumption maps, separating static urban morphology (conditioned on land use) from dynamic energy use (conditioned on month and climate prompts). Across New York, Washington, Norfolk, and Busan, it generates annotated synthetic energy data from **less than 25% labelled data while raising downstream prediction performance by 8% mIoU**, and reduces prediction error by 9% to 18% CVRMSE compared with existing methods.

papers.title: From Local Prediction Error to Final Outputs: A Theory of Expert Sharing in Multi-Step Reasoning
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can share experts across layers or computational steps, pooling training information from different contexts. This can reduce local prediction error, but multi-step systems are ultimately evaluated by their final outputs. We study when these local gains survive composition. In specified linear regression models, we derive exact sharing and merging criteria by balancing variance savings against bias from sharing across roles with different target behavior. Under a common fixed linear propagation map, we characterize expected squared final-output risk, retaining error directions and correlations. We construct cases where sharing lowers average local error yet increases final-output error. Within this setting, we also identify when orthogonal full pooling with isotropic noise preserves every local improvement at the final output. For general routed computations, we derive conditional end-to-end error bounds that account for distribution shifts, errors in surrounding components, and changes in expert selection. Separately, we show that correct predictions and route labels alone do not establish that individual experts implement the attributed operations. Controlled experiments realize a strict local-to-final risk reversal. In low-data symbolic settings, trained Transformers exhibit statistically supported teacher-forced one-step gains without statistically resolved free-running final-output gains. Separate intervention tests distinguish successful multi-layer actions from single-expert attribution and generalization to unseen transitions. Together, these results distinguish when sharing improves local estimation, when those gains survive to the final output, and what evidence is needed to attribute reusable operations to individual experts.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can share experts across layers or computational steps to reduce local prediction error, but it is unclear when those gains carry through to a multi-step system's final output. In linear regression settings the authors derive exact criteria for sharing and merging that balance variance savings against bias, characterize final-output risk under a fixed linear propagation map, and give conditional end-to-end error bounds for general routed computations. They **construct cases where sharing lowers average local error yet increases final-output error**, and controlled experiments realize this reversal. In low-data symbolic tasks, trained Transformers show statistically supported one-step gains under teacher forcing without resolved gains in free-running final outputs.

papers.title: Soteria: Formally Verified Planning with Runtime Enforcement for Safe LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents that execute multi-step tool calls must satisfy two objectives simultaneously: completing the user's task (utility) and conforming to domain policies and correctness constraints (safety). These objectives are in tension -- blocking an unsafe action prevents a violation but can leave the agent stranded with no principled way to recover. Existing approaches sacrifice one objective for the other. We introduce Soteria, a framework that reconciles safety and utility through verified hierarchical planning and runtime enforcement of specifications. Before execution, the agent generates a structured plan that is formally verified against the specifications prior to any tool invocation. During execution, the verified plan serves dual roles: it ensures that the agent takes specification-conformant trajectories and provides guidance when unsafe actions are blocked. Across multiple benchmarks covering a diverse range of tool-use tasks, Soteria achieves 1.7 times the average task success rate of the best baselines, with no violations of policy specifications, demonstrating that safety and utility need not be traded off.
papers.summary: LLM agents that execute multi-step tool calls must both finish the user's task and comply with domain policies, and blocking an unsafe action can leave the agent stranded with no way to recover. `Soteria` has the agent generate a structured hierarchical plan that is formally verified against the specifications before any tool is invoked, then enforces the specifications at runtime while using the verified plan as guidance when an action is blocked. Across multiple tool-use benchmarks it achieves **1.7 times the average task success rate of the best baselines with no policy violations**.

papers.title: Photogrammetric 3D Model-Based Animal Behavior Classification
papers.abstract: Video-based behavior estimation is often implemented end-to-end from image sequences. We advocate a two-stage alternative: reconstruct 3D body and object geometry before classifying behavior. This makes ambiguities of the ill-posed 2D-to-3D inverse problem explicit and potentially correctable. We demonstrate the strategy with simulated interacting mice and extend it to real video.
papers.summary: Video-based behavior estimation is usually done end-to-end from image sequences. The authors instead argue for a two-stage approach that **reconstructs 3D body and object geometry before classifying behavior**, which makes the ambiguities of the 2D-to-3D inverse problem explicit and potentially correctable. The strategy is demonstrated on simulated interacting mice and extended to real video.

papers.title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems by Design
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, delegating the subtasks to agents, and aggregating the agents' responses using an aggregation rule. Malicious agents can manipulate the final solution by providing malicious responses to their assigned subtasks. In this paper, we first propose response manipulation attacks (ReMA), which iteratively optimize malicious responses to maximize attack effectiveness. Specifically, we formulate untargeted and targeted attacks as optimization problems and develop an approach to approximately solve these problems by iteratively refining malicious responses based on feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system. To defend against such attacks, we further propose SecMAS, a secure aggregation rule that leverages the semantic similarities among agent responses to select the response that is most consistent with a sufficiently large subset of the other responses. We theoretically establish security guarantees for SecMAS against both untargeted and targeted attacks. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to ReMA, whereas SecMAS effectively defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants of ReMA, while maintaining utility comparable to that of existing aggregation rules.
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems split a task into subtasks, delegate them to agents, and aggregate the responses, which lets a malicious agent steer the final answer. The authors introduce response manipulation attacks (`ReMA`), which iteratively refine malicious responses using feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system, for both untargeted and targeted goals. As a defense they propose `SecMAS`, an aggregation rule that selects the response most semantically consistent with a sufficiently large subset of the others, and they prove security guarantees for it. In evaluations, existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to `ReMA`, whereas **`SecMAS` defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants, while keeping utility comparable to existing rules**.

papers.title: Quantum Graph Neural Networks: Architectures, Trainability, and Applications
papers.abstract: Quantum graph neural networks (QGNNs) apply parametrized quantum circuits to graph-structured data, with the aim of overcoming limits of classical graph neural networks in scalability, expressivity, and long-range information flow. Since the first Hamiltonian-based model in 2019, the field has produced many architectures, applications, and claims, but the evidence behind them has not been assessed systematically. This survey introduces a unified formalism that describes every QGNN as an encoder, a graph-conditioned circuit, observables, and an optional classical head, together with a circuit-level condition for permutation equivariance and a resource model for comparing costs. We organize the literature into five architecture families (convolutional, equivariant, message-passing and recurrent, Hamiltonian, and hybrid) and compare them by qubit cost, symmetry, scalability, and evidence. We then review symmetry and geometric inductive biases (permutation, rotation, and Lorentz), the results on expressivity, trainability, noise, and scalability, and applications in high-energy physics, chemistry, finance, healthcare, earth observation, and transportation. An audit of datasets and evaluation practices leads to a minimum reporting protocol. Our main finding is that the design space is rich and symmetry is the best-supported inductive bias, whereas the evidence remains thin: results are mostly simulated, on small graphs, at parity with classical models or with fewer parameters, and no advantage has yet been established on tasks over classical graph data. We identify five open challenges and a research agenda covering provable advantage, equivariant and geometric designs, fault-tolerant implementations, and shared benchmarks. The coverage extends through 2026 and emphasizes recent work.
papers.summary: Quantum graph neural networks (QGNNs) apply parametrized quantum circuits to graph-structured data, and the field has accumulated many architectures and claims without a systematic assessment of the evidence. This survey gives a unified formalism (an encoder, a graph-conditioned circuit, observables, and an optional classical head), a circuit-level condition for permutation equivariance, and a resource model, then organizes the literature into five architecture families and reviews expressivity, trainability, noise, and applications. Its main finding is that symmetry is the best-supported inductive bias, but **no advantage over classical models has yet been established on classical graph data**, with results mostly simulated on small graphs. The authors also propose a minimum reporting protocol and list five open challenges.

papers.title: Hierarchical Bayesian physics-augmented neural networks for populations of hyperelastic laws: specimen variability and uncertainty from scarce, noisy data
papers.abstract: The hyperelastic law of a material such as soft tissue differs between specimens, and often only a few specimens can be tested. Physics-augmented neural networks (PANNs) learn such laws from data without a prescribed functional form while keeping them physically admissible, and Bayesian versions of related models quantify the uncertainty of the law of one specimen or of a pooled group of specimens. A pooled fit, however, attributes the differences between specimens to measurement noise or to uncertainty about a mean law, and neither describes a new specimen. We first develop a Bayesian PANN for one specimen, whose priors keep the learned law plausible for few, noisy data. We then extend it to a hierarchical Bayesian PANN, a nonlinear mixed-effects model in which all specimens share learned polyconvex features and each specimen is a draw from a population of laws. Features, specimens, and population are inferred jointly by variational inference, with a separate model of the measurement noise, so that the variability between specimens is not mistaken for noise, the population carries its own uncertainty, and every specimen drawn from it is polyconvex. The population predicts the response of new specimens with credible intervals, without data or from a partial test, and assigns them to cohorts with quantified uncertainty, all without a prescribed form of the law. On synthetic populations, it recovers the population from few specimens and predicts new specimens more reliably than three published methods. On Treloar's rubber and on healthy and aneurysmal aortas, it reaches the accuracy of a deterministic PANN and assigns no aorta specimen to the wrong cohort with confidence, although it underestimates the uncertainty of untested curves.
papers.summary: The hyperelastic law of materials such as soft tissue varies between specimens, and pooled fits misattribute that variation to measurement noise or to uncertainty about a mean law. The authors build a hierarchical Bayesian physics-augmented neural network (PANN), a nonlinear mixed-effects model in which all specimens share learned polyconvex features and each specimen is a draw from a population of laws, fitted jointly by variational inference with a separate noise model. On synthetic populations it recovers the population from few specimens and predicts new specimens more reliably than three published methods. On Treloar's rubber data and on healthy and aneurysmal aortas, it **matches the accuracy of a deterministic PANN and assigns no aorta specimen to the wrong cohort with confidence**, though it underestimates the uncertainty of untested curves.

papers.title: More Genes, Faster Inference: Efficient Large-Panel Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) prediction from histology aims to infer spatially resolved gene expression profiles directly from tissue images. This is a challenging problem that is currently often addressed with complicated model architectures, additional inputs, and complicated training procedures, while remaining limited to fixed, small gene panels. This raises a natural question: Is there an efficient method for large-panel ST prediction? Here, we present GeneFlow, a simpler yet effective framework for large-scale spatial gene expression prediction that unifies flow-matching generative modeling with structured multimodal fusion. Specifically, GeneFlow first encodes both histological morphology and cross-gene interactions in spatial spots through histology and gene tokenizers. The model directly predicts spatial gene expression, rather than an intermediate velocity field, while being trained with a velocity-based flow-matching objective. We show that, even without relying on heavy generative pipelines, GeneFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple ST benchmarks, with up to 56.8% gains in 1,000-gene prediction. Extensive experiments further show that GeneFlow produces biologically meaningful spot profiles while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude, thereby improving efficiency and scalability, particularly in clinical settings. We believe GeneFlow provides an opportunity for leveraging widely available histology images for downstream biological discovery. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZZhangsm/GeneFlow
papers.summary: Predicting spatial transcriptomics (ST), meaning spatially resolved gene expression, from histology images is typically done with complicated architectures and training procedures that remain limited to small, fixed gene panels. `GeneFlow` combines flow-matching generative modeling with multimodal fusion, using histology and gene tokenizers to encode tissue morphology and cross-gene interactions, and predicts expression directly while training with a velocity-based flow-matching objective. The authors report state-of-the-art results across multiple ST benchmarks, with **up to 56.8% gains in 1,000-gene prediction**, alongside a reduction in computational cost of orders of magnitude.

papers.title: AmbiSteer: Selectively Eliciting Ambiguity-Aware Responses in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often exhibit overconfidence, providing firm answers even when visual evidence is insufficient. A prominent case is referential ambiguity in Visual Question Answering (VQA), where multiple entities in an image are plausible referents of a question. Addressing such cases requires recognizing when ambiguity is present: ambiguous questions can be handled by asking for clarification or enumerating plausible referents, while unambiguous questions should receive a direct answer. Current VLMs struggle with this distinction, often defaulting to a single interpretation. To investigate whether activation steering can serve as an inference-time mechanism to elicit such behaviors, we introduce AmbiSteer, a lightweight framework to selectively elicit ambiguity-aware behavior. Across three VLMs, we find that steering alone has limited and model-dependent effects, while prompting is generally more effective. Combining prompting and steering substantially increases clarification and enumeration behaviors, but also elicits them on unambiguous cases. AmbiSteer addresses this using a linear classifier to predict input ambiguity and condition the steering direction accordingly, increasing the proportion of inputs handled appropriately from 59.0% to 77.0% on average across models. Our work sets the ground for lightweight approaches to reduce model overconfidence in uncertain multimodal settings.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often answer confidently when a question in Visual Question Answering (VQA) could refer to several entities in the image, instead of asking for clarification or listing the plausible referents. The study tests activation steering as an inference-time fix and finds that steering alone has limited, model-dependent effects, prompting works better, and combining the two triggers clarification even on unambiguous questions. `AmbiSteer` adds a linear classifier that predicts whether the input is ambiguous and conditions the steering direction on that prediction. Across three VLMs this raises the **share of inputs handled appropriately from 59.0% to 77.0% on average**.

papers.title: Adversarially Attacking Symbolic Vocabulary Vulnerabilities In LLM Planners
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, their abilities in navigating automated planning tasks have become essential. However, despite their strengths, LLMs' planning ability is not robust, particularly when they are not allowed to exploit commonsense cues in the symbolic vocabulary (e.g., names of actions, predicates, and objects) used to define planning tasks. This makes LLMs unreliable compared to symbolic planners. With recent reasoning models showing improved planning performance on tasks with obfuscated symbolic vocabularies, we utilize an adversarial attack framework to reveal to what extent the crucial weaknesses of LLM agents at joint symbolic interpretation and planning remain and whether they can reason properly when presented with severe cases. As such, our main contribution is devising an LLM-based attack model, which we call Symbolic Swapper, to automatically generate obfuscated planning domains with non-standard symbolic vocabularies that systematically break strong reasoning models' ability to plan. In doing so, we reveal how much LLMs' planning abilities can be further degraded under more advanced obfuscation schemes, allowing us to ascertain their success when having to rely on their pure planning ability. We find that attacks can decrease the planning performance of base models and even robust planning frameworks by over 70%. We further analyze the factors behind how LLM planning abilities break down and find that successful obfuscation causes models to appear to significantly degrade in reasoning quality despite them showing some inherent ability to understand the domain, revealing a gap in the perception of a task domain and being able to plan under it.
papers.summary: LLM planning is known to degrade when the names of actions, predicates, and objects in a planning task no longer carry commonsense cues, although recent reasoning models handle obfuscated vocabularies better. The authors build `Symbolic Swapper`, an LLM-based attack model that automatically generates obfuscated planning domains with non-standard symbolic vocabularies designed to break strong reasoning models. The attacks **reduce planning performance of base models and even robust planning frameworks by over 70%**. Further analysis indicates that models retain some ability to understand the obfuscated domain while their reasoning quality degrades, pointing to a gap between perceiving a domain and planning within it.

papers.title: SWIFT: Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning of Time-Series Foundation Models for Forecasting
papers.abstract: While current few-shot adaptation strategies for time series forecasting foundation models are predominantly dataset-centric, the necessity of obtaining an additional dataset for the finetuning process poses a significant hurdle for adoption. To address this constraint, we propose Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a novel forecasting adaptation framework that achieves fine-grained specialization by leveraging structural priors from the target instance's own history. This shift allows the fine-tuning process to be entirely transparent to the end-user, which significantly enhances the ease of adoption. To implement this framework, SWIFT synergizes Self-Retrieval for historical mining and Frequency-Aware Loss for spectral consistency, while employing Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion to balance adaptation with general knowledge preservation. Extensive experiments across four TSFM backbones and three long-history benchmark subsets validate SWIFT, yielding average MASE and WQL reductions of 6.41% and 4.83% across 24 combinations of four backbones and six Chronos Benchmark II datasets. To the best of our knowledge, SWIFT is the first framework to investigate sample-wise instance fine-tuning of time-series foundation models, specializing the model for an individual prediction window using only the corresponding forecasting sample's own observed history.
papers.summary: Few-shot adaptation of time-series foundation models normally requires an additional fine-tuning dataset, which is a barrier to adoption. Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning (`SWIFT`) instead specializes the model for a single prediction window using only that sample's own observed history, combining self-retrieval over the history, a frequency-aware loss, and a deviation-aware fusion step that balances adaptation against the model's general knowledge. Across 24 combinations of four backbones and six `Chronos Benchmark II` datasets, it yields **average reductions of 6.41% in MASE and 4.83% in WQL**.

papers.title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes CARVE.CARVE uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, respectively.The median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.
papers.summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) teams learn coordination conventions that can become obsolete or unsafe when deployment requirements change, and runtime shielding or existing unlearning methods do not remove a convention that different agents can reproduce across different histories. `CARVE` formalizes this as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning, using causal attribution to find influential interactions, retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference, counterfactual re-coordination to learn alternatives, and adversarial auditing to check whether the convention can still be recovered. Across five cooperative MARL benchmarks it **reduces mean convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4% and 83.3% with a median utility loss of 5.9%**, and inference latency matches the original policies.

papers.title: Condensing Law of Security Information
papers.abstract: Scaling laws indicate that the generalization error of a large language model (LLM) decreases monotonically with model size once data is sufficient, and the corollary that larger models outperform smaller ones is now widely accepted. We argue that this corollary fails in security: decisions there hinge on anomalous inputs, which are long-tailed (e.g., zero-day attacks) and therefore poorly served by likelihood fitting. Worse still, the capability brought about by scale (e.g., inferring the intended whole from a corrupted part) leads a LLM silently \emph{repair} the anomaly before any downstream security head ever sees it. We formalize this as a tradeoff between two quantities: the cognitive capability $K(W)=I(W;P)$ that a model holds about the world distribution, and the security-information retention $R(W)=\frac{I(Z;S)}{I(A;S)}$ that survives in its intermediate representation. We derive three information-theoretic bounds to connect them: an upper bound on restoration accuracy in terms of $K(W)$, an upper bound on $R(W)$ in terms of the restoration error, and a Fano lower bound on security-task error in terms of $R(W)$. These theorems approximately imply that usable security information is a product of how much security information survives and how well it can be extracted, indicating that optimal usable security information can be achieved at a certain model size. We state this as the \emph{condensing law of security information}: usable security information is unimodal in model size, so security generalization error is U-shaped and is minimized at a finite $N^{\star}$ rather than decreasing without bound. The experiments on various real-world LLMs validate the condensing law, indicating that there is an optimal model size to solve security issues.
papers.summary: Scaling laws suggest larger language models generalize better, but the authors argue this fails for security tasks, where decisions depend on rare anomalous inputs and a more capable model tends to silently repair the anomaly before a downstream security head sees it. They formalize a tradeoff between a model's cognitive capability and the security information retained in its intermediate representations, and derive three information-theoretic bounds linking the two to security-task error. From these they state a condensing law: **usable security information is unimodal in model size, so security generalization error is U-shaped and minimized at a finite model size**. Experiments on several real-world LLMs are reported as consistent with this claim.

papers.title: RecMem: Recurrent Memory Compression for Long-Sequence Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but the cost of processing them directly grows with history length. We propose RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework guided by three desiderata: space invariance, semantic fidelity, and lifelong evolvability. RecMem compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and slot-wise forget-gated updates. Recommendation supervision trains the memory to preserve predictive information, while stream-consistency training aligns predictions from sequential and packed processing. By construction, the memory state and decoder context are independent of history length; under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency, we further derive a horizon-independent bound on the state discrepancy between these two processing orders. On MerRec, RecMem uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context, compared with 1,200 tokens for HSTU-1200, while retaining 87.9% of HSTU-1200's Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200. It outperforms PHSTU and the evaluated recent-only and retrieval baselines, and analyses of distant history show that archived interactions contribute predictive signal.
papers.summary: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but processing them directly costs more as the history grows. `RecMem` recurrently compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using an encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and forget-gated slot updates, trained with recommendation supervision and a consistency objective that aligns sequential and packed processing. On `MerRec`, it uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context instead of the 1,200 tokens of `HSTU-1200`, while **retaining 87.9% of that model's Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200**. It also outperforms `PHSTU` and the evaluated recent-only and retrieval baselines.

papers.title: TIDE: Reclaiming Lost Performance In On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Synchronous, colocated RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) today suffers from severe under-utilization due to long-tail rollouts. Inference engines fall idle waiting for long-tail rollouts or decode at low, inefficient batch sizes. To address this, we present TIDE, an RL training system that preserves on-policy training semantics while recovering resource utilization. TIDE does so by two complementary techniques: (1) dynamically repurposing rollout GPUs for training while long-tail rollouts complete and (2) dynamically migrating rollouts between inference engines to boost decoding throughput. TIDE automatically determines the right time to repurpose rollout resources through an adaptive migration policy, obtaining performance improvements that generalize across multiple applications and hardware configurations without requiring bespoke configuration. In our evaluation, TIDE provides end-to-end speedups of up to 1.36x over colocated systems, outperforming all evaluated on-policy baselines and achieving up to 97% of optimal throughput.
papers.summary: Synchronous, colocated reinforcement-learning post-training of large language models wastes GPU capacity because inference engines sit idle or decode at small batch sizes while a few long-tail rollouts finish. `TIDE` keeps on-policy semantics but repurposes rollout GPUs for training during that tail and migrates rollouts between inference engines to raise decoding throughput, with an adaptive policy choosing when to switch. The evaluation reports **end-to-end speedups of up to 1.36x over colocated systems**, reaching up to 97% of optimal throughput and beating all evaluated on-policy baselines.

papers.title: What Balanced Accuracy Cannot Identify in Neural-Signal Decoding under Test-Time Adaptation
papers.abstract: Adaptation for neural-signal classification is usually transductive: each batch is scored after updating on it, and the gain depends on the adapted model [4]. This paper asks what an aggregate change fails to characterise inside the cohort. Full test-time adaptation (full_ttt) was evaluated in 11 dataset-encoder cells (four each on Siena/EEG and PTB-XL/ECG, three on Sleep-EDF/EEG), with splits and source-model evaluation fixed; the subject was the unit, exact sign tests were Holm-corrected and conditional on the shared stream, and bootstrap intervals accompanied a dependence audit. Two results of different kinds follow. In the binary case balanced accuracy gives a one-class decoder the same value as one reporting both classes at 50%, so the aggregate cannot identify a class that stopped being reported; a class covering a tenth of a subject's samples went unpredicted in 26-47 of 112 subject-cells, against 7-9 for the controls, which is a descriptive count. With cohort, split and update rule fixed, the within-subject class contrast follows the encoder, tested directly rather than inferred from tests against zero: two of six Siena encoder pairs survive the dependence readings at their nominal reference and one at a fold-level reference, while two of ten Sleep-EDF stage pairs pass the run-clustered gate at its nominal reference; aggregate and contrast named different encoders in 10 of 11. The protocol bounds both results, since a stream-interleaving effect reverses sign with state sharing (+3.5 to -2.4 pp). An aggregate score can hide individual harm, as [1] showed, but it cannot distinguish a uniform loss from a deleted class; class-level change should therefore be reported alongside the aggregate and subject-level change alongside it, with both results conditional on the cell, the rule and the stream construction.
papers.summary: Aggregate balanced accuracy is examined as a measure of test-time adaptation for neural-signal classifiers, using full test-time adaptation across 11 dataset-encoder combinations on `Siena` (EEG), `PTB-XL` (ECG) and `Sleep-EDF` (EEG) with the subject as the statistical unit. In the binary case, balanced accuracy scores a decoder that predicts only one class the same as one that reports both classes at 50%, so it cannot reveal that a class has stopped being predicted. A class covering a tenth of a subject's samples **went unpredicted in 26-47 of 112 subject-cells, against 7-9 for the controls**, and the aggregate score and the within-subject class contrast favored different encoders in 10 of 11 cells. The authors recommend reporting class-level and subject-level change alongside the aggregate.

papers.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Scientific Paper Search: Retrieval Success and Inference Latency on Mac Studio and NVIDIA A100
papers.abstract: Scientific literature search can benefit from locally deployed LLM assistants, which reduce reliance on hosted model providers while giving research teams greater control over their data and infrastructure. This work investigates whether open-weight models can support web-assisted paper retrieval under practical computing constraints. We first characterize inference latency as the input context grows from 512 to 128k tokens on a Mac Studio and a server equipped with two NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We then evaluate eight models on the retrieval of 70 papers from seven scientific repositories, using queries that represent three levels of domain knowledge. The results show that retrieval success depends strongly on the selected model and the specificity of the query. And that A100 GPUs are generally faster than the Mac Studio, but its unified memory allows larger models that could not be loaded in the tested GPU configuration.
papers.summary: Open-weight language models are tested as locally deployed assistants for web-assisted scientific paper search under practical hardware limits. Inference latency is measured as input context grows from 512 to 128k tokens on a `Mac Studio` and on a server with two `NVIDIA A100` GPUs, and eight models are then evaluated on retrieving 70 papers from seven repositories using queries at three levels of domain knowledge. Retrieval success depends strongly on the model and on query specificity, and **the A100s are generally faster while the Mac Studio's unified memory can load larger models that did not fit in the tested GPU configuration**.

papers.title: MineralExp: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Experimental Design in Real-World Mineral Exploration
papers.abstract: In mineral exploration, verifying geological hypotheses relies on designing a variety of geochemical experiments. While large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate downstream geoscientific data analysis, a crucial upstream capability remains largely unexplored: automated geochemical experimental design, i.e., deciding which experiments to conduct before committing to costly laboratory work. Evaluating this capability of LLM agents is difficult for two reasons. First, geochemical experiments exhibit high methodological diversity and subjectivity: to test the same hypothesis, different geologists may choose different minerals and instruments, so no single protocol can serve as the reference answer. Second, open-ended experimental plans resist representation as structured labels, which makes objective scoring difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce MineralExp, a benchmark that reformulates geochemical experimental design as a hypothesis-based experiment selection problem, i.e., a multi-label classification problem. We abstract concrete instrument names and procedural details into a shared taxonomy of 19 experimental types across five mineral-system processes: Source, Transport, Deposition, Modification, and Preservation. This taxonomy yields deterministic multi-label targets while accommodating diverse experimental protocols. Constructed from published ore-deposit literature and verified by domain experts, MineralExp comprises 277 cases and 1,572 reference experimental plans. Given a geological hypothesis and initial context, an LLM agent selects the relevant tasks and generates concrete experimental plans, which are scored by multi-label classification metrics and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric. The experimental results show that current agents generally achieve high recall but low precision, tending to propose more experiments than are necessary to test the hypothesis.
papers.summary: Deciding which geochemical experiments to run before committing to costly laboratory work is an upstream skill for LLM agents in mineral exploration that is hard to score, because different geologists would legitimately choose different protocols. `MineralExp` recasts the task as multi-label selection over a taxonomy of 19 experiment types across five mineral-system processes, with 277 expert-verified cases and 1,572 reference plans drawn from published ore-deposit literature. Agents select the relevant experiment types and write concrete plans, which are scored with multi-label classification metrics and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric. Current agents show **high recall but low precision, proposing more experiments than are needed to test the hypothesis**.

papers.title: OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination
papers.abstract: In many long-horizon settings, an agent's own choices create future constraints: committing finite capacity establishes future obligations and forecloses later opportunities. Sustaining performance therefore requires both keeping evolving plans feasible and comparing the value of resource allocations with the alternatives they displace. Recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate LLM agents in continuing operations, but give less attention to how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing resource allocations as opportunities change. We introduce OutfitterBench, where agents manage an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, purchasing from a 46-product catalog and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests. Under a fixed capital ceiling, reservations and uncertain walk-in demand compete for reusable equipment whose availability changes over time. Experiments with seven frontier LLMs show that several agents underperform a simple rule-based baseline, while only the leading agent consistently surpasses it. Trajectory analysis shows that some agents apply known constraints inconsistently and make new decisions that conflict with existing commitments. Agents with more reliable fulfillment can still secure low returns from comparable commitments or delay resource reallocation. The leading agent better connects preparation with economic choices but also misses opportunities for more profitable asset use. These findings highlight limitations in sustaining coherent resource plans and reassessing their value over time. The benchmark code is publicly available at https://github.com/adminblackjack/OutfitterBench.
papers.summary: `OutfitterBench` tests whether LLM agents can keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing how finite resources are allocated over a long horizon. Agents run an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, buying from a 46-product catalog under a fixed capital ceiling and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests that compete with uncertain walk-in demand for reusable equipment. Across seven frontier LLMs, **several agents underperform a simple rule-based baseline and only the leading agent consistently beats it**. Trajectory analysis finds agents applying known constraints inconsistently, making decisions that conflict with existing commitments, and delaying reallocation of resources.

papers.title: Tracing Actual Causes with Counterfactual Witness Maps
papers.abstract: Halpernian actual causation, the formal study of which events in a specific situation caused a specific outcome in acyclic structural causal models, underpins legal responsibility, moral blame, and the assessment of causal harm. Despite the rich logical framework, no prior sound and complete enumeration procedure is known for finding all actual causes in a given setting, blocking downstream tasks such as responsibility attribution, blame assessment, and causal-harm grading that aggregate over the full cause set. We close this gap by introducing witness targets: sets of joint configurations containing every counterfactual witness. In combination with an ancestor intervention grammar we derive a finite directed acyclic witness map. We prove that for every actual cause there exists a contingency set such that the joint intervention set appears as a node of this map, and present an algorithm for Tracing Actual Causes (TrAC) that is sound and complete for enumerating all actual causes of any target event. We compare TrAC empirically with existing single-cause baselines on random Boolean structural causal models, demonstrating practical feasibility for graphs of up to 15 nodes.
papers.summary: Halpern-style actual causation asks which events in a specific situation caused a specific outcome in an acyclic structural causal model, but no sound and complete procedure was previously known for enumerating all actual causes. The authors introduce witness targets, sets of joint configurations containing every counterfactual witness, and combine them with an ancestor intervention grammar to build a finite directed acyclic witness map. They prove that every actual cause appears in this map with some contingency set, giving the `TrAC` (Tracing Actual Causes) algorithm, which is **sound and complete for enumerating all actual causes of any target event**. Experiments on random Boolean structural causal models show feasibility for graphs of up to 15 nodes.

papers.title: Measured from the feed: the unsustainable growth of AI video generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-video generation runs at commercial scale, but its broader environmental impacts remain, to our knowledge, understudied. Providers rarely disclose video volumes or energy needs; we measured the yearly video output of two commercial platforms and built a prospective model of such services' absolute footprint from training to storage. Our projections suggest that reducing emissions depends on both limiting growth in video generation and achieving substantial efficiency gains. Under continued growth, emissions rise nearly seventy-five-fold by 2030 despite technological improvements. When usage remains at 2026 levels, the same improvements reduce emissions by about two-fifths. These estimates are a conservative lower bound: they cover one AI service among many; other services and uses would push the total higher.
papers.summary: The environmental footprint of commercial text-to-video generation is estimated despite providers rarely disclosing video volumes or energy use. The authors measured the yearly video output of two commercial platforms and built a prospective model of such services' absolute footprint from training through storage. Under continued growth, **emissions rise nearly seventy-five-fold by 2030 despite technological improvements**, whereas holding usage at 2026 levels lets the same improvements cut emissions by about two-fifths. The estimates are described as a conservative lower bound because they cover only one kind of AI service.

papers.title: Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? Drift, Diagnosis and Auditable Intervention on One Shipped Financial Research Agent
papers.abstract: Can you trust a finance agent you did not build? We take the reference agent shipped with the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark v2, leave it untuned, and ask four questions a leaderboard score does not answer. Is the score stable? Seven identical runs on 18 questions pass between 105 and 123 of 149 rubric criteria, and the bill varies by up to 17%. When the agent fails, who owns the fix? We classify 20 failed trajectories, from three runs of nine held-out questions, by the layer whose owner would remedy them, under a taxonomy frozen in advance: 13 belong to the agent's instructions, 3 to its tools, 4 to the model, none to its data. Can that diagnosis be trusted? Four blind readers from three model families, given only the traces, name the same fault as our LLM analyzer in 94% of cases, the rate at which they agree with one another (93%). Can a change be trusted? An optimization loop reads the traces, makes one targeted change per round and keeps it only if it clears a fixed threshold. Under a cost objective its final configuration costs 0.34x the baseline on the held-out questions (95% CI [0.22, 0.58]) at accuracy within noise. Under an accuracy objective it gains 14 points on the development questions and 1.5 on the held-out ones (CI [-5.3, +7.2]). Judged against the measured run-to-run noise, under a rule written before the test was opened, the first is a real saving and the second is not. This is a case study of one agent and nine test questions, not a general result.
papers.summary: The untuned reference agent shipped with the `Vals Finance Agent Benchmark v2` is used as a case study of what a leaderboard score leaves unanswered. Seven identical runs on 18 questions passed between 105 and 123 of 149 rubric criteria with cost varying by up to 17%, and of 20 classified failed trajectories, 13 were attributed to the agent's instructions, 3 to its tools, 4 to the model and none to its data. An optimization loop that makes one trace-informed change per round and keeps it only if it clears a fixed threshold produced a configuration costing **0.34x the baseline on held-out questions at accuracy within noise**, while the accuracy-targeted run gained 14 points on development questions but only 1.5 on held-out ones, which is not distinguishable from run-to-run noise. The authors stress that the study covers one agent and nine test questions.

papers.title: Differentially Private Federated Class-Incremental Learning for EEG Mental State Classification
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) under differential privacy (DP) is typically evaluated on large client cohorts, where subsampling and cross-client averaging amplify privacy and smooth injected noise. Personal biosignal applications such as wearable EEG instead involve small federations of a handful of subjects, a regime whose interaction with formal client-level DP is largely uncharacterized. We study differentially private federated class-incremental learning in this small-cohort regime, combining a public EEG dataset with a custom four-channel MUSE 2 recording set into a K=5-client federation, and give a masked per-class training protocol that avoids degenerate gradients and missing negative supervision under class-incremental streaming. We propose FedEEG, combining Synaptic-Intelligence consolidation with a lagged adaptive FedProx term, and show it reduces catastrophic forgetting relative to FedAvg, FedProx, and a federated Learning-without-Forgetting baseline; on-device balanced-batch replay reduces mean forgetting by a further 56.7%. A class-scoping diagnosis yields $50.5\%\pm3.6\%$ accuracy with 6 seeds and 2.02 times chance. We also introduce head-scoped client-level DP, which protects the classification head and alone reduces the achievable $\varepsilon$ by 200 times at a matched round budget; combined with fewer communication rounds it reaches $\varepsilon\!\approx\!10.4$ with utility not statistically distinguishable from non-private training.
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) under differential privacy (DP) is usually studied with large client cohorts, whereas wearable EEG applications involve only a handful of subjects. A five-client class-incremental federation is built from a public EEG dataset plus custom four-channel `MUSE 2` recordings, and the proposed `FedEEG` combines Synaptic-Intelligence consolidation with a lagged adaptive `FedProx` term, reducing catastrophic forgetting relative to `FedAvg`, `FedProx` and a federated Learning-without-Forgetting baseline; on-device balanced-batch replay cuts mean forgetting by a further 56.7%. A head-scoped client-level DP scheme that protects only the classification head reduces the achievable ε by 200 times at a matched round budget, and with fewer communication rounds reaches **ε ≈ 10.4 with utility not statistically distinguishable from non-private training**.

papers.title: Toward Interference-Agnostic RF Source Separation
papers.abstract: Separating a radio-frequency signal of interest from a co-channel interference is mostly addressed with specialized separators, each trained for one pair of signal and interference types and therefore relying on a label that a heavily jammed receiver cannot identify. We show that this reliance is not benign: applied to an interference it was not trained on, such a separator usually fails to recover the signal, and in most of the cases we measure it leaves the signal worse than no processing at all. We then train a single separator over every pair, giving it no indication at test time of which one it faces, on two architectures with no component in common: the convolutional WaveNet of the ICASSP 2024 RF Challenge, and a band-split transformer that we adapt from music source separation. Both behave the same way. At the size of one specialized model, the unified separator stays close to the whole models it replaces, keeping the bit error rate close on almost every pair, better on one and worse on another. On an interference absent from every training set, it does as well as the best specialized model, without anyone having to choose which one to deploy.
papers.summary: Separators that recover a radio-frequency signal from co-channel interference are usually trained for one signal-interference pair, which requires knowing the interference type, something a heavily jammed receiver cannot determine. The authors show that such a specialized separator applied to an unseen interference usually fails and in most measured cases leaves the signal worse than no processing. They then train a single separator over every pair with no test-time indication of the interference type, using both the convolutional `WaveNet` from the `ICASSP 2024 RF Challenge` and a band-split transformer adapted from music source separation. At the size of one specialized model, the unified separator keeps bit error rate close to the specialized models on almost every pair, and **on an interference absent from all training sets it matches the best specialized model**.

papers.title: Domain Adaptation Based Pipeline for Character Classification and Handwritten Text Recognition
papers.abstract: Character classification and handwritten text recognition, particularly in specialized tasks, often suffer from limited labeled data, while a large amount of unlabeled data remains unused. To address this challenge, we propose a novel unsupervised domain adaptation-based pipeline to reduce the distribution gap between source and target domains. Our pipeline follows three main steps. In the first step, we pretrained an expert model on source data, to learn a strong general representation. In the second step, we perform unsupervised domain adaptation to leverage unlabeled target data, adapting the model to the specific characteristics of the target domain. In the third step, we trained the expert model on source data in the target style. By aligning the feature distributions between the source and target, our method enables the model to generalize effectively across diverse datasets.
