The unsupervised training increases the computation time only during training not in inference. We evaluate the pipeline on both character-level and historical handwritten line recognition tasks, demonstrating its flexibility. We establish a new state-of-the-art on the Safran-MNIST-DLS dataset defined in Track 2 of the DAGECC competition with 76.17% Macro F1-score and achieve competitive results on each of the specific datasets of READ 2018 without using the labels of the target data. Code is available at https://github.com/simon-corbi/DRANet-for-classification-and-htr
papers.summary: Character classification and handwritten text recognition in specialized settings often have little labeled data but plenty of unlabeled data. The proposed three-step pipeline pretrains an expert model on source data, applies unsupervised domain adaptation using unlabeled target data, and then trains the expert on source data rendered in the target style, adding compute only at training time. It reaches **76.17% Macro F1 on `Safran-MNIST-DLS`**, reported as a new state of the art for Track 2 of the `DAGECC` competition, and gives competitive results on the `READ 2018` datasets without using target labels.

papers.title: The Transformer Paradigm: Dynamic Processing and a New Principle of Inference
papers.abstract: We argue that the Transformer revolution is not adequately understood as a merely quantitative expansion of deep learning, but as the emergence of a new paradigm based on a different principle of inference. We interpret the Transformer as a system in which token representations are transformed by parameterized transformations, or transforming concepts. During inference, some of these transformations are dynamically constructed from the current input: previously acquired transformations are first adapted and then applied. At the mechanical-structural level, this dynamic processing is realized through output-weight interconnections, whereby outputs of some networks determine the weights of others. The resulting mode of processing, which we call Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (SIDPP), provides a framework for explaining strong prompt sensitivity and opens research directions concerning interpretability, control, alternative AI architectures, neuromorphic systems, and possible biological realizations of dynamic processing.
papers.summary: A conceptual argument is made that the Transformer represents a new principle of inference and not merely a quantitative scaling of deep learning. Token representations are described as being changed by parameterized transformations, some of which are **constructed dynamically from the current input during inference**, by adapting previously learned transformations before applying them. Mechanically this is attributed to output-weight interconnections, in which the outputs of some networks set the weights of others, a mode the authors call Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (`SIDPP`). They present the framework as an explanation for strong prompt sensitivity and as a basis for work on interpretability, control and alternative architectures.

papers.title: In the Eye of the Beholder: Human Label Variation in Textual and Visual Entailment
papers.abstract: Human Label Variation (HLV) is increasingly recognised as an informative signal that reflects meaningful differences in how people interpret the same input. While HLV has been studied extensively in Natural Language Inference (NLI), much less is known about HLV in Visual Entailment (VE; Xie et al., 2019), where the textual premise is replaced by an image, keeping the hypothesis and label space fixed. We introduce VariNLI-VE, a dataset for studying how HLV changes between paired NLI and VE instances. We re-annotate a subset of originally neutral SNLI (Bowman et al., 2015) instances and their visual counterparts, with the same annotators evaluating both the textual and visual versions. Each annotation includes a label, confidence score, and explanation, yielding 2,250 annotations. Labels and explanations are collected jointly, providing ecologically valid explanations. Because the image may reveal information not stated in the text, one might expect disagreement to decrease in VE. Instead, we find no clear overall reduction: disagreement decreases for some instances while it increases for others. Explanations reveal further variation, as annotators can retain the same label while changing their rationale. When evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on the paired data, we find lower accuracy, weaker alignment with human label distributions, and generally higher uncertainty in VE than in NLI.
papers.summary: Human Label Variation (HLV), meaning systematic differences in how annotators label the same input, has been studied widely in Natural Language Inference (NLI) but little in Visual Entailment (VE), where an image replaces the textual premise. `VariNLI-VE` re-annotates a subset of originally neutral `SNLI` instances and their image counterparts with the same annotators, collecting labels, confidence scores and explanations for 2,250 annotations. Contrary to the expectation that images would resolve ambiguity, there is **no clear overall reduction in disagreement in the visual setting**, with disagreement falling for some instances and rising for others. Vision-language models (VLMs) evaluated on the paired data show lower accuracy, weaker alignment with human label distributions and generally higher uncertainty on VE than on NLI.

papers.title: WebArena-Pro: A Heterogeneous, Multimodal, Reproducible Benchmark for Web Agents
papers.abstract: Web agents powered by large language and vision-language models are increasingly applied to realistic browser work that spans heterogeneous applications, multimodal content, and stateful workflows. However, existing reproducible web-agent benchmarks cover only a small number of web applications drawn from a few software categories, and restrict modality to text and vision. Live benchmarks broaden site coverage but sacrifice reproducibility, since pages and data drift between runs. Moreover, existing benchmarks do not meaningfully evaluate whether agents can understand and use audio and video content embedded within web tasks. To address these gaps, we introduce WebArena-Pro, a benchmark comprising 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications in six domain categories, spanning distinct interface conventions, workflows, and data models. Across the evaluated agents, the best performance is achieved by both Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 at 62.3%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro at 60.7%. The strongest GenericAgent configurations, Gemini 3.1 Pro omni and Gemma4 31B, both achieve 30.3%. Among reproducible, human-curated web agent benchmarks, WebArena-Pro provides the broadest application coverage and the most comprehensive multimodal support to date. The benchmark treats audio and video as core observations alongside text and vision, with dedicated actions for extracting information from each. WebArena-Pro runs each task in isolation and supports reproducible, parallel evaluation. Tasks are authored through a dedicated annotator interface, filtered by LLM-assisted triage, and finally validated by humans before release. Project page: https://webarena-pro.github.io
papers.summary: Reproducible web-agent benchmarks cover few applications and only text and vision, while live benchmarks drift between runs and none meaningfully test audio or video content embedded in tasks. `WebArena-Pro` provides 300 human-validated tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications in six domain categories, treats audio and video as core observations with dedicated extraction actions, and runs each task in isolation for reproducible parallel evaluation. The best results are **62.3%, reached by both `Codex` with `GPT 6.1 Sol` and `Claude Code` with `Claude Opus 5.5`**, followed by `OpenCode` with `Kimi 3.1 Pro` at 60.7%. The strongest `GenericAgent` configurations, `Gemini 3.1 Pro omni` and `Gemma4 31B`, both reach 30.3%.

papers.title: Reasoning Models Confabulate to Defend Injected Beliefs About Their Own Requests
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring and self-report are proposed as levers for AI oversight, on the assumption that a model's account of what it is doing is anchored to what it was asked. We show this anchor can be cut. An activation edit invisible in the prompt text, the injected forming-trace of an off-topic concept, overwrites a reasoning model's belief about its own request: across six models spanning scale, architecture, and recipe, the injected topic becomes the task it reasons about, reports back, and answers: the forced quote-back returns the injected topic in 47 of 48 model-concept cells, and on the four models with clean final haiku the injected answer follows in 99% of generations. Warnings barely move it: even one naming the true topic yields under 5% true-topic answers. Handed the truth in clean tokens, the model confabulates a story about the user ("maybe they got confused and corrected themselves") and answers with the injection anyway, its behavior and chain-of-thought corrupted together: a concrete limit on CoT monitorability. Opening the model up offers no reprieve: it attends to the true request even harder after edits, yet that attention is causally inert, and the injected content rides intact task circuits, so attention maps and circuit attributions read as on-task too; the same edit redirects the request's language and format, not only its topic. What the injection reaches is the model's reference to its own input; what it elicits is its defense of it.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring and self-report assume a model's account of what it is doing is anchored to what it was actually asked. The authors show that an activation edit invisible in the prompt text, injecting the trace of an off-topic concept, overwrites a reasoning model's belief about its own request across six models: **a forced quote-back of the request returns the injected topic in 47 of 48 model-concept cells**, and the injected answer follows in 99% of generations on the four models with clean outputs. Warnings barely help, with even one naming the true topic yielding under 5% true-topic answers, and when shown the truth the model invents a story about the user having changed their mind and answers with the injection anyway. Attention maps and circuit attributions still read as on-task, since attention to the true request increases but is causally inert.
papers.highlight_summary:
Chain-of-thought monitoring and self-report assume a model's account of its task is anchored to what it was actually asked. A prompt-invisible activation edit cuts that anchor: the model adopts an injected topic as its request, reasons and answers about it, and defends it when shown the truth.

- The method records the model's own residual-stream "forming-trace" for an off-topic concept, removes a shared substrate component via PCA, and adds the remainder at the final prompt positions over a per-model layer window at unit strength, then reads a forced verbatim quote-back and the final haiku across six 7–32B reasoning models including `R1-Qwen-7B/14B/32B`, `R1-Llama-8B`, `Nemotron-7B` and `QwQ-32B`.
- With no warning, the quote-back returns the injected topic in **47 of 48** model-concept cells, and on the four models with scorable final haikus the answer follows the injection in **99%** of sampled generations (95/96).
- Warnings barely help: clean recovery of the true topic stays at **3–4%** even when the warning names it, while hedged two-topic answers rise to 13% and, on `R1-Qwen-7B`, 29% of warned reasoning chains (46% under the explicit warning) invent a story that the user made a mistake or corrected themselves.
- Activation-level signals look on-task too, since attention to the true topic rises two to three times yet ablating it leaves the injected output unchanged, intact `IOI` name-mover heads write the injected name while attending to the true one, and a `CAA`/`ActAdd` steering baseline could not reproduce the effect without degenerating into repetition (26 of 32 configurations).
- The edit requires white-box activation write access and is shown only within-model on small open-weight reasoning models, a non-reasoning `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` reproduced it only weakly, and a per-layer logit-lens scan with full activation access can catch the demonstrated instance.

papers.title: DeltaVisionX: A Low-Cost Vision-Guided Automation System Using YOLOv11 and PLC-Based Actuation
papers.abstract: This paper presents DeltaVisionX, a low-cost industrial automation system that integrates real-time computer vision with PLC-based actuation for object classification and sorting. The system uses the YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once) deep learning model to detect objects on an operating conveyor belt and communicates detection results to a Delta DVP-SE PLC, which actuates pneumatic pistons for sorting. A custom dataset was created, labeled, and augmented to train the YOLOv11 model, achieving a mean average precision of 0.97 with real-time inference of 100 ms per frame. Encoder-based tracking ensures reliable synchronization between detection and actuation, supporting a throughput of 80 objects per minute. Results show that affordable, locally developed automation can reduce labor dependency and improve manufacturing efficiency. The novelty of the proposed system lies in its encodersynchronized vision-PLC integration rather than in the detection model itself. Future work includes integrating a highspeed Delta robot with EtherCAT-based servo control for advanced pick-and-place operations.
papers.summary: `DeltaVisionX` is a low-cost industrial sorting system that pairs real-time vision with programmable logic controller (PLC) actuation. A `YOLOv11` detector trained on a custom augmented dataset identifies objects on a moving conveyor and passes results to a `Delta DVP-SE` PLC that fires pneumatic pistons, with encoder-based tracking synchronizing detection and actuation. The detector reaches **a mean average precision of 0.97 at 100 ms per frame**, supporting a throughput of 80 objects per minute. The authors locate the novelty in the encoder-synchronized vision-PLC integration and not in the detection model.

papers.title: Toward Universal Translatability: On the Statistical Ontology of Generative AI
papers.abstract: This paper argues that the problem of translation functions both as a point of origin and as a normative horizon for contemporary generative AI. In current discourse around ''world models,'' their attainment is framed as the achievement of internal consistency, cross-modal alignment, and physical grounding. Taken together, these demands converge on an ideal of the model as a universal translation machine capable of establishing lossless correspondences across linguistic, visual, and physical representation spaces. I show that this ideal presupposes a metaphysical commitment that I call a statistical ontology: the belief that reality has an underlying, computable statistical structure that can be recovered through sufficient data and modeling, rather than being shaped and accessed through situated human interpretation and labor. Tracing this commitment back to Warren Weaver's 1949 Memorandum on machine translation, I outline how translation was historically recast as code deciphering and, later, as the alignment of probability distributions across structured outputs. Finally, I contrast this paradigm with approaches in Translation Studies that foreground opacity, power asymmetries, and the translator's positionality. I argue that generative AI's statistical ontology is pre-Kantian, pre-critical and obscures the infrastructures and human labor that make machine translatability---as alignment---possible in the first place.
papers.summary: A philosophical essay argues that translation serves as both the origin point and the guiding ideal of contemporary generative AI, with the pursuit of world models converging on the image of a universal translation machine that maps losslessly between linguistic, visual and physical representations. The author says this ideal rests on a **statistical ontology: the belief that reality has an underlying computable statistical structure recoverable from enough data and modeling**, as opposed to being accessed through situated human interpretation and labor. The commitment is traced to Warren Weaver's 1949 memorandum on machine translation and its later recasting as alignment of probability distributions. It is then contrasted with Translation Studies approaches that emphasize opacity, power asymmetries and the translator's position, and the author contends the paradigm obscures the infrastructure and human labor behind machine translatability.

papers.title: From Images to Grounded Edits: A Real-World Benchmark for Chinese Grammatical Error Correction in Handwritten Essays
papers.abstract: Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) is typically formulated as a text-to-text problem. While suitable for digital texts, this formulation falls short in real-world K-12 education, where AI-assisted corrections are expected directly on essay images, which are primarily handwritten and exhibit many irregularities. To bridge this gap, we introduce Grounded Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (G-CGEC), an image-to-grounded-edit task requiring systems to predict both corrections and their positions on essay images. We propose G-CGEC-Eval, a benchmark comprising real-world images of K-12 Chinese essays with fine-grained annotations. For evaluation, we adapt IoU-based metrics from object detection and propose a more tolerant alternative based on center-distance matching. Using this benchmark, we evaluate open-source and proprietary vision-language models under a direct single-pass setting, as well as settings with auxiliary components (OCR and character grounding) coordinated via pipelining or agentic harnessing. Results show that even top-tier proprietary models perform surprisingly poorly in the single-pass setting, while pipelining and agentic harnessing yield meaningful improvements. Notably, an error-type-based multi-agent workflow achieves the best performance, establishing it as the strongest baseline for future G-CGEC research. Through ablations and fine-grained analysis, we find the task remains far from solved, with linguistic error discovery and character-level grounding as the primary bottlenecks. This underscores the need for models that better integrate visual perception with linguistic reasoning and visual grounding.
papers.summary: Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) is normally treated as text-to-text, but in K-12 classrooms corrections need to be placed directly on images of handwritten essays. The authors define Grounded CGEC (`G-CGEC`), an image-to-grounded-edit task requiring both the correction and its position, and release `G-CGEC-Eval`, a benchmark of real essay images with fine-grained annotations scored by IoU-based metrics and a more tolerant center-distance matching alternative. Top proprietary vision-language models perform poorly in a single pass, while adding OCR and character-grounding components through pipelines or agentic harnesses helps, and **an error-type-based multi-agent workflow achieves the best performance**. The task remains far from solved, with linguistic error discovery and character-level grounding as the main bottlenecks.

papers.title: Analyzing Learning-Dynamics Across Loss and Prediction Choices for Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Denoising generative models predict clean data ($x$), noise ($\epsilon$), or velocity ($v$), while training losses can be measured in any of these spaces. Although the resulting nine combinations are algebraically related, they can yield substantially different denoising accuracy and sample quality. We disentangle the effects of prediction and loss spaces. For a fixed prediction target, we show that changing the loss space is exactly equivalent to timestep reweighting and provide a heuristic analysis of how this reweighting affects generation quality. We then show that a rank-$m$ linear bottleneck compressing a $D$-dimensional noisy input imposes an irreducible squared-error floor of $D-m$ on noise and velocity prediction, whereas clean-data prediction can exploit low-dimensional data structure. Combining this bound with prediction-dependent error conversion yields distinct necessary conditions on bottleneck capacity. Experiments with U-Net and JiT across CIFAR-10, Imagenette, and ImageNet-256 support these theoretical predictions. Under compression, prediction choice strongly affects both denoising accuracy and sample quality, with noise-prediction errors closely matching the theoretical lower bound. Our results provide a quantitative understanding of how architectural bottlenecks interact with prediction and loss choices in denoising generative models.
papers.summary: Denoising generative models can predict clean data, noise or velocity and measure the loss in any of those spaces, giving nine algebraically related combinations that nonetheless differ in denoising accuracy and sample quality. For a fixed prediction target, changing the loss space is shown to be exactly equivalent to timestep reweighting. The authors further prove that **a rank-m linear bottleneck on a D-dimensional noisy input imposes an irreducible squared-error floor of D − m on noise and velocity prediction**, whereas clean-data prediction can exploit low-dimensional data structure. Experiments with `U-Net` and `JiT` on `CIFAR-10`, `Imagenette` and `ImageNet-256` support the predictions, with noise-prediction errors closely tracking the lower bound under compression.

papers.title: TotalSegmentator Aorta Report: Automated Aortic Diameter Measurement at 11 Standardized Landmarks on CT Images
papers.abstract:
Purpose: To develop and evaluate a fully automated, open-source tool that measures aortic diameters at 11 standardized landmarks from the aortic annulus to the bifurcation on any CT image, following current guideline recommendations.
  Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 239 arterial phase CT angiography examinations of 230 patients (median age, 65 years [range, 18-99 years]; 163 men) performed between April 2025 and October 2026 (209 electrocardiographically [ECG] gated). The tool locates landmarks from TotalSegmentator segmentations of aortic branches and vertebrae and measures the maximum diameter at each. A senior radiologist reviewed and, where needed, corrected the automated measurements to create the reference standard. Agreement was assessed with mean absolute error (MAE), bias, and differences greater than 2 mm.
  Results: Across all landmarks, MAE was 1.06 mm (95% CI: 0.91, 1.22), and 86.6% (95% CI: 84.4, 88.5) of differences were 2 mm or less. The tool measured slightly larger diameters (bias, 0.45 mm [95% CI: 0.34, 0.57]). The sinuses of Valsalva had the largest MAE (2.17 mm [95% CI: 1.59, 2.86]). For 1.2% of landmarks, the automatic measurement failed. Examination-level MAE did not differ significantly by pathology, atherosclerosis grade (P=.95), or ECG gating (P=.14). Examinations with mural thrombus more often had an MAE greater than 2 mm (50% [95% CI: 31, 69] vs 20%; P=.03).
  Conclusion: The tool measured aortic diameters at 11 landmarks along the entire aorta with an MAE of about 1 mm, below published interreader variability. Agreement was lower at the aortic root and with mural thrombus.
  Code availability: The tool is open source and freely available at https://github.com/wasserth/TotalSegmentator.
papers.summary: An open-source tool built on `TotalSegmentator` automatically measures aortic diameter at 11 guideline-standardized landmarks from the aortic annulus to the bifurcation on CT images, locating landmarks from segmentations of aortic branches and vertebrae. In a retrospective single-center study of 239 CT angiography examinations from 230 patients, with a senior radiologist's reviewed and corrected measurements as reference, the **mean absolute error (MAE) was 1.06 mm across all landmarks** and 86.6% of differences were 2 mm or less. Agreement was weakest at the sinuses of Valsalva (MAE 2.17 mm) and in examinations with mural thrombus, and automatic measurement failed for 1.2% of landmarks.

papers.title: Efficient and Practical Clustering of Variables in Causal Graphs
papers.abstract: Clustering variables in a graph may improve visual clarity and simplify causal inference. Harnessing the full potential of clustering requires an automated method to detect useful clusters in a graph. We introduce a novel class of clusters called conduits, and present a sound, complete and efficient algorithm for detecting all conduits in the graph. In addition to algorithmic detectability, conduits appear naturally in causal graphs stemming from real-world applications, enabling substantial size reduction. Furthermore, the structure of conduits enables the application of known identifiability results regarding clustering. We demonstrate these properties in a simulation study with real-world graphs.
papers.summary: Grouping variables in a causal graph can make it easier to read and simplify causal inference, but useful clusters need to be found automatically. The authors define a new class of clusters called conduits and give **a sound, complete and efficient algorithm that detects all conduits in a graph**. Conduits occur naturally in causal graphs from real-world applications, allow substantial size reduction, and are structured so that existing identifiability results for clustered graphs apply, which a simulation study on real-world graphs illustrates.

papers.title: Algorithmic Opacity as a Principal-Agent Problem
papers.abstract: Concerns about gaming and trade secrecy, frequently invoked to justify algorithmic opacity, can also mask self-serving strategic behavior by decision-makers, who may prioritize private benefits over social welfare. We develop a principal-agent test for when algorithmic decision-making should trigger disclosure obligations even when concerns about gaming or trade secrecy exist. The test, which is anchored in decision quality, relies on two diagnostics that can be disclosed without enabling gaming or revealing trade secrets: the error profile (false positive and false negative rates, overall and for each group) and the distribution of decision outcomes across groups. These diagnostics make visible whether decision-makers align design and implementation with the public interest or instead use opacity to obscure bias, inefficiency, or strategic shirking. Strong disparities across social groups, and asymmetries in the distribution of decision errors across outcome types, should trigger rebuttable presumptions favoring further disclosure. Where ground-truth error rates are unavailable, outcome distributions across groups can support the same presumption, and a decision-maker's inability to produce an error profile is itself diagnostic. The test thus treats fairness metrics as triggers for further disclosure and extends to generative and agentic systems through analogous metrics. The framework informs differentiated disclosure regimes (staged, partial, mediated, or audience-segmented). Once such regimes are considered, the domain of justifiable algorithmic opacity is significantly narrower than commonly assumed: when gaming or trade secrecy risks are legitimate, actionable disclosures (such as training data characteristics and key system design parameters) ordinarily can be mandated without compromising innovation or enabling gaming, even for technically inscrutable algorithms.
papers.summary: Gaming and trade-secrecy concerns are often used to justify keeping algorithmic decision systems opaque, but they can also hide self-serving behavior by the decision-maker. The authors propose a principal-agent test based on two diagnostics that can be disclosed without enabling gaming or revealing secrets: the error profile (false positive and false negative rates, overall and per group) and the distribution of decision outcomes across groups. Strong group disparities or asymmetric error distributions create a rebuttable presumption in favor of further disclosure, and an inability to produce an error profile is itself treated as diagnostic. They argue that once staged, partial, mediated, or audience-segmented disclosure regimes are considered, **the domain of justifiable algorithmic opacity is significantly narrower than commonly assumed**.

papers.title: When Does Oversampling Help? A Decision Framework for Imbalanced Data Streams Under Label Delay and Concept Drift
papers.abstract: For imbalanced data streams with delayed labels, is it worth adding a streaming oversampler, or does continuous re-evaluation of earlier predictions already recover the cost of the delay? We address this through an extensive experimental comparison of streaming oversampling and continuous re-evaluation under joint class imbalance, concept drift, and label delay. Streaming oversamplers are typically evaluated under the test-then-train assumption of immediate labels; their behaviour under these conditions, assessed through re-evaluation, has not been systematically studied. We close this gap with a decision framework that predicts when oversampling adds value over re-evaluation, organised around three axes: drift density, minority-class learnability, and delay relative to the refinement window, and operationalised as a competition between a recovery channel (re-evaluation) and a minority-coverage channel (oversampling). Evaluating $15$ classifiers on $6$ synthetic and $6$ real streams, we find: re-evaluation recovers delay-induced loss on drift-active streams but is silent on stationary ones; oversampling's marginal contribution over re-evaluation is statistically detectable in only one real-data configuration; and cost--performance Pareto recommendations from synthetic streams do not transfer to real data, where fronts partition by drift regime. Method selection should therefore be conditioned on the stream's profile and re-estimated as it evolves, not inherited from synthetic benchmarks.
papers.summary: For imbalanced data streams where labels arrive late, the question studied is whether a streaming oversampler adds anything beyond continuously re-evaluating earlier predictions. The authors compare the two under joint class imbalance, concept drift, and label delay using 15 classifiers on 6 synthetic and 6 real streams, and organize the results into a decision framework built on drift density, minority-class learnability, and delay relative to the refinement window. Re-evaluation recovers delay-induced loss on streams with active drift but not on stationary ones, and **oversampling's marginal contribution over re-evaluation is statistically detectable in only one real-data configuration**. Cost-performance recommendations derived from synthetic streams do not transfer to real data, so method choice should be conditioned on the stream's profile and re-estimated as it evolves.

papers.title: Interactive deep-learning based interface for brain tumour segmentation
papers.abstract: Brain tumour segmentation from MR images is an integral part of their treatment, either through surgical resection or radiotherapy. Both applications require a high degree of precision that can be difficult to ensure for all patients due to the high degree of variability in the size, shape, number, and location of these tumours. This leads to difficulties with their automatic segmentation via deep learning, which can display catastrophic segmentation errors when presented with images that differ, even subtly, in terms of the specific MR sequence used, which varies from vendor to vendor. This article presents a deep-learning-based interactive segmentation system that, while being fully automatic by default, has the capability of being easily corrected by human users, allowing them ensure sufficiently high brain tumour segmentation accuracy for all patients. This interface is evaluated both in terms of the accuracy of its automatic approach as well as its usability through a preliminary observational expert user study.
papers.summary: Automatic deep-learning segmentation of brain tumours in magnetic resonance (MR) images can fail catastrophically when the MR sequence differs even subtly between scanner vendors, which is a problem for surgery and radiotherapy planning that need high precision. The authors present an interactive segmentation system that is **fully automatic by default but can be easily corrected by a human user** to reach sufficient accuracy for every patient. It is evaluated on the accuracy of its automatic mode and on usability through a preliminary observational study with expert users.

papers.title: LACCO: Local Accumulation with Computation--Communication Overlap
papers.abstract: Training language models across low-bandwidth networks requires reducing synchronization overhead. Local optimization methods such as DiLoCo communicate only after several local steps, but outer gradient averaging and the outer update remain on the critical path. Existing computation-communication overlap methods avoid this stall through delayed or replica-local updates, which can degrade convergence or cause replicas to drift. We propose LACCO (Local Accumulation with Computation-Communication Overlap), a two-stage algorithm that overlaps global communication with local computation while applying globally aggregated updates shared by every replica, without introducing staleness in the outer update. We establish convergence guarantees for smooth non-convex objectives. Experiments on language-model pre-training with FineWeb show that LACCO consistently outperforms communication-overlapped baselines such as Eager and Delayed DiLoCo. These gains remain robust as model size scales up to 0.5B parameters and across a range of communication intervals and numbers of replicas up to 16 workers, while incurring only negligible-or fully overlappable-computational or memory overhead, which demonstrates the strength of LACCO.
papers.summary: Training language models across low-bandwidth networks with local optimization methods such as `DiLoCo` still stalls while outer gradients are averaged and applied, and existing ways of overlapping communication with computation rely on delayed or replica-local updates that can hurt convergence or cause replicas to drift. `LACCO` (Local Accumulation with Computation-Communication Overlap) is a two-stage algorithm that overlaps global communication with local computation while applying the same globally aggregated update on every replica, without staleness in the outer update, and comes with convergence guarantees for smooth non-convex objectives. In language-model pre-training on `FineWeb`, it **consistently outperforms the communication-overlapped baselines `Eager DiLoCo` and `Delayed DiLoCo`**, with gains holding up to 0.5B parameters and 16 workers at negligible or fully overlappable overhead.

papers.title: Understanding the limits of snapshot-based fault diagnosis in distribution networks
papers.abstract: Inverter-based resources weaken fault currents in distribution networks, and snapshot-based diagnosis, which classifies a fault from voltage phasors at a few buses at one instant, offers a cheap first-stage screen. Its published accuracies, however, rest on different noise assumptions and do not show whether the error comes from the classifier, the features, the measurement error, or the fault resistance. This paper separates these sources on three IEEE test feeders and a public data set with distributed generation, using four feature sets, thirteen classifiers, and measurement error defined by total vector error classes. The classifier is not the limiting factor, because the full phasor snapshot classifies every fault correctly without noise, and the remaining error comes from measurement error on high-impedance faults. Three voltage sensors classify 90-96% of faults at the 1% accuracy class and 96-99% with distribution micro phasor measurement units (micro-PMUs). A discriminability-margin placement selects them from simulations alone in under one second and matches the best of twelve placement methods. The results show when snapshot-based diagnosis can be trusted.
papers.summary: Snapshot-based fault diagnosis in power distribution networks classifies a fault from voltage phasors at a few buses at a single instant, but published accuracies do not reveal whether errors come from the classifier, the features, measurement error, or fault resistance. The authors separate these sources on three IEEE test feeders and a public data set with distributed generation, using four feature sets, thirteen classifiers, and measurement error defined by total vector error classes. The classifier is not the limiting factor, since the full noiseless phasor snapshot classifies every fault correctly; the remaining error comes from measurement error on high-impedance faults. **Three voltage sensors classify 90-96% of faults at the 1% accuracy class and 96-99% with distribution micro phasor measurement units (micro-PMUs)**, and a discriminability-margin placement method picks those sensors from simulations in under one second.

papers.title: RiverScan: Learning to Accumulate on River Networks
papers.abstract: Accurate runoff prediction across large river basins requires models to capture heterogeneous local hydrological responses and their accumulation downstream. River-network connectivity provides a natural structure for this task, but using it effectively requires learning how to combine contributions from subcatchments of different sizes. We frame this challenge as learning to accumulate and introduce RiverScan, a spatial operator based on area-weighted selective state-space recurrence. RiverScan recursively combines local temporal representations with accumulated upstream states in topological order. Contributing-area fractions account for subcatchment size, while learned retention controls how upstream information persists downstream. Experiments on 608 stations in the Danube basin show that RiverScan outperforms the evaluated temporal and graph baselines in overall predictive performance. Structural controls and ablations demonstrate that composing heterogeneous subcatchment representations in a manner aligned with hydrological accumulation substantially improves runoff prediction, with the benefits of correct topology growing along the river-network hierarchy. These findings establish physically structured accumulation as an effective inductive bias for hydrological modeling and motivate finer-grained, fully distributed AI-based hydrological models.
papers.summary: Predicting runoff across a large river basin requires modeling both local hydrological responses and how they accumulate downstream through the river network. `RiverScan` is a spatial operator based on area-weighted selective state-space recurrence that combines local temporal representations with accumulated upstream states in topological order, using contributing-area fractions to account for subcatchment size and a learned retention term to control how upstream information persists. On **608 stations in the Danube basin it outperforms the evaluated temporal and graph baselines**, and ablations show the benefit of using the correct network topology grows along the river hierarchy.

papers.title: Sample-Efficient Control of Magnetoconvective Flows via Differentiable Simulation
papers.abstract: Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) fluid flows are central to demanding engineering applications, most prominently fusion blanket cooling, where flow control is a promising tool to optimize key properties such as heat transfer. While active flow control (AFC) has recently advanced through machine learning, its application to MHD flows remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present $\phi$-PICT, a novel differentiable GPU-accelerated MHD solver targeted at AFC. We validate $\phi$-PICT against MHD benchmarks and demonstrate its high computational efficiency. Integrated into FluidGym, $\phi$-PICT enables sample-efficient gradient-based algorithms to improve heat transfer by $>25$% and allows optimizers to achieve $10^3\times$ higher accuracy in inverse design than black-box methods. $\phi$-PICT is publicly available at https://github.com/upb-sciml/phiPICT.
papers.summary: Active flow control (AFC) with machine learning has rarely been applied to magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) flows, which matter for applications such as fusion blanket cooling. The authors introduce `phi-PICT`, a differentiable, GPU-accelerated MHD solver validated against MHD benchmarks and integrated into `FluidGym`. With it, sample-efficient gradient-based control algorithms **improve heat transfer by more than 25%**, and gradient-based optimizers reach about 1,000 times higher accuracy in inverse design than black-box methods.

papers.title: Conflict, Feasibility, Faithfulness, Displacement: Four Quantities That Come Apart in Federated Dual-Cone Aggregation
papers.abstract: FedFV, FedGH and FedMGDA+ aggregate client updates with multi-objective gradient aggregators to remove conflict between them. We examine this rationale with UPGrad, which increases no client's loss to first order, in a comparison that changes only the direction of FedAvg's update. Four quantities the rationale treats as one -- conflict between client updates, feasibility of their weighted mean, faithfulness of the transmitted updates to the clients' gradients, and displacement of the update -- come apart. Under Dirichlet partitioning UPGrad improves CIFAR-10 accuracy by +0.78 pp (14/15 seeds, p < 0.001), only with full participation; on Oxford-IIIT Pet its +0.52 pp gain vanishes (+0.07 pp) once the data our protocol left unused are kept. Varying only the Dirichlet concentration, the gain grows with heterogeneity, yet the split with the most conflict shows none. Uniform client weights, blind to conflict, match the CIFAR-10 gain and exceed the Pets gain; a matched random rotation does neither. No fairness effect survives multiplicity correction, and on CIFAR-10 the guarantee does not reach the clients' gradients. We state what evaluations should report.
papers.summary: Federated learning methods such as `FedFV`, `FedGH` and `FedMGDA+` aggregate client updates with multi-objective gradient aggregators on the rationale that this removes conflict between clients. The authors test that rationale with `UPGrad`, changing only the direction of the `FedAvg` update, and find that four quantities it treats as one (conflict between updates, feasibility of their weighted mean, faithfulness of transmitted updates to client gradients, and displacement of the update) come apart. `UPGrad` gains 0.78 percentage points on `CIFAR-10` only under full participation, its `Oxford-IIIT Pet` gain nearly vanishes once previously unused data are kept, and **uniform client weights that ignore conflict match the `CIFAR-10` gain and exceed the Pets gain**. No fairness effect survives multiplicity correction, and the authors list what such evaluations should report.

papers.title: JaRS: Contrast-Free Localization of Memorized Regions in Diffusion Models via Jacobian Row Sums
papers.abstract: Diffusion models sometimes memorize and reproduce regions of their training images, raising privacy and copyright concerns. We aim to localize these regions. Existing contrast-based methods use the diagonal of the denoiser Jacobian, which reflects the posterior variance of each pixel. However, a small diagonal entry is ambiguous: it signals either memorization or averaging over many neighboring pixels in smooth or predictable regions. To resolve this ambiguity, these methods subtract a reference map, which requires a second evaluation with a null prompt or an earlier checkpoint. Unconditional models have no null prompt, and earlier checkpoints are unavailable in general. We show that Jacobian row sums (JaRS), unlike the diagonal, separate memorization from local averaging without a reference map. Pairing JaRS with an image-level detection score that uses the same statistic at an early denoising step yields JaRS+. Across Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.1, Realistic Vision v5.1, and an unconditional diffusion Transformer (DiT), JaRS+ outperforms contrast-based localization methods.
papers.summary: Diffusion models sometimes reproduce regions of their training images, and existing methods for locating those regions use the diagonal of the denoiser Jacobian, which cannot distinguish memorization from averaging over smooth areas without subtracting a reference map from a null prompt or an earlier checkpoint. The authors show that Jacobian row sums (`JaRS`) **separate memorization from local averaging without any reference map**, which also makes the approach usable on unconditional models. Combined with an image-level detection score from the same statistic at an early denoising step, the resulting `JaRS+` outperforms contrast-based localization methods on `Stable Diffusion v1.4` and `v2.1`, `Realistic Vision v5.1`, and an unconditional diffusion Transformer (`DiT`).

papers.title: A Generalizable Approach to Safety-Aware Robotic Behavior Planning with an Explicit Constraint Space
papers.abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive plans, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation,context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.
papers.summary: Robot planners built on language and vision-language models struggle with tabletop safety because the relevant constraints depend on the scene and are often not stated in the instruction. The proposed framework keeps reusable textual safety rules in an explicit `Constraint Space` and **selects applicable rules with a lightweight dual-tower model conditioned on the task and environment rather than by semantic similarity alone**, passing them with the task and image to a multimodal planner. A multimodal `Safety Inspector` then checks the generated primitive plans, reconstructs the full applicable constraint set, and returns corrective feedback. Validated feedback drives test-time adaptation of the selector and LoRA adaptation of the inspector, and newly identified constraints are added to the store.

papers.title: Beyond Bot Labels: Retrospective Consequence-Grounded Ranking of Attributed Cache Harm in E-Commerce Logs
papers.abstract: Web caches reduce origin load and latency, but automated traffic can either warm them or evict objects shoppers reuse, lowering the cache hit ratio (CHR). Existing bot defenses generally infer automation from User-Agent (UA) strings or behavior rather than identify sessions that impose cross-session cache harm. We instead formulate the task as ranking sessions by eviction damage and propose consequence-grounded session ranking. A single chronological replay attributes each eviction-induced miss by a protected shopping session (a victim) to the session whose insertion last evicted the object. A behavioral model predicts the target from session behavior alone. Selected sessions bypass the cache but remain origin-served. In a controlled check of 539 non-victim sessions selected across harm levels, attribution order tracks victim-hit changes after removal (Spearman correlation 0.80). On a 12.7-million-request real trace, the top 1% of sessions carry 48.8% of attributed harm. Sessions without bot tags contribute 49.1% of this tier's harm. At the 20% request-volume target, the default conditional CHR difference reaches 93% of the UA baseline, which selects 47 times as many sessions. Six training seeds show little variation. This comparison conditions on the victims that remain, so we also report victim bypass. Local replay and retraining on a second store reproduce harm concentration and a top tier dominated by sessions without bot tags. These results establish attributed cross-session harm as an outcome-based target for retrospective cache audits and selective intervention design.
papers.summary: Automated traffic can evict objects from a web cache that real shoppers would have reused, lowering the cache hit ratio (CHR), yet bot defenses typically flag automation from User-Agent (UA) strings or behavior rather than from the harm caused. The authors instead rank sessions by eviction damage: a chronological replay attributes each eviction-induced miss suffered by a protected shopping session to the session whose insertion evicted the object, and a behavioral model predicts that target so selected sessions can bypass the cache while still being served. On a 12.7-million-request real trace, **the top 1% of sessions carry 48.8% of attributed harm**, and about half of that tier's harm comes from sessions with no bot tag. At a 20% request-volume target the method reaches 93% of the UA baseline's conditional CHR difference while selecting 47 times fewer sessions, and the harm concentration reproduces on a second store.

papers.title: PerfArena: Ranking LLMs by Code Performance
papers.abstract: Industry now relies on LLMs to write a large share of production code. Although that code is mostly, but not always, correct, correctness alone does not determine whether it is fit for repeated and extensive use, which depends on what the code costs in time, memory and energy. Most code-generation benchmarks nonetheless evaluate correctness in isolation, and most performance-oriented benchmarks cover few languages and rarely measure energy consumption. To address this gap, we present PERFARENA, an open-source, reproducible arena that ranks LLMs by the performance of their generated code across multiple languages and competitions. PERFARENA executes the solutions of each LLM on a Unix-like host and reports correctness together with latency, peak memory, and energy consumption. Correctness oracles, performance oracles, profilers, and code-generation workflows are pluggable in PERFARENA, enabling the integration of new judging backends and measurement tools without changing the pipeline. We evaluate PERFARENA on two competitions: CLBGComp, 10 compute-intensive benchmarks from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game, and LeetCodeComp, 99 LeetCode problems whose accepted solutions differ measurably in latency. Currently, PERFARENA holds 9,455 correct and measured solutions from 13 state-of-the-art LLMs across 7 programming languages. Across both competitions, got-6-astra is the only LLM that no other LLM beats significantly in latency, energy consumption, or peak memory, solving 99.7% of LeetCodeComp and 100% of CLBGComp. All PERFARENA leaderboards and measured solutions are publicly available, providing a continuously updated reference that helps developers choose an LLM per language and metric, instead of relying only on correctness rates or pricing.
papers.summary: Code-generation benchmarks mostly score correctness, leaving out what the generated code costs in time, memory and energy. `PerfArena` is an open-source, reproducible arena that executes each model's solutions on a Unix-like host and reports correctness alongside latency, peak memory, and energy consumption, with pluggable oracles, profilers, and generation workflows. It is run on two competitions, `CLBGComp` (10 compute-intensive tasks from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game) and `LeetCodeComp` (99 LeetCode problems), and currently holds 9,455 correct, measured solutions from 13 LLMs across 7 programming languages. Across both, **`got-6-astra` is the only model that no other model beats significantly in latency, energy, or peak memory**, solving 99.7% of `LeetCodeComp` and 100% of `CLBGComp`.

papers.title: RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$: On-Device Reinforcement Learning Runtime
papers.abstract: On-device reinforcement learning runs a periodic actor and a learner on one embedded GPU shared with other workloads. Because the learner produces the actor's weights, existing designs stall the actor or let its policy drift. We present RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$, an on-device runtime that makes this coupling a tunable parameter: a refresh bound limits actor releases between refreshes, and a GPU permit with slack-aware admission prioritises the actor and fills spare time with training atop any base scheduler. Under the real refresh cost on two Jetson boards, RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$ keeps a 16.8 M-parameter policy's deadline misses below 1%, against 85 to 100% without it.
papers.summary: On-device reinforcement learning runs a periodic actor and a learner on a single embedded GPU shared with other workloads, and because the learner produces the actor's weights, existing designs either stall the actor or let its policy drift. `RL^RT` is a runtime that makes this coupling tunable: a refresh bound limits how many actor releases can occur between weight refreshes, and a GPU permit with slack-aware admission prioritizes the actor while filling spare time with training on top of any base scheduler. On two Jetson boards under the real refresh cost, it **keeps deadline misses for a 16.8M-parameter policy below 1%, against 85 to 100% without it**.

papers.title: Enrichment-Oriented Virtual Screening of Perovskite Solar Cells through Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Experimental optimization of perovskite solar cells is constrained by combinatorial diversity in absorber compositions, device layers, and processing, which makes virtual screening attractive for prioritizing recipes before fabrication. We develop a surrogate-guided reinforcement-learning framework that casts recipe generation as virtual screening, enriching candidate shortlists near high-performing experimental neighbors. A frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) guides recipe generation, while a reference pool of 890 measured devices enables neighborhood-based assessment. Five-fold evaluation on 1,846 devices shows top-ten selection raises mean power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 19.68\% to 23.74\%. Three learned policies are compared with six baselines under 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run. In top-100 shortlists, Proximal policy optimization (PPO) and recurrent PPO (RPPO) achieve neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23\% and 24\% (7.9- and 8.3-fold Pure Random's 2.9\%), versus 10\% (3.4-fold) for the baselines with the highest supported hit rate (L-SHADE and Ax BO, tied) at $K = 100$. Gains coexist with weak-support fractions. Of 9,000 recipes, 65.4\% match a composition family at similarity 0.80, falling to 11.7\% at 0.90. Results support enrichment-oriented prioritization but not experimental performance, seed robustness, or matched-budget advantage.
papers.summary: Optimizing perovskite solar cells experimentally is limited by the combinatorial space of absorber compositions, device layers, and processing steps. The authors cast recipe generation as virtual screening, using reinforcement-learning policies guided by a frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (`TabPFN`) surrogate and a reference pool of 890 measured devices for neighborhood-based assessment. In top-100 shortlists, proximal policy optimization (`PPO`) and recurrent PPO reach **neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23% and 24%, versus 10% for the best baselines** and 2.9% for random sampling. The authors state that the results support enrichment-oriented prioritization but not experimental performance, seed robustness, or a matched-budget advantage.

papers.title: FEND: Far-End Detection in Outbound Voice AI Calls
papers.abstract: When a conversational Voice AI agent places an outbound call, the far end may be a live person, a voicemail greeting, an interactive voice response (IVR) system, or increasingly another AI system answering on the callee's behalf. Standard Answering Machine Detection (AMD) reports only whether a human or a machine picked up, a design meant for human call centres, where one machine is as uninteresting as another. That single bit does not tell a Voice AI agent what to do, since leaving a voicemail message, navigating an IVR and holding a short exchange with another AI are three different actions and a two-valued label cannot distinguish them. In 1,000 randomly sampled calls from our own outbound deployment, a live person answered 48.1%, a voicemail system 44.6%, an AI 6.9% and an IVR 0.4%. Our proposed framework, FEND, reads the far end's audio and its streaming transcript and runs one detector for each automated class (voicemail, IVR, AI callee), with human the default when nothing fires, returning a single label within 20 seconds. On a public benchmark the voicemail components reach 100% accuracy without ever misclassifying a live human, where Asterisk's AMD misclassifies 30 to 66% of them. For the AI callee, acoustic features do not transfer across recording conditions, but speech timing does, separating AI from human at 0.952 ROC-AUC, because synthesised speech leaves far shorter gaps between words. On production traffic, separating a live person from any automated far end reaches F1 0.979, and only 2.9% of live people are given an automated label, the error that matters most for an agent acting on the result.
papers.summary: When a voice AI agent places an outbound call, standard Answering Machine Detection (AMD) only reports human versus machine, which does not tell the agent whether to leave a voicemail, navigate an interactive voice response (IVR) menu, or talk to another AI answering for the callee. `FEND` reads the far end's audio and streaming transcript and runs one detector per automated class (voicemail, IVR, AI callee), defaulting to human, and returns a label within 20 seconds. On a public benchmark its voicemail components reach 100% accuracy without misclassifying a live human, where Asterisk's AMD misclassifies 30 to 66% of them, and speech timing separates AI from human callees at 0.952 ROC-AUC because synthesized speech leaves much shorter gaps between words. On production traffic, **distinguishing a live person from any automated far end reaches F1 0.979**, with 2.9% of live people given an automated label.

papers.title: A$^3$: Adaptive Audio Agent Framework for Collaborative Edge Computing
papers.abstract: Embedded audio agents need a nearby edge server for speed, but a server-dependent agent returns nothing when the link fails. We present A$^3$, an adaptive audio agent framework that places whole pipeline stages on the server, keeps a complete fallback agent on devices that can host one, and hedges both paths with a link-aware deadline that decides when to give up on the server. On Jetson devices and an RTX A4500 server, A$^3$ matches the server-only agent on a healthy link, answers every request in a full outage on the AGX, and beats a percentile hedge in simulated outages.
papers.summary: Embedded audio agents rely on a nearby edge server for speed, but an agent that depends entirely on the server returns nothing when the link fails. `A^3` places whole pipeline stages on the server, keeps a complete fallback agent on devices able to host one, and hedges both paths with a link-aware deadline that decides when to give up on the server. On Jetson devices with an RTX A4500 server, it matches the server-only agent on a healthy link, **answers every request during a full outage on the AGX**, and beats a percentile-based hedge in simulated outages.

papers.title: Product units in gated recurrent networks enhance prediction of nuclear masses and charge radii
papers.abstract: The prediction of nuclear properties using machine learning can complement theoretical models and advance the exploration of poorly known domains of the nuclear chart. We propose a machine learning technique for predicting nuclear masses and charge radii based on gated recurrent units (GRU) that integrates learnable product-unit mappings into the candidate state to model multiplicative dependencies among neighboring nuclei. Computations are performed in the complex domain to jointly capture amplitude and phase dynamics. Across three data partitions and three training seeds per partition, AM-PU-GRU achieves a mean mass interpolation RMSE of 0.2698 MeV and a temporal RMSE of 0.1905 MeV. Configuration comparisons support the integration of learned products into gated recurrence. Without mass inputs, MI-PU-GRU predicts charge radii with an RMSE of 0.019947 fm, 14.40% below the fixed WS* prior. Matched radius controls further show how candidate fusion shapes the benefit of learned products. Paired errors, nuclide-resolved maps, and inference measurements characterize predictive gains and computational cost. This article is an extended version of our ICCS 2026 conference paper (doi:10.1007/978-3-032-29921-5_10).
papers.summary: Machine learning can complement theoretical models in predicting properties of atomic nuclei in poorly measured regions of the nuclear chart. The authors modify gated recurrent units (GRU) by adding learnable product-unit mappings to the candidate state, computed in the complex domain, to capture multiplicative dependencies among neighboring nuclei. Their `AM-PU-GRU` model reaches a mean mass interpolation RMSE of 0.2698 MeV, and `MI-PU-GRU` predicts charge radii without mass inputs at an RMSE of 0.019947 fm, **14.40% below the fixed `WS*` prior**.

papers.title: Agent-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has progressed from task-specific systems toward general models spanning perception, generation, reasoning, and autonomous interaction, making reliable evaluation essential for comparison, deployment, and post-training feedback. At scale, modern evaluation pipelines increasingly rely on LLM-as-a-Judge to produce scores, preferences, and critiques; in its fixed-context setting, the judge relies on the supplied evaluand and evaluation materials. Yet a reliable verdict may require evidence beyond the supplied evaluand and context---either because critical environmental states remain unrecorded in the static execution log, or because controversial factual claims require external verification. Passive judges cannot obtain that missing evidence before deciding, especially when evaluating agent trajectories, executable artifacts, or domain-specific reports. Recent work therefore develops active evaluators that seek missing evidence and update their grounds for judgment before deciding. We bring these advances together through Agent-as-a-Judge, focusing on how evaluators construct and control checking processes within the broader LLM-based judging landscape. We define the scope through evaluation-directed checks and the use of their results, covering both structured workflows and observation-driven control. We organize the design space by multi-agent collaboration, tool integration, memory, and planning, and show how these mechanisms supply the checks and evidence on which a verdict rests. We consolidate published scores and reproduce missing entries for key agentic judges; the comparison reveals uneven agentic gains and motivates dedicated agentic evaluation. We conclude by characterizing application demands and open challenges in cost, reliability, safety, and governance that condition trusted deployment of agentic judges at scale.
papers.summary: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation works from a fixed context, but a reliable verdict sometimes needs evidence that is not in the supplied material, such as unrecorded environment state or external verification of contested claims. This survey covers active evaluators that seek missing evidence before deciding, defining their scope through evaluation-directed checks and organizing the design space by multi-agent collaboration, tool integration, memory, and planning. The authors consolidate published scores and reproduce missing entries for key agentic judges, and **the comparison shows uneven gains from making judges agentic**. They close with open challenges in cost, reliability, safety, and governance.

papers.title: Learning nonlinear interactions and cross-feature couplings with product-unit residual networks
papers.abstract: Understanding nonlinear feature interactions is crucial in science and engineering, yet standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) often capture such interactions only implicitly, leading to entangled representations that can impair robustness and interpretability. We investigate complex-valued product-unit residual networks (CV-PURe) that integrate multiplicative product units with residual connections to explicitly model cross-feature couplings while stabilizing optimization. We conduct a systematic evaluation on an interaction-driven synthetic benchmark and real-world datasets and evaluate prediction together with input-level interaction recovery under a reproducible protocol. Across five data splits and five training seeds, CV-PURe achieves the lowest mean RMSE on four of six scientific benchmarks, reducing Friedman error by 53.9% relative to MLP. Its Friedman interaction maps assign 60.7% of total strength to the known interacting pair, compared with 31.0% for MLP. On a synthetic task containing third- and fourth-order products and 20 distractors, CV-PURe reduces RMSE from 0.1376 to 0.0797 relative to a complex-valued MLP and recovers all nine true pairwise projections in every training/sampling repetition. Bike Sharing experiments connect improved prediction to the contribution of temporal, calendar, and seasonal context through paired ablations of both PURe variants. Parkinsons Telemonitoring extends the context analysis to repeated measurements. Noise and learning-curve evaluations demonstrate sustained predictive gains under perturbed inputs and limited supervision, while inference measurements quantify computational cost. This article extends our ICCS 2026 paper, Modeling Nonlinear Feature Interactions with Product-Unit Residual Networks (doi:10.1007/978-3-032-29921-5_6).
papers.summary: Standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) capture nonlinear feature interactions only implicitly, which can hurt robustness and interpretability. The authors study complex-valued product-unit residual networks (`CV-PURe`), which combine multiplicative product units with residual connections to model cross-feature couplings explicitly while keeping optimization stable. Across five data splits and five seeds, `CV-PURe` has the lowest mean RMSE on four of six scientific benchmarks and **cuts error on the `Friedman` benchmark by 53.9% relative to an MLP**, while assigning 60.7% of interaction strength to the known interacting pair versus 31.0% for the MLP. On a synthetic task with third- and fourth-order products and 20 distractor features, it recovers all nine true pairwise projections in every repetition.

papers.title: TelePhysica: Agentic Reconstruction of Physically Interactive Scenes
papers.abstract: Direct image-to-video diffusion models entangle pixel synthesis with implicit latent motion, precluding persistent 3D mechanical equilibrium, mid-rollout intervention, and counterfactual force control. Conversely, single-pass programmatic 3D reconstruction from an uncalibrated photograph leaves monocular depth and support clearance underconstrained, causing reconstructed scenes to interpenetrate or collapse under gravity. We present TelePhysica, a closed-loop framework that reconstructs an executable, multi-regime physical world from a single photograph to drive stateful 3D interaction and trajectory-grounded video synthesis. A vision-language coding agent synthesizes separable visual meshes and declarative physical models within a two-stage verification loop that pairs pixel-aligned silhouette critique with a zero-force gravitational equilibrium preflight. The verified world compiles into a unified solver coupling rigid bodies, articulated chains, co-dimensional cloth shells, and 3D tetrahedral elastodynamics, whose simulated rollouts condition pretrained video diffusion models through pixel-aligned structural streams. On a 100-scene single-image benchmark, closed-loop execution raises equilibrium-verified world recovery from $0\%$ in single-pass synthesis to $81\%$. Controlled constitutive ablations show over an order-of-magnitude larger localized corner displacement and out-of-plane pleating in finite-element cloth than in matched rigid-plate proxies. Conditioning video diffusion on simulated trajectories increases dynamic motion-mask overlap by $2{\times}\text{--}5{\times}$ and preserves motion direction under counterfactual force reversals where direct image-to-video models fail.
papers.summary: Reconstructing a physically interactive 3D scene from a single photograph is underconstrained, so single-pass reconstructions interpenetrate or collapse under gravity, while image-to-video diffusion models offer no persistent physical state or force control. `TelePhysica` has a vision-language coding agent write visual meshes and declarative physical models inside a verification loop that combines a silhouette critique with a zero-force gravitational equilibrium check. The verified scene compiles into a unified solver for rigid bodies, articulated chains, cloth, and elastic solids, and its simulated rollouts condition pretrained video diffusion models. On a 100-scene benchmark, the closed loop raises equilibrium-verified world recovery **from 0% in single-pass synthesis to 81%**, and trajectory conditioning increases motion-mask overlap by 2–5× while preserving motion direction under reversed forces.

papers.title: Two-Clustering Regime of Token Dynamics in Causal Attention
papers.abstract: We partially resolve Conjecture 1 of [Karagodin et al., Clustering in Causal Attention Masking (NeurIPS 2024)] and extend it to time-dependent parameter regimes. The conjecture predicts that causal attention dynamics converge to two clusters aligned with the eigenvectors associated with the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}$ of the value transformation. We prove that this behavior holds when $\lambda_{\max}>0$ and is generally false when $\lambda_{\max}\le0$. The resulting two-cluster regime is common in practice and substantially more challenging than the classical single-cluster setting studied previously. A central contribution of our work is the identification of a rigorous dimension reduction phenomenon: despite evolving in a high-dimensional embedding space, token trajectories collapse onto a two-dimensional structure governed by a small number of dominant directions. Building on this insight, we introduce a new analytical framework--instability within the flow--inspired by instability phenomena in physical systems. This framework enables the analysis of steady-regime behavior in non-monotone, non-autonomous attention dynamics. Our theoretical findings are illustrated through simulations and experimental studies using Group Query Attention (GQA) layers.
papers.summary: A conjecture from Karagodin et al. (NeurIPS 2024) predicts that token dynamics under causal attention converge to two clusters aligned with the eigenvectors of the largest eigenvalue λ_max of the value transformation. The authors prove that **the two-cluster behavior holds when λ_max > 0 and is generally false when λ_max ≤ 0**, and extend the analysis to time-dependent parameters. The proof rests on a dimension reduction result showing that token trajectories collapse onto a two-dimensional structure, plus a new analytical framework called instability within the flow for non-monotone, non-autonomous attention dynamics. Simulations and experiments with `Group Query Attention` (GQA) layers illustrate the theory.

papers.title: Deep Latents, Long Memory: Latent persistence explains temporal correlations in transformer activations
papers.abstract: The hidden layers of Large Language Models (LLMs) are believed to encode representations of the data whose abstraction increases with depth. However, in the absence of an operational notion of abstraction, this statement is hard to test quantitatively. Here, we propose an alternative view, building on the principle that the correlations of a sequence reflect the structure of the process that generated it. We define the autocorrelation function of a layer as the average dot product between its activations at two context positions separated by a lag. Latent variables encoded persistently along the context create slowly decaying tails in the autocorrelation, and we find these tails to grow across layers in both synthetic and natural data. In synthetic data with controlled hierarchical latent structure, this growth stems from the encoding of abstract latent variables, which govern long stretches of the input. Indeed, the persistence of latent codes predicts the qualitative structure of autocorrelations and accounts for most of the empirical measures. In real text, we take sparse-autoencoder features as proxies for latent variables, and find that their persistence correlates strongly with the magnitude of autocorrelations across datasets and LLMs. In particular, the persistence time increases with depth, as do autocorrelations, implying that deeper latent features persist for longer context spans. We complement this analysis by explicitly ablating the persistent sparse-autoencoder features and observing a consequent decrease in the autocorrelations.
papers.summary: The claim that deeper layers of Large Language Models (LLMs) encode more abstract representations is hard to test without an operational definition of abstraction. The authors instead measure a layer's autocorrelation function, the average dot product between its activations at two context positions separated by a lag, and argue that persistently encoded latent variables produce slowly decaying tails. On synthetic data with controlled hierarchical latents and on real text, where sparse-autoencoder features serve as proxies for latents, **both autocorrelation tails and feature persistence times grow with depth**, meaning deeper features persist over longer context spans. Ablating the persistent sparse-autoencoder features reduces the autocorrelations.
papers.highlight_summary:
Language models are thought to build more abstract representations in deeper layers, but that claim is hard to test without an operational definition of abstraction. The proposal here is to measure how slowly a layer's activations decorrelate across context positions, on the argument that abstract latent variables govern long stretches of input and leave long autocorrelation tails when their codes persist.

- The layer autocorrelation is the average dot product between standardised activations at two positions separated by a lag, which reduces to token-coincidence probability at the embedding layer and, under the linear representation hypothesis, counts latents encoded along aligned directions at both positions.
- In a 5-block GPT-2-style transformer trained on the `Random Hierarchy Model`, the autocorrelation forms a staircase whose steps fall at the span ends of the known latents (lags 2, 4 and 8), with persistent codes accounting for **55–95%** of the measured value and each plateau appearing in training exactly when the corresponding hierarchy level is learned.
- Across `Gemma 2 2B`, `Gemma 2 9B`, `Pythia-160M`, `Llama-3-8B` and `Qwen3-8B` on `WikiText` and `The Pile`, the median persistence of sparse-autoencoder features and the integrated autocorrelation both grow with depth and correlate strongly, and a position-shuffling control shows that feature activation frequency does not explain the growth in persistence.
- Projecting out a single persistent SAE feature within its firing episode lowers the mean autocorrelation there by about **3–13%**, three features by roughly **4–24%** and all active latents by **44–68%**, whereas a non-persistent control feature changes it by **under 1%**.
- The evidence has clear limits: the synthetic results come from a single grammar and training run, SAE features are an imperfect proxy whose full ablation never removes all the autocorrelation, the ablations cover only the deepest layer with an available SAE, and the measure misses latents whose encoding direction changes across positions.

papers.title: Training-point consistency of kernel ridge regression with varying correlation scales
papers.abstract: The scale parameter in kernel ridge regression plays a pivotal role in modeling the correlation structure of data. In modern applications, sampling density and the underlying correlation range often change simultaneously, making a fixed-scale assumption highly restrictive. However, establishing asymptotic theories under varying scale parameters is fundamentally challenging. To address this gap, this paper develops a unified theoretical framework for kernel ridge regression under varying scale parameters. We establish that, on uniform tensor grids with product exponential kernels, the consistency of the training-point risk holds if and only if the effective local sample size diverges to infinity. This sharp criterion universally covers all regimes along arbitrary deterministic scale sequences, seamlessly unifying the long-range, fixed-scale, and short-range. Furthermore, we provide an explicit, signal-independent construction of a deterministic regularization penalty that guarantees this consistency. Numerical experiments illustrate the criterion and the corresponding penalty across all the three regimes.
papers.summary: Kernel ridge regression theory usually assumes a fixed kernel scale, even though sampling density and correlation range often change together in practice. For uniform tensor grids with product exponential kernels, the authors prove that **the training-point risk is consistent if and only if the effective local sample size diverges to infinity**, a criterion covering long-range, fixed-scale, and short-range regimes along any deterministic scale sequence. They also give an explicit, signal-independent construction of a regularization penalty that guarantees this consistency, with numerical experiments illustrating all three regimes.

papers.title: VEPO: Mitigating Multilingual Hallucinations in LVLMs via Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization
