papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) achieve strong multimodal performance, yet they remain prone to object hallucination---generating answers that are linguistically fluent but visually ungrounded. This issue is especially severe in low-resource languages, where weaker cross-modal alignment causes models to rely more on language priors than on image evidence. Existing remedies either require costly multilingual annotations or external translation/reward models, or intervene at inference time in ways that can distort the output language. We propose VEPO(Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization), a training-time method that transfers reliable visual grounding from English to other languages without external models. VEPO first localizes key visual evidence using English queries via mid-layer cross-modal attention, then constructs preference pairs that share the same correct answer but differ in evidence sufficiency (full image vs.\ key-region masked image). Direct preference optimization on these pairs encourages low-resource inputs to prefer answers supported by complete visual evidence. Experiments on multilingual POPE and MME with Chinese, French, and Hindi show consistent hallucination reduction and perception gains, with the largest improvements on the lowest-resource language. Analyses further confirm that VEPO sharpens question-relevant attention and that evidence-guided masking outperforms random masking.
papers.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) hallucinate objects more often in low-resource languages, where weaker cross-modal alignment makes them lean on language priors instead of image evidence. `VEPO` (Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization) is a training-time method that localizes key visual evidence using English queries and mid-layer cross-modal attention, then builds preference pairs with the same correct answer but either the full image or an image with the key region masked. Applying direct preference optimization to these pairs, without external translation or reward models, reduces hallucination on multilingual `POPE` and `MME` in Chinese, French, and Hindi, with **the largest improvements on the lowest-resource language**. Evidence-guided masking also outperforms random masking.

papers.title: AG-JEPA: Anatomically Guided Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Neurodegenerative Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Brain MRI can reveal early signs of Alzheimers disease (AD) before measurable cognitive decline becomes apparent. However, during the transition from cognitively normal (CN) to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), the disease-related signals are often subtle and confined to only a few brain regions. Existing Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models learn general structural representations but do not explicitly capture the anatomical regions affected in AD. We propose Anatomically Guided JEPA (AG-JEPA), which introduces anatomical tokens that interact with patch tokens during pretraining to learn region-specific representations from brain regions relevant to neurodegeneration. Building on this representation space, we further propose Prog-AG-JEPA, which models disease progression trajectory as a conditioned latent displacement within this space. We evaluate AG-JEPA across five downstream tasks spanning Alzheimer's disease diagnosis and progression prediction. AG-JEPA improves diagnosis and MCI prognosis, achieving an 8.4 percentage point AUROC gain over the strongest baseline on CN/MCI classification and a 7.1 percentage point gain on out-of-distribution CN/AD classification on the MR-RATE dataset, highlighting its effectiveness across both early-stage detection and cross-cohort generalization. For disease progression modeling, Prog-AG-JEPA consistently outperforms all baselines on future diagnosis and brain volume change prediction, demonstrating the value of anatomically grounded neurodegeneration representations for diagnosis and prognosis.
papers.summary: Early Alzheimer's disease (AD) signals in brain MRI are subtle and confined to a few regions during the transition from cognitively normal (CN) to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and existing Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models do not explicitly capture those regions. `AG-JEPA` adds anatomical tokens that interact with patch tokens during pretraining to learn region-specific representations, and `Prog-AG-JEPA` models disease progression as a conditioned latent displacement in that space. Across five downstream tasks, `AG-JEPA` achieves **an 8.4 percentage point AUROC gain over the strongest baseline on CN/MCI classification** and a 7.1 point gain on out-of-distribution CN/AD classification on the `MR-RATE` dataset. `Prog-AG-JEPA` outperforms all baselines on future diagnosis and brain volume change prediction.

papers.title: Do Machines Learn Deviance From Their Peers? A Randomized Test of Differential Association With AI Agents
papers.abstract: Differential association theory and its extension, social learning theory, hold that rule-breaking, and the definitions that make it acceptable, are learned through interaction with others. Because people choose their friends, this claim has been hard to test. We addressed this selection problem with AI agents, which learn only through communication and can be assigned to peers at random. In a preregistered experiment, 420 teams of three agents (1,260 agents; seven AI models) worked on coding tasks that could not be solved honestly. A scripted teammate said that it had cheated (deviant peer), that it had reported the problem honestly (honest peer), or said nothing (silent peer). Half of the teams were told that an auditor read their chat. Compared with a silent peer, a deviant peer increased cheating (66.2% vs. 62.9%; OR = 1.96) and an honest peer reduced it (55.7%; OR = 0.35). Among agents that cheated, a deviant peer increased claims that cheating was normal (13.7% vs. 3.4%), often as the team's norm. Monitoring did not suppress prohibited discussion; it doubled it. Peers mattered only for models that had not yet decided. AI agents offer a new way to test criminological learning theories without selection effects.
papers.summary: Differential association theory holds that rule-breaking is learned from peers, but the claim is hard to test in humans because people choose their friends. In a preregistered experiment, 420 teams of three AI agents (1,260 agents across seven models) worked on coding tasks that could not be solved honestly, alongside a scripted teammate who said it had cheated, said it had reported the problem honestly, or said nothing. Compared with a silent peer, **a deviant peer increased cheating (66.2% vs. 62.9%; odds ratio 1.96) and an honest peer reduced it (55.7%; odds ratio 0.35)**, and cheating agents with a deviant peer more often claimed cheating was normal (13.7% vs. 3.4%). Telling teams that an auditor read their chat doubled prohibited discussion instead of suppressing it, and peers only influenced models that had not already decided.

papers.title: EcoVGGT: Pinned-Key Inference for Efficient and Streamable Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Long Videos
papers.abstract: Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content, and our experiments on VGGT and $\pi^3$ support it: a few dozen evenly spread frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) matches the success rate of $\pi^3$ on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos at 13.8 times its speed. With refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate of VGGT from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times its speed on 500 frames. EcoVGGT reconstructs 4,000 frames on one GPU, and EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 frames per second with the lowest online absolute trajectory error.
papers.summary: Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as `VGGT` recover cameras and geometry in one pass, but their cross-frame attention cost grows quadratically with frame count and accuracy drops on long videos. `EcoVGGT` is a training-free inference framework built on the finding that a few dozen evenly spaced frames, chosen without looking at content, can serve as attention keys for every frame: 31 pinned frames are cached and all other frames read that cache in independent batches at constant cost per frame. An attention-based `Alignment Score` flags failures, and fine-tuning only six middle global blocks for 3.6 GPU hours reduces them. `EcoVGGT` with `π³` **matches the success rate of `π³` on 1,000-frame `ScanNet` videos at 13.8 times its speed**, and the `VGGT` variant raises success from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times the speed on 500 frames while reconstructing 4,000 frames on one GPU.

papers.title: Contagious Fingerprints: When LLMs Inherit Another Model's Identity
papers.abstract: The fingerprint by which a classifier recognizes the LLM behind a text is usually treated as a fixed property of the model. We show that it is contagious: a model that continues a conversation begun by another model inherits that model's fingerprint. This undermines audits of API relays, which can serve the first turns of a conversation with the model a customer pays for and silently hand the rest to a cheaper one. After such a handoff, detection of the substitute by a text classifier drops from 0.97 to 0.72 (DeepSeek replacing Claude Sonnet) and from 0.87 to 0.54 for a same-vendor downgrade (Haiku), and retraining on handoff data repairs only substitutes seen in training. Preregistered experiments trace the contagion to imitation of the history's style. History also moves a model away from its own fingerprint: active probes are not camouflaged, but when calibrated on fresh conversations they flag \emph{honest} models on long contexts at rates up to 1.00, and a standard MMD equality test rejects all nine models we test. Both failures come from comparing a history-dependent reply with a history-free reference. We propose \textsc{Lineup}, which samples references from the claimed model \emph{on the same history} and tests the audited reply by its rank among them. \textsc{Lineup} controls false positives by exchangeability and needs no fitted threshold or log-probabilities. With contemporaneous references on two closed models, its false-positive rate is 0.056 (preregistered bound 0.10), and it detects 0.81 of substitute sessions across six pairs after four audited turns.
papers.summary: Text classifiers that identify which LLM produced a reply assume the model's fingerprint is fixed, but a model continuing a conversation begun by another model inherits that model's fingerprint by imitating the history's style. This lets an API relay serve the first turns with the paid-for model and silently hand off to a cheaper one: **classifier detection of the substitute drops from 0.97 to 0.72** when `DeepSeek` replaces `Claude Sonnet`, and from 0.87 to 0.54 for a downgrade to `Haiku`. History dependence also causes probes calibrated on fresh conversations to flag honest models on long contexts at rates up to 1.00. The proposed `Lineup` test samples reference replies from the claimed model on the same history and ranks the audited reply among them, needing no fitted threshold or log-probabilities; it shows a false-positive rate of 0.056 and detects 0.81 of substitute sessions after four audited turns.

papers.title: An In-Silico Audit of Topographic Organization in a Multimodal Brain-Response Model
papers.abstract: TRIBE v2 (d'Ascoli et al., 2026) predicts fMRI responses across the cortical surface from video, audio and text. Its authors validated it with category-selective localizers (faces, places, bodies, words) and language contrasts, but not with the classic topographic organization of sensory cortex: retinotopy, tonotopy, and motion selectivity in area MT+. There is a clear architectural reason to expect retinotopy to fail: TRIBE's video features are averaged over space before the response head, which should discard visual-field position. I present mapping stimuli, a fitting pipeline adapted from standard fMRI mapping analyses, and a stand-in model with known ground truth that serves as a positive and negative control, and apply them to TRIBE v2's predictions, comparing the fitted maps with human atlases using spin tests. TRIBE v2 shows a sharp split. There is no contralateral hemifield response and no polar-angle map, robustly across stimulus controls. There is no tonotopic gradient in primary auditory cortex: best frequencies span an interquartile range of only 0.14 octaves across core and belt, and the null persists with loudness-equalized tones. An eccentricity-like gradient appears only when the ring geometry changes, consistent with global image statistics rather than a positional code. In contrast, motion selectivity is strong and precisely localized: 22% of the 1% most motion-selective vertices fall in MT+, which covers 0.42% of cortex. In-silico experiments that depend on feature identity appear viable with TRIBE v2, while those that depend on visual-field or frequency position are not supported by the current model.
papers.summary: `TRIBE v2` predicts fMRI responses across the cortex from video, audio, and text, but it was never validated against the classic topographic maps of sensory cortex: retinotopy, tonotopy, and motion selectivity in area MT+. The author builds mapping stimuli, a fitting pipeline adapted from standard fMRI analyses, and a ground-truth stand-in model as a control, then compares the fitted maps with human atlases. The model shows **no contralateral hemifield response, no polar-angle map, and no tonotopic gradient**, consistent with its video features being spatially averaged before the response head. Motion selectivity, by contrast, is strong and well localized, with 22% of the top 1% motion-selective vertices falling in MT+, which covers 0.42% of cortex.

papers.title: Folding Language Models into Themselves
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation usually trains a compact student from scratch, which needs a large amount of data even though the teacher's weights already encode most of what the student has to learn. In this work, we explore building the student directly from the teacher's weights. We propose Concertina, which folds every group of N adjacent teacher layers into one shared block that is executed N times. Each loop step carries a low-rank correction initialized from the layer it replaces, and a per-token gate mixes these corrections, to let every token recover the behavior of the original layers from a single shared block. We further design a distillation data recipe that balances general, mathematical, academic and targeted multiple-choice data, to recover all capabilities of the teacher together rather than one at the expense of another. On Qwen3-4B, a 2.27B Concertina model distilled on 22B tokens retains about 90% of the teacher on commonsense and mathematical reasoning and 84% on average across eight benchmarks. It outperforms same-size dense and layer-sharing baselines, as well as Qwen3-1.7B, which is trained on over a thousand times more data. These results suggest that a compact model need not be retrained at scale, since folding the teacher into itself and distilling it on the right data recovers most of its capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/myboker/concertina.
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation normally trains a compact student from scratch on large amounts of data, even though the teacher's weights already encode most of what the student must learn. `Concertina` builds the student from the teacher by folding each group of N adjacent layers into one shared block executed N times, with a low-rank correction per loop step initialized from the replaced layer and a per-token gate that mixes the corrections. Paired with a distillation data mix spanning general, mathematical, academic, and multiple-choice data, a 2.27B-parameter model folded from `Qwen3-4B` and distilled on 22B tokens **retains about 90% of the teacher on commonsense and mathematical reasoning** and 84% on average across eight benchmarks. It outperforms same-size dense and layer-sharing baselines as well as `Qwen3-1.7B`, which was trained on over a thousand times more data.

papers.title: Interpretable weight-space programming builds transparent transformers and brain encoding models
papers.abstract: Neural networks are powerful predictors, yet their opacity limits their usefulness in science, where the goal is explanation rather than mere prediction. In neuroscience, for example, deep encoding models accurately predict brain activity in response to natural stimuli, but struggle to reveal which stimulus features drive those predictions. Here we introduce interpretable weight-space programming (iWSP), a method in which an LLM agent iteratively builds interpretable models by explicitly programming their weights and features in code, without gradient-based training (backpropagation). Without backpropagation to tune parameters, the agent must draw on its prior knowledge and reason over previous trials to hypothesize, hand-craft, and refine human-interpretable computations mirroring the workflow of a human scientist. LLM audits confirm the interpretability of the hand-crafted models. We first validate iWSP by tasking it with constructing transformers for canonical benchmarks such as arithmetic and sentiment classification, finding that LLM agents can successfully craft compact, accurate networks directly. Next, we apply iWSP to build neural encoding models across vision, language, and audition. In the visual cortex, iWSP outpredicts existing interpretable baselines, uncovers distinct computations across early/higher visual areas, and generalizes to unseen data. In language fMRI, iWSP surfaces a confound in the data and in auditory ECoG, it systematically discovers interpretable acoustic features that predict neural activity. Together, these results establish iWSP as a general paradigm for aligning high predictive performance with human-interpretable scientific discovery.
papers.summary: Deep encoding models predict brain activity well but do not reveal which stimulus features drive their predictions. Interpretable weight-space programming (`iWSP`) has an LLM agent iteratively build models by writing their weights and features directly in code, with no gradient-based training, relying on prior knowledge and reasoning over earlier trials. The agent **successfully hand-crafts compact, accurate transformers for benchmarks such as arithmetic and sentiment classification**, and LLM audits confirm the resulting models are interpretable. Applied to neural encoding, `iWSP` outpredicts existing interpretable baselines in visual cortex, surfaces a confound in language fMRI data, and discovers interpretable acoustic features that predict auditory ECoG activity.

papers.title: Optimizing Drilling Trajectories in Multi-Material Structures Using Quantum Annealers
papers.abstract: In this work we present a quantum-hybrid optimization approach for planning drilling trajectories on multi-material structures, with the objective of minimizing total energy consumption. The proposed formulation models the drilling process as a constrained routing problem in which each hole must be visited while accounting for heterogeneous material properties, material-dependent drilling costs and displacement energy, as well as tool-wear penalties. Our method incorporates realistic industrial constraints, including open-path routing and mandatory grouping of holes belonging to the same material to avoid frequent tool-bit changes. The modeled problem is solved using D-Wave's Leap Constrained Quadratic Model Hybrid Solver. To evaluate performance, we benchmark instances ranging from 10 to 55 holes with varying material distributions and cost matrices. The results highlight the capability of quantum-hybrid optimization to handle complex multi-physics constraints and to generate energy-efficient drilling sequences under realistic manufacturing conditions.
papers.summary: Planning the order in which to drill holes in multi-material structures is framed as a constrained routing problem that minimizes total energy consumption. The formulation accounts for material-dependent drilling costs, displacement energy, tool-wear penalties, open-path routing, and mandatory grouping of holes in the same material to avoid frequent tool-bit changes. It is solved with `D-Wave`'s `Leap Constrained Quadratic Model Hybrid Solver` on instances of 10 to 55 holes, where the authors report that **the quantum-hybrid solver handles the full constraint set and produces energy-efficient drilling sequences**.

papers.title: Muon Attains $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ Iteration Complexity under Shuffling
papers.abstract: Muon is a stochastic first-order optimizer for matrix-valued parameters. It maintains an exponential moving average of stochastic gradients in a momentum buffer with coefficient $\beta$, and orthogonalizes the buffer to obtain the update direction. Muon has been reported to accelerate and stabilize the training of large language models. In practice, it is often used with shuffling (sampling without replacement), where each epoch visits the components of a finite-sum objective in a permuted order. However, its iteration complexity in this setting remains open. We analyze Muon under shuffling, with the momentum buffer orthogonalized by the polar map. For smooth nonconvex finite-sum problems, we establish an $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ iteration complexity for finding an $\varepsilon$-stationary point. This guarantee holds for every sequence of permutations, covering random reshuffling, shuffle once, and the incremental gradient method. This complexity matches that of stochastic gradient descent under shuffling in its dependence on $\varepsilon$, and improves on Muon's $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ complexity under sampling with replacement. Our guarantee requires a problem-dependent $\beta$ that approaches one as the number of components grows. In contrast, no fixed $\beta$ guarantees convergence to stationarity for every number of components. We show this by constructing a family of smooth convex problems on which, for any fixed $\beta\in[0,1)$, Muon remains bounded away from stationarity once the number of components is sufficiently large. This failure occurs for every sequence of permutations and persists even with small stepsizes. These results suggest two practical tuning rules: if the training loss stops decreasing even after reducing the stepsize, increase $\beta$; when increasing $\beta$, reduce the stepsize accordingly.
papers.summary: `Muon` is an optimizer for matrix-valued parameters that orthogonalizes an exponential moving average of gradients, and it is typically run with shuffling (sampling without replacement), a setting where its iteration complexity was unknown. For smooth nonconvex finite-sum problems, the authors prove that `Muon` under shuffling reaches an ε-stationary point in **O(ε⁻³) iterations, improving on its O(ε⁻⁴) complexity under sampling with replacement** and matching shuffled stochastic gradient descent, for every sequence of permutations. The guarantee requires a momentum coefficient β that approaches one as the number of components grows, and a constructed family of convex problems shows that no fixed β guarantees convergence for every problem size. The practical tuning rules that follow are to increase β if the loss stalls even after reducing the stepsize, and to reduce the stepsize when increasing β.

papers.title: Efficient Poincar\'e Convolutions through Patch-Statistics Factorization
papers.abstract: Published implementations of the Poincar\'e convolution in Hyperbolic Neural Networks++ (HNN++) map every overlapping image patch to the Poincar\'e ball before evaluating its score. We show that the clipped score depends on each patch only through two statistics, its squared norm and its inner products with the filters, which a native convolution and a single-channel box filter compute directly. The factorized layer therefore evaluates the specified score exactly, without constructing ball-valued patches, and its single-precision outputs and gradients agree with double-precision evaluations at least as closely as those of the explicit reference. On an RTX A6000 under two versions of JAX, complete training updates of a Poincar\'e U-Net and a Poincar\'e ResNet-20 are 1.5 to 1.8 times faster than the faster of two explicit implementations that map patches to the ball (1.2 to 1.4 times against an explicit implementation that skips this mapping); on a V100, the gain over the gather-based one persists as the ResNet-20 is widened eightfold. In 15 paired training runs per task, updates are 2.0 and 1.8 times faster than a reference that follows the published execution order, with no consistent change in final segmentation or classification quality, and peak memory falls by 38 to 55% in a U-Net scaling study. Replacing the convolutions of the official PyTorch Hyperbolic U-Net makes its training step 1.4 times faster with half the memory. Evaluating an existing layer from its patch statistics thus makes Poincar\'e convolutional networks cheaper to train in the tested models and software stacks.
papers.summary: Published implementations of the Poincaré convolution from Hyperbolic Neural Networks++ (`HNN++`) map every overlapping image patch to the Poincaré ball before scoring it. The authors show the clipped score depends on each patch only through its squared norm and its inner products with the filters, which a native convolution and a single-channel box filter compute directly, so the layer can be evaluated exactly without constructing ball-valued patches. In `JAX`, full training updates of a Poincaré U-Net and Poincaré ResNet-20 run **1.5 to 1.8 times faster than the faster explicit implementation**, with peak memory down 38 to 55% in a U-Net scaling study and no consistent change in final quality. Swapping the layer into the official `PyTorch` Hyperbolic U-Net makes its training step 1.4 times faster with half the memory.

papers.title: PRISM: A Post-Prediction Reliability Framework for Evidence-Guided Correction and Selective Abstention
papers.abstract:
A model may produce a prediction with high confidence and still get the outcome wrong. This is a challenge in sequential applications, where the system evolves over time and deployment data may differ from the data used during training. To address this issue, we propose PRISM (Prediction Reliability and Intelligent Self-Correction Mechanism), a framework that evaluates prediction reliability after the initial output is generated. It estimates the risk of error and examines predictions identified as potentially unreliable. For these cases, PRISM analyses available signals, retrieves similar situations from historical data, and verifies whether an alternative prediction is supported by the evidence. It can then retain the original prediction, apply a verified correction, or abstain when the evidence is insufficient.
  We evaluate PRISM on second-innings match prediction in the Indian Premier League (IPL). Ball-by-ball records are converted into over-level observations to capture changes in match conditions throughout an innings. To preserve temporal order, earlier IPL seasons are used for training, IPL 2024 for validation, and IPL 2025-2026 for out-of-time testing. The dataset contains 8,665 over-level observations from 475 matches, with the test partition comprising 2,568 observations from 142 matches. In one experimental record, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and HistGradientBoosting achieve accuracies of 65.2%, 68.4%, and 70.2%, respectively. The corresponding PRISM evaluation reports a selective accuracy of 82.4% at 88.5% coverage, with a Brier score of 0.126 and an expected calibration error (ECE) of 0.019.
papers.summary: Models can be confidently wrong, particularly in sequential settings where deployment data drifts from training data. `PRISM` (Prediction Reliability and Intelligent Self-Correction Mechanism) assesses a prediction after it is made: it estimates error risk, retrieves similar historical situations for flagged cases, and then keeps the prediction, applies a verified correction, or abstains when evidence is insufficient. It is evaluated on second-innings match prediction in the Indian Premier League (IPL) using 8,665 over-level observations from 475 matches with an out-of-time test split. In one experimental record, baseline classifiers reach 65.2% to 70.2% accuracy while `PRISM` reports **a selective accuracy of 82.4% at 88.5% coverage**, with a Brier score of 0.126 and an expected calibration error (ECE) of 0.019.

papers.title: JFinBench: A Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to finance, creating a need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities across financial systems with different regulations and practices. However, existing financial benchmarks provide limited coverage of country-specific financial systems, and they are difficult to keep up to date as released questions leak into training data. We introduce JFinBench, a Japanese financial benchmark comprising 321 examples from the 2026 editions of six regularly administered certification exams covering accounting, tax, financial planning, and banking. To construct it, we develop a human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline in which a coding agent writes exam-specific conversion code and a review page, while a human verifies every example and feeds corrections back to the agent. This pipeline adapts to heterogeneous exam formats and reduces the effort of incorporating new exam editions, enabling periodic refreshes that mitigate data contamination. Evaluating 12 recent LLMs, we find that Claude Fable 5 and GPT-6 Astra exceed 93% overall, while even the best open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, trails Claude Fable 5 by 12 percentage points. When models can additionally use a terminal and web access, they retrieve the knowledge they lack and every model improves. The gap narrows but about 4 points remain, and the ranking of models stays largely the same, suggesting that knowledge held in the model itself remains valuable even with tools. We release the dataset, the evaluation code, and the construction pipeline.
papers.summary: Financial benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) cover country-specific systems poorly and go stale as released questions leak into training data. `JFinBench` contains 321 examples from the 2026 editions of six Japanese certification exams covering accounting, tax, financial planning, and banking, built with a human-in-the-loop pipeline in which a coding agent writes exam-specific conversion code and a review page while a human verifies every example. Among 12 evaluated models, `Claude Fable 5` and `GPT-6 Astra` exceed 93% overall, while **the best open-weight model, `Kimi K3.1 Pro`, trails `Claude Fable 5` by 12 percentage points**. Giving models a terminal and web access improves every model and narrows that gap to about 4 points, but the ranking stays largely the same.
papers.highlight_summary:
Financial LLM benchmarks are mostly English and U.S.-centric and go stale as questions leak into training data, so `JFinBench` builds a refreshable Japanese benchmark from the newest certification exams. A human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline converts the exam PDFs into structured examples, making each new exam edition cheap to add.

- The benchmark holds **321 examples** from the 2026 editions of six exams (CPA, tax accountant, financial planning, bank counter services, and two bookkeeping tests), spanning multiple choice, short answer, structured forms and essays, with 12 image-dependent questions.
- To build it, `Gemini 3.8 Flash` transcribes each page to layout-preserving markdown, `Claude Code` writes exam-specific conversion code and a review page, and a native-speaker author verifies every example against the source, taking about **12 hours** in total.
- Without tools, across 12 models at maximum reasoning effort, `Claude Fable 5` scores **95.8%** and `GPT-6 Astra` **93.6%** (equal-weight mean over the six exams), while the best open-weight model, `Kimi K3.1 Pro`, reaches **83.4%** and every open-weight model ranks below every proprietary one.
- With terminal and web access every model improves, by up to 29.9 points for `GLM 5.3 Flash`, and taking each model's best harness the proprietary-to-open gap narrows from **12.4 to 4.4 points** (`GPT-6 Astra` at 97.3 versus `Kimi K3.1 Pro` at 92.9), yet the ranking barely changes (Spearman **ρ = 0.87**).
- Most failures come from missing knowledge rather than calculation errors, and the main limitations are saturation (the two leaders score 96–100 on every exam except the tax accountant exam, where the best is 79.4) and contamination that cannot be ruled out because knowledge cutoffs are self-reported.

papers.title: PUMA-Former: Uncertainty-Aware Agentic Computation Offloading in MEO-LEO Satellite Networks With Incomplete Information
papers.abstract: Satellite edge computing distributes mobile workloads across moving processors whose service capacity must be coordinated over time. In medium Earth orbit (MEO)--low Earth orbit (LEO) networks, periodic reports leave CPU states stale or missing, making offloading sensitive to uncertain capacity and shared-destination congestion. We propose PUMA-Former, an uncertainty-aware agentic framework for cooperative offloading under incomplete information that balances completed work, service delay, and execution cost. A MEO coordinator maintains distinct-report memory and closes the loop between available evidence, capacity estimates, allocation commands, and execution feedback. Latent-delay attention weights plausible measurement-age hypotheses, and historical innovations refine CPU estimates around the latest received report. Queue-error-aware fusion incorporates auxiliary pressure while accounting for backlog uncertainty. The inferred resource moments condition a structured Transformer allocator for joint destination, partition, bandwidth, CPU, and power decisions. Bounded risk-aware calibration then adjusts workload splits to reflect uncertainty and shared destination load. In traffic-driven development evaluation, PUMA-Former increases admitted compute-work completion by 8.62%, reduces mean modeled service delay by 34.78%, and reduces mean episode-P95 delay by 71.08% relative to ATLA-adapt. It also improves completion and normalized energy over fixed-half round-robin offloading. Service gains over the learning baselines involve higher normalized energy.
papers.summary: In satellite edge computing across medium Earth orbit (MEO) and low Earth orbit (LEO) networks, periodic status reports leave CPU states stale or missing, making computation offloading sensitive to uncertain capacity and congestion at shared destinations. `PUMA-Former` has a MEO coordinator maintain a memory of reports, estimate capacity using attention over plausible measurement-age hypotheses, and feed the inferred resource estimates to a Transformer allocator that jointly decides destination, partition, bandwidth, CPU, and power, followed by a risk-aware calibration of workload splits. Relative to the `ATLA-adapt` baseline, it increases completed compute work by 8.62% and **reduces mean service delay by 34.78%** and mean 95th-percentile episode delay by 71.08%. These service gains over the learning baselines come with higher normalized energy use.

papers.title: Large Language Model-Empowered Intelligent Agent for Adaptive Fast-Charging Control of Lithium-Ion Batteries
papers.abstract: Fast charging of lithium-ion batteries is a multi-objective control problem that requires reducing charging time and sustaining high energy throughput while suppressing accelerated degradation and safety-critical electrochemical reactions. Conventional protocols are easy to implement but have limited ability to adapt to variations in battery chemistry, operating conditions, and aging state. Model-based optimization and conventional data-driven control often require accurate models, costly iterative search, or task-specific policies. We develop a large language model (LLM)-empowered intelligent agent for adaptive battery fast-charging control. In this closed-loop framework, the agent interprets structured battery states, generates executable charging actions, observes the resulting battery response, and continuously adjusts subsequent decisions. We construct a large-scale simulation corpus with PyBaMM across five battery chemistries and 11 parameter sets and convert the resulting state-action-response trajectories into structured process data for agent training. Our two-stage strategy combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). SFT establishes battery-control semantics and feasible decision priors from simulation-derived demonstrations. GRPO aligns the agent with a multi-objective control objective covering energy throughput, degradation mitigation, and operational constraints. Closed-loop simulations show that, under matched energy-throughput requirements, the agent achieves longer cycling life than conventional charging baselines and optimization-based strategies across heterogeneous battery configurations. This study provides a simulation-grounded proof of concept for using LLM agents as sequential decision makers in battery management and takes a step toward language-model-enabled control of physical energy systems.
papers.summary: Fast charging of lithium-ion batteries must trade off charging time and energy throughput against degradation and safety, and conventional protocols adapt poorly to different chemistries, conditions, and aging states. The authors train an LLM agent that reads structured battery states, issues executable charging actions, observes the response, and adjusts subsequent decisions in a closed loop. Training uses a `PyBaMM` simulation corpus spanning five battery chemistries and 11 parameter sets, with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) against a multi-objective reward. In closed-loop simulation under matched energy-throughput requirements, **the agent achieves longer cycling life than conventional charging baselines and optimization-based strategies** across heterogeneous battery configurations.

papers.title: When Copying Is Hard to Beat: A Negative Result in Clinical Assessment Forecasting
papers.abstract: We report a negative result in next-day clinical assessment forecasting: the evaluated models show no consistent advantage over strong persistence-based baselines. Clinicians can view the previous day's questionnaire answers, a plausible source of documentation persistence. Predicting 45 items on 29,715 ICU day-pairs with patient-disjoint splits, a physiology-informed gated model improves item-macro-F1 over a one-line clinical rule by +0.0019 [+0.0006,+0.0031], while losing accuracy. No macro-F1 advantage is established when the physiology window ends at the previous form's reference time (+0.0001 [-0.0006,+0.0008]), or when scoring excludes the 68.5% of cells derived from parent answers; combining both changes yields a small disadvantage. Four checkpoints across three families underperform persistence, and a fine-tuned one differs from it on only two cells. A categorical read-out raises changed-cell accuracy eightfold, but a state-only read-out scores higher overall than forecast-only decoding and matches a transition matrix. This negative result highlights how the documentation process, input cutoff, observation mask and decoding rule shape conclusions about forecasting recorded assessments.
papers.summary: Forecasting the next day's clinical assessment answers for intensive care patients is tested against persistence baselines that simply copy the previous day's answers, which clinicians can see when filling in the form. Across 45 items on 29,715 ICU day-pairs with patient-disjoint splits, **the evaluated models show no consistent advantage over persistence**: a physiology-informed gated model gains only +0.0019 item-macro-F1 over a one-line clinical rule while losing accuracy. That margin disappears when the physiology window ends at the previous form's reference time or when the 68.5% of cells derived from parent answers are excluded from scoring. Four checkpoints across three model families underperform persistence, and the authors show that the documentation process, input cutoff, observation mask, and decoding rule shape the conclusions drawn.

papers.title: STAMP: Manufacturing-Informed Generative Design and Shape Optimization of Sheet Panels
papers.abstract: Generative design of formed sheet panels must preserve geometric manufacturing conditions while exploring layouts and improving performance. STAMP embeds these conditions directly in the shape representation. Each panel is described by its material layout and a reference surface with one height at each occupied position in a plane perpendicular to the drawing direction. Nominal thickness is prescribed along the normal. The representation allows curved surfaces, ribs, and openings. It excludes reference-surface undercuts and keeps nominal thickness fixed without manufacturing penalty terms. Because these conditions belong to the representation, every generated and optimized panel satisfies them regardless of training-set size. Boundary-conditioned diffusion generates alternative layouts, and predictor gradients guide a surface optimization that retains outlines, openings, and designated fixed regions. We demonstrate STAMP on automotive hood inner panels using CarHoods10k. With a comparable number of stored values, depth maps reconstruct surfaces more accurately than point-cloud and voxel baselines. From only five training designs, one of three training runs yields novel and varied layouts. A generator trained on 500 designs, 6.5% of the training set, already reaches the layout variety of the full-data model. Across 11 held-out design families, predictor-based selection among existing dataset designs yields an average gap of 0.18 mm to the best available FEA deformation, versus an expected 1.59 mm for random selection. It does better than random selection in all 11 families. At a 10% depth-change bound, a network not used in the search predicts an average deformation reduction of 24.8% for six generated and existing panels, with a 3.2% average mass increase computed from geometry. Engineers can thus explore and optimize panels within this manufacturing-informed design space.
papers.summary: Generative design of formed sheet-metal panels has to respect manufacturing conditions while exploring layouts and improving performance. `STAMP` builds those conditions into the shape representation itself: each panel is a material layout plus a depth map giving one height per occupied position perpendicular to the drawing direction, with fixed nominal thickness, so undercuts are excluded by construction and no penalty terms are needed. Boundary-conditioned diffusion proposes layouts and predictor gradients guide surface optimization. On automotive hood inner panels from `CarHoods10k`, a generator trained on 500 designs (6.5% of the training set) matches the layout variety of the full-data model, and at a 10% depth-change bound an independent network predicts an **average deformation reduction of 24.8%** for a 3.2% average mass increase.

papers.title: Compiling Specialized GPU-Initiated Networking
papers.abstract: Machine learning systems specialize computation to the workload and hardware, but communication remains in generic libraries whose device code and transport decisions are not visible to high-level compilers. We present Obaleth, a compiler that makes GPU-initiated communication part of a kernel's intermediate representation, co-optimizes it alongside computation, and lowers it to specialized transport code. Obaleth plans completions around buffer lifetimes and optimizes memory ordering, synchronization, and batching across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. On H100 GPUs, Obaleth sends small messages up to 3.3$\times$ faster, and on 256 GPUs runs all-to-all 1.25$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ faster than NVSHMEM and NCCL GIN, with much smaller memory and register use. In vLLM, it serves Qwen3-235B on 16 B200 GPUs and answers requests up to 1.29$\times$ faster than with DeepEP.
papers.summary: Machine learning systems specialize computation to the workload and hardware, but communication is left to generic libraries whose device code and transport decisions are invisible to high-level compilers. `Obaleth` is a compiler that makes GPU-initiated communication part of a kernel's intermediate representation, co-optimizes it with computation, and lowers it to specialized transport code, planning completions around buffer lifetimes and tuning memory ordering, synchronization, and batching on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. On H100 GPUs it sends small messages up to 3.3x faster, and on 256 GPUs it runs all-to-all **1.25x and 2.3x faster than `NVSHMEM` and `NCCL GIN`** with much smaller memory and register use. Integrated into `vLLM`, it serves `Qwen3-235B` on 16 B200 GPUs and answers requests up to 1.29x faster than with `DeepEP`.

papers.title: Which Model, For Which Variable? Per-Variable Forecast Combination in Sparse ICU Time Series
papers.abstract: Clinical forecasting papers typically report a single best architecture. We show that on multivariate ICU physiology this question conceals variable-specific differences: no architecture is best on every variable, and which model wins changes from variable to variable. Across five ICU databases (MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, eICU, HiRID, and UMM (University Medicine Mannheim), a German single-center ICU) we forecast 94 channels over a 24-hour horizon with a pool of 14 models, and combine them with weights fitted per variable. On test, the combination beats the best single model on all five databases by 6.1-11.0% mean squared error (mean 8.7%). The gain is concentrated where clinical data is thinnest: the sparsest third of channels improves by 11.9% and laboratory values by 7.5%, against 3.1% for the densest third. Rank-based harmonic weighting of the best five models per variable, with no fitted weights at all, recovers about four-fifths of the gain. Extending the pool afterwards with a per-channel gradient-boosted tree, ARIMA and ETS makes the tree the validation-selected best single model on all five databases; per-variable combination still improves on it by 2.9-5.9% (significant on four of five), while equal weighting of the same members does not. As on univariate benchmarks, learned combination beats simple averaging - but only once the weights are constrained. We also report which model to prefer when, and show that the ordering changes with database size.
papers.summary: Clinical forecasting studies usually report one best architecture, but on multivariate intensive care unit (ICU) physiology no model wins on every variable. Across five ICU databases (`MIMIC-III`, `MIMIC-IV`, `eICU`, `HiRID`, and `UMM` from University Medicine Mannheim), the authors forecast 94 channels over a 24-hour horizon with a pool of 14 models and combine them with weights fitted per variable. The combination **beats the best single model on all five databases by 6.1-11.0% mean squared error**, with the largest gains on the sparsest channels and laboratory values. A rank-based harmonic weighting of the top five models per variable, with no fitted weights, recovers about four-fifths of the gain, and learned combination beats simple averaging only once the weights are constrained.

papers.title: Who Should Be on the Panel? Task-Conditioned Persona Selection for LLM Trading Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are built by fixing a cast of roles and then designing how the cast coordinates. Which agents should make up the group for a given task is left to the designer, and the same cast is reused for every task. Financial trading makes the cost of that choice visible: stocks trade differently, and the trading styles suited to one need not suit another. We study task-conditioned persona selection, composing the group from the characteristics of the task it will face, and instantiate it with FinPanel, an LLM multi-agent trading system in which a recruiter selects a panel of named trader personas for each stock from a direction-blind statistical sketch of how the stock trades, each persona gives an independent daily call in its own style, and a manager commits the trade after reading the panel's arguments and their desk-kept, hierarchical track records. Because nothing is returned to the traders, the panel stays the panel that was selected, and it can trade a new stock from an empty record. On eight US stocks over the out-of-knowledge year 2025, against three prior LLM trading agents re-implemented in the same framework and against rule-based, predictive and reinforcement-learning baselines, the selected panel is ahead of a fixed panel of the same size and of the prior agents run as their papers prescribe, with a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold on every stock; it keeps its performance with no warm-up and with no record at all, whereas the memory-augmented agents' returns swing with their warm-up; and neither more seats nor the manager's reading of the arguments substitutes for selecting the right ones. Who is in the group is a design decision to be made per task, before how the group coordinates.
papers.summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems usually fix a cast of roles and reuse it for every task, leaving group composition to the designer. `FinPanel` instead has a recruiter select a panel of named trader personas for each stock from a direction-blind statistical sketch of how it trades; each persona makes an independent daily call, and a manager commits the trade after reading the arguments and the personas' track records. On eight US stocks over 2025, a year outside the models' knowledge, **the selected panel outperforms a fixed panel of the same size** and three re-implemented prior LLM trading agents, with a shallower drawdown than buy-and-hold on every stock. It holds its performance with no warm-up or track record, and neither adding seats nor the manager's reading of arguments substitutes for selecting the right personas.

papers.title: A Multi-Layered AI Pipeline for BPMN Generation from Natural Language
papers.abstract: The automated transformation of unstructured natural language process descriptions into Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams remains a challenging task, due to linguistic ambiguity and the difficulty to detect non-adjacent control-flow relationships. This paper proposes a solution for generating BPMN models from natural language descriptions through a multi-layered pipeline that integrates transformer-based architectures, Large Language Models and ontology population. The proposed method starts with natural language descriptions and separates textual processing, control-flow relation extraction, and structural validation into dedicated components. Entity extraction is performed using a fine-tuned RoBERTa-based transformer model while a control-flow engine captures non-adjacent relationships through LLM-based inference. To improve generalization under limited available data, the approach uses a dynamic few-shot strategy with con- trolled template input construction, enabling improved generalization under limited data availability. Additionally, an ontology population mechanism is introduced to represent the generated process models as semantic knowledge structures. For evaluation purposes we have used from the literature and industry reference processes. Additionally, we have validated the proposed method on a real-world heart disease patients transitional care process, capturing practical constraints and multi-actor collaboration, and serving as an expert-defined benchmark scenario. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance in the relation extraction task, achieving an accuracy of 90.7%, as well as maintaining structural alignment between the generated and reference BPMN models across multiple evaluation scenarios scenarios.
papers.summary: Turning unstructured natural language process descriptions into Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams is hard because of linguistic ambiguity and control-flow relationships between non-adjacent steps. The proposed pipeline splits the work into dedicated components: a fine-tuned `RoBERTa`-based model extracts entities, a large language model with dynamic few-shot prompting infers control-flow relations, and an ontology population step represents the resulting process as a semantic knowledge structure. Evaluated on reference processes from literature and industry plus a real-world transitional care process for heart disease patients, it reaches **90.7% accuracy on relation extraction** while keeping generated models structurally aligned with the references.

papers.title: On the Limits of Sufficient Explanations
papers.abstract: We formally characterize the conditions under which sufficient explanations exist for classifiers on structured data such as graphs and strings. We focus on post-hoc explainers that select parts of the input as sufficient explanations. An explanation is sufficient if the selected part alone ensures the predicted label. Sufficient explanations have been widely adopted across data modalities, including graphs, strings, and images. However, a unified formal analysis of sufficient explanations remains missing. We bridge this gap with four main contributions: (i) We define a general explanation formalism consisting of an instance space, a classifier, and a select relation. The select relation specifies which potential sub-instances or feature subsets can be selected as explanations from each instance; (ii) We show that the existence of sufficient explainers is fully characterized by the interplay between the classifier and the select relation; (iii) We extend this analysis to practically relevant variants of sufficiency, including probabilistic sufficiency and deletion sufficiency; (iv) Based on the formal analysis, we devise statistics that bound the maximum achievable sufficiency for a given task. We evaluate these statistics on language, protein, and molecular classification datasets and find that full sufficiency is unattainable on most of them. Since these bounds hold for every explainer, they provide a task-level reference against which any explainer's sufficiency can be judged in absolute terms.
papers.summary: Post-hoc explainers often select a part of the input as a sufficient explanation, meaning the selected part alone ensures the predicted label, but there has been no unified formal account of when such explanations exist. The authors define a formalism consisting of an instance space, a classifier, and a select relation that specifies which sub-instances may serve as explanations, and show that the existence of sufficient explainers is fully characterized by the interplay between classifier and select relation. They extend the analysis to probabilistic and deletion sufficiency and derive statistics that upper-bound achievable sufficiency for a task regardless of the explainer. On language, protein, and molecular classification datasets, **full sufficiency is unattainable on most of them**.

papers.title: Detection and Classification in Latent Spaces: High-Dimensional Analysis and Validation
papers.abstract: Foundation models produce high-dimensional latent representations in which suitably designed statistical decision rules can be effective yet analytically tractable. We study such detectors in the high-dimensional regime, where latent dimension and training sample size grow proportionally. For linear and quadratic statistics, we derive explicit large-deviation characterizations of false-alarm and miss-detection performance under the Neyman-Pearson paradigm, and show how the binary analysis extends to multi-class classification. The resulting error probabilities and corresponding decay rates exhibit non-monotonic dependence on the shape parameter, including double-descent and, in some regimes, multiple-descent. Experiments on vision, text, and audio datasets using modern foundation models show close agreement between theoretical predictions and empirical performance. In particular, the proposed framework allows us to set a prescribed false-alarm level and accurately predict the corresponding miss-detection probability. Overall, our results provide a theoretically grounded and interpretable framework with competitive empirical performance across different modalities.
papers.summary: Statistical decision rules applied to the latent representations of foundation models are analyzed in the high-dimensional regime where latent dimension and training sample size grow proportionally. For linear and quadratic statistics, the authors derive explicit large-deviation characterizations of false-alarm and miss-detection performance under the Neyman-Pearson paradigm and extend the binary analysis to multi-class classification. The error probabilities and decay rates depend non-monotonically on the shape parameter, showing double descent and in some regimes multiple descent. Experiments on vision, text, and audio datasets show that the theory lets one **fix a false-alarm level and accurately predict the resulting miss-detection probability**.

papers.title: Explanations that Transfer: Interpreting Medical Retrieval with Sparse AutoEncoders
papers.abstract: Medical AI systems that answer users' queries rely on retrieving medical knowledge from large document collections. In this context, finetuning general models on medical datasets can improve retrieval relevance. Yet the dense embeddings underlying modern retrieval systems remain largely opaque, making it difficult to understand the mechanics behind their results. Moreover, adapting to a specific medical dataset risks losing transferability to new clinical corpora. In this work, we tackle these issues by applying Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to medical information retrieval, transforming dense text embeddings into semantically interpretable representations. To do so, our model combines a reconstruction objective with an InfoNCE contrastive loss that directly preserves query-document relevance. We evaluate three embedding models across six medical retrieval datasets, both in-domain and out-of-domain. Trained on a medical corpus, our sparse codes improve in-domain retrieval over the original embeddings, and lose less out-of-domain performance than their dense counterparts, especially when the target corpus is distant from the training one. Importantly, our experiments show that the method yields interpretable features whose semantic content can be inferred from the queries and documents that activate them most strongly. The interpretation of these features sheds light on why a particular document was retrieved, and transfers beyond the training distribution.
papers.summary: Dense embeddings used for medical document retrieval are opaque, and fine-tuning them on one medical dataset risks losing transferability to other clinical corpora. The authors train Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on text embeddings with a reconstruction objective combined with an `InfoNCE` contrastive loss that preserves query-document relevance, producing sparse, interpretable codes. Across three embedding models and six medical retrieval datasets, the sparse codes **improve in-domain retrieval over the original embeddings and lose less out-of-domain performance than dense fine-tuned counterparts**, especially when the target corpus is far from the training one. The learned features can be interpreted from their top-activating queries and documents, which helps explain why a given document was retrieved.

papers.title: LaMe: a Joint Latent Mediation Framework for High-Dimensional Systems
papers.abstract: Mediation analysis seeks to understand how an exposure influences an outcome through intermediate variables. However, as increasingly rich datasets become available, hundreds to thousands of potential mediators make these systems difficult to model and hard to interpret. Latent-variable approaches offer a natural way to accommodate these high-dimensional settings. However, existing latent mediation methods face limitations, including overparameterization, biased inference, or limited scalability. We develop LaMe, a joint linear-Gaussian framework that summarizes a high-dimensional exposure-mediator-outcome system through a small number of latent variables. We identify natural direct and indirect effects under an explicit assumption that the manifest measurements fully capture the latent mediators, and characterize conditions under which the latent representation effectively restricts the observed cross-covariance structure. Simulations assess recovery of observed association parameters, natural effects, and manifest features associated with latent mediation pathways across a range of challenging settings. Four real-world applications demonstrate competitive predictive performance with compact latent representations, including single-dimensional representations of biomarker and proteomic measurements. Together, these results establish LaMe as a practical framework for estimating and summarizing multivariate mediation systems under explicit structural and measurement assumptions.
papers.summary: Mediation analysis asks how an exposure affects an outcome through intermediate variables, which becomes hard to model and interpret when there are hundreds or thousands of candidate mediators. `LaMe` is a joint linear-Gaussian framework that summarizes a high-dimensional exposure-mediator-outcome system with a small number of latent variables, identifying natural direct and indirect effects under an explicit assumption that the measurements fully capture the latent mediators. Simulations assess recovery of association parameters, natural effects, and the features tied to latent pathways, and four real-world applications show **competitive predictive performance with compact latent representations**, including single-dimensional summaries of biomarker and proteomic measurements.

papers.title: MarathonTS: a benchmark of long synthetic time series from window assembly and long-series generators
papers.abstract: Many applications of synthetic time series require a series that is much longer than the windows on which a generative model is trained. Such a series can be assembled from a pool of short generated windows, which requires deciding which windows are taken, in what order, and how their seams are processed, or it can be produced directly by a long-series generator. This study presents MarathonTS, to our knowledge the first open benchmark that compares both families under one protocol. Every method produces a series of the same length on 9 open hourly datasets with 10 seeds. The series is evaluated by its fidelity to the real data (83 metrics in 12 groups, against three real references: train, validation and an out-of-time split), by its utility (models are trained on the synthetic series only and tested on real data, TSTR against TRTR, in 14 classification and regression tasks), by its memorisation of the training data and by its computational cost. The statistical analysis is carried out as a separate stage that reads the published tables and gives the rankings of every method in every slice, the answers to the research questions with tests and uncertainty, and the results of a pre-specified confirmatory family. In the main run, the methods differ in both confirmatory cells; the choice of windows matters more than the processing of their seams, which does not improve the series, and no method trains the downstream models as well as the real series. The top tier of the leaderboard is reproduced on other hardware, whereas the exact places within it are not. For the reproducibility of the study, the code, the data hashes and all results are publicly available (links below).
papers.summary: Many uses of synthetic time series need sequences far longer than the windows a generative model is trained on, obtained either by assembling short generated windows or by a dedicated long-series generator. `MarathonTS` is an open benchmark comparing both families under one protocol on 9 hourly datasets with 10 seeds, scoring fidelity (83 metrics in 12 groups), utility for training downstream models tested on real data across 14 tasks, memorisation, and computational cost, with a pre-specified statistical analysis. The choice of which windows to use matters more than how their seams are processed, which does not improve the series, and **no method trains downstream models as well as real data does**. The top tier of the leaderboard reproduces on other hardware, but exact rankings within it do not.

papers.title: T2ST: Data-Efficient Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models via Temporal Data and Knowledge Transfer
papers.abstract: Spatio-temporal foundation models (STFMs) require large-scale training corpora, yet synchronized observations and spatial metadata are costly to acquire and curate, limiting the availability of suitable data. By contrast, time-series data are abundant and easier to collect. Since observations at each location form a time series, this motivates a natural question: can abundant time-series data enhance STFMs when spatio-temporal observations are scarce? To bridge this gap, we propose T2ST, a data-efficient training framework that augments limited spatio-temporal observations with selected auxiliary time series and transfers knowledge from a frozen time-series foundation model. Our key insight is that temporal pattern learning can benefit from abundant external time series, while spatial dependency learning remains grounded in real spatio-temporal observations. Guided by this insight, T2ST retrieves matched sequences to reinforce sparsely observed temporal patterns and selects reliable complementary sequences to broaden temporal coverage. Temporal relation distillation aligns relationships among historical patches, while multi-scale prediction distillation transfers forecasting behavior at fine and coarse temporal resolutions, enabling knowledge transfer across heterogeneous architectures. Using only 10\% of the original spatio-temporal data, T2ST enables STFMs to achieve overall forecasting performance competitive with or superior to their full-data counterparts across six long-term and twelve short-term forecasting datasets. These results establish a new paradigm for data-efficient training of spatio-temporal foundation models. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/T2ST-65F3/.
papers.summary: Spatio-temporal foundation models (STFMs) need large corpora of synchronized observations with spatial metadata, which are costly to collect, whereas plain time series are abundant. `T2ST` augments scarce spatio-temporal data with retrieved and selected auxiliary time series and distills knowledge from a frozen time-series foundation model, using temporal relation distillation over historical patches and multi-scale prediction distillation, while spatial dependency learning stays grounded in real spatio-temporal observations. With **only 10% of the original spatio-temporal data**, models trained this way reach forecasting performance competitive with or better than their full-data counterparts across six long-term and twelve short-term forecasting datasets.

papers.title: From Pen-and-Paper to Machine-Checked Proofs: Lean for System Identification
papers.abstract: Mathematical proofs in scientific papers are often long and intricate, relying on chains of references to earlier results. This makes it difficult for readers and reviewers to verify each and every step. Interactive theorem proving offers a complement: the theorem and its proof are written as code, and every inference is checked by a small, trusted piece of software called the kernel. This paper serves as an introduction to the Lean 4 proof assistant for a system identification and control audience, assuming no prior exposure to formal methods. We first show how a Lean proof is read using two elementary examples: the first on identifiability, the second on set invariance. We then illustrate how Lean can be used to analyse results from the literature, taking as example a classic lemma on the inversion of the noise filter in prediction-error identification (Ljung, 1999, Lemma 3.1). Since in Lean every step must be justified, the formalization brings to light a subtle point: the original claim of that lemma holds almost surely, although not for every realisation, as its statement may suggest. A simple counterexample makes this concrete. Finally, the paper discusses guidelines and perspectives on the use of Lean in system identification research.
papers.summary: Long pen-and-paper proofs in scientific papers are hard for readers and reviewers to verify step by step. This tutorial introduces the `Lean 4` proof assistant to a system identification and control audience with no formal methods background, walking through two elementary examples on identifiability and set invariance and then formalizing a classic lemma on noise-filter inversion in prediction-error identification (Ljung, 1999, Lemma 3.1). The formalization exposes a subtlety: **the lemma's original claim holds only almost surely, not for every realisation** as its statement may suggest, which a simple counterexample makes concrete. The authors close with guidelines for using `Lean` in system identification research.

papers.title: Personalization of Basic and Moral Values Guiding LLM-Controlled Assistant Robots
papers.abstract: Personal assistant robots powered by large language models (LLMs) are likely to enter everyday life within the next decade, but the values that should guide their behaviour remain largely unspecified. Current alignment practice steers a single model toward an aggregate of human values, ignoring that individual users may prefer a robot whose value profile differs from their own. We administer parallel self- and robot-targeted versions of three established psycho-metric instruments - the simplified Schwartz Values Survey (SVS), the Portrait Values Questionnaire (PVQ-21), and the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ) - to potential future users (N=22), capturing both their personal values and the values they would want an assistant robot to embody. We compare the three instruments as personalization tools using the UEQ-S and benchmark fifteen contemporary LLMs against the resulting profiles. Participants wanted their robot to score markedly lower than themselves on personal-focus values and higher on social-focus values; moral profiles were nearly identical. LLMs prompted to act as robots shifted only weakly toward the desired profile, indicating that default model behaviour and prompt engineering are no substitute for explicit value personalization.
papers.summary: Assistant robots driven by large language models (LLMs) will need guiding values, yet current alignment targets an aggregate of human values rather than what individual users want from their robot. The authors gave 22 prospective users parallel self- and robot-targeted versions of the simplified Schwartz Values Survey (SVS), the Portrait Values Questionnaire (`PVQ-21`), and the Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ), and benchmarked fifteen LLMs against the resulting profiles. Participants wanted their robot to score markedly lower than themselves on personal-focus values and higher on social-focus values, while moral profiles were nearly identical. **LLMs prompted to act as robots shifted only weakly toward the desired profile**, suggesting default behaviour and prompting do not replace explicit value personalization.

papers.title: NeoResearch: Literature- and Experience-Guided Autonomous Time Series Model Discovery
papers.abstract: Developing effective forecasting models for diverse time-series domains requires substantial expert knowledge, evidence from scientific literature on the web, and iterative experimentation. However, translating this knowledge and research experience into model designs requires preserving source context and testing applicability under task-specific assumptions. In this paper, we propose NeoResearch, a literature- and experience-guided autonomous research framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) as researchers to discover lightweight, domain-specific forecasting models. Specifically, NeoResearch establishes an expert-inspired dual-loop research workflow, coupling hypothesis-driven architecture exploration with iterative training and hyperparameter optimization through experimental feedback. To enable knowledge-grounded discovery, the agent autonomously mines scientific literature from the Web, extracting modeling mechanisms, empirical evidence, and applicability conditions to formulate task-grounded, testable architecture hypotheses. Furthermore, a hierarchical experience memory links literature findings to experimental outcomes and consolidates conditional lessons, guiding architecture discovery and training optimization while supporting reuse across forecasting tasks. Experiments on ten datasets show competitive performance and support dual loops, literature extraction, and memory reuse. Our code is available.
papers.summary: Designing forecasting models for a new time-series domain takes expert knowledge, evidence from the literature, and repeated experimentation. `NeoResearch` uses large language models (LLMs) as autonomous researchers in a dual-loop workflow that couples hypothesis-driven architecture exploration with iterative training and hyperparameter optimization driven by experimental feedback. The agent mines scientific literature from the web for modeling mechanisms, evidence, and applicability conditions to form testable architecture hypotheses, and a hierarchical experience memory links those findings to experimental outcomes for reuse across tasks. Experiments on ten datasets show **competitive forecasting performance with lightweight discovered models**, and ablations support the dual loops, literature extraction, and memory reuse.

papers.title: Small Is Not Dead: Distance-Aware Cluster Revival for e-means
papers.abstract: e-means (Bessa et al., 2026) is a recent mini-batch k-means algorithm, now part of the FAISS library, that reaches the error of Lloyd's algorithm about an order of magnitude faster on large embedding datasets. Every five mini-batches, it removes every cluster whose running point count falls below a tenth of the average and reuses its centre to split a large cluster. In the authors' ablation, removing this mechanism, called dead-cluster revival, raises the error more than removing any other component added to the moving-average update. The rule, however, considers only cluster size: it cannot distinguish a cluster that is small because it is redundant from one that covers a rare, isolated group of points, and on data with such groups it repeatedly removes centres whose removal is costly. We add a second condition, based on the distance between centres: a small cluster is removed only if its centre is close to another centre, relative to a running estimate of the mean squared error. When a centre equals the mean of its points, this squared distance is an upper bound on the average increase in squared error, per point of the cluster, caused by removing the centre. The condition costs one nearest-centre search for the small clusters every five mini-batches and adds no measurable running time. On the e-means paper's embedding benchmarks, it never prevents a removal, so the results are identical to those of FAISS. On datasets with small isolated groups not used during development, it reduces the test error after two epochs by roughly 10% to 80% relative to count-based revival, and it preserves the advantage of k-means++ initialization; on the other evaluation datasets, it stays within about 1% of the better of revival enabled and disabled. We also report two failure modes that the analysis predicts. This is a CPU proof of concept; GPU implementations are left to future work.
papers.summary: `e-means`, a recent mini-batch k-means algorithm included in `FAISS`, periodically removes clusters with few points and reuses their centres to split large clusters, but this size-only rule cannot tell a redundant cluster from one covering a rare, isolated group. The authors add a distance condition: a small cluster is removed only if its centre lies close to another centre relative to a running estimate of mean squared error, a quantity shown to upper-bound the per-point error increase from removal. The check adds no measurable running time and leaves results on the original embedding benchmarks identical to `FAISS`. On datasets with small isolated groups it **reduces test error after two epochs by roughly 10% to 80%** relative to count-based revival, and elsewhere stays within about 1% of the better of revival enabled or disabled.

papers.title: Neural Classifiers as Error-Correcting Codes
papers.abstract: A unified framework is proposed that characterizes supervised deep classification as the decoding of error-correcting codes in the Shannon sense. Cross-entropy optimization is shown to align softmax classifiers with maximum-likelihood decoding, where logits map to Hamming distances to class-specific codewords. This correspondence explains the emergence of standard divergence objectives (e.g., Kullback-Leibler, Jeffreys) and provides a geometric basis for the stability of decision boundaries. Furthermore, the geometries of Neural Collapse and LeJEPA are identified as optimal constellations for decoding under isotropic noise. Unlike classical Error-Correcting Output Codes, deep networks are shown to learn effective codebooks in the feature space implicitly. This insight is leveraged to derive novel criteria for lossless quantization, improved knowledge distillation, and architectural regularization based on code redundancy. Finally, this perspective is extended to self-supervised encoders, offering a cohesive explanation for the geometry of latent representations in modern neural models.
papers.summary: Supervised deep classification is recast as decoding of error-correcting codes in the Shannon sense.
