The authors show that **cross-entropy training aligns softmax classifiers with maximum-likelihood decoding**, with logits corresponding to Hamming distances to class-specific codewords, which accounts for standard divergence objectives and the stability of decision boundaries. The geometries of Neural Collapse and `LeJEPA` are identified as optimal constellations for decoding under isotropic noise, and networks are shown to learn codebooks implicitly in feature space, unlike classical Error-Correcting Output Codes. From this view they derive criteria for lossless quantization, improved knowledge distillation, and redundancy-based regularization, and extend the account to self-supervised encoders.

papers.title: RACE: Ranking-Uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation
papers.abstract: Efficient sequential recommendation has emerged as a promising paradigm for providing real-time personalized service. To deploy models under resource-constrained environment, model compression becomes a necessity, yet existing methods typically apply uniform compression ratios, overlooking the heterogeneity in user intent complexity. This "one-size-fits-all" approach leads to a fundamental Capacity-Complexity Mismatch, where computational resources are either wasted on simple instances or insufficient for complex ones. To address this, we propose RACE (Ranking-uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation), a framework that dynamically adapts both model structures and input sequences with uncertainty-aware compression ratios. To ensure capacity-adaptive inference, RACE captures the model's intrinsic uncertainty of its predictions and transforms it into a proactive resource allocator. Specifically, we derive a list-wise ranking-uncertainty metric from the distributional stability of top-$K$ predictions, which serves as a measurable proxy for instance complexity. A lightweight predictor is then trained via self-supervision to anticipate this uncertainty from early-layer features. Guided by this signal, RACE performs instance-specific slimming in two dimensions: a hypernetwork-style channel sensitivity extractor identifies parameter redundancy, while importance-aware progressive sequence filtering mitigates data redundancy. Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate that RACE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability.
papers.summary: Compressed sequential recommendation models usually apply one compression ratio to every request, wasting computation on simple users and under-serving complex ones. `RACE` (Ranking-uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation) derives a list-wise ranking-uncertainty measure from the stability of top-K predictions and trains a lightweight predictor to anticipate it from early-layer features. That signal drives per-instance slimming along two axes: a hypernetwork-style extractor prunes redundant channels, and progressive importance-aware filtering shortens the input sequence. On four datasets, the method is reported to **outperform state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability**.

papers.title: Probabilities of Causation in Nondeterministic Causal Models
papers.abstract: We study probabilities of causation in nondeterministic causal models, where mechanisms may remain intrinsically stochastic even after all latent variables are fixed. Focusing on binary treatments and outcomes, we develop a generic identification program that represents observational and interventional data as moment constraints on latent stochastic mechanism types and computes minimal/maximal values of counterfactual quantities via constrained optimization. Within this framework, we derive sharp analytic bounds on the probabilities of causation under several assumptions tailored to nondeterministic models. Resulting identification regions are often more informative than those attainable under deterministic alternatives. We illustrate the practical relevance of these results in a case study on personalized treatment decisions and experiments on semi-synthetic datasets. Our results clarify how classical bounds relate to nondeterministic causal semantics, generalizing previous works and providing a unified route from qualitative structural restrictions to computable partial identification regions.
papers.summary: Probabilities of causation are studied in nondeterministic causal models, where mechanisms remain intrinsically stochastic even after all latent variables are fixed. For binary treatments and outcomes, the authors represent observational and interventional data as moment constraints on latent stochastic mechanism types and compute minimal and maximal values of counterfactual quantities by constrained optimization, deriving sharp analytic bounds under several assumptions. The resulting **identification regions are often more informative than those obtainable under deterministic models**. A case study on personalized treatment decisions and semi-synthetic experiments illustrate the bounds.

papers.title: Dancing Tokens on the Vocabulary Network from LLM Generation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, yet how a particular generation relates to the geometry learned in pre-training remains unclear. The fundamental explainability of LLMs is elusive. Here, we build a similarity network from the input embeddings of six open LLMs and map generation onto it. The token-embedding network is scale-free while heavy-tailed, as are random embeddings with matched covariance, but far more fragmented. Distillation barely changes this topology because input embeddings are largely inherited. The knowledge space is thus deterministic from pre-training. Consecutive generated tokens are rarely graph neighbours and, in most models, no more often than in shuffled order, so generation is not a walk on the predefined network, although the tokens it visits are concentrated within it. Through the logit lens in a layer- wise manner, tokens settle late in depth in most models, and repetitive models remain confined to small domain-specific sub-graphs. These observables could serve as inference-time monitors of degeneration. We thus provide a fresh perspective on understanding LLM generation in the microscopic way from node or link prediction by graph learning.
papers.summary: To relate large language model (LLM) generation to the geometry learned in pre-training, the authors build a similarity network from the input token embeddings of six open LLMs and map generated text onto it. The network is scale-free and heavy-tailed, as are random embeddings with matched covariance, but far more fragmented, and distillation barely changes it because input embeddings are largely inherited. **Consecutive generated tokens are rarely graph neighbours, and in most models no more often than in shuffled order**, so generation is not a walk on this network even though visited tokens concentrate within it. Logit-lens analysis shows tokens settling late in depth in most models, and repetitive models stay confined to small domain-specific sub-graphs, which the authors suggest could serve as inference-time monitors of degeneration.

papers.title: ParetoM$^3$: Learning on the Pareto Set under Preference Guidance via Min-Max-Min Optimization
papers.abstract: Learning across multiple inherently conflicting objectives requires selecting desirable trade-offs from the Pareto set. In this work, we study preference-guided multi-objective optimization, where a predefined preference function is minimized over the weak Pareto set of multiple nonconvex objectives. Leveraging a merit function that vanishes on the weak Pareto set, we propose a penalty-based min-max-min formulation, termed the M$^3$ problem, which unifies preference optimization and the enforcement of weak Pareto optimality in a single objective. We further develop ParetoM$^3$, a single-loop first-order algorithm for computing stationary solutions of the resulting M$^3$ problem. Under a local Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz assumption, we prove that ParetoM$^3$ finds an $\epsilon$-stationary point of the M$^3$ problem that is also approximately weakly Pareto optimal for the original multi-objective problem when the penalty parameter is sufficiently large, with explicit non-asymptotic convergence rates. We also show that this stationarity notion recovers existing optimality criteria, including approximate preference stationarity and approximate Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, under the same assumptions used in prior works. Experiments on a synthetic benchmark, image classification, regression, and math reasoning demonstrate that ParetoM$^3$ reliably attains preferred weak Pareto optimal solutions while achieving strong practical performance. Code is available at https://github.com/tpgoodboy/ParetoM3.
papers.summary: Preference-guided multi-objective optimization seeks the point on the weak Pareto set of several nonconvex, conflicting objectives that minimizes a given preference function. Using a merit function that vanishes on the weak Pareto set, the authors fold preference optimization and Pareto enforcement into a single penalty-based min-max-min problem and propose `ParetoM3`, a single-loop first-order algorithm for it. Under a local Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz assumption they prove it **finds an epsilon-stationary point that is also approximately weakly Pareto optimal, with explicit non-asymptotic convergence rates**, when the penalty parameter is large enough, and that this stationarity notion recovers existing optimality criteria. Experiments cover a synthetic benchmark, image classification, regression, and math reasoning.

papers.title: NER-D: A cross-domain benchmark for German NER
papers.abstract: We present NER-D, a cross-domain benchmark for German NER comprising 13 datasets spanning 9 domains, including General/Politics, Wikipedia, Legal, Medical, Historical, Financial, Agriculture and Archaeology. We examine the performance of both proprietary LLMs and state-of-the-art small open-source models using normal prompting and further examine the performance gains achievable via in-context learning and LoRA fine-tuning. Our results show that without any sort of optimization a proprietary model (GPT-5.4 mini) outperforms the smaller open-source models on 6 out of 13 datasets, but LoRA fine-tuning enables the smaller models to substantially outperform the proprietary baseline. We further analyze the influence of the domain and the tagset used in each task on the performance achieved in the different evaluation settings. Our benchmark will be available as a resource for the development of future German NER methods on both general and specialized domains.\footnote{We make our code, data, and models publicly available upon acceptance of this paper.
papers.summary: `NER-D` is a cross-domain benchmark for German named entity recognition, made up of 13 datasets covering general and specialized domains such as legal, medical, historical, financial, agriculture and archaeology. The authors compare proprietary large language models with small open-source models under plain prompting, in-context learning and `LoRA` fine-tuning. Without any optimization `GPT-5.4 mini` beats the smaller open models on 6 of the 13 datasets, but **`LoRA` fine-tuning lets the small open-source models substantially outperform the proprietary baseline**. They also analyze how the domain and the tagset affect performance in each setting.

papers.title: MamaReason: Unfinished Reasoning and Answer Recovery in Clinical Language Models
papers.abstract: Answer continuation often returns a diagnosis already stated in unfinished clinical reasoning. We study this behavior in MamaReason, adapted from dense Gemma 4 31B, on MamaBench's 217 paired maternal and child-health presentations. An explicit-commitment extractor identifies a diagnosis in 75 of 94 failed RL first passes and 75 of 93 failed SFT first passes. The continuation matches that diagnosis in 67/75 RL cases and 58/75 SFT cases, using diagnosis strings alone. Reading these commitments without additional generation recovers 30 of the 40 RL pairs restored by continuation under the archived correctness labels. Recurrence controls distinguish routine mentions from repeated answer selection. An offline second-commitment trigger measures the tradeoff between earlier readout and paired accuracy. The resulting decomposition separates diagnostic content already present in a trace, completion of an accepted answer, and paired diagnostic correctness. For clinical language-model evaluation, these are distinct outcomes that become visible when the same reasoning trace is examined through multiple readouts.
papers.summary: When a clinical language model's reasoning is cut off before it gives a final answer, letting it continue often just returns a diagnosis it had already stated. The authors study this in `MamaReason`, a model adapted from `Gemma 4 31B`, on the 217 paired maternal and child-health cases of `MamaBench`, using an extractor that finds explicit diagnostic commitments in failed first passes of the reinforcement-learning and supervised fine-tuned variants. The continuation matches the extracted diagnosis in 67 of 75 reinforcement-learning cases and 58 of 75 supervised cases, and **reading those commitments with no further generation recovers 30 of the 40 pairs that continuation restores**. They argue that diagnostic content already present in a trace, completion of an accepted answer, and paired correctness are distinct outcomes that an evaluation should report separately.

papers.title: From Bytes to Behavior: Request-Level Attribution from Live GPU Hidden States
papers.abstract: Existing memory forensics for machine learning systems typically targets static artifacts, such as model weights or prompt logs, rather than the transient computational states of a live inference process. This gap limits an examiner's ability to analyze the specific behavior of a running large language model (LLM) service that cannot be restarted or modified. We present a method for acquiring per-layer residual-stream activations from a live GPU process using a non-modifying debugger, without requiring prior knowledge of the model's architecture parameters or weights. The approach employs a general six-stage process with platform-specific adapters, utilizing either a PyTorch allocator clock or a kernel-launch clock to identify and read tensor allocations from video memory. We validate this acquisition on 33 open-source decoder-only models across nine architecture classes, demonstrating that the recovered bytes are byte-exact and usable for downstream analysis. As a use case, we apply linear probes trained on standard framework activations to the recovered states, successfully distinguishing refusal from compliance with an AUROC of 0.88 on held-out prompts. This work establishes that live, observational access to intermediate hidden states is feasible on named inference platforms, providing a new source of evidence for examining the operational behavior of deployed AI systems.
papers.summary: Memory forensics for machine learning systems usually targets static artifacts such as weights or prompt logs, which leaves an examiner unable to analyze a running large language model service that cannot be restarted or modified. The authors describe a six-stage method that reads per-layer residual-stream activations out of a live GPU process with a non-modifying debugger, locating tensor allocations in video memory through either a `PyTorch` allocator clock or a kernel-launch clock, without knowing the model's architecture or weights. Across 33 open-source decoder-only models in nine architecture classes the recovered bytes are byte-exact. Linear probes trained on ordinary framework activations and applied to the recovered states **separate refusal from compliance with an AUROC of 0.88** on held-out prompts.

papers.title: Right Token, Right Time: From Per-Token Gating to Trajectory-Aware Activation Steering
papers.abstract: Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning. Yet, standard methods apply the steering signal at every generated token, displacing representations from the distribution the model was trained on and eroding generation quality. We show that \emph{when} along a generation the intervention is applied is a decisive axis of control. We cast steering as a per-token allocation problem under a fixed budget of steerable tokens, so that methods differ only in which tokens they select, making allocation the sole variable. Within this framework we introduce two gates. The first, Contrastive Feature Projection (CFP), is memoryless and selects the tokens least aligned with the target behavior through a sparse, interpretable feature projection. The second, Closed-Loop Adaptive Bernoulli Steering (CLABS), is trajectory aware. It treats allocation as closed-loop feedback control, tracking the alignment a generation has accumulated so far and spending budget where the trajectory falls behind. On a linear steering-response model we derive an explicit gain region that guarantees closed-loop stability of CLABS and show that its integral term reduces the steady-state tracking offset. Empirically, CFP and CLABS achieve the largest behavioral shift among budgeted gates at matched budgets, with CLABS strongest under the tight budgets where allocation matters most, while best preserving fluency.
papers.summary: Steering a language model with sparse autoencoder (SAE) features is normally applied at every generated token, which pushes representations off the training distribution and degrades output quality. The authors recast steering as choosing which tokens to steer under a fixed budget and propose two gates: Contrastive Feature Projection (`CFP`), a memoryless rule that picks the tokens least aligned with the target behavior, and Closed-Loop Adaptive Bernoulli Steering (`CLABS`), a feedback controller that tracks accumulated alignment and spends budget where the generation falls behind. For a linear steering-response model they derive a gain region that guarantees `CLABS` is stable. Empirically, **both gates produce the largest behavioral shift among budgeted gates at matched budgets while best preserving fluency**, with `CLABS` strongest under tight budgets.

papers.title: GT-FENG: General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding in Language Models *Author(s)
papers.abstract: Whether a language model's answer is correct often depends on context: the same value can be right under one jurisdiction, date, or legal definition and wrong under another. We introduce GT-FENG (General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding), the first general framework to unify contextual/temporal correctness and rule-based error attribution across law, policy, and other rule-governed domains. GT-FENG checks answers against the applicable rules and identifies documented rules that match incorrect answers. It shows that when multiple rules give the same value, the answer alone cannot tell which rule the model used. In Medicaid income-limit answers from two models, documenting the asked state's own records reduces the number of wrong answers that match only other states' values by 68-78%, and more than half of stable wrong answers then match two or more documented sources. GT-FENG provides a foundation for evaluating language models in rule-governed domains and for future benchmarks and evaluation toolkits. We release GT-FENG as an open-source Python package, gtfeng.
papers.summary: Whether a language model's answer is correct can depend on jurisdiction, date or legal definition, so the same value may be right in one context and wrong in another. `GT-FENG` (General Theory of Factual Evaluation and Normative Grounding) is a framework and open-source Python package that checks answers against the applicable rules and identifies which documented rules match an incorrect answer, showing that when several rules yield the same value the answer alone cannot reveal which rule the model used. On Medicaid income-limit answers from two models, **documenting the asked state's own records cuts the number of wrong answers that match only other states' values by 68-78%**. More than half of the stable wrong answers then match two or more documented sources.

papers.title: Clean Tickets, Wrong Orders: Catching Silent Errors with a Language Model in Your Browser Tab
papers.abstract: A small language model that turns a typed order into structure can fail in two ways. It can print something broken, which any system rejects. Or it can print a clean, well formed order that nobody placed. Our companion work calls the second kind a silent error, and it is the dangerous one. We present a web demo in which a fine-tuned 0.8B parameter model runs entirely inside the visitor's browser tab, through llama.cpp compiled to WebAssembly. No order text leaves the device. The page parses orders as the visitor types, scores every ticket with the PIZZA benchmark's own matcher ported to TypeScript, refuses anything off the menu with "?" so the model can face the open web, and lets visitors hunt for silent errors or try to cause one. Run in the browser on all 1,357 PIZZA test orders, the deployed model writes the same output as the server evaluation for 99.0% of them and reaches the same exact match (0.882); we also report its latency on 3 consumer laptops. Demo: https://wrong.cuyor.com
papers.summary: A small model that converts a typed order into structured output can fail silently by producing a clean, well-formed order that nobody placed, and this web demo lets visitors look for such errors. A fine-tuned 0.8B-parameter model runs entirely inside the browser tab through `llama.cpp` compiled to WebAssembly, so no order text leaves the device; the page scores each ticket with a TypeScript port of the `PIZZA` benchmark's matcher and refuses off-menu items with a question mark. Run in the browser on all 1,357 `PIZZA` test orders, **the deployed model produces the same output as the server evaluation for 99.0% of them and reaches the same exact match of 0.882**. Latency is reported on three consumer laptops.

papers.title: PrivacyPR: A Dataset of Real-World Privacy Fixes for Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review
papers.abstract: Coding agents increasingly review code, yet whether they catch the privacy defects that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid remains largely untested, partly because few datasets connect real privacy defects to their accepted fixes and review context. We present PrivacyPR, a dataset of 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests (PRs) from 1,469 repositories, created between June 2018 and January 2024. Each PR includes its commits, diffs, review discussion, and LLM-generated labels for privacy relevance, fix type, and GDPR principles. PrivacyPR provides 1,169 high-confidence privacy fixes and 1,643 non-fix PRs, together with Verified, a manually checked split of 250 privacy fixes and 250 non-fix PRs, and Small, a 100 + 100 subset for evaluation. On Verified, both annotators endorsed 72% of the LLM's GDPR-principle assignments. Beyond supporting empirical study of how privacy defects arise and are fixed, PrivacyPR provides a benchmark for privacy-aware code review on real, developer-accepted fixes. Its evaluation harness reverts each fix to reintroduce the defect. On Small, two coding agents detect only 42-51% of defects under a generic review prompt, but 88-91% when explicitly asked to check privacy, while flagging 11-15% of non-fix PRs. These results show that privacy defects can be detected by coding agents, but that detection depends strongly on review intent and comes with false alarms. Data, code, reviews, judge verdicts, and an extensible evaluation harness are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23744765.
papers.summary: Few datasets link real privacy defects to their accepted fixes, so it is largely untested whether coding agents catch the problems that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid. `PrivacyPR` collects 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests (PRs) from 1,469 repositories with commits, diffs, review discussion and LLM-generated labels, and includes a manually checked `Verified` split of 250 privacy fixes and 250 non-fix PRs plus a 100 + 100 `Small` subset; its evaluation harness reverts each fix to reintroduce the defect. On `Small`, **two coding agents detect only 42-51% of defects under a generic review prompt but 88-91% when explicitly asked to check privacy**, while flagging 11-15% of non-fix PRs. Both annotators endorsed 72% of the LLM's GDPR-principle assignments on `Verified`.

papers.title: When evaluation becomes intervention in clinical AI
papers.abstract: AI judges, models that grade another system's output against a rubric, extend clinical review to the scale at which clinical AI writes. When teams use judge assessments to select a prompt or train a model, the judge becomes part of the intervention. Selection can then favor errors the judge overlooks. We describe what a judge's report must contain and the independent clinical test each judge-driven change needs.
papers.summary: AI judges, meaning models that grade another system's output against a rubric, are used to extend clinical review to the volume at which clinical AI produces text. The authors argue that **once judge assessments are used to select a prompt or train a model, the judge becomes part of the intervention and selection can favor the errors it overlooks**, and they set out what a judge's report must contain and the independent clinical test each judge-driven change needs.

papers.title: AI for Parameter Selection in Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization
papers.abstract: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) methods provide a way to compute molecular ground-state energies, but their accuracy and runtime depend sensitively on configuration choices such as the subspace dimension, propagation timestep, and the allocation of a fixed sampling budget across circuits, for which no formal selection method exists. In this work, we explore whether oracle models can predict the quantum runtime and approximation error from the Hamiltonian and the candidate configuration. Using synthetic Hamiltonians with controllable spectral properties, we show that machine-learned models can map a Hamiltonian directly to the best-ranked configuration within a predefined grid for the SKQD algorithm, validated against classical Krylov propagation, achieving strong rank correlations between true and predicted error and runtime, Spearman $\rho = 0.969$ and $\rho = 0.905$, respectively. Extending the approach to 50 molecular Hamiltonians (20-50 qubits), with reference ground-state energies from classical calculations, we train regressors that predict the simulation error and runtime for a given molecule--configuration pair ahead of execution, and classifiers to distinguish, from 600 SqDRIFT quantum-hardware runs, whether a configuration achieves a ground-state energy within chemical accuracy ($1.6\times10^{-3}$ Ha $\approx 1$ kcal/mol). For the molecular Hamiltonians, the models additionally provide an a priori feasibility and resource estimate, predicting whether a molecule can reach chemical accuracy on current hardware and at what runtime, thus correctly classifying held-out molecules at the molecule level, achieving balanced accuracy 61.8% in-distribution and 100% for five larger held-out molecules.
papers.summary: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) methods compute molecular ground-state energies, but their accuracy and runtime depend on configuration choices such as subspace dimension, propagation timestep and sampling-budget allocation, for which no formal selection method exists. The authors train machine-learned models to predict quantum runtime and approximation error from the Hamiltonian and a candidate configuration. On synthetic Hamiltonians for the `SKQD` algorithm, **predicted and true values reach Spearman rank correlations of 0.969 for error and 0.905 for runtime**. On 50 molecular Hamiltonians of 20-50 qubits and 600 `SqDRIFT` quantum-hardware runs, classifiers predicting whether a molecule reaches chemical accuracy score 61.8% balanced accuracy in-distribution and 100% on five larger held-out molecules.

papers.title: Experts Across Schemas: Agent-Guided Mixture-of-Relational-Experts for Cross-Database Generalization
papers.abstract: Web platforms record user and item activity in relational databases whose schemas differ from platform to platform, which makes it difficult to transfer predictive models between them. Relational foundation models address this through cross-database pretraining, yet recent improvements have relied on increasingly large pretraining corpora. We ask whether a better architecture, together with features specific to the target database, can deliver comparable gains from far less pretraining data. We introduce MoREGT, a mixture-of-relational-experts graph transformer that represents both rows and cells as tokens, adds the log-ages of rows and the names of foreign-key relationships to attention, and routes cells and rows to experts by column metadata rather than by values. A label-blind LLM agent complements the model: it reads the target database's schema and column statistics and adds validated single-row derived columns, without access to labels or model scores. On 21 RelBench tasks with leave-one-database-out pretraining on six databases, the MoREGT backbone improves on the Relational Transformer pretrained on the same databases by 2.25 points of mean AUROC and 5.83 points of mean nMAE. The agent's columns raise mean AUROC from 78.45 to 79.63 and lower mean nMAE from 27.91 to 26.98, the highest means on both metrics among the compared methods, including RT-J, which pretrains on about 400 times as many databases.
papers.summary: Relational databases differ in schema from one platform to the next, which makes predictive models hard to transfer, and recent relational foundation models have improved mainly by pretraining on ever larger corpora. `MoREGT` is a mixture-of-relational-experts graph transformer that tokenizes both rows and cells, adds row log-ages and foreign-key relationship names to attention, and routes tokens to experts by column metadata; a label-blind LLM agent reads the target schema and column statistics and adds validated derived columns. On 21 `RelBench` tasks with leave-one-database-out pretraining on six databases, the backbone beats the `Relational Transformer` pretrained on the same data by 2.25 points of mean AUROC and 5.83 points of mean nMAE. With the agent's columns, **mean AUROC rises from 78.45 to 79.63, the best among compared methods including `RT-J`, which pretrains on about 400 times as many databases**.

papers.title: Learning Word-Level Explanations of Text Reuse in Latin Literature with Little Annotation
papers.abstract: Detecting an intertextual reference is only the first step; philologists also need to know how a later author reworked the source. We explain a reuse pair word by word: each word of the reusing passage is first aligned to its source word, then labeled with the operation that transformed it, such as a copy, a change of inflection, or a substitution. Such word-level operations are expensive to annotate, and only a few corpora annotated at this level exist for text reuse in Latin literature. We describe a procedure that needs only a limited number of annotations: synthetic pairs, built by applying known operations to Latin text, train a first model, and active learning chooses the pairs an annotator corrects. Among several architectures, a model that links and labels together performs best: a pointer network that, for every reuse word, chooses a source word and names the operation in the same step. We show that with active learning, 200 pairs chosen by uncertainty are enough for the model to match one trained on every annotated pair of the 1,490 references of the Loci Similes benchmark. We release our code, word-level predictions for all references, and an interactive demo.
papers.summary: Philologists studying text reuse in Latin literature want to know how a later author reworked a source, not only that a reference exists. The authors explain each reuse pair word by word, aligning every word of the reusing passage to a source word and labeling the operation that transformed it, such as a copy, a change of inflection or a substitution. To limit annotation cost, a first model is trained on synthetic pairs built by applying known operations to Latin text, and active learning then chooses which pairs an annotator corrects; a pointer network that picks the source word and names the operation in one step performs best. **With 200 pairs chosen by uncertainty, the model matches one trained on every annotated pair of the 1,490 references in the `Loci Similes` benchmark**.

papers.title: Causal AI-Driven Secure mmWave Beam Alignment with Defensive Variational Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Efficient and secure beam alignment is essential for mmWave communication systems. However, existing deep learning (DL)-based beam alignment methods often neglect causal relationships between inputs and outputs, resulting in limited interpretability, poor generalization, and excessive beam sweeping. Moreover, these DL solutions are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small perturbations in received power measurements can mislead beam classifiers. To overcome these issues, we propose a causally-aware DL framework integrating causal discovery into beam alignment. A two-stage causal beam selection algorithm learns a Bayesian graph capturing dependencies between received signal strength indicators (RSSI) as inputs and the optimal beam index as the target variable, then uses it to select a minimal set of relevant input features for the DL classifier. To mitigate adversarial attacks, we introduce a defensive variational autoencoder (DVAE) that maps potentially perturbed inputs back to their clean versions. End-to-end fine-tuning of the downstream beam classifier on the DVAE-reconstructed RSSI representations further boosts prediction accuracy. Simulation results show that causal beam selection achieves accuracy comparable to conventional methods while providing an \(\mathbf{829\times}\) lower per-sample computational cost than SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations), a widely used explainable AI (XAI)-based feature selection method. It further reduces beam-sweeping overhead by \(\mathbf{59.4\%}\) and \(\mathbf{89.8\%}\), compared to conventional DL-based beam selection and exhaustive search, respectively. The DVAE-based defense effectively denoises adversarial inputs, sustaining 85\% accuracy across different perturbation bounds, retains baseline performance on unperturbed RSSI inputs and surpasses defensive distillation defense scheme by 15--20\% on average under different attack scenarios.
papers.summary: Deep learning methods for aligning millimeter-wave (mmWave) beams tend to ignore causal structure, require excessive beam sweeping and can be misled by small adversarial perturbations of received power measurements. The authors learn a Bayesian graph relating received signal strength indicators (RSSI) to the optimal beam index and use it to select a minimal set of input features, then add a defensive variational autoencoder (`DVAE`) that maps perturbed inputs back to clean ones before a fine-tuned beam classifier. In simulation, causal beam selection matches the accuracy of conventional methods at **829x lower per-sample computational cost than `SHAP`-based feature selection**, and reduces beam-sweeping overhead by 59.4% against conventional deep learning selection and 89.8% against exhaustive search. The `DVAE` defense sustains 85% accuracy across perturbation bounds and beats defensive distillation by 15-20% on average.

papers.title: Marimba: A System One Model for Speech
papers.abstract: Speech applications require decisions about term presence, turn completion, and language within an audio window. We present Marimba, an interface for typed speech decisions built on frozen Qwen3-ASR 0.6B features. Lexical questions use zero-shot scoring of ASR transcripts; non-lexical questions use a question-conditioned head and a separate layer-18 turn-end readout. Language identification uses the ASR model's own language scores. On private conversational test sets, decoder AUROC is 0.80-0.92; on public read speech it is 0.92-0.97. Speech Commands four-way accuracy is 0.93; binary lexical ECE is at most 0.08. Personal-information detection, which passes the greedy transcript to a private, curated PII pipeline, reaches item-level F1 0.904 on synthetic Brazilian Portuguese speech (1.000 on reference transcripts). Layer-12 speaker readouts detect speaker change with AUROC 0.966-0.980 on AMI and VoxConverse, above an ECAPA baseline, and count speakers (0, 1, 2, or 3+) more accurately than pyannote 3.1. The turn-end readout reaches AUROC 0.930 versus Smart Turn v3.2 at 0.982 on Smart Turn's own test set. On a subset of ICSI meetings labeled by next speaker, AUROC is 0.716 versus 0.712; the paired confidence interval includes zero.
papers.summary: Speech applications need quick decisions about an audio window, such as whether a term was spoken, whether a turn has ended, and which language is in use. `Marimba` exposes these as typed questions on top of frozen `Qwen3-ASR 0.6B` features, using zero-shot scoring of transcripts for lexical questions, a question-conditioned head and layer readouts for non-lexical ones, and the speech recognizer's own scores for language identification. Decoder AUROC is 0.80-0.92 on private conversational test sets and 0.92-0.97 on public read speech, and **layer-12 speaker readouts detect speaker change with AUROC 0.966-0.980 on `AMI` and `VoxConverse`, above an `ECAPA` baseline**, while counting speakers more accurately than `pyannote 3.1`. Its turn-end readout reaches AUROC 0.930, below the 0.982 of `Smart Turn v3.2` on that model's own test set.

papers.title: Emulating physics-based XCO2 retrievals across OCO-2 viewing modes with compact neural networks
papers.abstract: Operational full-physics retrieval of the column-averaged dry-air mole fraction of carbon dioxide from satellite spectra is computationally demanding. We use singular value decomposition to compress spectra from the Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 separately by band. Compact multilayer perceptrons use the resulting spectral scores, prior information, and viewing geometry to predict the difference between the full-physics retrieval and its operational prior. Adding the predicted difference to the prior yields an estimate of the retrieved mole fraction. The models were trained on 2015-2019 observations and validated on 2020 observations. In 2021-2025 tests, the mean annual root-mean-square errors relative to the Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide Observations from Space retrieval product were 0.89, 1.35, and 1.43 parts per million for ocean glint, land glint, and nadir observations, respectively. On East Asian nadir observations screened using the published criteria for the spectral Transformer, our model yielded a lower mean annual error than reported for that model in 2020-2022. These results show that compact neural networks using compressed spectra can efficiently emulate the full-physics retrieval across multiple viewing modes and years.
papers.summary: Full-physics retrieval of column-averaged carbon dioxide from satellite spectra is computationally demanding. The authors compress `Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2` spectra band by band with singular value decomposition and train compact multilayer perceptrons on the spectral scores, prior information and viewing geometry to predict the difference between the full-physics retrieval and its operational prior. Trained on 2015-2019 data and tested on 2021-2025, the models reach **mean annual root-mean-square errors of 0.89, 1.35 and 1.43 parts per million for ocean glint, land glint and nadir observations** relative to the operational retrieval product. On East Asian nadir observations they report a lower mean annual error than a published spectral Transformer for 2020-2022.

papers.title: VLAN: Vision-Language Accessible Navigation
papers.abstract: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. Yet, existing benchmarks evaluate traversability under a fixed and limited embodiment. We present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), containing 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes across diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. For each trajectory, VLAN provides embodiment-specific actions and accessibility features for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, while everyday obstacles and accessibility labels are categorized as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk, and Blocked. Unlike goal-only evaluation, our benchmark measures physical safety and alignment with user-specific constraints via goal-reaching, collision-aware, and accessibility-aligned metrics. We benchmark modern vision-language models and find they often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, path selection, and safety criteria across user profiles, suggesting accessibility-aware navigation requires dedicated datasets, tasks, and metrics beyond conventional embodied navigation evaluation. All data and code open-source at https://github.com/InSAI-Lab/VLAN.
papers.summary: Whether a path is walkable depends on who or what is travelling it, yet existing navigation benchmarks evaluate traversability for a single fixed embodiment. The `VLAN` benchmark provides 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories and 160K keyframes with embodiment-specific actions for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, and labels obstacles as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk or Blocked. Its metrics cover goal-reaching, collisions and alignment with user-specific accessibility constraints. Benchmarked vision-language models **often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, path selection and safety criteria across user profiles**.

papers.title: Online Switching Control as Learning with Experts
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the problem of online switching control for discrete-time nonlinear systems where a controller is sequentially selected from a finite set of candidates. The goal is to generate an adaptive sequence of controllers to minimize the cumulative cost under unknown disturbances and cost functions. Specifically, we consider a full-information feedback setting where realized disturbance effects and cost functions are available after each selection. Using counterfactual costs computed from historical data, we reduce the online switching control problem to the experts problem with switching costs. Then, we propose an adaptive switching algorithm based on the Hedge algorithm with a switching suppression mechanism. Notably, the proposed algorithm achieves an expected regret of $O(\sqrt{T\log N})$, where $T$ is the time horizon and $N$ is the number of candidate controllers, while ensuring uniform boundedness of the state. This matches the optimal regret order for the standard experts problem.
papers.summary: Online switching control picks one controller at a time from a finite set of candidates for a discrete-time nonlinear system, aiming to minimize cumulative cost under unknown disturbances and cost functions. In a full-information setting where disturbance effects and costs are revealed after each choice, the authors use counterfactual costs computed from historical data to reduce the problem to prediction with experts under switching costs, and propose an algorithm based on `Hedge` with a mechanism that suppresses switching. The algorithm achieves **expected regret of O(sqrt(T log N)) for horizon T and N candidate controllers while keeping the state uniformly bounded**, matching the optimal order for the standard experts problem.

papers.title: Envisioning Agentic Robotics: A New Era of Robotic Systems
papers.abstract: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.
papers.summary: A position paper on what the authors call agentic robotics: applying a foundation model with an agentic harness to open-world embodied tasks in a closed loop of observing, reasoning, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes and adapting, instead of training a dedicated policy per task family. The authors state that after the release of `GPT-6 Astra`, frontier models with such harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks, and note that the field lacks a shared definition, evaluation framework or roadmap. They argue that **an `Embodied System 2`, a foundation model paired with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics**, with the central challenge being to turn general reasoning into verifiable actions under physical constraints. They propose an evaluation framework covering both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance, and a roadmap toward sustained autonomy.
papers.highlight_summary:
Frontier models wrapped in agentic harnesses now match or beat task-specific robot policies on many embodied benchmarks, yet the field has no shared definition, evaluation framework, or roadmap for this shift. This position paper proposes **Embodied System 2** — a foundation model plus an embodied harness that interprets intent, orchestrates skills and tools, verifies outcomes, and adapts — as the decision-making core of agentic robotics.

- The reference architecture separates three functional roles — `S2` for deciding and verifying, `S1` for callable skills such as VLA policies, perception and motion planning, and `S0` for real-time body control — with a real-time event monitor alongside that can interrupt `S2` or trigger a protective stop in `S0` under predefined safety rules.
- A component counts as `S2` only if it makes both decisions on how to proceed and decisions on outcomes in a way identifiable from outside, which excludes latent-only upper modules such as those in `Helix` and `GR00T N1`, while the harness contributes five core parts: context manager, tool interface, planner, memory, and verifier.
- Cited results, not new experiments, show how much the harness matters: a frozen `GPT-6 Astra` holding a whole episode in context solved **92.1%** of 800 `RoboMME` test episodes at **18.3 s** per call with the simulator paused, and a skill-only interface raised `GPT-5.6-Sol` from **11% to 63%** but dropped `GPT-6 Astra` from **92% to 61%**.
- The authors argue for "capped scaling" — gaining capability within a fixed decision deadline rather than by reasoning longer — noting that `GPT-6 Astra` used directly takes **7.7 to 39.86 s** per decision, roughly **40 to 8,000 times** slower than `S1` control skills.
- The contribution is conceptual — a nine-dimension evaluation framework and a roadmap from executing primitives (L1) to fulfilling standing roles (L4) — and the paper itself concedes that the cited latency figures come from non-comparable settings, the capped-scaling curve is schematic, and whether concise reasoning improves correctness on physical tasks remains open.

papers.title: Adaptable Watermarking: Transforming Image Watermarking Models via Lightweight Adapters
papers.abstract: We explore the adaptability of neural image watermarking models; the extent to which one watermarking method can be transformed into another through lightweight adaptation. We introduce a framework that enables encoder-decoder watermarking architectures to become modular and upgradable, supporting multiple watermarking styles without re-training full models. Adaptation is performed by attaching a compact parameter-efficient adapter and fine-tuning under a multi-domain residual alignment loss (spatial, gradient, and frequency) while preserving bit accuracy via a secret-loss term. We evaluate this approach across a suite of recent watermarking models, including TrustMark, InvisMark, RoSteALS, HiDDeN, and WAM, demonstrating that adapted encoders closely reproduce target residuals and that adapted decoders recover messages with near-optimal accuracy under standard augmentations and distortions. We show that cross-model adaptation, with applications in interoperable and upgradable watermarking, can be achieved with as few as 1-2M trainable parameters per component (e.g., the 2M decoder adapter used in our multi-decoder inference pipeline).
papers.summary: The authors ask how far one neural image watermarking model can be transformed into another through lightweight adaptation instead of full retraining. They attach compact parameter-efficient adapters to encoder-decoder watermarking architectures and fine-tune them with a residual alignment loss over spatial, gradient and frequency domains plus a secret-loss term that preserves bit accuracy. Across `TrustMark`, `InvisMark`, `RoSteALS`, `HiDDeN` and `WAM`, adapted encoders closely reproduce the target model's residuals and adapted decoders recover messages with near-optimal accuracy under standard augmentations and distortions. **Cross-model adaptation works with as few as 1-2M trainable parameters per component**.

papers.title: DECODE: Decomposable Environments for COntrolled Sequential-Decision Evaluation
papers.abstract: When a sequential decision system falls short of an optimum, its score does not reveal which modifications would improve its decisions. DECODE is a benchmark for testing such modifications through controlled experiments on planning and available information. Its consumer-credit collections generator provides five partially observed environments that share known dynamics matrices and vary a memory parameter and process noise. The experiments change selected inputs or planning rules while keeping the rest of the solver fixed. Each comparison specifies the solver's state inputs, response inputs and planning horizon. On the deterministic base environment, which was selected for a large gap between six-month and one-month planning with the hidden state, extending planning from one to six months increases the scores of two gradient-boosted solvers by 15 to 17 percentage points of the exact optimum, computed with the hidden state and borrower traits. Even at this horizon, the best graded solver, whose repayment response is fitted on logs, remains 15.6 points below that optimum. In a specified intervention sequence, three changes to its state inputs and their evaluation during search lower its score by 6.3 points, and replacing its fitted repayment model with the true response, evaluated with hidden borrower traits, then raises it by 15.6, a net recovery of nine of those points. Because the intermediate effects are conditional on the repayment model and the order of the changes, they do not uniquely assign the gap to separate causes. Within these limits, DECODE makes hypotheses about solver performance testable through specified interventions under known dynamics and explicit information conditions.
papers.summary: A single score does not reveal which changes would improve a sequential decision system that falls short of the optimum. `DECODE` is a benchmark built on a consumer-credit collections generator with five partially observed environments sharing known dynamics, in which controlled experiments change selected solver inputs or planning rules while everything else stays fixed. On the deterministic base environment, **extending planning from one to six months raises two gradient-boosted solvers' scores by 15 to 17 percentage points of the exact optimum**, yet the best graded solver still sits 15.6 points below that optimum. In one intervention sequence, three changes to state inputs lower the score by 6.3 points and substituting the true repayment response then raises it by 15.6; the authors caution that such order-dependent effects do not uniquely assign the gap to separate causes.

papers.title: f-Divergence Self-Play for Tabular Anomaly Detection via Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection in tabular data poses significant challenges due to heterogeneous feature types-mixing numerical, categorical, and textual attributes, which complicate learning meaningful representations of normality. Recent work has applied large language models (LLMs) to this problem by serializing table rows as text sequences, yet these approaches rely on one-shot supervised fine-tuning that offers limited signal to tighten the model's description of normality. We propose DiSPaT, a self-play fine-tuning framework that strengthens the model's understanding of normal data. Building on the theoretical foundation of f-divergence minimization, we derive a tight approximation connecting our training objective to reducing the distributional gap between real normal data and model-generated samples. DiSPaT operates through an alternating optimization: at each iteration, the current policy generates synthetic samples that serve as pseudo-anomalies, while a critic discriminator learns to distinguish these from real normal samples; this signal drives policy updates that progressively align the model distribution with the true normal-data distribution. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DiSPaT consistently outperforms prior LLM-based methods, deep learning approaches, and classical unsupervised detectors for tabular anomaly detection.
papers.summary: Anomaly detection in tabular data is complicated by mixed numerical, categorical and textual features, and existing large language model approaches that serialize rows as text rely on one-shot supervised fine-tuning. `DiSPaT` is a self-play fine-tuning framework grounded in f-divergence minimization: the current model generates synthetic rows that serve as pseudo-anomalies, a critic discriminator learns to tell them from real normal rows, and that signal updates the model so its distribution moves toward the true normal-data distribution. The authors derive an approximation linking the training objective to the distributional gap between real and generated samples. In experiments on diverse benchmarks, **`DiSPaT` consistently outperforms prior LLM-based methods, deep learning approaches and classical unsupervised detectors**.

papers.title: Evaluating Human Sensitivity to Gender Biased AI-Generated Content through Human Assessment of Google's Autocomplete Function
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly present, but their effects on human users remain underexplored. We tested whether AI-attributed information influences views regarding gender-related statements, a domain where biases are pervasive. Spanish-speaking participants recruited through Prolific evaluated biased statements derived from Google's autocomplete function and human-authored, non-biased gender-related facts. Participants were either informed that some of the material was AI-generated or received no information about its origin. AI attribution did not affect reaction times or agreement judgments. This result suggests that AI-generated content does not automatically raise credibility concerns and may be evaluated with less scrutiny compared to human-produced content.
papers.summary: Whether labelling content as AI-generated changes how people judge gender-related statements is tested with Spanish-speaking participants recruited through `Prolific`. Participants rated biased statements derived from Google's autocomplete function alongside human-written, non-biased gender facts, and only some were told that part of the material was AI-generated. **AI attribution had no effect on reaction times or agreement judgments**, which the authors read as a sign that AI-generated content does not automatically prompt extra scrutiny.

papers.title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($\pi_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, and this survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026 on manipulation, navigation, humanoid control and evaluation. It follows a VLA through seven axes spanning design, training and deployment, and compares 22 models on training data, size, inference speed and hardware. Training data has broadened to community-collected and egocentric human video, generalists such as `UniVLA` and `Qwen-VLA` now handle both manipulation and navigation, and **model sizes have split between 3-7 billion parameters and a sub-one-billion group that runs on consumer GPUs**. The survey also reviews evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly.

papers.title: AI-Based Multi-View Echocardiographic Image Synthesis using Dynamic Shape Control
papers.abstract: Although automated methods have improved echocardiographic workflows, progress remains constrained by the need for large, well-annotated datasets. As the development of clinical databases is often limited by ethical and logistical challenges, synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising alternative. However, existing approaches commonly rely on left ventricle shape-based supervision or are tailored to specific cardiac views, limiting the generation of additional standard and unconventional imaging planes and the preservation of multi-view consistency across cardiac chambers. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework for shape-controlled synthesis of multi-view echocardiographic sequences. First, multi-view cross-sections are extracted from dynamic whole-heart meshes. Ultrasound-like appearance is then introduced through a two-stage AI-based pipeline. In Stage 1, an unpaired GAN-diffusion model translates these cross-sections into realistic echocardiographic frames. As this translation is performed independently at the frame level, Stage 2 employs masked video reconstruction to improve temporal coherence and cardiac motion. Evaluation demonstrated high frame-level realism for both stages, while the integration of Stage 2 substantially improved video-level motion quality and temporal consistency. Overall, the proposed framework enables the generation of realistic multi-view echocardiographic sequences from diverse cardiac models, providing a scalable source of annotated data for dataset augmentation and the development of multi-view cardiac assessment methods.
papers.summary: Synthetic echocardiography data is usually limited to specific cardiac views or to left-ventricle shape supervision, which prevents consistent multi-view generation across heart chambers. The proposed framework extracts multi-view cross-sections from dynamic whole-heart meshes, translates them into ultrasound-like frames with an unpaired GAN-diffusion model, and then applies masked video reconstruction to restore temporal coherence. Both stages produce realistic individual frames, and **the second stage substantially improves video-level motion quality and temporal consistency**, yielding annotated multi-view sequences for dataset augmentation.

papers.title: Structure makes quantum circuits trainable
papers.abstract: The scalability of variational quantum algorithms is limited by barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially in system size. This worst-case result raises fundamental questions about the trainability of quantum AI models. We present a major advance towards resolving this trainability question by answering whether a given quantum circuit has a barren plateau. We do this using an analytical framework that bounds the gradient variance for arbitrary input states $\rho$ and observables $\mathcal{M}$ by decomposing the unitary representation of the associated compact Lie group. When the circuit segments on both sides of a gate form $2$-designs, we obtain the variance exactly and prove a sufficient condition for trainability: if $\rho^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mathcal{M}^{\otimes 2}$ are sufficiently concentrated on the same irreducible invariant subspace of polynomial dimension, and the differentiated gate moves this subspace by an inverse-polynomial amount, then the gradient variance is at least inverse-polynomial. We further present a sampling algorithm that estimates the gradient variance from runs of the ansatz, without constructing the representation-theoretic projectors. Our algorithm decides whether the variance exceeds a tolerance $\tau$ with the number of runs polynomial in $1/\tau$, including cases in which the bounds are inconclusive. This resolves the question of the trainability of the circuit before expensive training procedures.
papers.summary: Variational quantum algorithms suffer from barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially with system size, and it has been hard to tell in advance whether a given circuit has one. The authors bound the gradient variance for arbitrary input states and observables by decomposing the unitary representation of the circuit's associated compact Lie group, and they prove a sufficient condition for trainability when the state and observable concentrate on the same polynomial-dimension invariant subspace. They also give a sampling algorithm that **decides whether the gradient variance exceeds a tolerance using a number of circuit runs polynomial in the inverse tolerance**, including in cases where the analytical bounds are inconclusive.

papers.title: Where Tree Ensembles Decide: Structural Local Explanation with Decision Predicate Graphs
papers.abstract: Tree ensembles are among the most accurate models for tabular data, yet the computation behind a single prediction is spread over hundreds of decision rules. Feature attributions and counterfactuals explain such predictions through the influence of features or a change of the input, leaving open which of the thresholds applied by the trees a prediction responds to, while structural explanations compress these rules and lose the trees behind them. To address this gap, we propose a local Decision Predicate Graph (local DPG), which gathers the rules executed for a sample into a verifiable record of the computation, with a class support that reproduces every explained prediction. From these rules we select the critical predicate, the executed predicate whose crossing is estimated to move the model most strongly toward a chosen class, which offers the user a concrete threshold and the trees that share it, without an external explainer. Across 16 datasets and four ensemble families, it separates differently predicted neighbours better than random and nearest-threshold predicates. A single crossing recovers the true class in 46-69% of wrong predictions, against 29-50% when the same rule is applied to the feature ranked first by TreeSHAP, a measure close to the selection criterion, and on planted faults it finds the faulty threshold in 46-71% of the resulting errors, against 6-21% at random. Although training-free edits of these predicates did not reduce the error on unseen data, the critical predicate complements attributions and counterfactuals by naming where a prediction can be changed.
papers.summary: Explanations of tree-ensemble predictions usually report feature influence or counterfactual inputs, without saying which of the trees' decision thresholds a prediction actually depends on. The local Decision Predicate Graph (`local DPG`) collects the rules executed for one sample into a verifiable record and selects a critical predicate, the threshold whose crossing is estimated to move the model most toward a chosen class. Across 16 datasets and four ensemble families, **a single crossing recovers the true class in 46-69% of wrong predictions, against 29-50% for the top `TreeSHAP` feature**, and it locates planted faulty thresholds in 46-71% of resulting errors. Training-free edits of these predicates did not reduce error on unseen data.

papers.title: A systematic comparison of physics-informed neural networks and mechanistic models for epidemic modeling and forecasting
papers.abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently been applied to epidemic modeling and forecasting with promising results. These methods integrate mechanistic knowledge with data-driven learning. Yet, their comparative performance against well-established, and simpler epidemic models is underexplored. Here, we conduct a systematic comparison of a PINN-based framework and a stochastic mechanistic model. Both approaches share the same age-structured SEIRD core and rolling-window forecasting pipeline, in a deliberately minimal setting. We evaluate their retrospective fits and probabilistic forecasts in two synthetic scenarios and the first COVID-19 wave in London. Interestingly, while PINNs underperform in synthetic scenarios, they achieve better performance on real data. Furthermore, PINNs provide narrower uncertainty intervals and sharper estimation of parameters in synthetic scenarios. Our findings confirm PINNs as a promising tool in epidemiology. At the same time, the results reaffirm the value of simpler approaches such as traditional compartmental models, and promote additional benchmarking studies.
papers.summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have been applied to epidemic forecasting, but rarely compared head to head with simpler established models. This study pits a PINN framework against a stochastic mechanistic model, both built on the same age-structured SEIRD core and rolling-window forecasting pipeline, on two synthetic scenarios and the first COVID-19 wave in London. **The PINNs underperform on the synthetic scenarios but do better on the real London data**, while giving narrower uncertainty intervals and sharper parameter estimates in the synthetic cases.

papers.title: VelServe: Taming Decode Jitters in LLM Inference with Tail-Calibrated Scheduling
papers.abstract:
Interactive LLM services must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs) for the time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (TBT), as streaming and soft real-time applications require predictable token delivery. We identify decode jitters in both aggregated and disaggregated serving. A jitter delays every request in the batch, and long responses span hundreds of steps, so even rare overruns cause many SLO violations. In aggregated serving, SLO-aware schedulers set each step's prefill budget until its predicted latency just meets the TBT target, leaving no room for mispredictions or host stalls. Disaggregation meets average TBT targets at a cost in capacity, yet the steps that admit new requests still run late.
  We present \sysname, a scheduler that calibrates how much prefill work each decode step carries using the measured tail of its own iteration latency. The SLO determines how rare a late step must be, and \sysname leaves enough headroom in each iteration to prevent overruns and meet the target decode latency. This headroom slows prefill, so \sysname serves the shortest waiting prompt first. When TTFT deadlines grow with prompt length, the long prompts it delays have the most time to spare. Under disaggregation, it spaces admissions so that no request waits on more slow admission steps than its P99 target allows. On three attention families and varying workloads, \sysname sustains 2.4--2.9$\times$ the SLO goodput of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4$\times$ on DeepSeek-V2-Lite. With prefill and decode disaggregated on eight GPUs, \sysname meets the SLO for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.summary: Interactive LLM serving must meet latency targets for time to first token (TTFT) and time between tokens (TBT), but occasional slow decode steps delay every request in a batch and cause many violations over long responses. `VelServe` sizes the prefill work attached to each decode step using the measured tail of its own iteration latency, serves the shortest waiting prompt first, and spaces admissions when prefill and decode are disaggregated. It sustains **2.4-2.9x the goodput of the strongest baseline** on `Qwen3-8B` and `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` and at least 4.4x on `DeepSeek-V2-Lite`, and meets the latency target for more than twice as many requests in an eight-GPU disaggregated setup.

papers.title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
papers.abstract: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.
papers.summary: Machine learning weather models still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation systems that are typically updated every six hours. `WeatherDreamer` is a world model that learns the assimilation-and-forecast cycle end to end from 18 global observing systems without reanalysis, inferring a latent state, stepping it forward hourly, and correcting it with new observations. At held-out stations its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (`GEFS`) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 hours, though its errors are up to five times larger than the operational first guess for temperature-sounding channels. It produces **an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU**.

papers.title: Lipschitz-Constrained Discriminators in Generative Modeling: Asymptotic Behavior and Support Mismatch
papers.abstract: We study the asymptotic behavior of optimal discriminators associated to $L-$Lipschitz regularized KL-divergences of two probability distributions $Q$ and $P$ that interpolate between the rescaled Wasserstein$-1$ metric by some parameter $L>0$ and the KL divergence. The parameter $L$ plays the role of a Lipschitz constraint and is viewed as a regularization parameter: small values of $L$ enforce a more geometry-aware discriminator, while as $L$ increases the geometric regularization is progressively relaxed. It is a known result [3] that such divergences converge to the KL divergence as $L\to\infty$. In this paper, we characterize the asymptotic behavior of the optimal discriminators as $L\to\infty$ in different regimes: Firstly, under $Q\ll P$ and the Radon-Nikodym derivative $\frac{dQ}{dP}$ is bounded from above and bounded away from zero. Secondly, when $Q$ and $P$ are discrete distributions satisfying $Q\ll P$, and finally when $Q$ and $P$ are non absolutely continuous discrete distributions. This result motivates training strategies which involve discriminators, such as adversarial generative models. In practice, the data distribution is often represented by a discrete empirical measure, while, especially at the early stages of the training, the model distribution may have little or no overlap with the empirical data distribution.
papers.summary: Lipschitz-regularized KL divergences interpolate between a rescaled Wasserstein-1 metric and the KL divergence through a Lipschitz constant L, and are known to converge to KL as L grows. This work characterizes **how the optimal discriminators themselves behave as L goes to infinity** in three regimes: bounded density ratios, discrete distributions with absolute continuity, and discrete distributions with mismatched support. The mismatched-support case is relevant to adversarial generative training, where the empirical data distribution and the early model distribution may barely overlap.

papers.title: Smart Home Agents Make Capable but Unpredictable Grid Operators
papers.abstract: AI-enabled smart homes are becoming more common across the grid edge. However, there has not been much work on failure response. This area is critical because smart homes operate on the grid edge where failures can cascade down. If a power outage happens within a smart home, a user has to manually troubleshoot their smart home to include tasks such as power load balance and device recovery. We conduct the first resilience analysis of smart home agents across a full power outage, providing a suite of outage simulations in a live environment that measures resilience before, during, and post power outage. We show that smart home agents can act as grid operators in power outages and identify several new failure categories highlighting the current limitations across all of our models. These findings establish the groundwork for smart home agents as grid operators to increase overall resilience on the grid edge.
papers.summary: AI agents that control smart homes have not been studied for how they respond to failures, even though outages at the grid edge can cascade. The authors build a suite of outage simulations in a live environment and measure agent resilience before, during and after a full power outage, covering tasks such as load balancing and device recovery. They report that **smart home agents can act as grid operators during outages**, but identify several new failure categories shared across all tested models.

papers.title: Deep Neural Networks Training Efficiency: Does Grokking Modify its Dynamics?
papers.abstract: We study whether grokking, the delayed emergence of out-of-distribution generalization after apparent overfitting, alters training efficiency in deep neural networks, where efficiency is measured as accuracy per unit energy. Using two canonical settings, modular arithmetic and MNIST, we analyze two neural network models under 16-, 32-, and 64-bit precision and use Orthograd to test whether grokking produces noticeable deviations from the typically decreasing dynamics of training efficiency. We consider both short training runs of up to 500 epochs and long training runs of up to 20,000 epochs, and in both cases identify grokking as a sharp improvement in test accuracy after a sustained train-test gap. In the short-horizon experiments, applying Orthograd at progressively stronger levels during early training does not induce grokking, and efficiency remains smoothly decreasing.
