In the long-horizon experiments, Orthograd induces grokking, but the efficiency curves remain approximately monotonic and show no appreciable local increase at the grokking transition. These results suggest that, in our setting, grokking does not materially alter overall training-efficiency dynamics.
papers.summary: Grokking is the delayed jump in generalization after apparent overfitting, and this study asks whether it changes training efficiency measured as accuracy per unit energy. Two network models are trained on modular arithmetic and `MNIST` at 16-, 32- and 64-bit precision, using `Orthograd` to induce grokking in runs of up to 500 and up to 20,000 epochs. Grokking appears only in the long runs, and **efficiency curves stay approximately monotonic with no appreciable local increase at the grokking transition**.

papers.title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
papers.abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.
papers.summary: `Gamer` is a generalist vision-language-action agent for long-horizon, real-time play that operates both 2D graphical interfaces and 3D simulated worlds through keyboard and mouse. It is pre-trained on tens of thousands of hours of device-level interaction trajectories, tuned with sparse-thinking instruction tuning to cut redundant reasoning, and trained with a multi-turn reinforcement learning method aimed at finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors and sparse rewards. A cloud-edge inference engine keeps latency low across many concurrent environments. The authors report **operational efficiency comparable to skilled players in several 3D open-world games**, plus competitive results on 2D game benchmarks.
papers.highlight_summary:
Playing modern 3D games for hours in real time, from raw pixels and native keyboard-and-mouse input with no game APIs, strains a vision-language model's control, memory and inference latency all at once. `Gamer` trains a single `Qwen3-VL-8B` policy in three stages — continued pre-training, sparse-reasoning fine-tuning and online reinforcement learning — and pairs it with a low-latency serving engine.

- The policy sees the screen at **5 Hz** and emits six key/button blocks per step for roughly **30 Hz** control, with pre-training that randomly remaps keys and down-weights repeated actions, which make up **over 85%** of steps.
- Fine-tuning teaches the model to act directly on routine steps, reason only at key decisions and write its own memory summaries, using about **1K hours** of curated `Honkai: Star Rail` play (filtered from **11K hours**) annotated with roughly **1.2M** reasoning notes, **63K** task segments and **223K** memory summaries.
- `TA-GRPO` splits long rollouts into memory-linked segments and scores them against each other on environment-verified outcomes, with no critic or learned reward model and more weight on later steps, collecting **128 rollouts per iteration in groups of 8**.
- `Streaming-vLLM` reuses KV-cache state across memory compaction, drafts predictable structural tokens with a finite-state machine that the model verifies, and dispatches the first action block before decoding finishes, with **64 H200 GPUs serving 32 parallel game environments**.
- The authors claim **efficiency comparable to skilled human players** on 3D open-world game tasks and competitive results on 2D benchmarks (the extracted text cuts off before the numbers), while noting that extra pre-training data brings **no sustained gains on distant unseen games** and that only the inference engine and scaling-study checkpoints are released.

papers.title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs
papers.abstract: Research in the domain of Physics-Informed Neural Networks applied to PDE modelling has advanced significantly in recent years, providing a wide ecosystem of novel methods. However, one frequent limitation is the inability of PINNs to scale out on High-Performance Computing architectures to address more ambitious challenges, particularly non-linear physics models with turbulent dynamics in large spatial domains. Typical studies restrain demonstrations to toy models with simple physics equations, few variables, and rarely any complex non-linear dynamics evolved over long timescales. Part of the AI community has even adopted the idea that "PINNs don't scale". This work proves otherwise. We present a mathematically robust formulation of Finite-Element-Method for Neural Networks (FEM-NN) implemented into a comprehensive, modular framework: Fuse-PINN. This formulation provides the basis for a sclable parallelisation of Physics-Informed Neural Networks on GPU-based HPC systems. Furthermore, an Energy Natural Gradient Descent optimiser is implemented to allow high-precision convergence. Fuse-PINN is demonstrated on physics models relevant to Magnetic Confinement Fusion, including non-linear convective models with fine-scale dynamics. Near-perfect scaling is achieved on multi-GPU runs with increasing problem size.
papers.summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are widely believed not to scale to large non-linear, turbulent problems on High-Performance Computing systems. `Fuse-PINN` is a modular framework built on a Finite-Element-Method formulation for neural networks, which allows parallelisation across GPUs, combined with an Energy Natural Gradient Descent optimiser for high-precision convergence. Demonstrated on magnetic confinement fusion models including non-linear convective dynamics, it achieves **near-perfect scaling on multi-GPU runs as problem size increases**.

papers.title: LitArc-Bench: Disentangling Text-Specific Reader-Response Dynamics from Position and Lexical Affect
papers.abstract: When model predictions track an unfolding human affect trajectory, alignment may reflect narrative position, affective words, or text-specific reader-response dynamics. We introduce LitArc-Bench to separate these explanations: 39 Chinese-language literary excerpts segmented into seven checkpoints, with 430 questionnaires from 81 adults in two classroom groups (9,020 VAD ratings). We compare three future-blind model runs with leave-one-text-out position priors, lexical affect, and human-human references. Position alone reaches r = .470 for arousal, making raw alignment insufficient. Yet all six V/A transition advantages over a joint position-lexicon control have text-bootstrap intervals above zero. Cross-fitted models match the correct human text better than 38 mismatched texts in all nine model-dimension cells (p < .0001); a text-invariant negative control returns chance (p = 1). On human transitions at least 0.5 points against the position trend, models recover 69-76% of valence directions and 53-68% for arousal and dominance. Under crossed participant-text resampling, all nine identity intervals remain above zero; joint-control advantages are robust for valence and directional but less certain for arousal. High shape agreement still coexists with scale bias. LitArc-Bench identifies which components of literary reader response are recoverable beyond shallow explanations and why shape, calibration, and human variability require separate evaluation.
papers.summary: When a model's predictions track readers' unfolding emotional response to a story, the match could come from narrative position or affective vocabulary instead of anything specific to the text. `LitArc-Bench` separates these explanations with 39 Chinese-language literary excerpts split into seven checkpoints and 9,020 valence-arousal-dominance ratings from 81 adults, compared against position priors, lexical affect and human-human references. Position alone reaches a correlation of .470 for arousal, yet models still beat a joint position-lexicon control and **recover 69-76% of valence directions on human transitions that run against the position trend**. High agreement in trajectory shape coexists with scale bias.

papers.title: CoPre-MoE: Consolidating and Preserving MoE for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
papers.abstract: Multimodal continual instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to sequentially acquire new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising way to mitigate task interference through expert specialization and combination. However, while existing MoE-based methods avoid overwriting shared parameters by allocating separate experts for each task, this progressive expansion incurs severe cross-task redundancy and linear parameter growth. Specifically, experts across tasks often learn overlapping functions alongside task-specific capabilities. For instance, ScienceQA and TextVQA both locate relevant image regions. To curb parameter redundancy without inducing forgetting, we propose Consolidating and Preserving MoE (CoPre-MoE). For each incoming task, CoPre-MoE first learns task-specific MoE to capture specialized capabilities. To eliminate redundancy and reduce parameter growth across tasks, we design a shared-and-private expert architecture. Specifically, we first evaluate functional overlap to selectively consolidate overlapping experts across tasks into a fixed-capacity generic expert pool. We then factorize the remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact task-specific cores within a private expert pool. To mitigate forgetting, we construct the router by pairing each expert with learnable retrieval keys, where historical keys remain frozen during continual updates while newly added keys are regularized with an orthogonality penalty. At inference, input-dependent routing dynamically combines both pools without test-time task labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPre-MoE achieves superior performance while substantially reducing parameter overhead.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models that learn tasks sequentially often use mixture-of-experts (MoE) designs that add separate experts per task, which avoids forgetting but causes redundancy and linear parameter growth. `CoPre-MoE` merges functionally overlapping experts into a fixed-capacity generic pool, factorizes the remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases with compact private cores, and routes inputs with retrieval keys whose historical entries stay frozen. Routing needs no task labels at test time, and the authors report **superior performance with substantially lower parameter overhead** than prior MoE-based methods.

papers.title: LECAT: Measuring LLM Category Learning from Pretraining Data
papers.abstract: Humans know that airplanes are fast, that this extends to red airplanes, but that it does not hold for broken airplanes. How do LLMs acquire category knowledge that humans learn and apply effortlessly? We introduce LeCat, a two-part framework to analyze LLM's Learning of Category knowledge. First, we use LeCat to evaluate models on their ability to learn category knowledge, distinguishing between three cases: memorization of in-domain category knowledge, generalization to unseen instances, and ability to flexibly use knowledge in appropriate contexts. Then, we use LeCat to trace how this knowledge can be learned in pretraining from text that may encode category knowledge in various ways, such as verbatim repetition or exceptions, which we refer to as forms of "knowledge expression". We first assess open-source pretrained models using 199 curated category-feature pairs and analyze their training data. Our findings suggest that strengthening context and category-feature co-occurrence likelihood (PMI) improve learning for larger models and verbatim rule-like statements diminish flexible category learning. To systematically isolate these effects, we then train a 68M model from scratch with precise control over the categorical information each sees in their training data, confirming that verbatim repetition reduces flexible learning but mixture of diverse knowledge expressions lead to more robust category learning. Together, our findings highlight that while contextual flexibility is persistently difficult for models, how category knowledge is expressed in pretraining greatly impacts models' acquisition of robust category knowledge.
papers.summary: How LLMs pick up category knowledge, such as that airplanes are fast but broken airplanes are not, is examined with `LeCat`, a framework that separates memorization, generalization to unseen instances, and flexible use in context. The authors evaluate open-source pretrained models on 199 category-feature pairs, analyze their training data, and then train a 68M-parameter model from scratch with controlled data. **Verbatim repetition of rule-like statements reduces flexible category learning, while a mixture of diverse knowledge expressions makes it more robust**, and contextual flexibility remains persistently difficult for models.

papers.title: Graph diffusion transformer for interpretable generation and inverse design of disordered atomic structures
papers.abstract: Atomic disorder offers a potent degree of freedom to tailor material properties, yet the resulting vast configuration space obscures structure-property relations and hinders rational inverse design. Here we introduce Graph Amorphous Diffusion Transformer (GaDiT), a generative model that combines dynamic periodic graphs, masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution. GaDiT generates high-quality disordered structures while accelerating sampling by two orders of magnitude compared with existing corrector-based approaches, as demonstrated across two-dimensional amorphous carbon and three-dimensional amorphous silicon and silica. Moreover, GaDiT supports conditional generation under single or combined structural features, physical properties and preparation conditions in a unified model, and enables inverse design that expands accessible structure-property ranges beyond the training distribution. To interpret these structures and the trained network, we propose a conditioned atomic response mapping analysis, revealing both the global structural descriptors and the local atomic environments that govern target properties. Overall, GaDiT establishes a general framework for interpretable generation, inverse design and structure-property discovery for disordered atomic structures.
papers.summary: Disordered atomic structures have a vast configuration space that obscures structure-property relations and makes inverse design difficult. The Graph Amorphous Diffusion Transformer (`GaDiT`) combines dynamic periodic graphs, masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution to generate amorphous carbon, silicon and silica structures, with **sampling two orders of magnitude faster than corrector-based approaches**. One model supports conditioning on structural features, physical properties and preparation conditions, and inverse design reaches structure-property ranges beyond the training distribution. A conditioned atomic response mapping analysis is proposed to identify the descriptors and local environments that govern target properties.

papers.title: The State Is Not the Bottleneck: A Paged-State Gated-DeltaNet Tile on a Tri-Mode Multicast Mesh, Bit-Exact from RTL to Silicon
papers.abstract: Linear-attention language models replace a growing key-value cache with a recurrent state of fixed size. On an edge FPGA, this state can exceed the on-chip memory and must be paged to external memory. This paper asks whether such paging dominates the cost of decoding (generating tokens). We built a hardware tile that computes one complete layer of a custom 369-million-parameter hybrid Gated DeltaNet model on an Agilex 5 FPGA and pages its recurrent state. The model state needs 6.2 MiB, whereas the device has 0.87 MiB of block memory. Paging adds 26.0 MB of memory traffic per decoded token, at most 11.2 percent of the calculated total. On the board at 75 MHz, with synthetic weights, one token takes 11.15 ms in this layer. The matrix-vector products with the weights take about 62 percent of this time and the state phase, including the paging, 13 percent. The tile is one node of a multicast mesh of tri-mode processing elements. We measure the error of the fixed-point arithmetic against floating point and check that the hardware agrees bit for bit with a fixed-point reference. In simulation, the state logic agrees with the reference on all 18 recurrent layers. On the board, six builds pass all 30 runs of 64 tokens and two runs of 1,024 tokens. For this model and memory interface, the delivery of the weights limits the decoding performance, and the recurrent state does not. State paging is therefore practical for such a model on an edge FPGA.
papers.summary: Linear-attention language models keep a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value cache, but on an edge FPGA that state can exceed on-chip memory and must be paged to external memory. The authors built a hardware tile computing one full layer of a 369-million-parameter hybrid `Gated DeltaNet` model on an `Agilex 5` FPGA, where the state needs 6.2 MiB against 0.87 MiB of block memory. **Paging accounts for at most 11.2 percent of per-token memory traffic**, and of the 11.15 ms per token in this layer, weight matrix-vector products take about 62 percent and the state phase 13 percent. The hardware matches a fixed-point reference bit for bit, and weight delivery, not the recurrent state, limits decoding speed.

papers.title: Towards Explainable Sleep Stage Classification using Single-Channel Electroencephalogram
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging has achieved strong bench- mark accuracy; however, clinical adoption remains limited due to a lack of interpretability. In this work, we fill the research gap by extending the SleepXAI sleep staging framework to systematically compare five different XAI methods. Further, attribution fidelity is evaluated using Spearman rank correlation with AASM-defined EEG frequency bands, serving as clinically grounded reference signals. In this paper, we focus on single- channel Electroencephalogram (EEG), which is more amenable to practical clinical deployment compared to full polysomnography setups. Experiments are conducted on the Sleep-EDF benchmark dataset and the DREAMT dataset. In DREAMT, we stratified subjects based on OSA into four Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) severity groups. We observed that the SleepXAI model achieves strong classification performance on both datasets. Among the evaluated methods, Integrated Gradients (IG) consistently achieves the highest mean attribution fidelity across all five sleep stages on Sleep-EDF and across all AHI groups on DREAMT, outperforming all other evaluated methods under the Spearman rank correlation metric. These findings highlight the importance of attribution method selection as a key factor for ensuring reliable and clinically interpretable automated sleep staging systems.
papers.summary: Automated sleep staging is accurate on benchmarks but sees limited clinical use because its decisions are hard to interpret. This work extends the `SleepXAI` framework for single-channel electroencephalogram (EEG) to compare five explanation methods, scoring each by Spearman rank correlation between its attributions and the clinically defined EEG frequency bands. On `Sleep-EDF` and on `DREAMT`, with subjects grouped by Apnea-Hypopnea Index severity, **`Integrated Gradients` consistently gives the highest attribution fidelity** across all sleep stages and severity groups.

papers.title: Between Obligations and Evidence: A Participatory Study of Translating the EU AI Act into Technical Requirements
papers.abstract: The EU AI Act imposes technical and organizational requirements for high-risk AI systems, but applying these requirements involves contextual choices about what to measure and what evidence supports a compliance claim. We investigate these challenges through a participatory workshop involving 32 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners from different disciplines, using realistic scenarios in healthcare, recruitment, and public transport to examine how regulatory obligations are interpreted, translated into technical requirements, and evaluated in practice. Through a thematic analysis of workshop data, we identify recurring tensions between how regulatory obligations are translated into measurable system properties, how responsibility and human oversight are exercised in practice, and how the validity of compliance evidence is affected by changing operational conditions and system uses. For example, participants highlighted how fairness metrics could conceal discrimination in recruitment, how time pressure and limited information could undermine human oversight in public transport, and how changes in patient populations could invalidate previously established evidence of system performance. Our findings suggest that technical, organizational, and evidentiary challenges are interdependent, and that establishing and maintaining compliance requires attention not only to technical assessments but also to how AI systems are used, governed, and monitored over time. We discuss implications for supporting context-sensitive and ongoing compliance.
papers.summary: The EU AI Act sets technical and organizational requirements for high-risk AI systems, but applying them requires contextual choices about what to measure and what counts as compliance evidence. A participatory workshop with 32 researchers, policymakers and practitioners worked through realistic scenarios in healthcare, recruitment and public transport, and the results were analysed thematically. Participants noted that fairness metrics can conceal discrimination, that time pressure can undermine human oversight, and that shifts in patient populations can invalidate earlier performance evidence. The authors conclude that **technical, organizational and evidentiary challenges are interdependent**, so compliance has to be maintained over time and not established once.

papers.title: PACT: A Decoder-Confidence-Guided Two-Round Receiver for Joint Channel and Phase-Noise Estimation in Sub-THz OFDM
papers.abstract: Frequency-selective fading and oscillator phase noise (PN) jointly impair coded sub-THz OFDM reception. We propose a decoder-confidence-guided two-round receiver combining a {pilot-aware complex transformer} (PACT) estimator, banded linear minimum mean-square error equalization, and neural normalized min-sum decoding. PACT jointly estimates the frequency-domain channel and effective time-domain PN through interacting complex-valued branches. Decoder-derived pseudo-pilots and continuous constellation-aware confidence guide second-round refinement through PACT inputs and attention, with parameters shared across rounds. At $E_b/N_0=30$~dB, the PACT receiver achieves approximately $70\%$ and $57\%$ lower code-block error rates than the best-performing learning-based baseline in the two benchmark settings, respectively. Frozen-weight tests further demonstrate applicability across channel/PN models, carrier frequencies, and FFT/bandwidth configurations.
papers.summary: Coded sub-terahertz OFDM reception suffers from the combined effect of frequency-selective fading and oscillator phase noise (PN). The proposed two-round receiver pairs a pilot-aware complex transformer estimator, `PACT`, with banded linear minimum mean-square error equalization and neural normalized min-sum decoding, feeding decoder-derived pseudo-pilots and confidence values back into a second estimation round that shares the same weights. At an Eb/N0 of 30 dB it achieves **roughly 70% and 57% lower code-block error rates** than the best learning-based baseline in two benchmark settings, and frozen-weight tests indicate it transfers across channel and PN models, carrier frequencies, and FFT/bandwidth configurations.

papers.title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
papers.abstract: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.
papers.summary: Black-box uncertainty methods for large language models (LLMs) usually collapse to a single score that cannot separate prompt ambiguity (aleatoric uncertainty) from model knowledge gaps (epistemic uncertainty). The proposed two-level ensemble samples multiple stochastic decodings per prompt and repeats this across meaning-preserving paraphrases of the prompt, then applies the law of total covariance in an embedding space to split within-perturbation from between-perturbation variability. Supporting theory includes a bias-corrected epistemic estimator for nested Monte Carlo, a bound relating the estimates to Bayesian targets, and a proof that consistency-only black-box methods miss a class of failures that perturbation-based estimates detect. Across five short question-answering benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs, the estimator **matches leading black-box methods on error ranking at an equal generation budget while also decomposing the two uncertainty types**, which respond selectively to prompt ambiguity and knowledge gaps in controlled interventions.

papers.title: When to Trust Simulated Patient Responses:Support-Gated World Models for Vasopressor Decision Support
papers.abstract: Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support, a lightweight extension of a propose--simulate--refine agent. A recurrent dynamics ensemble predicts short-horizon physiological responses to documented norepinephrine dose categories, while a behavior model estimates observational action support. The interface withholds predictions with insufficient support or excessive ensemble disagreement and abstains when no candidate qualifies. Evaluation on eICU-CRD includes 70 hospitals and 30,700 decision transitions, with 14 hospitals held out for testing. At 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating yields a MAP mean absolute error of 7.3 mmHg, compared with 9.2 mmHg for random selection at the same coverage. The gated agent achieves 60.0% agreement with recorded actions at 81.0% decision coverage, compared with 55.0% agreement and 99.5% coverage for an ungated ensemble agent. Component ablations show lower factual risk with joint gating than with either gate alone.These results characterize a reliability--coverage trade-off in selective clinical simulation; they do not identify individualized treatment effects or establish improved patient outcomes.
papers.summary: Clinical world models that let language-model agents preview predicted patient responses can be unreliable for rarely used treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. `Support-Gated World-Model` decision support extends a propose-simulate-refine agent with a recurrent dynamics ensemble that predicts short-horizon responses to norepinephrine dose categories and a behavior model that estimates how well each action is supported by observational data, withholding predictions with weak support or high ensemble disagreement and abstaining when no candidate qualifies. On `eICU-CRD` with 14 of 70 hospitals held out, joint gating gives a mean arterial pressure error of **7.3 mmHg at 62.0% coverage versus 9.2 mmHg for random selection** at the same coverage, and the gated agent agrees with recorded actions 60.0% of the time at 81.0% decision coverage compared with 55.0% at 99.5% for an ungated agent. The authors state that the results characterize a reliability-coverage trade-off and do not establish individualized treatment effects or improved patient outcomes.

papers.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
papers.abstract: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.
papers.summary: Frequent context edits in agent sessions invalidate cached key-value (KV) attention state, forcing requests to wait for a full re-prefill before decoding can begin. `Callo` is a serving system with separate prefill and decode stages that uses the invalidated KV to generate speculative draft tokens during the wait, then verifies them against the exact KV once prefill finishes before committing anything. It schedules speculation into idle decode capacity and preempts drafts that are unlikely to be accepted. On a two-GPU testbed running `SWE-agent` sessions across three model families it delivers **all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over `vLLM`** at moderate load, with trace-driven cluster simulations indicating the gains persist at scale.

papers.title: Sample-efficient prediction of high-entropy alloy strength through outcome-aware robust sequential learning
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of high-entropy alloy (HEA) strength can guide composition and processing decisions; however, obtaining tensile-test data for HEAs can be costly and experimentally demanding. This study proposes Robust Outcome-aware Sequential Experimentation for High-Entropy Alloys (ROSE-HEA), a sample-efficient framework for predicting ultimate tensile strength (UTS) from alloy composition and processing conditions. Its acquisition policy anticipates how possible UTS outcomes update predictions and the support for complementary Gaussian process (GP) descriptions. It then reassesses the worst-case expected predictive risk remaining across a reference domain to select informative candidates. A retrospective evaluation on 501 HEA records compares ROSE-HEA with expected-improvement (EI) and upper-confidence-bound (UCB) Bayesian optimization (BO), random GP sampling, and eight conventional regressors across 30 matched runs with shared initial observations and test conditions. Starting from 25 initial observations and acquiring 100 additional responses, ROSE-HEA achieves the lowest mean root-mean-square error (RMSE), at 152.84 MPa, and the highest mean R^2, at 0.7443. Mean RMSE is reduced by 6.16% and 6.37% relative to EI and UCB, respectively. The selected observations improve prediction across six regressor families and provide broader design-space coverage. ROSE-HEA also surpasses the strongest conventional regressor's mean predictive performance using 125 rather than 185 observations, corresponding to 32.4% fewer training observations. These findings demonstrate the potential of outcome-aware robust sequential learning to improve UTS prediction in HEAs under constrained training budgets.
papers.summary: Tensile-test data for high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is expensive to collect, which limits models that predict ultimate tensile strength from composition and processing conditions. `ROSE-HEA` is a sequential experiment-selection framework whose acquisition policy anticipates how possible outcomes would update several complementary Gaussian process models and then picks candidates that reduce the worst-case expected predictive risk over a reference domain. In a retrospective evaluation on 501 HEA records, starting from 25 observations and acquiring 100 more, it reaches the lowest mean root-mean-square error of 152.84 MPa, about 6% below expected-improvement and upper-confidence-bound Bayesian optimization. It also exceeds the best conventional regressor's performance with **125 rather than 185 observations, 32.4% fewer**.

papers.title: Typing Matters: Muscle, Language and Typing Behaviour in Live Keystroke Decoding from sEMG
papers.abstract: Surface electromyography (sEMG) from the wrists can recover typed text without a keyboard. It is usually posed as a signal-inference problem: characters are read out of the muscle signal and character error rate is reported offline. We argue that this framing removes most of the problem. The decoder is constrained simultaneously by the muscles, by the language being typed, and by typing behaviour such as typos, corrections, backspaces and line breaks, and a usable system must predict keys live while the hand keeps moving. Existing systems fall short on two counts: (1) they process sEMG in fixed windows and carry nothing from one window to the next, discarding context accumulated over a session, and (2) they lack any understanding of the linguistic structure that drives typing, so every keystroke is inferred from the muscle signal alone. We propose a fully causal, zero-lookahead sEMG typing decoder built on a state space model (SSM), in which a single model decodes a whole session without windowed partitions, conditioned on what has already been typed. We achieve this by fusing a traditional typing decoder with an efficient autoregressive language model, instilling both sEMG and linguistic understanding in one model. To train such a model for per-character typing rather than whole-word text, we introduce a retokenization method that rewrites ordinary prose as human-like typing, with keystrokes, typos, backspaces and line breaks included, converting WikiText into a large typing corpus where none existed. Our model, having never seen a single sEMG-to-character transcript in typing, achieves a state-of-the-art character error rate of 25.13% on emg2qwerty's cross-user benchmark, a 5.4% relative improvement over the previous best with 6.7 times fewer parameters, while running strictly causally with no future context.
papers.summary: Decoding typed text from wrist surface electromyography (sEMG) is usually treated as offline signal inference over fixed windows, ignoring language structure and typing behaviour such as typos, backspaces and corrections. The proposed decoder is fully causal with zero lookahead, built on a state space model that processes an entire session without windowing and fuses a conventional typing decoder with an efficient autoregressive language model conditioned on what has already been typed. To train it, a retokenization method rewrites `WikiText` prose as human-like keystroke sequences including typos, backspaces and line breaks. The model reaches a **25.13% character error rate on the `emg2qwerty` cross-user benchmark**, a 5.4% relative improvement over the previous best with 6.7 times fewer parameters.

papers.title: Score-based neural ordinary differential equations for reaction-diffusions
papers.abstract: A diffusion equation can be rewritten as a transport equation driven by the score function of the evolving density. Conventional probability-flow formulations, which move particles deterministically with this score-driven velocity, typically conserve total mass. In this work, we develop a Lagrangian method for reaction-diffusion equations in which each particle carries a position and a physical weight. The characteristic ODEs incorporate source terms into the evolution of the log-density and its gradient, while particle weights track changes in mass. We combine this representation with a learned velocity field and weighted particle training to approximate these dynamics. For non-increasing reaction rates, a relative-entropy inequality supports the mass-normalized self-consistency residual as the training objective. This objective can control the error of the induced density when the growth rate is bounded. The algorithm divides the time interval into short windows. In each window, a frozen velocity generates the particle data for a regression of the network velocity. We draw the particles from period-adapted initial sampling distributions and weight them in the loss partly by their predicted future mass, because the reaction can make regions with little initial mass important later. We numerically investigate the method on the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck (OU) equation with a linear source term, Fisher--KPP equations, and Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao gradient flows.
papers.summary: Score-driven probability-flow methods move particles deterministically to solve diffusion equations but typically conserve total mass, so they do not directly handle reaction terms that create or destroy mass. The proposed Lagrangian method gives each particle a position and a physical weight, with characteristic ordinary differential equations that fold source terms into the evolution of the log-density and its gradient while weights track mass changes, and a neural velocity field trained window by window on particles generated with a frozen velocity. For non-increasing reaction rates, **a relative-entropy inequality justifies the mass-normalized self-consistency residual as the training objective**, which controls the density error when the growth rate is bounded. Numerical experiments cover an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck equation with a linear source, Fisher-KPP equations, and Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao gradient flows.

papers.title: Contrastive latent representation learning with denoising score matching
papers.abstract: Contrastive representation learning methods operate by pulling different views of the same data sample together while pushing them away from views of different samples. A fundamental challenge is the estimation of the repulsive force, which typically requires large batch sizes, can exhibit high variance, and is susceptible to the curse of dimensionality. We introduce ScoreCLR, a contrastive representation learning method that offers a novel way to estimate this repulsion term. We consider the framework of representation learning by maximizing the mutual information between two latent views of a sample. By deriving the gradient of the Shannon entropy with respect to the encoder parameters, we obtain an equivalent objective that involves the score of the latent representation. We then use denoising score matching techniques to estimate this score with a lightweight network that is trained jointly with the encoder. We further propose regularization techniques using different noise levels and a Gaussian prior on the latent representation. ScoreCLR replaces the batch of explicit negative samples in contrastive methods with a learned repulsion whose cost is linear in the batch size rather than quadratic. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 it does so with minimal loss of linear-probe accuracy compared to SimCLR under a shared recipe, while producing projector outputs of higher effective rank, closer to the Gaussian prior.
papers.summary: Contrastive representation learning depends on a repulsive force between different samples whose estimation typically needs large batches, has high variance, and suffers in high dimensions. `ScoreCLR` derives the gradient of the latent entropy term in a mutual-information objective, which yields an equivalent objective involving the score of the latent distribution, and estimates that score with a lightweight network trained jointly with the encoder via denoising score matching, regularized by multiple noise levels and a Gaussian prior. This replaces explicit negative samples with a learned repulsion whose **cost is linear rather than quadratic in batch size**. On `CIFAR-10` and `ImageNet-100` it shows minimal loss in linear-probe accuracy relative to `SimCLR` under a shared recipe, while producing projector outputs of higher effective rank.

papers.title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation
papers.abstract: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.
papers.summary: LLM-based verifiers that judge agent executions are usually validated on a single representation of the trajectory, even though deployed systems expose the same run through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories. `Verification Transport` tests whether a verifier's judgment stays stable by building matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, outcome, ground truth, criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, **transport failure reaches about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation**; direct verification tends to produce wrong verdicts, while evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain. Restoring the execution provenance recovers 85.5% of the failures, with lower recovery when provenance is lossy or unavailable.

papers.title: Evaluating Feedback-Driven Black-Box Processes via Stochastic Modeling and Simulation
papers.abstract: We study feedback-driven black-box processes across software engineering and machine learning. These processes are inherently sequential: policies generate inputs, observe outputs/feedback from systems, and use the feedback to guide the design of subsequent inputs. While many policies are developed under structural assumptions on the underlying systems, many real-world systems operate without such knowledge, necessitating black-box policies that lack a unified evaluation framework. We introduce a stochastic framework that models and evaluates such policies using Markov chains and simulation, thereby connecting empirical practice with theory. We instantiate the framework in mutation-based fuzzing (widely used for discovering software bugs via sequential input mutation), by a novel Markov chain model of fuzzing whose transitions are governed by the mutation strategy and whose feedback is given by program execution. We develop a rigorous evaluation paradigm with new performance measures, sound estimators, and evaluation procedures with provable guarantees. Guided by the theory, we evaluate 9 fuzzers on 18 widely used fuzzing benchmarks and conduct case studies in 4 non-fuzzing domains. These results show that the framework provides a principled basis for evaluation while connecting to practice, with implications beyond fuzzing.
papers.summary: Sequential black-box processes, in which a policy generates inputs, observes system feedback, and uses it to design the next inputs, lack a unified evaluation framework across software engineering and machine learning. The proposed stochastic framework models such policies with Markov chains and simulation, and is instantiated for mutation-based fuzzing with a Markov chain whose transitions are governed by the mutation strategy and whose feedback comes from program execution. It supplies new performance measures, sound estimators, and evaluation procedures with provable guarantees. Guided by the theory, the authors **evaluate 9 fuzzers on 18 widely used fuzzing benchmarks** and run case studies in 4 non-fuzzing domains.

papers.title: Bregman geometry in regular exponential families: dual representations and relative smoothness
papers.abstract: Regular exponential-family distributions are ubiquitous in statistics due to their appealing and convenient properties. Notably, they can be expressed in terms of Bregman divergences, revealing fundamental connections between statistics, convex analysis, and information geometry. However, this geometric structure has not been systematically exploited to characterize these distributions with respect to their expectation parametrization. Building on a projective characterization, we establish a general construction of equivalent dual Bregman representations, together with normalization and uniqueness results. These representations express log-densities as ordinary Bregman divergences in dual coordinate systems, providing geometric characterizations of the parameter space. So-called $\beta$- and $\alpha$-scaled dual representations emerge as particular instances of this framework. We further derive dual Bregman representations of conjugate priors and establish that they preserve conjugacy. Applications to classical distributions illustrate the geometric structures underlying seemingly different statistical models. Moreover, we show that these representations provide natural reference geometries for establishing relative smoothness of the primal Bregman representation of the distribution, with explicit bounds that are sharp in the scalar and separable settings. An illustrative application to the Poisson distribution sheds new light on several works in the literature, providing complementary geometric justifications for reference geometries while deriving existing algorithms.
papers.summary: Regular exponential-family distributions can be written in terms of Bregman divergences, but this geometry has not been systematically used to characterize them in the expectation parametrization. Building on a projective characterization, the authors give a general construction of equivalent dual Bregman representations with normalization and uniqueness results, recovering beta- and alpha-scaled representations as special cases and showing that the corresponding representations of conjugate priors preserve conjugacy. These representations also serve as reference geometries for proving relative smoothness of the primal representation, **with explicit bounds that are sharp in the scalar and separable settings**. An application to the Poisson distribution gives geometric justifications for reference geometries used in prior work and rederives existing algorithms.

papers.title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
papers.abstract: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.
papers.summary: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is moving from passive data collection toward agentic systems that interpret patient state, coordinate care, and initiate actions at home and in clinics. A structured scoping review finds that **mature agentic care has not yet emerged**: most systems remain human led, and tighter decision-action coupling and embodied AI are largely confined to prototypes and pilots. The authors argue that healthcare robotics makes embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance core design requirements, and propose "agentic robotics" as a direction for supervised systems that connect AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable, interruptible workflows.

papers.title: Interactive Program Induction with Language Model Priors
papers.abstract: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\gamma}\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.
papers.summary: Recovering a program from a handful of input-output examples is inherently ambiguous, since infinitely many programs fit any finite set of examples. Framing the problem in Bayesian terms with a language model as the prior over programs, the authors derive a greedy algorithm that picks maximally informative inputs to ask an oracle (such as the user) about, estimating the selection objective by importance sampling under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence. They prove it terminates after a number of informative queries logarithmic in the inverse prior probability of the target program and returns that program up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. On the `CodeARC` benchmark it **improves accuracy over a language-model-only agent by up to 22 percentage points** while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.

papers.title: TradeGauntlet: Evaluating Compliance Controls for Autonomous Trading Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.
papers.summary: Controls on autonomous trading agents must block problematic orders without making legitimate trading impractical. `TradeGauntlet` is a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separately measures detection, prevention, and execution cost; in 1,680 sessions with `Claude Haiku 5.5` and `Claude Sonnet 5.5`, every conduct alert was a self-match, and gates that reject self-crossing orders removed them while the aggregate gate cut `Sonnet`'s two-sided fills by about 15%. Search methods then found **split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules**; a learned baseline caught all 2,400 searched episodes but also flagged 15% of a large market maker's sessions. The authors conclude that zero alerts alone do not establish compliance, and note the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.

papers.title: ARCHER: From Rationale Imitation to Executable Reasoning in Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Small language models are attractive for local, low-cost, and privacy-sensitive deployment, but they remain unreliable on mathematical reasoning tasks that require decomposition, exact computation, tool use, and verification. We introduce \textbf{ARCHER}: \textbf{A}ction-trace \textbf{R}einforcement for \textbf{C}alculator-grounded \textbf{H}ierarchical \textbf{E}xecutable \textbf{R}easoning, a two-stage framework for training small language models (SLMs) to produce executable and auditable reasoning trajectories. In the first stage, ARCHER compiles free-form chain-of-thought rationales into typed action traces containing reasoning steps, calculator calls, deterministic runtime observations, verification actions, and final answers. This shifts the supervision target from imitating explanatory text to learning a tool-grounded reasoning policy. In the second stage, ARCHER refines this policy through asymmetric hierarchical reinforcement learning, using grouped and conditionally gated trajectory rewards for answer correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace alignment. Across five standard sub-10B backbones, ARCHER improves over the strongest tool-augmented baseline by 5.51 percentage points on macro-average across benchmark accuracies, including gains of 8.95 points on MATH-500 and 5.33 and 5.34 points on AIME-2024 and AIME-2025. Evaluations on two additional reasoning-specialized 7B backbones further show that executable grounding remains beneficial after reasoning-focused reinforcement learning or distillation. These results demonstrate that executable supervision and reward-guided behavioral refinement provide a general and effective training paradigm for compact mathematical reasoners.
papers.summary: Small language models (SLMs) are appealing for local, low-cost deployment but are unreliable on math problems requiring decomposition, exact computation, tool use, and verification. `ARCHER` first compiles free-form chain-of-thought rationales into typed action traces containing reasoning steps, calculator calls, deterministic runtime observations, verification actions, and final answers, then refines the resulting policy with hierarchical reinforcement learning using gated rewards for answer correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace alignment. Across five sub-10B backbones it **beats the strongest tool-augmented baseline by 5.51 percentage points on macro-average**, including 8.95 points on `MATH-500` and about 5.3 points on `AIME-2024` and `AIME-2025`. Tests on two reasoning-specialized 7B models indicate that executable grounding still helps after reasoning-focused reinforcement learning or distillation.

papers.title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.
papers.summary: Circuits that operate on information protected by quantum error-correcting codes, such as logical state preparation, logical gates, and routines like code-switching and code growth, are still largely designed by hand for individual cases. The authors cast the design problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, in which a large language model with tool access, guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for each of a curated set of tasks. The approach **finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of the tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults**.

papers.title: Agentic induction of common data elements and information extraction from sarcoma case report abstracts
papers.abstract: Common data elements (CDEs) support clinical data comparability but are usually defined manually. We investigated whether large language model agents could derive a CDE schema from sarcoma case report abstracts and apply it at scale. An agent proposed 72,909 candidate CDEs from 24,588 PubMed abstracts; agentic consolidation yielded 1,570 CDEs. We retained 53 supported by at least 50 abstracts and attempted evidence-linked extraction across the corpus. Processing succeeded for all retained CDEs in 79.2% of abstracts, including responses indicating non-mention. Two human reviewers approved 83.0% of retained CDEs for relevance, 67.9% for clarity, and 56.6% for correctness. In 100 sampled abstracts, exact agreement with the value extracted by the LLM was 94.9% among 1,116 pairs with a non-empty answer (abstract-level bootstrap 95% CI, 93.0-96.4%). Errors concentrated in anatomical and temporal fields. These findings support agent-assisted schema drafting followed by expert curation before large-scale extraction.
authors: Daniel Reichenpfader (Institute for Patient-Centered Digital Health
Bern University Hospital and University of Bern
Fabio Dennst\"adt (Data Semantics and Decision Making Institute
Bern University Hospital and University of Bern
papers.summary: Common data elements (CDEs), the standardized fields that make clinical data comparable, are usually defined by hand. Here a large language model agent proposed 72,909 candidate CDEs from 24,588 PubMed sarcoma case report abstracts, agentic consolidation reduced them to 1,570, and the 53 supported by at least 50 abstracts were used for evidence-linked extraction across the corpus. Two human reviewers approved 83.0% of the retained CDEs for relevance, 67.9% for clarity, and 56.6% for correctness, while in 100 sampled abstracts **extracted values matched exactly in 94.9% of 1,116 non-empty pairs**, with errors concentrated in anatomical and temporal fields. The authors conclude that agent-drafted schemas need expert curation before large-scale extraction.

papers.title: Asymptotic Margins and Feature Confinement in Conic Classification Heads under Softmax Cross-Entropy
papers.abstract: Classification heads built on conic functions give each class a bounded region of the feature space, and such regions are used to reject samples of unseen classes. We ask whether these regions also keep the features bounded when the head is trained with softmax cross-entropy. For a head whose class scores combine a linear term with a Euclidean norm, we first show that the region of each class is bounded by a quadric of revolution, whose eccentricity is the reciprocal of one learned ratio. We then attach to each class an asymptotic margin, which compares the growth of its score with the growth of all the other scores and can be computed by a second-order cone program. The loss of a class has infimum zero exactly when its margin is positive, and it then approaches zero only along diverging features. When the margin is negative, the loss is coercive and its minimizers lie in an explicit ball. Since softmax depends only on the differences between scores, a class with a bounded region can still have a positive margin, so bounded regions do not confine the features. The result extends to other norms, including the polyhedral conic functions. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, all 1210 cells of 67 trained conic heads have positive margins, whereas a prototype head keeps nine of its ten cells bounded, as the theory predicts.
papers.summary: Classification heads built on conic functions assign each class a bounded region of feature space, which is used to reject samples from unseen classes; the question is whether training with softmax cross-entropy also keeps features bounded. For heads whose class scores combine a linear term with a Euclidean norm, each class region is shown to be bounded by a quadric of revolution, and each class gets an asymptotic margin, computable by a second-order cone program, that compares the growth of its score with all others. A class's loss has infimum zero exactly when its margin is positive, and is then approached only along diverging features, so **bounded class regions do not confine the features**, because softmax depends only on score differences. On `CIFAR-10` and `CIFAR-100`, all 1210 cells of 67 trained conic heads have positive margins, whereas a prototype head keeps nine of its ten cells bounded.

papers.title: On numerical issues of divergences between nearly equal distributions
papers.abstract: Barron et al. (2026) recently identified numerical issues in the softmax and soft cross-entropy loss. We show that similar issues are present in standard divergence operations between categorical distributions. This includes the forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), as well as Monte Carlo KL estimates and entropy. When the distributions are nearly equal, rounding and cancellation issues affect the forward and gradient computations. These issues can affect settings using divergences in optimization objectives, such as knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. We propose numerically stable reformulations and provide example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests.
papers.summary: Following recently identified numerical problems in softmax and soft cross-entropy, the authors show that standard divergence computations between categorical distributions have similar flaws. Forward and reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence, Monte Carlo KL estimates, and entropy all **suffer rounding and cancellation errors in both forward values and gradients when the two distributions are nearly equal**. These issues can affect objectives used in knowledge distillation, reinforcement learning, and proximal methods. The authors propose numerically stable reformulations with example implementations for each setting, validated by property-based tests.

papers.title: MeReader: An Offline, Privacy-Preserving, Progress-Aware AI Assistant for Narrative eBook Reading
papers.abstract: This paper introduces MeReader, a privacy-preserving, offline and progress-aware AI assistant designed to function as a contextual companion for narrative reading on consumer hardware. Unlike conventional Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems that process documents/books online in an all-texts-at-once type of way, thereby risking narrative spoilers, MeReader confines both retrieval and generation to the reader's distinct position in the text. The system integrates a hybrid retrieval architecture, combining vector similarity, BM25, and summary embeddings, to ensure high fidelity to the reader's current context. We evaluate the system across classical English books using both quantitative comprehension metrics and qualitative LLM-based independent judging. The results identify a quality-latency frontier, showing that mid-sized local models (2b-4b) can achieve comprehension parity with larger counterparts (5b+) while maintaining acceptable response quality. Importantly, the proposed progress-aware boundary mechanism is shown to prevent future content leakage without compromising retrieval quality and correctness. These findings suggest that a localized, privacy-centric approach can augment, rather than replace, the digital reading experience, offering a good alternative to cloud-dependent services. Therein, there remains a lack of amalgamate systems which combine progress-aware, privacy-preserving, and narrative eBook reading with AI support. It is in this very gap that the development of MeReader came to be; synthesizing said strands into an offline, book-constrained assistant focused on enhancing comprehension without compromising narrative continuity or user privacy.
papers.summary: AI reading assistants that ingest an entire book at once risk revealing plot points the reader has not yet reached. `MeReader` is an offline assistant for narrative eBooks on consumer hardware that restricts both retrieval and generation to text up to the reader's current position, using hybrid retrieval that combines vector similarity, `BM25`, and summary embeddings. Evaluated on classic English books with comprehension metrics and LLM-based judging, **mid-sized local models (2-4 billion parameters) reach comprehension parity with larger ones (5 billion and up)** while keeping acceptable response quality. The progress-aware boundary is reported to prevent leakage of future content without reducing retrieval quality or correctness.

papers.title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.
papers.summary: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) tools are tested on a realistic failure of Large Language Model (LLM) agents: web agents hallucinating actions that a website does not offer. Working with `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` on live websites, the authors find that a linear probe on the last prompt token predicts hallucinations before generation starts (0.80 AUC), and **steering along the probe direction corrects 85% of hallucinations but disrupts 7% of valid actions**. The explanation remains partial: the probe direction loses much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are formatted, and circuit identification is hard because the computation is spread across many components and positions and varies between examples. The authors discuss how this challenges the assumptions behind standard circuit-discovery and feature-identification methods.

papers.title: StreamEmbed: Real-Time Indexing from Pixels for Screenshot Retrieval
papers.abstract: Screen history can serve as searchable visual memory for people and agents, but unlike an offline corpus, it must be encoded and indexed as each screenshot arrives. OCR-based indexing is fast but loses visual information; visual encoding takes over two seconds. Yet screens change incrementally: most pixels repeat within and across screenshots. This raises a question: do visual encoders need to recompute their representations from scratch for every new screenshot? We present StreamEmbed, a system for incremental visual embedding that exploits this redundancy. Guided solely by pixel differences, it combines spatial token pruning, which skips blocks that repeat a neighbor, with temporal KV reuse, which reuses cached keys and values for blocks unchanged across screenshots. A small learned adapter compensates for pruning and reuse to preserve fidelity to full-screenshot embeddings. On ScreenMemEval, our benchmark of 10,426 questions over 184 hours of screen histories from two humans and a computer-use agent, StreamEmbed sets a new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier on an M2 Pro GPU: it encodes up to 3.7x faster than full-screenshot encoding without sacrificing accuracy and improves accuracy over OCR-based indexing by up to 6.3 Recall@10 points at matched latency. A memory-efficient vector index stores a simulated year of screenshots in 0.13 GB of RAM. Together, these results make real-time indexing of screen history in its native visual form practical, laying a foundation for fully local visual assistants.
papers.summary: Searchable screen history has to be indexed as each screenshot arrives, but OCR-based indexing discards visual information and full visual encoding takes over two seconds per screenshot. `StreamEmbed` exploits the fact that screens change incrementally: guided only by pixel differences, it prunes blocks that repeat a neighbor, reuses cached keys and values for blocks unchanged since earlier screenshots, and uses a small learned adapter to stay faithful to full-screenshot embeddings. On `ScreenMemEval`, a new benchmark of 10,426 questions over 184 hours of screen history from two humans and a computer-use agent, it **encodes up to 3.7x faster than full-screenshot encoding on an M2 Pro GPU without losing accuracy**, and beats OCR-based indexing by up to 6.3 Recall@10 points at matched latency. Its vector index holds a simulated year of screenshots in 0.13 GB of RAM.

papers.title: WaferTetris: Efficient Freeform Mapping on Wafer-Scale Accelerators
papers.abstract:
Wafer-scale accelerators offer massive compute capacity through hundreds of thousands of processing elements (PEs) interconnected across a single wafer, but realizing this potential requires efficient application mapping. Their scale makes programming these systems and mapping applications onto them challenging. Existing approaches rely on template-based mappings to maintain productivity, but these templates restrict the mapping design space. In particular, they impose fixed geometric layouts over the PE grid, often leaving compute and memory resources underutilized.
  In this work, we present WaferTetris, a system that removes these geometric restrictions through freeform mapping. Its Tetris-like strategy flexibly packs computation across the wafer, improving PE utilization and usable memory capacity while preserving PE-task code. We develop a recurrence-based throughput model that captures branch-and-join dependencies to guide spatial parallelism, and an architecture model with per-color gates that enable existing FPGA place-and-route algorithms to enforce WSE routing constraints.
  We evaluate WaferTetris on Cerebras WSE-3 using LLM decoding and scientific stencil benchmarks. For LLM decoding, it achieves up to $4.42\times$ the system throughput of a template-based automatic mapping baseline on the same fabric size. Compared with the manually optimized WaferLLM, WaferTetris supports $1.8\times$ the context length for LLaMA3.1-8B (80k versus 44k), while delivering equal or higher per-user throughput at matched context lengths, up to $1.10\times$.
papers.summary: Wafer-scale accelerators contain hundreds of thousands of processing elements (PEs), and current template-based mapping tools impose fixed geometric layouts that leave compute and memory unused. `WaferTetris` instead packs computation freely across the wafer, guided by a recurrence-based throughput model for branch-and-join dependencies and an architecture model that lets existing FPGA place-and-route algorithms enforce the wafer's routing constraints. On the `Cerebras WSE-3`, it reaches **up to 4.42x the LLM decoding throughput of a template-based automatic mapping baseline** on the same fabric size. Against the hand-optimized `WaferLLM`, it supports 1.8x the context length for `LLaMA3.1-8B` (80k versus 44k tokens) with equal or higher per-user throughput at matched context lengths.

papers.title: Understanding Contextual Bias in Agricultural CNNs Through Hidden-Neuron Concept Induction
papers.abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can classify images using background-dominated patches that contain little or none of the target object, showing that they exploit contextual information. Previous studies detected this behavior through classification accuracy but say little about what CNN hidden layers represent. We investigate whether Concept Induction can reveal interpretable visual properties associated with hidden-neuron activations on contextual image patches.
