Using five agricultural datasets with high, moderate, and low contextual bias, we analyze four CNN architectures at three network depths and five patch locations. Quantitative image descriptors of each patch are encoded in a knowledge graph and used as background knowledge for Concept Induction, which derives logical expressions characterizing neuron activation. These expressions are tested on held-out images using the Mann-Whitney U test and Cliff's delta. Of 48,013 tested neuron-feature pairs, 13,164 (27.4%) were validated. Validation was most frequent at intermediate depths (mean 40.2% at mid layers versus 12.0% at deep layers), and no patch location dominated across datasets. Among the tested descriptors, edge, Gabor, and Tamura texture features had the highest validation rates. Stronger contextual bias did not correspond to higher neuron-feature validation rates: moderately biased Sugarcane had the highest rate (40.5%) and highly biased Cassava the lowest (19.2%). These results suggest that behavioral context dependence and the semantic interpretability of hidden neurons capture different aspects of CNN behavior, and that Concept Induction can complement patch-based bias detection.
papers.summary: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can classify images from background patches containing little of the target object, but accuracy-based tests of this contextual bias do not show what hidden layers represent. The authors apply `Concept Induction`, which derives logical expressions over a knowledge graph of quantitative image descriptors, to characterize hidden-neuron activations in four CNN architectures across five agricultural datasets, three depths, and five patch locations. **Of 48,013 tested neuron-feature pairs, 13,164 (27.4%) were validated on held-out images**, most often at intermediate depths and for edge, Gabor, and Tamura texture features. Stronger contextual bias did not produce higher validation rates, which the authors read as evidence that behavioral context dependence and neuron interpretability capture different aspects of a network.

papers.title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.
papers.summary: An evolutionary model is used to study how selection shapes an AI agent's choices when completing a task conflicts with following rules of conduct. Copies of an agent face a shared uncertain reward state and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce, so long-run growth is maximized by taking each action as often as the environment rewards it. A task-only policy fails once conduct matters and a fixed linear policy drifts toward task completion as stakes rise, whereas **a learned policy converges to the tradeoffs its environment rewards**, which the authors call socialization when humans supply the rewards. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to undo under later task-only training, though finite memory weakens that protection and hard prohibitions are costly when mistaken; small neural network experiments illustrate these effects.

papers.title: ModHarness-RL: Recasting Harnesses as Learnable and Evolving Programs for Agentic RL
papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly relies on a harness, the scaffold around the model that decides what it sees of its own interaction and what guidance it receives. Most existing approaches train under a hand-written harness that stays fixed throughout. However, an effective harness depends on the domain, the data and the model, and keeps changing as the model trains. We introduce ModHarness-RL, which recasts the harness as programs that are learned from data and evolve as the model trains with RL. ModHarness-RL records the interaction as structured State, a set of typed blocks, and two core components of the harness are programs over these blocks, a Compression program that assembles the accumulated history into the model's context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During RL training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories, so the harness tracks how the model's behavior shifts. We study CodeSearch in depth and further analyze ALFWorld and BIRD SQL, with models from 1.5B to 8B. The proposed Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over the fixed-harness baseline in most settings. These results suggest that a harness for agentic RL can be learned from the task's data and evolved with the model.
papers.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) usually trains a model under a hand-written, fixed harness, even though the best scaffold depends on the domain, data, and model and shifts as training proceeds. `ModHarness-RL` treats the harness as programs over a structured, typed record of the interaction: a Compression program that assembles history into the model's context and a Steering program that supplies guidance when behavior deviates. During training, candidate programs are proposed from recent trajectories, verified by execution, and replayed over past trajectories so the harness tracks the model's changing behavior. On `CodeSearch`, `ALFWorld`, and `BIRD SQL` with models from 1.5B to 8B parameters, **the learned Compression and Steering mechanisms improve held-out performance over a fixed-harness baseline in most settings**.

papers.title: Why Finite Intelligence Works in an Infinite World: A Mathematical Theory
papers.abstract: An information system often has to learn before it knows what it will be asked. A finite representation can succeed without recording an infinite environment in full when those asks share collective structure, rather than demand unrelated facts scattered arbitrarily across it. We formalize this phenomenon through future-task information, the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value relative to the available evidence. A joint decision-regret state records posterior comparisons among actions for every permitted task. Under compactness assumptions, every retained representation admits a calibrated replacement based on this state, preserving all task regrets without increasing information; the resulting information-regret curve equals an operational coding rate. Two exact boundaries govern finite preservation: weak-star closure for a fixed action count, and the singular mass of the source-evidence law when all finite action menus are admitted. Collective structure determines information requirements beyond individual-question difficulty. Families with identical source laws, pairwise task metrics, and individual-task rates can have different high-resolution exponents. Covariance-identical coordinate and parity families have different exact rate-distortion curves, with optimal parity retention characterized by a sharp Fourier-entropy inequality. For balanced nested task families, refinement sizes and weighted reach determine the rate within an additive constant, attained by prefix coding under explicit decay conditions. Nonlinear learning and computational separations distinguish preservation from efficient discovery and use. The proposed mathematical theory identifies which shared decision requirements allow finite information to remain useful for infinitely many possible purposes.
papers.summary: A mathematical framework addresses why a finite representation, learned before its future tasks are known, can remain useful in an infinite environment. It defines future-task information as the minimum retained information needed to preserve decision value, and shows under compactness assumptions that any representation can be replaced by a calibrated one based on a joint decision-regret state without increasing information, giving an information-regret curve equal to an operational coding rate. The central claim is that **the collective structure of a task family, not the difficulty of individual questions, determines information requirements**: families with identical source laws, pairwise task metrics, and individual-task rates can still have different high-resolution exponents. Further results give exact rate-distortion curves for coordinate and parity families and separate preserving information from efficiently discovering and using it.

papers.title: Elliptic Sampling: Optimal Interpolant Schedules for Gaussians and Beyond
papers.abstract: Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev's optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number $\kappa$ of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit $\kappa \rightarrow 1$. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error $\varepsilon$ using $\Theta(\log\kappa\,\log(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most $\varepsilon$ 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d} \, \mathrm{polylog}(\kappa, 1/\varepsilon))$ score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.
papers.summary: Generative models built on stochastic interpolants need both a schedule bridging the initial and target distributions and a discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. The authors design the two jointly from the analyticity of the complexified ODE trajectories, solve the problem exactly by conformal mapping to obtain variance-preserving elliptic schedules based on Jacobi elliptic functions, and pair them with a tailored discretization called `Zoloflow` that depends on the target's condition number κ. For Gaussian targets, `Zoloflow` is **minimax optimal among oblivious score-span algorithms, reaching total-variation error ε with Θ(log κ · log(√d/ε)) score queries**, and for log-concave targets the elliptic schedule needs roughly √d · polylog(κ, 1/ε) score evaluations for 2-Wasserstein error ε. Experiments compare the elliptic schedule with alternatives on synthetic benchmarks and image generation datasets.

papers.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
papers.summary: Demonstrations speed up single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) one person cannot teleoperate several agents at once; Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (`R2BC`) works around this by having the demonstrator control one agent at a time, yet its policies are capped by demonstration quality. `IBMARL` extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (`IBRL`) to cooperative teams: each agent gets an action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, an ensemble of centralized critics picks among the combinations, and a gated penalty pulls the RL policy toward imitation only where the critics prefer the imitation action. On four cooperative benchmarks, it **surpasses its imitation policies 2.6-4.2x faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks and is the only method to surpass them on the other two**, exceeding the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations it still beats imitation learning alone, more than twice as fast as the best baseline.

papers.title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.
papers.summary: Weight-Space Programming (WSP) is the ability of large language models (LLMs) to read, repair, and write the parameters of other neural networks directly, without gradient descent. `WeightBench` evaluates it with 42 tasks in five tracks (reading, fixing, and writing weights, recognizing impossible edits, and data-free compression) on networks ranging from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Frontier agents can **read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one**. `Claude Opus 5.5` scores 0.535 macro across all 42 tasks, ahead of `Sonnet 5.5`, `Haiku 5.5`, and `DeepSeek v4-flash`, while on the 38 tasks it was run on `GPT-6.1-sol` scores 0.568 against 0.546 for Opus.
papers.highlight_summary:
A benchmark for Weight-Space Programming, the emerging practice of having LLM agents read, repair, and write other networks' parameters directly without gradient descent, tests whether that ability is real reasoning or disguised trial and error. `WeightBench` scores agents on **42 tasks** across five tracks while metering and auditing every computation they perform on the weights.

- The tasks cover reading weights, surgical fixes, writing networks from scratch, recognizing infeasible edits, and data-free compression, on subject networks ranging from **2K-parameter** control policies to **7B-parameter** language models.
- Agents run in an OS-level sandbox with a metered NumPy subclass that detects forward-pass chains, a hash-chained ledger, and 28 audit flags that quarantine suspect runs, and the composite score multiplies task gain by penalties for collateral damage, edit size, and compute use.
- On all 42 tasks `Claude Opus 5.5` reaches a macro score of **0.535** (`Sonnet 5.5` 0.466, `Haiku 5.5` 0.402, `DeepSeek v4-flash` 0.215), while on the 38 tasks it was run on `GPT-6.1-sol` scores **0.568** against Opus's **0.546**.
- Strong agents can already write working control policies from all-zero weights (**0.829** for Opus, **0.863** for `GPT-6.1-sol`) and read small networks (0.744 and 0.928), but the three Claude models sit at roughly chance (**about 0.49–0.50**) on telling infeasible edits from hard ones, every model scores only **0.177–0.238** on data-free compression, and patching language models remains largely unsolved.
- The leaderboard is preliminary, since every score is a lower bound with quarantined runs counted as zero pending human review (11 of 77 for Opus, 13 of 42 for DeepSeek), runs use a single seed with one or two samples per task, and only 21 of the 42 reference solutions work with the same access the agents get.

papers.title: BAL: Bidirectional Autoregression in Latent Space for Learning Human Movement Representations
papers.abstract: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.
papers.summary: Self-supervised methods for learning human movement representations from 3D pose sequences typically rely on augmentation invariance or masked reconstruction, whose heuristic hyperparameters influence what semantics get learned. `BAL` instead uses the natural ordering of everyday behavior as supervision, predicting autoregressively in an abstract latent space both forward and backward in time so that representations can draw on past and future context. To prevent representation collapse, each prediction target is split into a global sequence-level component and a local context-independent component, and the authors prove the local targets keep nontrivial angular diversity unless representations fully collapse. On large-scale datasets, the learned representations **outperform baselines on most evaluation metrics for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation**.

papers.title: FETTUCCINE: Fast and efficient brain-to-text decoding on mobile devices
papers.abstract: Recent advances in speech neuroprostheses have enabled new communication avenues for people who have lost the ability to speak due to neurological illness or injury. These systems can decode neural activity during attempted speech into text by relying on language priors to achieve high decoding accuracy. This performance currently comes at the cost of using a compute-intensive language modeling stack, presenting a major bottleneck for real-world use. Further, current language models incur highly variable and disruptive inference latencies, limiting communication throughput and preventing users from reliably participating in natural conversation. We introduce FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end brain-to-text framework that leverages the speed and portability of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to address the aforementioned practical challenges, while achieving usable (<10%) word error rates (WER), efficient adaptation to neural non-stationarities, and reliable performance on mobile devices. When evaluated using publicly available data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user, FETTUCCINE outperforms previous end-to-end methods, achieving as low as 4.39% WER. Most notably, our models successfully run on a commercially-available mobile device with throughput reaching up to 370x real-time, providing the first demonstration of brain-to-text decoding on a mobile device. We also show that our models can be successfully finetuned to extend usable performance to future days. Beyond performance, our approach enables localization of the neural features most relevant for decoding via gradient-based saliency maps, which we show align with well-established physiological priors across different ASR model families. Taken together, our results show that FETTUCCINE overcomes core infrastructural and computational barriers, yielding a new class of portable brain-to-text communication.
papers.summary: Speech neuroprostheses decode neural activity during attempted speech into text, but they depend on a compute-heavy language modeling stack with variable latency that hinders real-world conversational use. `FETTUCCINE` is an end-to-end brain-to-text framework built on automatic speech recognition (ASR) models, chosen for their speed and portability. On public data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user it reaches **a word error rate (WER) as low as 4.39%**, outperforming previous end-to-end methods, and runs on a commercially available mobile device at up to 370x real-time. The models can be fine-tuned to maintain usable performance on later recording days, and gradient-based saliency maps locate decoding-relevant neural features that match established physiological priors.

papers.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
papers.abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $\pi_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $\pi_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.
papers.summary: Robot-use agents (RUAs), which control robots the way computer-use agents control software, have so far worked well only with frontier proprietary models. The authors train an open-weight 27B reasoning model with reinforcement learning entirely in simulation and without demonstrations, using their Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (`PEAR`); the model observes the scene, reasons in a chain of thought, and outputs the next end-effector pose with no harness. After training on `LIBERO` and `RoboDojo`, it **succeeds in 60% of trials on a real dual-arm robot where the base model succeeds in none**, and its `LIBERO` success rate rises from 1.6% to 74.4%. On `LIBERO-Pro` it handles new tasks in familiar scenes 57.4% of the time versus 0.75% for the demonstration-fine-tuned `π0.5`, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding, and vision benchmarks.

papers.title: Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
papers.abstract: Monitoring maritime activities is important for safety and security, particularly for detecting illegal activities, but remains challenging due to the size and complexity of the maritime domain. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is commonly used for this purpose, despite its known vulnerabilities. In contrast, space-based radio frequency (RF) observations provide an independent source of vessel activity but lack ship identification and therefore cannot identify vessels on their own. Following the CRISP-DM process, this study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to align individual RF detections with AIS trajectories, using temporal and spatial information while modeling noise and timing discrepancies. We evaluate it on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections against nearest-neighbor baselines and analyze its errors with bias tests on trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity and AIS--RF distance. The length-corrected Forward score reaches a top-1 precision of $0.7776$ on the validation split of multi-candidate detections, where errors are possible, and an AUC of $0.637$ for detecting dark vessels among the detections that pass the prefilter. With a single RF detection, the score mostly reflects the AIS trajectory itself, and its errors favor longer and more stationary trajectories. A log-odds score, which compares the full model with a null model without match transitions, raises precision to $0.8580$ and AUC to $0.852$. Its length-corrected variant no longer shows a significant bias towards stationary trajectories and short inter-message distances, but still favors candidates farther from the RF detection. A time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline without fitting remains ahead (precision $0.9013$, AUC $0.904$), so this single-detection, hand-designed PHMM formulation approaches but does not beat it.
papers.summary: Maritime monitoring relies on the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which has known vulnerabilities, while space-based radio frequency (RF) detections are independent of it but carry no ship identity. The study applies a Pair Hidden Markov Model (PHMM) to match individual RF detections to AIS trajectories, evaluated on NOAA AIS data with synthetic RF detections and analyzed for biases in trajectory length, sampling density, stationarity, and distance. The best PHMM variant, a log-odds score against a null model, reaches a top-1 precision of 0.8580 and an AUC of 0.852 for detecting dark vessels. However, **an unfitted time-weighted nearest-neighbor baseline remains ahead (precision 0.9013, AUC 0.904)**, so the hand-designed single-detection formulation approaches but does not beat it.

audio.title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
audio.script: Today's pick from the AI Paper Digest. Playing a modern video game for hours is hard for an AI. It has to watch the screen, remember what happened, and react fast, using only keyboard and mouse. The authors built one model, called Gamer. It learned in stages, first from about a thousand hours of recorded play, then by practicing in the game itself. A fast serving engine keeps its reactions quick. The authors claim it matches skilled human players in efficiency. But extra training data did not keep helping on very different, unseen games.
